**Ethiopia, its own centre.** The Ethiopian highlands domesticated a unique set of plants: **teff** (the tiny grain of *injera*), **enset** (the "false banana", whose stem is eaten), **noog** (an oilseed), probably **finger millet**, and **coffee**. **When** is poorly known, because the highlands are little excavated. They also adopted wheat and barley from the Near East.

**Egypt and the north.** Egypt's farmers used the **Near Eastern** package — wheat, barley, sheep and goats — arriving by about **5200 BC** at the **Fayum** lake and Merimde in the Delta.

**East and south.** Herders reached the shores of **Lake Turkana** in Kenya by about **3000 BC**, where they built large communal cemeteries marked with stone pillars, such as **Lothagam North**. Farming and herding reached southern Africa much later, in Stage 5; the South African story is told in the South African Politics curriculum.

**Why it mattered.** Sorghum and millets became the staple grains of much of Africa and spread to India. And the West African yam-and-palm farmers were the ancestors of the **Bantu-speaking** peoples, whose expansion across central and southern Africa began, by most estimates, around the end of this period, and is told in the next stages.
Farmers on the move: the Neolithic reach:
Farming spread outwards from its first centres. A long argument was how: did **people** move, or only **ideas**? Ancient DNA has largely answered it for Europe.

**Into Europe.** Farming crossed from Anatolia into **Greece and the Balkans by about 6500 BC**, then went two ways:

| Route | When (approximate) | How it shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The Danube, inland** | central Europe by about **5500 BC** | the **Linear Pottery culture** (LBK), with **longhouses** up to 40 m long, from Hungary to the Paris basin |
| **The Mediterranean coast** | Italy, southern France and Spain by about **5800–5000 BC** | **Cardial ware**, pottery decorated with cockle shells; probably spread by boat |
| **The north-west** | **Britain, Ireland and southern Scandinavia** about **4000 BC** | a late arrival, after a long pause |

**The old debate: migrants or ideas?** For most of the 20th century archaeologists argued whether European hunter-gatherers **adopted** farming from neighbours (cultural diffusion) or were **replaced** by incoming farmers (demic diffusion).

**What ancient DNA showed** (from about 2010 onward): Europe's first farmers were mostly **descended from Anatolian farmers**. They were a migrating population. Hunter-gatherers lived beside them, sometimes for **two thousand years**, and slowly mixed in. The question here is now **largely settled**: people moved, and ideas went with them. It is a good example of new evidence closing a debate.

**Not peaceful everywhere.** At **Talheim** in Germany, about **5000 BC**, a pit held **34 people**, men, women and children, killed by blows from stone axes of the kind the LBK farmers themselves used. Similar massacre sites are known from the end of the LBK. Whether violence was common or a crisis at that time is debated.

**Into South Asia: Mehrgarh.** At the foot of the **Bolan Pass** in Balochistan, Pakistan, **Mehrgarh** was a farming village by about **7000 BC**, with mud-brick houses, **barley** and **wheat**, goats and sheep, and later **zebu cattle**, perhaps domesticated there. Its people also practised the first known **dentistry**: molars drilled with flint, about 7000–5500 BC.

Was Mehrgarh's farming **brought** from the Near East or partly **local**? Its wheat must have come from the west; its barley and zebu may be local. Ancient DNA suggests early South Asian farmers descended from a population related to ancient **Iranians**, but one that split off before farming began — which would mean the **idea and the crops** came, more than many people. That is a reading of thin evidence, and still debated.

**Elsewhere in South Asia.** Rice was being cultivated in the **Ganges** valley by the 3rd millennium BC, possibly earlier; in **South India**, millet and pulse farmers with cattle left great **ash mounds**, burnt cattle pens, from about **3000 BC**.

**Into South-East Asia and the Pacific.** Rice and millet farmers from southern China reached **Taiwan** by about **3000 BC** and **mainland South-East Asia** around **2500–2000 BC**. From Taiwan, speakers of **Austronesian** languages began moving south into the Philippines by about 2000 BC — the start of the greatest sea migration in history, continued in Stage 3.

**Why it mattered.** By 2000 BC, farming had spread over most of the lands that could be farmed with the crops then available. Where it went, it usually brought **more people**, and in Europe the farmers' descendants are still a large part of the population's ancestry.
The price of farming: health, work and i:
Farming fed more people. It did not, at first, make most of them healthier or freer. This is one of the clearest findings of archaeology, and one of the most argued over in its meaning.

**What the skeletons show.** Compare foragers with the early farmers who followed them, in many regions:

| Sign | What changed with farming |
| --- | --- |
| **Height** | early farmers were often **shorter**, by several centimetres, than the foragers before them |
| **Teeth** | many more **cavities**, from starchy grain |
| **Childhood stress** | more lines in tooth enamel (*hypoplasia*) showing hunger or illness in childhood |
| **Anaemia** | more signs of iron deficiency in skulls |
| **Infection** | more disease from crowding, dirty water, and living close to animals |
| **Work** | heavy, repetitive labour: grinding grain on a stone wore down women's knees, toes and backs |

**Why worse?** A narrower diet based on one or two grains; **crop failures** that hit everyone at once; diseases that need crowds to survive; and much more work.

**Why farm anyway?** Because farming produces **far more food per acre**. Birth rates rose sharply — a **"Neolithic demographic transition"**, as the demographer Jean-Pierre Bocquet-Appel called it. A farming village could raise more children than a foraging band, and grow, and spread, even if each person lived less well. Once numbers had grown, there was no going back.

**Inequality: when and why.** Early farming villages like Çatalhöyük were fairly **equal**. Inequality grew slowly, as **land, herds and stores** became wealth that could be inherited. A 2017 study (Kohler and colleagues) measured house sizes across many ancient sites and found that inequality rose more in the Old World than in the Americas after a few thousand years of farming, probably because **draft animals** and ploughs let some households farm much more land than others.

**The strongest readings, side by side:**

| Reading | The argument |
| --- | --- |
| **"The worst mistake"** | Jared Diamond (1987), and later Yuval Noah Harari ("history's biggest fraud"): farming brought disease, toil, inequality, war and kings. Foragers worked fewer hours and ate better |
| **"Against the grain"** | James C. Scott (2017): grain was the first crop that could be **seen, measured and taxed**, which is why early states were built on it — and many people fled them |
| **"A necessary step"** | farming made possible everything that came later: cities, writing, science, medicine, art on a large scale, and eventually the higher living standards of modern times. Its early costs were real, but temporary on the scale of history |
| **"Neither"** | the comparison is too general: some foragers lived hard lives, some farmers lived well, and the outcome depended on place, crop and time |

**What would settle it.** Partly, it can't: "better" depends on what you value. But the facts can sharpen: more skeletons studied from the **same regions** before and after farming, better estimates of foragers' working hours (modern studies vary widely), and closer dating of when inequality first appears in each region.

**What is not in doubt.** Farming led to **many more people**. The world's population, perhaps a few million at 10,000 BC, was somewhere in the tens of millions by 2000 BC (estimates vary widely, roughly 25 to 70 million). Nearly all of them farmed or herded.
Copper, megaliths and the steppe: Europe:
While cities rose in Mesopotamia and Egypt, Europe and the western steppe went their own way: no cities and no writing, but metal, great stone monuments, and a migration that rewrote the population of a continent.

**The first metal.** **Copper** was hammered cold for thousands of years before anyone **smelted** it from ore. Smelting appears by about **5000 BC**, in the **Balkans** (at Belovode in Serbia) and in Iran. This begins what is called the **Copper Age**, or **Chalcolithic**. Bronze, a harder alloy of copper and tin, spread in the Near East from about **3000 BC** and in Europe from about 2200 BC.

**Varna, Bulgaria, about 4500 BC.** A cemetery near the Black Sea, found in **1972**, held the **oldest large hoard of worked gold** in the world: over **6 kg** of gold objects in all. One man (grave 43) was buried with gold bracelets, a gold-sheathed sceptre and gold on his body, while most graves held little. This is one of the earliest clear signs of a **rich elite**.

**Ötzi the Iceman, about 3300 BC.** A man who died high in the **Ötztal Alps** on the Italian–Austrian border and was found, freeze-dried, in **1991**. He carried a **copper axe**, a bow, arrows, and dried fungus for kindling, and had **61 tattoos**. An **arrowhead in his left shoulder** shows he was killed. He is the most detailed single body from prehistoric Europe.

**Megaliths: the great stones.** From about **4500 BC**, people along Europe's Atlantic coast began building tombs and monuments from huge stones:

| Monument | Where | When (approximate) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Barnenez** and the Carnac alignments | Brittany, France | about 4500 BC onwards |
| **Ġgantija** and the temples of Malta | Gozo and Malta | about 3600 BC onwards |
| **Newgrange** | Ireland | about 3200 BC; its passage is lit by the sunrise at the winter solstice |
| **Stonehenge** | southern England | a ditch and bank about **3000 BC**; the great **sarsen** circle about **2500 BC**; smaller **bluestones** brought some 225 km from the Preseli Hills in Wales |

A 2019 study of radiocarbon dates argued that megalith building began in **north-west France** and spread **by sea**. What the monuments meant — tombs, calendars, gathering places, all three — is debated for each one.

**Giant villages on the steppe edge.** In Ukraine and Moldova, the **Cucuteni–Trypillia** culture built settlements of hundreds of hectares around **4000–3600 BC**, such as **Talianki**, bigger in area than the first Mesopotamian cities. How many people lived in them at once — perhaps over 10,000, or far fewer, using them seasonally — is **argued**, and so is why they were regularly **burned**.

**The steppe herders: Yamnaya, about 3300–2600 BC.** On the grasslands north of the Black and Caspian seas, herders with **wagons**, cattle and sheep buried their leaders under earth mounds (*kurgans*). From about **3000 BC** their descendants spread **west into Europe** and **east to the Altai**. Ancient DNA (2015 onwards) shows that in central Europe, and later in Britain after about **2450 BC**, a large share of the population's ancestry was replaced by people with steppe ancestry.

**Why so complete?** One proposal is **plague**: *Yersinia pestis*, the plague bacterium, has been found in skeletons of this period across Eurasia. Whether it emptied Europe ahead of the migrants is **not settled**.

**The language question.** Many scholars link this migration to the spread of the **Indo-European** languages (from which come English, Latin, Greek, Persian and Sanskrit). The **steppe hypothesis** (Marija Gimbutas, David Anthony) fits the DNA for Europe. The **Anatolian hypothesis** (Colin Renfrew, 1987) linked the languages to the first farmers instead; few now hold it in its original form, but a recent "southern arc" proposal places the deepest root south of the Caucasus. More ancient DNA from the Caucasus and Anatolia is what will decide it.

**The wheel.** Wheeled vehicles appear about **3500–3300 BC**, almost at once from Mesopotamia to Poland. Where they were invented is unknown.
Uruk: the first city:
On the Euphrates in southern Iraq, about **3500–3100 BC**, a town grew into something new: the first place that clearly deserves the name **city**.

**Where.** **Uruk** (modern Warka; the Bible's *Erech*), in **Sumer**, the flat, hot, marshy land of southern Mesopotamia. Rain is too scarce for farming there, but the rivers, led out in **irrigation canals**, made the soil extremely fertile. Barley, dates, fish, sheep and reeds were the wealth of the land.

**Before Uruk: the Ubaid, about 6500–3800 BC.** Irrigation farming villages spread over southern Mesopotamia, with mud-brick **temples** rebuilt again and again on the same spot. At **Eridu**, the Sumerians' own "first city", archaeologists found a sequence of temples, one on top of the other, going back to about **5400 BC**.

**The Uruk period, about 4000–3100 BC.** Uruk grew to about **250 hectares** by **3100 BC**, perhaps twice the size of any other settlement, with **tens of thousands** of people — estimates vary, commonly **25,000 to 50,000**. Later its wall ran **9 km** around the city; the Sumerians said **Gilgamesh** built it.

**What made it a city, not just a big village:**

| Feature | At Uruk |
| --- | --- |
| **Monumental public buildings** | the **Eanna** precinct, sacred to the goddess **Inanna**, with huge temples decorated with cone mosaics; the **White Temple** on a high platform in the precinct of the sky god **Anu** |
| **Specialists** | potters, metalworkers, weavers, scribes, priests, administrators, who did not grow their own food |
| **Mass production** | millions of crude **bevelled-rim bowls**, perhaps for rations of grain to workers (the most common reading, still debated) |
| **Administration** | **cylinder seals**, rolled on clay to mark ownership; and then **writing** |
| **Hierarchy** | a figure archaeologists call the **"priest-king"**, shown on seals and on the carved **Uruk Vase**, leading offerings and fighting enemies |

**The Uruk Vase**, about 3200–3000 BC, shows the whole order of society in bands: water and crops at the bottom, then animals, then naked men carrying offerings, then a ruler presenting gifts to the goddess Inanna. It was looted from the Iraq Museum in **2003** and returned, damaged, the same year.

**The "Uruk expansion".** Uruk-style pottery, buildings and seals appear far up the Euphrates in Syria and Turkey, at sites like **Habuba Kabira**, and in Iran. Guillermo Algaze argued (1993) for an early **"world system"**: Uruk planted trading colonies to get timber, metal and stone, which Sumer lacked. Others argue the northern sites were local societies that **copied** Uruk, or that the relationship was mixed. That debate continues.

**Not the only early city.** At **Tell Brak** in north-eastern Syria, a large settlement grew from about **4000 BC**, **earlier** than once thought and independently of the south. So urban life had more than one root even in Mesopotamia.

**Why it mattered.** Uruk showed what a city was: a place of **gods, rulers, scribes and specialists**, fed by farmers in the countryside. Almost every city since has been a version of it.
From tokens to cuneiform: writing in Sum:
The first writing was invented in southern Mesopotamia about **3300–3200 BC**. It began as **bookkeeping**.

**Before writing: tokens.** From about **8000 BC**, people across the Near East used small clay **tokens**: cones, spheres, discs and cylinders. The archaeologist **Denise Schmandt-Besserat** argued (from the 1970s) that each shape stood for a quantity of a good: a measure of grain, a jar of oil, a sheep.

**The steps she proposed:**

| Step | When (approximate) | What happened |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Tokens** | from about 8000 BC | counters, one per item |
| **Envelopes** (*bullae*) | about 3500 BC | tokens sealed inside hollow clay balls as a record of a deal; the shapes pressed on the outside, so the contents could be "read" without breaking it |
| **Numerical tablets** | about 3400 BC | the marks alone, pressed into a flat clay tablet: the envelope without the tokens |
| **Proto-cuneiform** | about **3300–3100 BC**, at Uruk | signs for goods drawn with a stylus, beside number marks |

Her reading is widely taught, but critics argue that she grouped very different tokens together, and that many could have been gaming pieces or something else. What is not doubted is that **the earliest writing was accounting**.

**The first tablets.** About **5,000 tablets** from Uruk, of the period about **3300–3000 BC**, are the oldest large body of writing on earth. Roughly **85 per cent** are **administrative**: rations, fields, animals, workers. Most of the rest are **lists** of signs and words — professions, animals, vessels — copied by scribes learning their trade, some for centuries.

**How it worked.**
- The writer pressed a cut **reed** into soft **clay**. Over time the drawn pictures became groups of wedge-shaped marks: hence **cuneiform**, from Latin *cuneus*, "wedge".
- At first there were roughly a thousand signs; the number later fell to about 600 in regular use.
- The leap that made it real writing was the **rebus principle**: using a sign for its **sound**. The Sumerian word *ti* meant "arrow", and also "life"; so the sign for arrow could write "life". With sound-signs, scribes could write names, grammar, and in time whole sentences.

**Who wrote it.** The language of the first texts was **Sumerian**, a **language isolate**, related to no known language. From about **2600 BC** we have literature: proverbs, hymns, the first stories. Cuneiform was then adopted for **Akkadian**, a Semitic language, and later for Elamite, Hittite, Old Persian and others.

**How long it lasted.** About **3,000 years**. The last known datable cuneiform tablet is an **astronomical text of about AD 79–80**.

**How we can read it.** Cuneiform was forgotten for nearly 2,000 years, and deciphered in the **1850s**, mainly from the three-language inscription of the Persian king Darius at **Behistun** in Iran, copied by **Henry Rawlinson**. In **1857** four scholars translated the same new text separately and got the same meaning: proof it had been cracked.

**Why it mattered.** Writing began as a tool of the **temple and palace** to count what they owned and owed. It became a way to keep laws, letters, literature and science, and it is the reason we can call these people by their own names.
The Sumerian city-states: temples, ziggu:
After about **2900 BC**, Sumer was a land of a dozen or more rival **city-states**: each a city with its farmland and villages, its own god, and its own ruler. This is the **Early Dynastic period**, about **2900–2350 BC**.

**The cities and their gods:**

| City | Its god | Known for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Uruk** | Inanna and Anu | the oldest great city; Gilgamesh's city |
| **Ur** | Nanna, the moon god | the Royal Cemetery; later the ziggurat |
| **Nippur** | **Enlil**, the chief god | the **religious centre** of all Sumer; never the seat of a great dynasty |
| **Kish** | Zababa | in the north; "king of Kish" became a title of overlordship |
| **Lagash** and **Umma** | Ningirsu; Shara | neighbours who fought for generations |
| **Eridu** | Enki, god of fresh water and wisdom | the oldest temple site |

**Rulers.** Inscriptions use several titles: ***en*** (lord, at first with a priestly role), ***ensi*** (governor or city ruler) and ***lugal*** (literally "big man": king). Kingship grew stronger over the period, often through **war**.

**The temple and the palace.** Each city's temple owned land, herds and workshops, and fed many dependants. Scholars in the early 20th century read Sumer as a **"temple-state"**, where the god owned everything and the priests ran it. Later work, notably by Igor Diakonoff and Ignace Gelb, showed that **palaces, families and private owners** held much land too; the temple-state picture rested mainly on one archive from Lagash. The balance between them, and how it changed, is still debated.

**The first recorded war: Lagash against Umma.** The two fought over a fertile border district, the **Gu-edena**, for about 150 years. The **Stele of the Vultures** (about **2450 BC**, now in the Louvre) shows King **Eannatum** of Lagash leading a phalanx of soldiers with spears and shields, and vultures carrying off the heads of the dead. Later, **Uru-inimgina** of Lagash (about **2350 BC**) proclaimed **reforms** to protect widows and orphans and curb officials — the first known such decree. Soon after, Lagash was sacked by **Lugal-zage-si** of Umma, who went on to rule much of Sumer until Sargon defeated him.

**The Royal Cemetery of Ur, about 2600–2450 BC.** Excavated by **Leonard Woolley** in **1922–34**: about 1,800 graves, and 16 extraordinary "royal" tombs. In the tomb of **Queen Puabi** and in the **"Great Death Pit"**, dozens of attendants — **74** in the Death Pit — lay in rows in their finery: gold, silver, lapis lazuli from Afghanistan, harps, the famous **"Ram in a Thicket"** and the **Standard of Ur**. Woolley thought they had drunk poison willingly. CT scans of some skulls (2009) suggested several were **killed by blows** to the head. Why the practice existed, and whether it was voluntary, is unknown.

**The ziggurat.** A stepped, solid mud-brick tower with a shrine on top, the "mountain" of the god. It grew from the custom of raising temples on platforms, as at Uruk's White Temple. The best preserved, the **Ziggurat of Ur**, was built about **2100 BC** by King **Ur-Nammu**, with a base about 60 by 45 metres. It was not a tomb and not a place of public worship: the city's god lived there, and few were allowed up.

**The Sumerian King List**, composed about 2100–1800 BC, says kingship "descended from heaven" and passed from city to city, with a great **Flood** dividing early kings who reigned for thousands of years from later ones. It is propaganda and myth mixed with real names — a good example of a primary source to be read critically.

**Why it mattered.** Sumer created the pattern of the Near East for the next 2,000 years: rival cities, each under a god, competing for land and water, until one of them, or an outsider, united them by force.
Primary source: Gilgamesh, and the wild:
The oldest great story in the world contains a scene about this very stage: a wild man becomes human by eating farmed food.

**The epic.** **Gilgamesh** was remembered as a king of **Uruk**, perhaps a real ruler of about **2700 BC**, though no inscription of his own survives. Poems about him were written in Sumerian by about **2100 BC**. They were woven into one Akkadian epic, the version translated here, by about **1800 BC**, and the best-known "standard" version came later still. The gods make **Enkidu**, a wild man, to match Gilgamesh's strength. He lives with the animals until a woman of the temple (a "courtesan", in this translation) tames him, and then leads him to the city.

**The text** (the Old Babylonian "Pennsylvania tablet", column III; translated by **Morris Jastrow and Albert T. Clay**, *An Old Babylonian Version of the Gilgamesh Epic*, Yale, **1920**; square brackets are the translators' restorations of broken text):

> "Milk of the cattle
> He was accustomed to suck.
> Food they placed before him,
> He broke (it) off and looked
> And gazed.
> Enkidu had not known
> To eat food.
> To drink wine
> He had not been taught.
> The woman opened her mouth and
> Spoke to Enkidu:
> "Eat food, O Enkidu,
> The provender of life!
> Drink wine, the custom of the land!"
> Enkidu ate food
> Till he was satiated.
> Wine he drank,
> Seven goblets.
> His spirit was loosened, he became hilarious.
> His heart became glad and
> His face shone.
> [The barber(?)] removed
> The hair on his body.
> He was anointed with oil.
> He became manlike.
> He put on a garment,
> He was like a man."

**Two words to correct.** The Akkadian word translated **"wine"** is *šikaru*, which modern scholars render **"beer"**: barley beer was the everyday drink of Mesopotamia. And the **"food"** Enkidu breaks off is **bread**. Jastrow and Clay's own commentary calls it "bread and wine".

**Read it closely:**

| Line | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **"Milk of the cattle / He was accustomed to suck"** | before, he lived like an animal, eating what nature gave |
| **"He broke (it) off and looked / And gazed"** | bread is strange to him: food that has been **made**, by farming and baking |
| **"The provender of life … the custom of the land"** | bread and beer are what make people people. **Civilisation is defined by farmed food** |
| **"He was anointed with oil … He put on a garment"** | grooming, oil and woven cloth: all products of farming and herding |
| **"He was like a man"** | to become human is to join the farmed, settled world |

**What it reveals about its writers.** The Mesopotamians saw themselves as living in a **made world**: fields, canals, bread, beer, clothes and cities. The wilderness was the opposite of humanity. Immediately afterwards Enkidu protects the **shepherds** from lions: he has crossed over to their side.

**What it does not tell you.** It is a poem, not a record. It tells us what the scribes of about 1800 BC **valued**, not how farming began. And it is told from inside the city: no forager wrote down what he thought of bread.

**The tablet itself.** The Pennsylvania tablet is a clay tablet of six columns, now in the Penn Museum in Philadelphia. The epic was first recognised in **1872**, when **George Smith** at the British Museum read a later tablet from Nineveh telling of a great flood.
Egypt unified: Naqada, Narmer and the fi:
In the Nile valley, a single kingdom stretching some 1,000 km appeared around **3100 BC**, the first large territorial state in the world.

**The land.** Egypt is the **Nile**: a green strip, mostly a few kilometres wide, through desert, ending in the broad marshy **Delta**. Each summer the river flooded and left fresh black silt; Egyptians called their country *Kemet*, "the black land". **Upper Egypt** is the narrow valley in the south; **Lower Egypt** is the Delta in the north.

**Before the kings: the Naqada cultures**, named after a site in Upper Egypt:

| Phase | When (approximate) | What changed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Naqada I** | 4000–3500 BC | farming villages; fine pottery; graves with goods |
| **Naqada II** | 3500–3200 BC | larger towns; **rich elite graves**; the culture spreads north into the Delta; contacts with Mesopotamia |
| **Naqada III** ("Dynasty 0") | 3200–3100 BC | **kings** in Upper Egypt, at **Hierakonpolis**, Naqada and **Abydos** |

**The first signs of writing.** At Abydos, **tomb U-j** (about **3300–3200 BC**), excavated by **Günter Dreyer** in **1988**, held some 200 small bone and ivory labels with signs that seem to record places or goods. If they are writing, Egyptian writing is as old as Sumer's.

**Contact with Mesopotamia.** Late Naqada objects show Mesopotamian touches: **cylinder seals**, recessed brick façades, and the "master of animals" motif on the **Gebel el-Arak knife**. So Egypt was in contact with Sumer as its state formed, probably through trade.

**The Narmer Palette, about 3100 BC.** A shield-shaped stone slab about **64 cm** tall, found at **Hierakonpolis** in **1897–98** by **James Quibell** and **Frederick Green**, now in Cairo.

- On one side, King **Narmer** wears the tall **white crown of Upper Egypt** and strikes a kneeling enemy.
- On the other, he wears the **red crown of Lower Egypt** and inspects rows of beheaded bodies.
- His name is written in hieroglyphs: a catfish (*nar*) and a chisel (*mer*).

**Was Narmer the unifier?** Later Egyptian tradition, recorded by the priest **Manetho** in the 3rd century BC, named the first king **Menes**. Seal impressions from Abydos list **Narmer** at the head of the 1st Dynasty kings, so many scholars identify him with Menes; others favour his successor **Hor-Aha**.

**How did unification happen?** Two strong readings:

| Reading | The case |
| --- | --- |
| **Conquest** | the palette's battle scenes, and the tradition of a southern king conquering the north |
| **A slow process** | Upper Egyptian culture had spread into the Delta for generations before; several Dynasty 0 kings came before Narmer; and the palette may show a **ritual of kingship** rather than a single event |

Many now combine them: a **long cultural merging**, finished by **wars** between rival kings. More excavated Delta sites from the 4th millennium BC would sharpen the picture.

**The Early Dynastic period (1st and 2nd Dynasties), about 3100–2686 BC.** A capital at **Memphis**, near modern Cairo, where the valley meets the Delta. Kings were buried at **Abydos**, and in the 1st Dynasty, **hundreds of servants** were buried around royal tombs, apparently killed to serve the king after death; the practice ended soon after. The king was **Horus**, the falcon god, on earth.

**Nubia, to the south.** The **A-Group** people of Lower Nubia had their own chiefs and rich graves. One scholar argued in the 1980s that Egyptian kingship began there; most reject this. What is clear is that Egypt's early kings **raided Nubia**, and the A-Group disappears from the record soon after 3000 BC.
The Old Kingdom: the god-king and the fi:
The **Old Kingdom**, about **2686–2181 BC** (Dynasties 3 to 6), was the age of the great pyramids, and of the most absolute idea of kingship in early history.

**The king.** The pharaoh was **Horus** on earth and, from the 4th or 5th Dynasty, **son of Ra**, the sun god. His duty was to keep ***maat***: truth, justice and cosmic order, the opposite of chaos. Everything, in principle, belonged to him.

**How Egypt was run.**
- A chief minister, the **vizier**, ran the government.
- The land was divided into provinces (**nomes**), each under a governor (*nomarch*).
- Scribes counted **cattle, land and people**; a regular **"count"** of herds became a way of dating years.
- Hieroglyphs for monuments, and a faster hand, **hieratic**, for documents.

**Djoser and the first pyramid, about 2670 BC.** Before him, kings and nobles were buried under flat mud-brick tombs called **mastabas**. For King **Djoser** of the 3rd Dynasty, his official **Imhotep** stacked six mastaba-like stages of **stone**: the **Step Pyramid at Saqqara**, about **60 m** high. It is the **oldest large stone building** in the world. Imhotep's name is carved on a statue base there; later Egyptians revered him as a sage and even a god of medicine.

**Sneferu learns to build, about 2600 BC.** The first king of the 4th Dynasty built **three** large pyramids, learning as he went: **Meidum**, which partly collapsed; the **Bent Pyramid** at Dahshur, whose angle changes halfway up; and the **Red Pyramid**, the first true, smooth-sided pyramid.

**The great age of Giza** (next lesson) followed under his son **Khufu**.

**The 5th Dynasty, about 2494–2345 BC.** Smaller pyramids, and **sun temples** to Ra. Expeditions went south by sea to **Punt** (probably in the region of Eritrea and Sudan) for incense and gold. In the pyramid of the last king, **Unas** (about 2350 BC), the walls were carved with the **Pyramid Texts**, spells to help the king rise to the stars: the **oldest large body of religious writing** in the world.

**The 6th Dynasty, about 2345–2181 BC.** Provincial governors grew richer and more independent, building fine tombs at home instead of near the king. **Harkhuf**, governor at Aswan, led trading expeditions deep into Nubia, and carved on his tomb a letter from the boy-king **Pepi II**, excited about a dancing pygmy Harkhuf was bringing back. Pepi II's reign was very long; tradition says over **90 years**, which many scholars doubt, though it was certainly long.

**The end, about 2181 BC.** Central power broke up into the **First Intermediate Period** (about **2181–2055 BC**), with rival kings at Herakleopolis in the north and Thebes in the south. Its causes are debated in the lesson on the crisis around 2200 BC.

**Why it mattered.** The Old Kingdom set the model of Egyptian kingship, art and religion for the next 2,500 years. Later Egyptians looked back on it as a golden age.
Giza: how the Great Pyramid was built, a:
The largest of the pyramids, built for King **Khufu** (reigned about **2589–2566 BC**) on the Giza plateau west of Memphis, near modern Cairo.

**The facts:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Height** | about **146.6 m** when finished (about 138 m now, without its capstone and casing) |
| **Base** | about **230 m** a side, levelled to within a few centimetres, its sides aligned almost exactly to north, south, east and west |
| **Blocks** | about **2.3 million**, averaging over 2 tonnes; some granite beams in the king's chamber weigh dozens of tonnes |
| **Time** | about **20 years**, by tradition and by estimate |
| **Record** | the **tallest building on earth** for over 3,800 years, until the spire of Lincoln Cathedral in about AD 1311 |

Beside it, Khufu's son **Khafre** built the second pyramid and, it is usually agreed, the **Great Sphinx**; and **Menkaure** built the third, smaller one.

**Who built it?** The Greek historian **Herodotus**, visiting about **440 BC**, said **100,000 men** worked in three-month shifts. Films later showed **slaves** under the whip. The evidence says otherwise:

- **The workers' town.** Since **1988**, **Mark Lehner** and his team have excavated a town south of the plateau, with bakeries, breweries, barracks and storerooms. The bones show the workers ate a lot of **beef, sheep and goat**.
- **The workers' tombs.** Found in **1990** by **Zahi Hawass**: small tombs of overseers and workers, buried with honour near the king, some with healed fractures that show **medical care**.
- **The crews' graffiti.** Inside the Great Pyramid, work gangs painted their names, such as **"Friends of Khufu"**.
- **Modern estimates** of the workforce at any one time mostly run from about **10,000 to 30,000**: a permanent body of skilled craftsmen, and many more farmers serving in **rotating shifts** as a labour duty owed to the king.

Whether that duty was willing or forced is a matter of definition: it was **compulsory labour**, not chattel slavery, and it was fed and housed.

**The Diary of Merer.** In **2013**, the French Egyptologist **Pierre Tallet** found papyri at **Wadi al-Jarf** on the Red Sea: the **oldest inscribed papyri known**. One is the logbook of **Merer**, an inspector of a crew of about 40 men in about **Khufu's 27th year**. It records, day by day, ferrying **limestone blocks** by boat from the quarries at **Tura** across the Nile, through canals, to Giza, under the direction of **Ankhhaf**, Khufu's half-brother. It is direct evidence from the building of the Great Pyramid.

**How were the blocks raised?** Here there is genuine argument:

| Theory | For it | Against it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **One long straight ramp** | simple; ramps are found at other pyramids | it would have to be enormously long and as big as the pyramid |
| **A ramp spiralling round the sides** | uses less material | it would hide the corners needed to keep the shape true |
| **An internal ramp** (Jean-Pierre Houdin, 2007) | clever, and fits some features | little direct evidence |
| **Short ramps plus levers** | fits Herodotus's mention of machines | slow for the biggest blocks |

**Some things are known.** Blocks were dragged on **wooden sledges**; a Middle Kingdom tomb painting shows water poured on the sand in front of a sledge, and a 2014 experiment showed that **wet sand roughly halves the pulling force**. At the alabaster quarry of **Hatnub**, a steep ramp with stairs and post holes from Khufu's time was found in **2018**. More of these finds, at Giza itself, would settle the method.

**Claims that it was built by anyone other than Egyptians** have no support in the evidence: the quarries, tools, town, tombs, graffiti and papyri all point to Egypt's own people.
Writing invented more than once:
Writing is so useful that it looks inevitable. In fact it was invented from nothing **only a few times** in all of history.

**What counts as writing.** Many peoples used **symbols**: marks of ownership, tallies, pictures. Scholars call that **proto-writing**. **Full writing** is a system that can record **any sentence** in a language, by using signs for **sounds** as well as meanings. That is much rarer.

**The independent inventions:**

| Where | When (approximate) | Script | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Mesopotamia** | **3300–3200 BC** | cuneiform | the earliest; certainly independent |
| **Egypt** | **3250–3100 BC** | hieroglyphs | probably independent; see below |
| **China** | by about **1250 BC** | the Shang oracle-bone script, ancestor of Chinese characters | independent; Stage 3 |
| **Mesoamerica** | by about **600 BC**, perhaps earlier | Zapotec and Olmec scripts, later the Maya | independent; Stage 4 onward |

**Egypt: independent or inspired?** Two strong positions:
- **Inspired by Sumer.** Egypt was in contact with Mesopotamia just when its writing appeared. Perhaps Egyptians heard of the **idea** of writing and built their own system — **stimulus diffusion**. A modern parallel: **Sequoyah**, a Cherokee who could not read English, invented a Cherokee script around **1821** after seeing that marks on paper could carry speech.
- **Independent.** Egyptian signs, their sounds and their uses owe nothing to cuneiform, and the Abydos labels (about 3300–3200 BC) are as old as the earliest Sumerian tablets.
Firmer dates for the earliest signs in both places would settle which came first; even then, an idea leaves no trace.

**Scripts still unread from this stage:**
- **The Indus script**, about **2600–1900 BC**: thousands of short inscriptions, no bilingual text (see the Indus lessons).
- **Proto-Elamite**, about **3100–2900 BC**, from **Susa** in south-west Iran and across the Iranian plateau, used for accounts; still largely undeciphered. A later Iranian script, **Linear Elamite**, had a decipherment proposed in **2022** by François Desset and colleagues, which some specialists accept and others doubt.

**Proto-writing that did not become writing.** Signs on pots and figurines of the **Vinča** culture in the Balkans (about 5000 BC), and the shell marks at **Jiahu** in China (about 6000 BC), are sometimes claimed as early writing. Most scholars treat them as symbols, not full writing.

**What every early script was for.** Where we can tell, writing began in the service of **power and accounting**: Mesopotamian temple rations, Egyptian royal labels, Chinese divination for the king. Literature, letters and history came after.

**How many scripts descend from these few.** Most scripts in use today come down from Egyptian, through the alphabet (invented about **1850 BC** by Semitic speakers working in Egypt, Stage 3), or from Chinese. Cuneiform and the Mesoamerican scripts died out.

**Why it mattered.** Writing divides **prehistory** from **history**, by the convention of Stage 1. And it changed what states could do: with records, a ruler could tax, count and command people he would never see.
The Indus cities: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro:
The third of the great river civilisations, and the largest in area: the **Indus** or **Harappan** civilisation, in what is now **Pakistan** and **north-west India**.

**When.**

| Phase | When (approximate) |
| --- | --- |
| **Early Harappan** | 3300–2600 BC: towns, regional cultures, the first signs |
| **Mature Harappan** | **2600–1900 BC**: the great cities, the script, the seals |
| **Late Harappan** | 1900–1300 BC: the cities empty; village life continues |

**Where.** Over **a thousand** known settlements, across an area estimated at about **800,000 km²** or more — larger than Egypt and Mesopotamia together. From the Arabian Sea coast to the Himalayan foothills, and an outpost at **Shortugai** on the Amu Darya in northern Afghanistan.

**The great cities:**

| City | Where | Known for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Mohenjo-daro** | on the Indus, Sindh, Pakistan | the biggest excavated: a high **citadel** mound with the **Great Bath**, and a lower town in a **grid**; perhaps **40,000** people (estimates vary widely) |
| **Harappa** | on the Ravi, Punjab, Pakistan | the first found, which named the civilisation |
| **Dholavira** | the Rann of Kutch, Gujarat, India | great stone **reservoirs** to store rain; a "signboard" of ten large signs |
| **Rakhigarhi** | Haryana, India | perhaps the largest of all, still being excavated |
| **Lothal** | Gujarat, India | a large brick basin, read by some as a **dockyard**, by others as a reservoir |

**What made the cities remarkable.**
- **Planning.** Streets laid out in a broad grid, with houses opening onto lanes.
- **Water.** Wells in many houses, bathing platforms, and covered **drains** along the streets: sanitation not matched in many cities for thousands of years.
- **Standards.** Baked bricks made to the same **proportions (1:2:4)** across the whole region; stone cube **weights** in a fixed series, doubling from a small unit and then rising by decimals. One system for hundreds of thousands of square kilometres.
- **Crafts.** Long **carnelian beads**, drilled with great skill; shell bangles; bronze, including the small **"Dancing Girl"** from Mohenjo-daro.
- **Seals.** Small square stamp seals carved with animals — most often a one-horned bull-like beast called the **"unicorn"** — and a line of script.

**The Great Bath** of Mohenjo-daro, about 12 by 7 metres and over 2 metres deep, was made watertight with fine brick and **bitumen**. Most scholars think it was used for **ritual bathing**, and some see an early form of the later Indian concern with purity in water, but that link is a reading, not a proof.

**What is missing.** No clearly identified **palaces**, no **royal tombs**, no large **temples**, few weapons, and no pictures of kings at war. The stone bust nicknamed the **"Priest-King"** got that name from its excavators, not from any evidence of his role.

**Discovery.** Harappa's mounds were noticed in the 1820s, and partly dug for bricks to lay a railway in the 1850s. Excavations by **Daya Ram Sahni** at Harappa (**1921**) and **R. D. Banerji** at Mohenjo-daro (**1922**) led **John Marshall** to announce a new civilisation in **1924**.

**Why it mattered.** For seven centuries, the Indus people kept up an ordered, crafted urban life over a vast area, and traded as far as Mesopotamia. How they did it, and who ruled them, is the subject of the next lesson.
The Indus puzzles: an unread script and:
The Indus civilisation leaves three great questions open: what its script says, how it was governed, and why its cities emptied.

**1. The script.** About **4,000–5,000** inscribed objects survive, mostly seals. The script has some **400–700** signs, depending on how they are counted. Inscriptions are **very short**, on average about **five signs**, and mostly read from right to left. There is **no bilingual text**, nothing like the Rosetta Stone.

| Reading | The argument |
| --- | --- |
| **A language, probably Dravidian** | Iravatham Mahadevan and Asko Parpola argued that the signs write an early form of the **Dravidian** languages, now spoken mainly in southern India (Tamil, Telugu and others). Many find this plausible; no proposed reading has been proven |
| **A language, of unknown family** | others propose Indo-Aryan, Munda or a lost language. None has convinced most specialists |
| **Not a language at all** | Steve Farmer, Richard Sproat and Michael Witzel (2004) argued the inscriptions are too short and repetitive to be full writing: a system of **symbols**, like heraldry. Statistical work in 2009 (Rajesh Rao and colleagues) answered that the sign patterns look like those of languages. The argument continues |

**What would settle it:** a **bilingual** inscription, perhaps a Mesopotamian–Indus text from the trade with Sumer, or a **much longer** inscription.

**2. How it was governed.** No palaces and no kings in art, yet uniform weights and bricks across a huge area. Readings range from **one state** with an unusually faceless elite; to **several city-states** sharing a culture; to rule by **merchants, priests or councils** with no king at all. The evidence fits more than one, and the script would help most.

**3. Why the cities emptied, about 1900 BC.** After about 1900 BC, the big cities shrank and were abandoned; the script, seals and standard weights went out of use. People did not vanish: villages multiplied **eastwards**, into the upper Ganges plain, and **south** into Gujarat.

| Explanation | For it | Against it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Invasion by "Aryans"** | Mortimer Wheeler (1940s) pointed to skeletons in Mohenjo-daro's streets and the hymns of the Rigveda | the skeletons come from **different periods**, not one massacre (shown by George Dales, 1964); the Indo-Aryan speakers seem to arrive **after** the decline. Largely abandoned |
| **A weakening monsoon** | climate records show drier conditions around **2200–1900 BC** (the "4.2-kiloyear event") | the timing is not precise enough to show cause |
| **Rivers that moved or dried** | the **Ghaggar-Hakra** river, along which many sites lie, lost its water. Some identify it with the **Sarasvati** of the Rigveda | studies differ on **when** it dried; some argue it had already shrunk to a monsoon-fed stream long before |
| **Trade collapse** | Mesopotamian trade with "Meluhha" faded around the same time | it may be an effect, not a cause |

Most specialists now favour **several causes together**: climate stress, shifting rivers and the fraying of trade, with people choosing to leave the cities for villages.

**Who were they?** A genome from a woman buried at **Rakhigarhi**, published in **2019**, showed ancestry from early Iranian-related peoples and from ancient South Asian hunter-gatherers, with **no steppe** ancestry. That is one individual, but it fits the view that the Indus people were mainly the ancestors of later South Asians, and that steppe ancestry arrived later.

**Why it matters.** The Indus is the one great early civilisation we **cannot read**. Everything we know comes from the ground, which is why the questions stay open.
Before the Shang: Longshan towns, Taosi:
In China, the road from farming villages to the first state ran through walled towns, jade and bronze. It ends, just after this stage, at **Erlitou**, and the old question of the **Xia**.

**The Longshan world, about 3000–1900 BC.** Across the middle and lower Yellow River, villages grew into **walled towns** of **rammed earth** (*hangtu*: soil pounded in layers between boards, as hard as soft rock). Graves became sharply unequal: a few rich tombs, many poor ones. Craftsmen turned **eggshell-thin black pottery** on the wheel. Divination by **cracking heated bones** began, a practice the Shang later made famous.

**Liangzhu, on the lower Yangtze, about 3300–2300 BC.** Near modern Hangzhou, a **walled city of about 300 hectares**, with a huge raised palace platform and a system of **dams and embankments** in the hills, built about **3100 BC**, among the oldest large hydraulic works known. Its elite were buried with **jade**: the ***cong*** (a square tube with a round hole) and the ***bi*** (a flat disc), shapes used in Chinese ritual for thousands of years. Liangzhu was named a **UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019**, and some Chinese scholars call it China's first **state**. It ended about **2300 BC**, possibly after floods.

**Taosi, in Shanxi, about 2300–1900 BC.** A walled town of nearly **300 hectares**, with a palace area, storage pits, rich tombs, and a semicircular structure that its excavators read as an **astronomical observatory** for marking the solstices. That reading is argued over. Late in its history the town was violently sacked, and its elite tombs were desecrated.

**Shimao, in Shaanxi, about 2300–1800 BC.** A great **stone-walled** city on the northern loess plateau, with a stepped central pyramid-like platform. Under one gate, dozens of human **skulls**, probably of sacrificed captives.

**Erlitou, about 1900–1500 BC.** Near Luoyang in **Henan**, on the middle Yellow River, a city of about **300 hectares** that is the strongest candidate for China's **first state** in the full sense:

| Feature | At Erlitou |
| --- | --- |
| **Palaces** | large compounds on rammed-earth platforms, inside a walled palace zone |
| **Roads** | the oldest known grid of roads in China, around the palace zone |
| **Bronze** | workshops casting **ritual vessels** (such as the *jue*, a tripod wine cup) by **piece-mould casting**, the method later perfected by the Shang |
| **Treasure** | a **turquoise dragon**, about 70 cm long, made of over 2,000 pieces of turquoise, found in a tomb in 2002 |

**The Xia question.** China's first great historian, **Sima Qian** (about 100 BC), wrote of a **Xia dynasty** before the Shang, founded by **Yu the Great**, who tamed the floods. A Chinese state project (**1996–2000**) dated the Xia to about **2070–1600 BC**.

| Reading | The case |
| --- | --- |
| **Erlitou was the Xia** | it is in the right place and at the right time, as a powerful state before the Shang; many Chinese archaeologists hold this |
| **We cannot say** | no writing has been found at Erlitou to name it; the texts about the Xia were written over a thousand years later; many Western scholars call it "Erlitou culture" and leave the name open |

**What would settle it:** an **inscription** from Erlitou naming its rulers or its state. None has been found.

**Why it mattered.** Walled towns, jade ritual, bone divination and bronze casting all flowed into the **Shang dynasty**, from about **1600 BC**, the first Chinese state with writing (Stage 3).
Caral and Norte Chico: the first towns o:
On the desert coast of Peru, about **3000–1800 BC**, people built monumental towns at the same time as the pyramids of Egypt rose — without pottery, without writing, and perhaps without grain farming as their base.

**Where.** **Norte Chico** ("Little North"), about 150–200 km north of Lima, in four small river valleys running down from the Andes to the Pacific: the **Huaura, Supe, Pativilca and Fortaleza**. More than **30** sites have large platform mounds.

**Caral**, in the Supe valley about 23 km from the sea. The Peruvian archaeologist **Ruth Shady** began excavating in **1994**. In **2001**, she and her colleagues published radiocarbon dates showing the site was in use by about **2600 BC**, which made Norte Chico the **oldest known civilisation in the Americas** by well over a thousand years. Caral became a **UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2009**.

**What Caral has:**
- **Six large platform mounds**, faced with stone, the largest (the *Pirámide Mayor*) with a stairway to a summit with rooms and a fire altar.
- **Sunken circular plazas**, a feature that runs through Andean architecture for the next 2,000 years.
- **Housing of different quality**: fine stone rooms near the mounds, simpler homes on the edges, suggesting **ranks** in society.
- **Flutes** made from pelican and condor bones, and cornets of animal bone.
- **Construction with *shicras***: bags of woven reed filled with stones, stacked as fill inside the mounds.
- Perhaps **3,000 people** at Caral itself, by Shady's estimate.

**Aspero**, on the coast at the mouth of the Supe, is older still, with platform mounds from about **3000 BC**.

**What it does not have.** **No pottery**: the whole culture is "preceramic". **No writing**, as far as is known. And remarkably, **no clear signs of war**: no fortifications, few weapons, no burned layers. That is one of the reasons Caral interests historians: it is an early complex society that **seems** to have been held together without violence. The evidence is absence, which is never final.

**What fed it: the great debate.**

| Reading | The case |
| --- | --- |
| **The sea** ("maritime foundations") | Michael Moseley argued in **1975** that Andean civilisation began on **fish**: the Peruvian coast has one of the richest fisheries on earth. Norte Chico's middens are full of **anchovy and sardine** bones |
| **Cotton and exchange** | inland towns like Caral grew **cotton** (for fishing nets), squash, beans and fruit with irrigation, and traded with the coast for fish; the system needed both |
| **Maize** | a 2013 study (Haas and colleagues) found maize pollen and other traces and argued maize was a staple. Others disputed how much there was |

Most now agree on **fish plus irrigated crops, especially cotton**, with the role of maize unresolved. Analysis of the people's own bones, which would show their diet directly, would help settle it.

**Why it mattered.** Norte Chico shows that the Americas began building monumental towns about as early as the Old World, and with **a different recipe**: no cereals at the base, no pottery, no writing. It began the Andean tradition of platform mounds and sunken plazas that led to **Chavín** (Stage 3) and, much later, the Inca.
Sargon of Akkad: the first empire:
About **2334 BC**, a man from northern Mesopotamia conquered all the Sumerian cities and much beyond, and founded what is usually called the **first empire** in history.

**The dates.** By the most used ("middle") chronology, **Sargon** reigned about **2334–2279 BC**. Some scholars place him about 60 years later; the dates for this period are uncertain by decades.

**His name.** *Šarru-kīn*, Akkadian for **"the true king"** or "the legitimate king" — a name that may itself suggest he was **not** born to the throne.

**His rise, as later tradition told it.** A Sumerian story says he was **cupbearer** to **Ur-Zababa**, king of **Kish**, and overthrew him. A much later **birth legend**, known from copies of the 7th century BC, says his mother was a priestess who set him adrift in a **basket of reeds** on the Euphrates, and that he was raised by a water-drawer. These stories were written long after him and are **legend**, not evidence of his birth.

**His conquests, as his own inscriptions told it.** Copies of his victory inscriptions, made by later scribes at Nippur, say that he:
- defeated **Lugal-zage-si** of Uruk, who ruled much of Sumer, and brought him **in a neck-stock** to the gate of Enlil's temple;
- conquered the Sumerian cities and **"washed his weapons in the sea"**, the Persian Gulf;
- fought **34 battles**, and went up the Euphrates to **Mari** and **Ebla**, as far as the "Cedar Forest" and the "Silver Mountains" (probably Lebanon or the Amanus, and the Taurus);
- had **5,400 men eat daily before him**: a standing army, or a royal household;
- brought **ships from Meluhha, Magan and Dilmun** to moor at the quay of his capital.

**Akkad and its capital.** He ruled from a new city, **Agade**, which gave its name to the land (**Akkad**) and the language (**Akkadian**). Agade has **never been found**; it probably lies somewhere near the Tigris or the Euphrates in central Iraq.

**How the empire worked.** Sargon put **his own men** as governors over the old Sumerian cities, made **Akkadian**, a Semitic language, a language of government alongside Sumerian, and standardised some weights and measures. The Sumerian cities **rebelled** again and again.

**Enheduanna.** Sargon made his daughter **Enheduanna** high priestess of the moon god Nanna at **Ur**, binding the southern cult to his house. A carved disc from Ur shows her at an offering. Hymns to the goddess **Inanna**, including *The Exaltation of Inanna*, are attributed to her, which would make her the **first named author** in history. Some scholars doubt it: the copies date from about 1800 BC, and the attribution may be a later tradition. Most accept she was at least the patron of the hymns.

**His grandson Naram-Sin** (about **2254–2218 BC**) took the title **"King of the Four Quarters"**, meaning the whole world, and was the first Mesopotamian king to have himself **made a god**, with the divine sign before his name. His **Victory Stele**, now in the Louvre, shows him climbing a mountain over his defeated enemies, the Lullubi of the Zagros.

**Was it the first empire?** Earlier kings, such as Lugal-zage-si, had ruled several cities. Akkad was the first to rule **many peoples and languages** over a large area **through a central administration**, which is why most historians give it the title. The answer depends on the definition.

**Its fall, about 2150 BC.** After Naram-Sin, the empire shrank under revolts and invasion by the **Gutians** from the Zagros. Its end is the subject of the next lesson.

**Why it mattered.** Sargon became the model of the world-conquering king for 2,000 years: Assyrian kings took his name, and his legend was still being copied in the 7th century BC.
The crisis around 2200 BC: drought, the:
Around **2200 BC**, several of the first states broke down within about a century of each other. Was there a common cause?

**What fell, and when (approximate):**

| Where | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| **Mesopotamia** | the **Akkadian empire** collapsed about **2150 BC**; the **Gutians** from the Zagros took over much of the south |
| **Upper Mesopotamia** | many towns on the **Habur plains** of north-east Syria, such as **Tell Leilan**, were abandoned about **2200 BC** |
| **Egypt** | the **Old Kingdom** ended about **2181 BC**; the land split into rival kingdoms |
| **The Indus** | the cities began to decline, though later, after about **1900 BC** |
| **China** | Liangzhu had already ended about 2300 BC; Longshan towns were changing |

**The climate case: the "4.2-kiloyear event".** Climate records, from stalagmites, lake beds and ocean cores, show a spell of **drier, cooler** conditions across much of the northern hemisphere starting about **2200 BC** (4,200 years ago). Geologists took it in **2018** as the official start of the **Meghalayan age**, the latest slice of the Holocene, named after a cave in Meghalaya, India, whose stalagmite records it.

- **Harvey Weiss** argued in **1993** that the abandonment of Tell Leilan and its region showed **drought destroyed the Akkadian empire's grain base**.
- In Egypt, the tomb of **Ankhtifi**, governor at Mo'alla in the south (about **2150 BC**), boasts that he fed his province when all of Upper Egypt was dying of hunger (a paraphrase). Low Nile floods fit the drought.

**The human case.** Each collapse has its own causes:
- **Akkad** was always fragile: its Sumerian cities revolted constantly, and the Gutians attacked from outside.
- In **Egypt**, provincial governors had been growing more independent for a century, and the very long reign of **Pepi II** may have left a weak succession.
- Climate stress is **not** the same as collapse: societies with reserves and good government can ride out droughts.

**The strongest form of each:**

| Reading | The argument |
| --- | --- |
| **Climate was decisive** | the near-simultaneous breakdown across regions is too striking to be chance; all these states depended on rain or river floods |
| **Climate was one stress among many** | each state was already strained; the timing of the climate signal varies by region; and some societies in the same zone did not collapse |

**What would settle it:** **finer dating** of both the climate records and the collapses, region by region, to see whether the drought came **first** everywhere it is blamed.

**The Mesopotamians' own explanation.** A Sumerian poem, ***The Cursing of Agade***, written perhaps a century later, blamed **Naram-Sin** for desecrating **Enlil's temple** at Nippur, so that the gods sent the Gutians and famine. The **Sumerian King List** sums up the confusion after Akkad by asking, in effect, who was king and who was not.

**The recovery: the Third Dynasty of Ur, about 2112–2004 BC.** **Ur-Nammu** of Ur reunited Sumer and Akkad, built the great **ziggurat of Ur**, and issued the **Code of Ur-Nammu**, the **oldest surviving law code**, which set fines in silver for injuries. His son **Shulgi** (about 2094–2047 BC) made himself a god and ran a vast **bureaucracy**: tens of thousands of Ur III tablets survive, recording every sheep and worker. It ended in **2004 BC**, when the **Elamites** from Iran sacked Ur and led its last king, **Ibbi-Sin**, away. The **Lament for Ur** mourned it.

**In Egypt**, **Mentuhotep II** of Thebes reunited the country about **2055 BC**, founding the **Middle Kingdom** (Stage 3).

**Why it mattered.** The first states proved **fragile**, but the idea of the state did not die. In both Egypt and Mesopotamia, unity was rebuilt within about a century — a pattern of collapse and revival that recurs through all of ancient history.
Connections: the world of 2000 BC:
The stage closes about **2000 BC**. Seven thousand years earlier, everyone was a forager. Now there are farmers on every inhabited continent but Australia, states on four great rivers, and long-distance trade linking them.

**Who traded with whom.**

| Link | What moved |
| --- | --- |
| **Mesopotamia – the Gulf – the Indus** | Sumerian texts name **Dilmun** (Bahrain), **Magan** (Oman, a source of **copper**) and **Meluhha** (the Indus). Indus **seals** and **carnelian beads** have been found at Ur and other Mesopotamian cities; Sargon boasted of Meluhhan ships at his quay |
| **Afghanistan – everywhere** | **lapis lazuli**, a deep-blue stone mined in **Badakhshan**, reached the royal tombs of Ur and the graves of Egypt; the Indus outpost at **Shortugai** sat near the mines |
| **Egypt – the Levant** | **cedar** from Lebanon, shipped from **Byblos**, for Egyptian boats and temples; a royal record says King Sneferu brought 40 shiploads |
| **Egypt – Nubia and Punt** | gold, ebony, ivory and incense; trade, raiding and tribute |
| **Syria's cities** | the archive of **Ebla** (found **1974–76**, about **2400–2300 BC**) records trade in textiles and metals with Mari and other cities, and Egyptian objects were found there |
| **Across Eurasia** | **wheat and barley** reached northern **China** from the west by about 2500–2000 BC; Chinese **millet** moved west across Central Asia; African **sorghum** and **pearl millet** reached **India** by about 2000 BC |

**Who fought whom.** **Lagash and Umma** over a border field; **Akkad** against everyone; **Egypt** against Nubia and the desert peoples; the **Gutians** against Akkad; **Elam** against Ur. Walls rose around towns from Mesopotamia to China. War became an activity of **states**.

**What spread.**
- **Farming** across most of the farmable world, often carried by migrating farmers.
- **Metal**: copper, then **bronze**, from the Near East outward.
- **The wheel**, the **plough** and the **sail**.
- **Writing**, in the Near East; and the idea of it, perhaps, from Sumer to Egypt.

**Who is where, about 2000 BC:**

| Region | The state of things |
| --- | --- |
| **Mesopotamia** | Ur has just fallen to the Elamites (2004 BC); **Amorite** chiefs are taking over cities, among them a small town called **Babylon** |
| **Egypt** | reuniting under the **Middle Kingdom** |
| **Nubia** | the kingdom of **Kerma**, founded about 2500 BC, growing into Egypt's great southern rival |
| **The Indus** | the cities at their height, about to decline |
| **China** | Longshan towns; **Erlitou** is about to rise |
| **The steppe** | herders with steppe ancestry spread across Europe and Central Asia; the **spoked-wheel chariot** is about to appear |
| **Europe** | Stonehenge complete; the **Bronze Age** beginning; on **Crete**, the first Minoan palaces will soon be built |
| **Africa** | herders in East Africa; millet and sorghum farmers in the Sahel; **Bantu-speaking** farmers in West-Central Africa, whose great expansion is beginning, by most estimates |
| **The Americas** | Norte Chico's towns in Peru; maize villages forming in Mesoamerica |
| **The Pacific** | Austronesian farmers sailing south from Taiwan |
| **Australia** | Aboriginal peoples, foragers and land managers, across the continent |

**What carried over into Stage 3.**
1. **Babylon** and **Hammurabi**, heirs to Sumer's cities and to Akkad's idea of empire.
2. **Middle and New Kingdom Egypt**, built on the Old Kingdom's model of the god-king.
3. The **Shang**, heirs of Erlitou, with the first Chinese writing.
4. The **chariot**, and the Indo-European-speaking peoples who used it: **Hittites**, **Mycenaean Greeks**, and the Indo-Aryans who entered South Asia.
5. The **Olmec** in Mesoamerica and **Chavín** in the Andes.

**Look back at the whole stage:** farming was invented again and again; it brought more people, more work and more inequality; and in a few river valleys it fed **cities, kings and writing**. Most of the people in this stage are **unnamed** — but for the first time, a few speak to us in their own words.
Map: the world around 2000 BC:
This stage runs from about 2000 to 1000 BC: the Late Bronze Age in the Near East and the Mediterranean, and its equivalents elsewhere. Here is where everyone stands at the start.

**Bronze is the age's name and its engine.** Bronze is copper alloyed with roughly a tenth part tin. Copper is fairly common; **tin is rare**, found in a few places such as Cornwall, the Ore Mountains of central Europe, Iberia and Central Asia. So any kingdom that wanted bronze weapons and tools had to trade over long distances, and **long-distance trade is the thread that ties this whole stage together**.

| Region | Around 2000 BC |
| --- | --- |
| **Mesopotamia** | the Third Dynasty of Ur has just fallen (Ur was sacked by the Elamites about **2004 BC**). Its land splits into rival **Amorite** kingdoms: Isin, Larsa, Eshnunna, Mari and a small town called **Babylon** |
| **Assyria and Anatolia** | merchants from the city of **Ashur** run donkey caravans of tin and cloth to **Kanesh** (Kültepe, in central Turkey). Over 20,000 of their business letters survive, from about 1950–1750 BC |
| **Egypt** | reunited about **2055 BC** by Mentuhotep II of Thebes after a century of division: the start of the **Middle Kingdom** |
| **Nubia** | the kingdom of **Kush**, centred at **Kerma** on the Nile in what is now Sudan, is growing rich on trade |
| **The Aegean** | on Crete, the first great **Minoan palaces** are being built, about 1950 BC. Mainland Greece is a land of modest villages |
| **Europe beyond** | the **Únětice** culture of central Europe, rich in bronze and controlling routes for tin and amber |
| **The steppe** | in the southern Urals, the **Sintashta** people are building the first **spoked-wheel chariots** |
| **South Asia** | the great **Indus cities** (Harappa, Mohenjo-daro) are at the end of their peak; within a few centuries they will empty |
| **East Asia** | on the Yellow River, the **Erlitou** culture (from about 1900 BC) builds the first palace-centred town in China |
| **The Americas** | farming villages and pottery in Mesoamerica; in the Andes, coastal temple-centres; in Louisiana, **Poverty Point** will begin about 1700 BC |
| **Oceania** | Austronesian-speaking farmers have spread from Taiwan into the Philippines; the open Pacific beyond New Guinea is still empty of people |

**A word on dates.** Before about 1400 BC, Near Eastern dates can be **off by decades**, sometimes more. Scholars use competing systems ("high", "middle", "low" chronologies) because the king lists cannot yet be tied exactly to astronomy or to tree rings. This stage uses the commonly cited **middle chronology** and says "about".

**What to watch for.** Across this stage four things happen in many places at once: **kingdoms grow into empires**, **the horse and chariot spread**, **writing spreads and an alphabet is invented**, and, around 1200 BC, **much of the system collapses**. The last lesson asks what carried through.
Horse, chariot and the Indo-European lan:
Two of the biggest changes of the age came out of the Eurasian steppe: a way of fighting, and a family of languages that now has over three billion speakers.

**The horse.** People on the steppe hunted horses for millennia and some herded them. But a 2021 study of ancient horse DNA (Librado and colleagues) found that **the ancestors of all modern domestic horses were bred on the lower Volga–Don steppe in what is now southern Russia, about 2200 BC**, and spread across Eurasia within a few centuries. Earlier herds, such as those at Botai in Kazakhstan around 3500 BC, belonged to a different line.

**The chariot.** About **2100–1800 BC**, the **Sintashta** people of the southern Urals buried warriors with light, two-wheeled vehicles with **spoked wheels**, pulled by horses. Spokes made the wheel light, and lightness made it fast. Chariots reached the Near East by about **1700 BC**, Egypt during the Hyksos period (about 1650–1550 BC), Mycenaean Greece about 1600 BC, and China by about **1200 BC**. **For five centuries the chariot was the weapon that marked a great power**, used by an aristocracy of specialist warriors.

**The languages.** In 1786 the British judge William Jones noticed that **Sanskrit, Greek and Latin** shared roots too many to be chance: Sanskrit *pitar*, Greek *patēr*, Latin *pater*, English *father*. These languages, with the Germanic, Celtic, Slavic, Baltic, Iranian, Armenian, Albanian and the extinct Anatolian (Hittite) and Tocharian branches, form the **Indo-European family**, descended from one lost language, **Proto-Indo-European**.

**Where was it spoken? This is contested.**

| Reading | Strongest form |
| --- | --- |
| **The steppe hypothesis** (Marija Gimbutas; David Anthony) | Proto-Indo-European was spoken by steppe herders, the **Yamnaya** culture (about 3300–2600 BC). Its shared words for wheels, wagons and horses suggest a date after the wheel. Ancient DNA (2015) shows a **massive movement of steppe ancestry into Europe** after 3000 BC, and later into South Asia |
| **The Anatolian hypothesis** (Colin Renfrew) | the languages spread from Anatolia with the **first farmers**, after about 7000 BC. Farming was the one movement big enough to carry a language family so far |
| **Recent hybrids** | some studies (2023–2025) place the earliest stage south of the Caucasus or between the Caucasus and the Volga, with a later steppe branch carrying most of the family. Notably, **the Hittites show little or no Yamnaya ancestry** |

Most linguists and geneticists now favour a steppe origin for most branches. What would settle the remainder is **more ancient DNA from early Anatolian speakers** and from the Caucasus, and better dating of the shared vocabulary.

**Why it matters for this stage.** The Hittites, the Mitanni's rulers, the Mycenaean Greeks and the Vedic peoples of India all spoke Indo-European languages, and several of them fought from chariots.
Egypt's Middle Kingdom, about 2055–1650:
After the pyramid age broke down, Egypt was put back together, and its second great age is the one Egyptians themselves later looked back to as classical.

**The reunion.** About **2055 BC**, **Mentuhotep II**, a ruler of **Thebes** in the south, defeated the rival kings of Herakleopolis and reunited the Two Lands. The new order was firmed up by the **12th Dynasty**, founded about **1985 BC** by **Amenemhat I**, a former official who moved the capital north to a new city, **Itjtawy**, near modern Lisht.

**The great kings of the 12th Dynasty:**

| King | About | Known for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Amenemhat I** | 1985–1956 BC | new capital; probably murdered in a palace plot, which a text in his name describes |
| **Senusret I** | 1956–1911 BC | building across Egypt; the White Chapel at Karnak |
| **Senusret III** | 1870–1831 BC | conquered Lower Nubia to the **Second Cataract** and built a chain of mud-brick forts there (**Buhen, Semna**) |
| **Amenemhat III** | 1831–1786 BC | reclaimed farmland in the **Fayum** basin; a vast temple Herodotus later called the "labyrinth" |
| **Sobekneferu** | about 1777–1773 BC | the first woman securely known to have ruled as king |

**Power at home.** In the Old Kingdom's last years, provincial governors (**nomarchs**) had become nearly independent. Under Senusret III their great tombs stop being built. Most scholars read this as the crown curbing them; some think the families simply moved into court service. The evidence is the tombs and titles, and it supports both.

**Egypt's classical literature.** Middle Egyptian, the language of this age, became the model language that later scribes copied for 1,500 years. Its best stories are still read: **the Tale of Sinuhe**, an official who flees Egypt for the Levant and longs to come home to be buried; **the Shipwrecked Sailor**; and teaching texts on how to live.

**The afterlife opens up.** Old Kingdom spells for eternal life had been carved only in royal pyramids. Now the **Coffin Texts** were painted inside the coffins of officials and their families. Scholars once called this the "democratisation of the afterlife"; many now think the change was more in what got written down than in belief, so treat the phrase with care.

**Outside contact.** A tomb painting at **Beni Hasan** (about 1890 BC) shows a party of **Asiatics** from the Levant arriving with goods. People from the Levant were settling in the eastern Delta. That quiet movement is the background to the next great change.

**The end.** After about 1773 BC the 13th Dynasty's kings came and went quickly, and by about **1650 BC** Egypt had split again: the **Second Intermediate Period**, and the rule of foreign kings in the north.
Hammurabi and Old Babylon:
For about forty years in the 1700s BC, a king of a once-minor town made Babylon the centre of Mesopotamia, and it stayed the region's cultural capital for over a thousand years.

**Babylon before Hammurabi.** Babylon sat on the Euphrates, south of modern Baghdad. Its First Dynasty, founded about **1894 BC**, was **Amorite**: the Amorites were Semitic-speaking peoples from the Syrian steppe who had taken power in many Mesopotamian cities as Ur's empire broke up. Around 1800 BC there were half a dozen comparable kingdoms, and none could beat the rest.

**Hammurabi** reigned about **1792–1750 BC**. For thirty years he waited, allied and bargained. Letters from the palace at **Mari** on the middle Euphrates, where some 20,000 or more tablets were found from the 1930s on, show a world of shifting coalitions in which, as one envoy reported, no king was strong on his own, and each had other kings following him.

**Then he struck:**

| About | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **1763 BC** | conquers **Larsa** and its king Rim-Sin, taking the whole south |
| **1762 BC** | defeats **Eshnunna** to the east |
| **1761–1759 BC** | takes **Mari**, his former ally, and later destroys it |

By his death Babylon ruled from the Persian Gulf to the middle Euphrates. **His empire did not last**: under his son **Samsu-iluna** the far south broke away.

**How he ruled.** Hundreds of Hammurabi's letters survive. They show a king who dealt personally with canals, rents, temple land and lawsuits. His **laws**, set up on stone near the end of his reign, are the subject of the next lesson.

**Old Babylonian culture**, more lasting than the empire:
- **Scribal schools** (the *edubba*, "tablet house") taught **Sumerian**, by now a dead language kept for learning, as Latin was in medieval Europe.
- The first long versions of the **Epic of Gilgamesh** and the flood story **Atrahasis** were written down.
- **Mathematics** in base 60 reached a high level. The tablet **Plimpton 322** (about 1800 BC) lists sets of numbers related to right-angled triangles; how it was used is debated. Our 60 minutes and 360 degrees descend from this system.
- **Marduk**, Babylon's own god, began his rise to the head of the pantheon.

**The end of the dynasty.** About **1595 BC**, the Hittite king **Mursili I** marched well over 1,000 km from Anatolia, **sacked Babylon** and went home. (On the low chronology this happened decades later; the uncertainty in this whole period hangs on this date.) Into the gap came the **Kassites**, who ruled Babylon for over four centuries.

**Why Babylon mattered afterwards.** Even under foreign kings, Babylon was the city of learning. Its script, Akkadian cuneiform, became **the language of diplomacy** across the Near East, as the Amarna letters will show.
Primary source: Hammurabi's laws on eyes:
A few clauses from the most famous law collection of the ancient world, read slowly.

**The object.** A black stone stele about **2.25 metres** tall, set up about **1755–1750 BC**. At the top, Hammurabi stands before the seated sun god **Shamash**, the god of justice. Below, about **282 laws** are carved in Akkadian, framed by a prologue and an epilogue. In the 1100s BC an Elamite king carried it off as plunder to **Susa** in Iran, where French archaeologists found it in **1901–02**. It is now in the **Louvre**.

**The text** (laws 196–199 and 229–231; translated by **L. W. King, 1903**, as given in the Fordham Ancient History Sourcebook):

> "196. If a man put out the eye of another man, his eye shall be put out.
> 197. If he break another man's bone, his bone shall be broken.
> 198. If he put out the eye of a freed man, or break the bone of a freed man, he shall pay one gold mina.
> 199. If he put out the eye of a man's slave, or break the bone of a man's slave, he shall pay one-half of its value."

> "229 If a builder build a house for some one, and does not construct it properly, and the house which he built fall in and kill its owner, then that builder shall be put to death.
> 230. If it kill the son of the owner the son of that builder shall be put to death.
> 231. If it kill a slave of the owner, then he shall pay slave for slave to the owner of the house."

**Read it closely:**

| Feature | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **"If… then…"** | every law is a **case**, the same form as Babylonian omen texts. The laws were thought of as examples of justice, not a complete system |
| **Eye for eye** (196–197) | **retaliation in kind**, called *talion*. It appears again centuries later in the Hebrew Bible (Exodus 21). Whether one borrowed from the other, or both drew on shared custom, is debated |
| **Three classes** (196–199) | the same injury costs differently by **rank**. King's "freed man" translates *muškēnum*, which scholars now render as **commoner** or palace dependant. The full free man (*awīlum*) gets talion; the commoner gets silver; the slave's owner gets half a slave's price |
| **The builder's son** (230) | punishment falls on the builder's **family**: a son for a son. Justice here means balance between households, not only individual guilt |

**What Hammurabi says it is for.** In the epilogue, in King's translation: "That the strong might not injure the weak, in order to protect the widows and orphans, I have … set up these my precious words, written upon my memorial stone." **The stele is royal self-presentation as much as law**: proof to gods and successors that he was a just king.

**Was it law? Historians disagree.**
- **As a legal code**: it was copied by scribes for over a thousand years, and its rules on debt, rents and family match real practice in contracts.
- **As a royal monument and scholarly treatise**: among thousands of Old Babylonian court records, **almost none cites it**, and judges decided cases on their own. It was not the first, either: the laws of **Ur-Nammu** (about 2100 BC) and **Lipit-Ishtar** are older.

What would settle it is a body of court records that refers to the stele's rules by wording. So far it has not appeared.
Kerma: the kingdom of Kush that rivalled:
