South of Egypt, on the Nile in what is now northern Sudan, Africa's first great kingdom outside Egypt rose, flourished and fought Egypt for a thousand years.

**Where and when.** The town of **Kerma** lies just above the Nile's **Third Cataract**. It was a settled centre by about **2500 BC**, and the kingdom it led, which the Egyptians called **Kush**, reached its height in the **Classic Kerma** period, about **1750–1500 BC**. At its peak it controlled the Nile valley for over 1,000 km, from the First Cataract to beyond the Fourth.

**Why it was rich.** Kush sat on the route between Egypt and the lands to the south. Down that route came **gold** (Nubia was the Egyptian world's main source), **ivory, ebony, incense, animal skins and cattle**. Kerma was not a copy of Egypt: its pottery, its round huts and its religion were its own.

**What survives:**

| Site | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **The Western Deffufa** | a huge mud-brick temple, still about **18 metres** high, at the heart of the town |
| **The royal cemetery** | mounds (*tumuli*) up to about 90 metres across. In the largest, the dead king was accompanied by **hundreds of sacrificed people**, perhaps 300 or more in one, along with cattle skulls and fine goods |
| **The town** | palaces, workshops and a defensive wall with bastions |

The American archaeologist **George Reisner** excavated the cemetery in **1913–1916** and assumed Kerma was an Egyptian outpost. **The Swiss archaeologist Charles Bonnet, working there from the 1970s, showed it was an independent African capital.**

**Kush and Egypt.** The relationship ran both ways:
- In the **Middle Kingdom**, Egypt built forts at the Second Cataract to hold Kush back and control trade, with a boundary stela forbidding Nubians to pass except to trade.
- In the **Second Intermediate Period**, about 1650–1550 BC, Kush struck north. An inscription in the tomb of an Egyptian governor at **Elkab**, read in 2003, describes Kushite armies **raiding deep into Egypt**. Kush was also in contact with the **Hyksos** kings in the Delta: the Theban king **Kamose** boasted of intercepting a Hyksos messenger who was carrying a letter to the ruler of Kush, proposing that they divide Egypt between them.
- When the New Kingdom rose, Egypt turned on Kush. **Thutmose I** (about 1504–1492 BC) **destroyed Kerma**, and Egypt ruled Nubia for the next 450 years through a viceroy called the **"King's Son of Kush"**, mining its gold and building temples, including one to Amun at **Jebel Barkal**.

**Why it matters.** Kush did not disappear. Under Egyptian rule its people learned Egyptian writing and the cult of Amun, and about **750 BC** a Kushite dynasty would conquer Egypt itself. That is Stage 4.
The Hyksos: foreign kings in the Nile De:
For about a century, northern Egypt was ruled by kings from the Levant. Later Egyptians remembered it as a national humiliation; the evidence tells a more interesting story.

**Who.** *Hyksos* is a Greek form of the Egyptian ***heqau khasut*, "rulers of foreign lands"**. They were the **15th Dynasty**, about **1650–1550 BC**, and their names (Khyan, Apepi) and culture were **West Semitic**, from Canaan and Syria.

**Where.** Their capital was **Avaris** in the eastern Delta, now **Tell el-Dab'a**, excavated by the Austrian archaeologist **Manfred Bietak** from 1966. It was a big city with Levantine-style houses, temples and burials, including donkeys buried at tomb entrances, a Levantine custom. The south stayed under Egyptian kings at **Thebes** (the 17th Dynasty), who paid tribute to Avaris for a time.

**How did they take power? This is contested.**

| Reading | Strongest form |
| --- | --- |
| **Invasion** | the Egyptian priest **Manetho**, writing in the 200s BC (and known through the Jewish historian Josephus), describes them as invaders of unknown origin who took the land by force and burned cities and temples |
| **Gradual takeover** | Avaris had a Levantine population **for generations before** the Hyksos kings, since the late Middle Kingdom. A 2020 study of strontium isotopes in teeth from Avaris burials found many people raised outside Egypt, a good share of them **women**, across the late Middle Kingdom and the Hyksos period: the pattern of **long-term immigration**, not of a sudden army of men. On this reading, a settled immigrant community took power as the 13th Dynasty weakened |

Manetho wrote 1,400 years later and drew on hostile tradition; the archaeology is direct but cannot show what happened in a single year. Most specialists now lean to the gradual reading, perhaps with a final seizure of power. What would settle it is the excavation of the 13th Dynasty's last capital and more dated burials from the decades around 1650 BC.

**What they brought.** The Hyksos period is when Egypt adopted the **horse and chariot**, the **composite bow**, new bronze-working and new kinds of axe and dagger. Some of these may have arrived just before the Hyksos, but **Egypt came out of this period with a chariot army it had not had before.** Avaris also had contacts with Crete and Cyprus: a lid with Khyan's name was found at Knossos.

**The war of liberation.** The Theban kings fought back:
- **Seqenenre Tao** (about 1560 BC): his mummy shows **fatal head wounds**, consistent with Levantine-type axes, probably in battle.
- **Kamose** campaigned north and boasted of it on stelae at Karnak.
- **Ahmose I** (reigned about 1550–1525 BC) **took Avaris** and then besieged **Sharuhen** in southern Canaan for three years.

**Why it mattered.** The shock changed Egypt. Its kings no longer trusted to deserts and the Nile to protect them. **The New Kingdom that Ahmose founded would carry war into Asia and Nubia, and become an empire.**
The Hittites of Hattusa:
A people forgotten for three thousand years, rediscovered in the twentieth century as one of the great powers of the age.

**Where.** Central Anatolia, on a high, cold plateau. Their capital, **Hattusa**, lies beside the village of Boğazkale, about 150 km east of Ankara. It was a fortified city of temples and palaces with walls over 6 km round, gates guarded by carved lions and sphinxes.

**How they were found.** The Bible mentions "Hittites", but nobody knew who they were. In **1906** the German scholar **Hugo Winckler** began digging at Boğazkale and found **thousands of cuneiform tablets**, the royal archive. In **1915** the Czech scholar **Bedřich Hrozný** showed that their main language was **Indo-European**, the oldest written member of the family. (One clue was a sentence that, read with Hittite words like *wadar*, "water", meant "you will eat bread and drink water".)

**The story in outline:**

| About | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **1650 BC** | **Hattusili I** makes Hattusa his capital and campaigns into Syria |
| **1595 BC** | **Mursili I** sacks Babylon; soon after, he is murdered and the kingdom falls into civil wars |
| **1350–1322 BC** | **Suppiluliuma I** builds an empire: destroys **Mitanni**, takes Syria as far as Kadesh and Carchemish |
| **1274 BC** | **Muwatalli II** fights Ramesses II at **Kadesh** |
| **about 1259 BC** | **Hattusili III** makes peace with Egypt |
| **about 1185–1180 BC** | Hattusa is abandoned, and the empire ends |

**How the Hittites ruled.** The king was a high priest and judge as well as war leader. He bound lesser kings to him by **treaties**, many of which survive: the vassal swore loyalty before the gods of both sides and promised troops, and the treaty opened with a history of past favours. Scholars have compared their form to covenants in the Hebrew Bible; the likeness is real and its meaning is debated.

**The "thousand gods of Hatti".** The Hittites collected gods. They worshipped the Storm God and the Sun Goddess of Arinna, and took in Hattian, Hurrian, Luwian and Babylonian gods as they absorbed lands. Their archives also hold **Hurrian myths** of gods overthrowing gods in succession that closely resemble Hesiod's Greek *Theogony*, written centuries later.

**An episode from the archive.** In the **1320s BC** (some date it a decade earlier), an Egyptian queen, recently widowed, wrote to Suppiluliuma asking for one of his sons to marry and become pharaoh. He sent a prince, **Zannanza**, who was killed on the journey. Which queen wrote is debated (Tutankhamun's widow Ankhesenamun is the usual candidate). The letter tells us how close Egypt's throne came to a Hittite king.

**A myth to set aside.** The Hittites are often said to have **held a secret of iron**. They did work some iron, and a Hittite king's letter mentions sending an iron blade to Assyria, but iron was rare and costly everywhere in this age, and no monopoly is attested. **Iron became common only after the Bronze Age collapse.**

**The end.** Hattusa shows no sign of a great sack: the palace was cleared before it burned, which suggests the court **left** around 1185–1180 BC. Famine, revolt and attacks from the Kaska people of the north are all candidates. **Hittite kingship lived on in small "Neo-Hittite" states** in Syria and south-east Turkey, such as **Carchemish**, into the 700s BC.
Mitanni, the Kassites and the rise of As:
Between Egypt and the Hittites lay three more powers. Two are half-forgotten; the third would one day swallow the Near East.

**Mitanni (about 1550–1300 BC).** A kingdom across northern Syria and northern Mesopotamia, in the upper Khabur and Euphrates valleys. Its people were mostly **Hurrians**, speakers of a language unrelated to Semitic or Indo-European. Its capital, **Washukanni**, has never been certainly located.

**A puzzle in Mitanni's names.** Its kings had names that are **Indo-Aryan**, the branch of Indo-European that includes Sanskrit: Tushratta, Shattiwaza. In a treaty with the Hittites of about **1350 BC**, Mitanni's king swore by the gods **Mitra, Varuna, Indra and the Nasatyas**, gods also found in the Rigveda of India. A Hittite horse-training manual, by a Mitannian called **Kikkuli**, uses Indo-Aryan words for numbers (*aika*, "one"). **So an Indo-Aryan-speaking elite was ruling Hurrians in Syria by about 1500 BC**, while related speakers were reaching India. Both groups probably came from Central Asia; this is one of the main pieces of evidence for the Indo-Aryan migrations taught later in this stage.

**Mitanni's arc:**

| About | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **1500–1450 BC** | Mitanni is Egypt's great rival in Syria; Thutmose III fights it |
| **1400–1350 BC** | peace and royal marriages: Mitannian princesses (Gilukhepa, Tadukhepa) go to Egypt |
| **about 1340s BC** | Suppiluliuma of Hatti sacks Washukanni; Mitanni is split |
| **1300–1260 BC** | its remnant, **Hanigalbat**, is conquered by Assyria |

**Its warriors** were the **maryannu**, a chariot-owning aristocracy, a word borrowed across the region.

**The Kassites in Babylon (about 1595–1155 BC).** After the Hittite raid, a people from the Zagros mountains, the **Kassites**, took Babylon. They ruled for over **four centuries**, the longest dynasty in Babylon's history. They were not destroyers: they adopted Babylonian language, gods and learning, and copied and preserved its literature. They are known for **boundary stones** (*kudurru*) recording royal land grants, and a new royal city, **Dur-Kurigalzu**. Their kings wrote as equals to the pharaohs. The dynasty ended about **1155 BC**, when the Elamite king **Shutruk-Nahhunte** raided Babylon and carried off monuments, **Hammurabi's stele among them**, to Susa.

**Assyria rises.** **Ashur**, on the upper Tigris, had been a merchant city and then a Mitannian dependant. About **1363–1328 BC**, **Ashur-uballit I** threw off Mitanni and wrote to the pharaoh calling himself a **great king**, to Babylon's fury. His successors took Hanigalbat, and **Tukulti-Ninurta I** (about 1243–1207 BC) **sacked Babylon** itself. This is the **Middle Assyrian kingdom**: a hard, militarised state with deportations of conquered peoples and a law collection unusually harsh on women.

**Why it matters.** Assyria **came through the Bronze Age collapse** and, after 900 BC, became the first empire to rule the whole Near East. That is Stage 4.
Egypt's New Kingdom builds an empire:
After throwing out the Hyksos, Egypt did something new: it went abroad, and for four centuries it was an imperial power in Africa and Asia.

**Dates.** The **New Kingdom** runs about **1550–1069 BC**, the 18th, 19th and 20th Dynasties. Its religious and royal centre was **Thebes** (modern Luxor), home of the god **Amun**.

**Building the empire:**

| King | About | What he did |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Ahmose I** | 1550–1525 BC | expelled the Hyksos; began the recovery of Nubia |
| **Thutmose I** | 1504–1492 BC | **destroyed Kerma**; marched to the **Euphrates**, where he set up a boundary stela |
| **Thutmose III** | 1479–1425 BC | about **17 campaigns** in the Levant; made Egypt the leading power of the east |
| **Amenhotep III** | 1390–1352 BC | ruled at the empire's peak in peace and wealth |

**The Battle of Megiddo**, about **1457 BC**, is the first battle in history recorded in real detail. Thutmose III faced a coalition of Canaanite rulers led by the king of **Kadesh**, gathered at Megiddo in northern Israel. Against his generals' advice he led his army through a **narrow pass** the enemy had left unguarded, and appeared in front of the city. The coalition broke and fled inside; a seven-month **siege** followed. The account is carved in his **Annals** on the walls of the temple at **Karnak**. It is a royal text written to glorify him, but its practical details (the council of war, the route, the plunder list) suggest it drew on a campaign diary.

**How the empire worked.** Egypt did not govern the Levant directly. Local **city-kings** stayed in place as vassals, swore oaths, sent tribute, and sent their **sons to be educated at the Egyptian court**, partly as hostages. Egyptian garrisons held key towns such as Gaza. **Nubia** was different: it was annexed outright, ruled by the viceroy, and mined for **gold**, which paid for much of what followed.

**What the wealth built:**
- **Karnak**, the temple of Amun at Thebes, enlarged by almost every king until it became one of the largest religious complexes ever built.
- **The Valley of the Kings**, west of Thebes: New Kingdom kings were buried in hidden rock-cut tombs, not pyramids, to defeat robbers. It did not work; almost all were robbed in antiquity.
- **Deir el-Medina**, the village of the tomb-builders, whose thousands of notes on pottery and stone flakes (*ostraca*) record ordinary lives: wages, quarrels, sick days, and, about 1157 BC, **the first recorded strike**, when rations were late.

**The priesthood of Amun.** Kings gave a large share of plunder and land to **Amun's temples**, and the high priests of Amun became great landowners. **The power of that priesthood** is part of the background to the strange reign of Akhenaten, two lessons on.
Hatshepsut, the woman who ruled as king:
Egypt had queens of great power, but very few women took the throne itself. Hatshepsut did, for about twenty years, and made a success of it.

**Who.** Hatshepsut was the daughter of **Thutmose I** and the wife of her half-brother **Thutmose II**. When he died young, about **1479 BC**, the heir was a small boy, **Thutmose III**, son of a lesser wife. Hatshepsut acted as his **regent**. Then, about **1473 BC**, she went further and was crowned **king**, with the full royal titles. The two reigned together, with her as senior, until her death about **1458 BC**.

**How she presented herself.** Egyptian kingship was a male office, and there was no word for a female king. Her early images show her as a woman; later ones show her with **the king's kilt, headcloth and false beard**, the regalia of the office. Texts refer to her with a mix of feminine and masculine grammar. She claimed that the god **Amun** himself was her father, shown in reliefs of her divine conception and birth.

**What she did:**

| Work | About |
| --- | --- |
| **Djeser-djeseru** ("holiest of holy places") at **Deir el-Bahari**, her mortuary temple: terraces cut into the cliffs west of Thebes, one of the finest buildings of Egypt | 1470s–1450s BC |
| **The expedition to Punt**, a land of incense somewhere on the southern Red Sea coast (probably Eritrea or Sudan), carved in reliefs at the temple: ships, myrrh trees, and the Puntite queen | about 1463 BC |
| **Obelisks at Karnak**, one still standing, about 29 metres tall | |
| Building and repair across Egypt, and some military campaigns, in Nubia at least | |

Her chief official, **Senenmut**, steward and architect, rose from modest birth to great power; the nature of their relationship has been the subject of more speculation than evidence.

**Her erasure.** Late in Thutmose III's reign, about **twenty years after her death**, her images and names were chiselled off many monuments and her statues smashed and thrown into a quarry. Why? **Historians disagree:**

| Reading | Strongest form |
| --- | --- |
| **Revenge** | the old view: Thutmose III hated the woman who kept him from his throne |
| **Politics of succession** | the delay argues against personal hatred. The aim was probably to **make the line of kings run directly from Thutmose I to Thutmose III**, securing the throne for his son Amenhotep II, and perhaps to stop a female king serving as a precedent |

The second reading is now the more widely held. Neither is proven, because no text explains the erasure.

**Her body.** In **2007** a mummy from a minor tomb was identified as Hatshepsut's, partly by matching a loose tooth in a box bearing her name. Many accept the identification; some specialists think it unproven.

**Why it matters.** She shows the kingship was an **office**, which in a crisis a woman could hold, and how much later rulers could edit the record.
Akhenaten, the Aten and the city of Amar:
For about seventeen years, a pharaoh tried to change Egypt's religion, its art and its capital. Then almost everything he did was undone and his name was cut from the lists of kings.

**Who and when.** **Amenhotep IV** came to the throne about **1352 BC**, son of Amenhotep III, at the height of Egypt's wealth. Within a few years he had changed his name to **Akhenaten**, "effective for the Aten", and ruled until about **1336 BC**. His chief wife was **Nefertiti**.

**What he did:**

| Change | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| **One god above all** | he raised the **Aten**, the disc of the sun, from one form of the sun god to the god the king worshipped above all others. Its symbol: a disc whose rays end in **little hands**, holding the sign of life to the king and queen |
| **The other gods suppressed** | temples of Amun were closed and his name was **hacked out** of monuments, even the plural word "gods" in places |
| **A new capital** | about **1346 BC** he founded **Akhetaten**, "horizon of the Aten", on empty desert ground halfway between Thebes and Memphis; we call the site **Amarna** |
| **New art** | the king shown with a long face, heavy hips and belly, playing with his daughters: a deliberate break with idealised royal images |
| **Open-air temples** | the Aten was worshipped in the sunlight, not in a dark inner shrine |

**The Great Hymn to the Aten**, found in a tomb at Amarna, praises the sun as creator of all lands and peoples, not of Egypt only. Its likeness to **Psalm 104** in the Bible has long been noticed; whether there is any link, and how, is debated.

**Was it monotheism? Historians disagree.**
- **Yes, or close to it**: the Aten was hailed as the only god, other gods were persecuted, and this was without precedent.
- **No, a royal cult**: ordinary people at Amarna kept household gods; the Aten was approached only **through the king and his family**, and the change may be read partly as **a king taking power and wealth back from the priesthood of Amun**.

These are not exclusive, and many scholars hold a version of both. What would decide it more is evidence of what ordinary Egyptians outside Amarna believed in those years, which is thin.

**After him.** Who reigned right after Akhenaten is unclear: one or two short-lived rulers, one of them possibly Nefertiti. Then came a boy, **Tutankhaten**, who changed his name to **Tutankhamun**, returned the court to Memphis and Thebes, and restored Amun. Amarna was abandoned within about twenty years of its founding. Later kings, especially **Horemheb**, dismantled Akhenaten's temples, and the king lists left his line out. In later legal documents he is not even named, but referred to as the criminal of Akhetaten.

**Why we know so much.** Because Amarna was abandoned and never rebuilt over, it is the best-preserved **city plan** from ancient Egypt. Its finds include the painted **bust of Nefertiti** (found 1912, now in Berlin) and an archive of diplomatic letters, the subject of the next lesson. And Tutankhamun, a minor king, is famous only because his tomb was found nearly intact, by **Howard Carter in 1922**.
The Amarna letters and the club of great:
In 1887, villagers digging at Amarna found clay tablets covered in cuneiform. They turned out to be the foreign mail of the pharaohs, and the best picture we have of how the Bronze Age world was run.

**What they are.** About **380 tablets**, written from about **1360 to 1330 BC**, under Amenhotep III, Akhenaten and perhaps just after. They are mostly letters to the pharaoh, with some copies of his replies. Almost all are in **Akkadian**, the Babylonian language, written in cuneiform, even when neither writer nor reader was Babylonian. **Akkadian was the diplomatic language of the age**, as French was in eighteenth-century Europe, and scribes in Egypt, Canaan and Anatolia were trained to write it.

**Two kinds of correspondent:**

| Group | Who | Tone |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The great kings** | Babylon (the Kassite kings Kadashman-Enlil and Burna-Buriash), **Mitanni** (Tushratta), **Hatti** (Suppiluliuma), **Assyria** (Ashur-uballit, newly admitted), and **Alashiya** (Cyprus) | equals: they call each other **"brother"** |
| **The vassals** | the city-kings of **Canaan** and the Levant: Byblos, Tyre, Jerusalem, Megiddo, Gezer and others | subjects: they address the pharaoh as their lord and their sun, and by the set formula of the letters fall at his feet seven times and seven times |

**How the club worked.** Historians call it the **"great powers club"** or the Bronze Age **international system**. Its members:
- **Exchanged gifts** constantly: gold from Egypt (Nubia's gold); horses, chariots and lapis lazuli from Babylon and Mitanni; copper from Cyprus.
- **Married each other's daughters.** Mitannian and Babylonian princesses went to Egypt with huge dowries. But Egypt **would not send its own princesses abroad**, and a Babylonian king complained of it, asking at least for some beautiful Egyptian woman he could pass off as one.
- **Haggled** with frankness. Tushratta of Mitanni wrote that gold in Egypt was as plentiful as dust, and complained that the statues he was promised arrived as gilded wood, not solid gold.
- **Sent envoys** who could be held for years as a bargaining counter.

The letters are **gift exchange in the language of family**, but beneath it lay hard trade and rivalry.

**The vassals' letters** tell another story. **Rib-Hadda of Byblos** wrote dozens of letters begging for troops against his neighbours, especially **Abdi-Ashirta** and his son **Aziru** of Amurru, who were switching sides to the Hittites. **Abdi-Heba of Jerusalem** complained that the land was being lost to the **'Apiru**, bands of uprooted people living outside the cities' control. Some once connected the 'Apiru with the Hebrews; the word may be related, but the 'Apiru were a social class found across the region, not one people.

**What the trade looked like.** A ship found wrecked off **Uluburun** on the south coast of Turkey, about **1300 BC**, and excavated from **1984**, carried about **10 tonnes of copper and 1 tonne of tin** in ingots: the exact mix for bronze. Also aboard: glass ingots, ebony, ivory, ostrich eggs, Baltic **amber**, Canaanite jars of resin, Mycenaean pottery, and a gold scarab of Nefertiti. **One ship carried goods from at least seven cultures.**

**Why it matters.** The letters show a **system**: several states of roughly equal power, bound by marriage, trade and treaty. That interdependence made the age rich. It may also, as the collapse lesson argues, have made it fragile.
Ramesses II, Kadesh and the treaty with:
The best-known pharaoh, the best-known chariot battle of the ancient world, and a peace treaty whose two versions both survive.

**Ramesses II** reigned about **1279–1213 BC**, some 66 years, in the 19th Dynasty. He outlived many of his children, and fathered over a hundred. His capital was **Pi-Ramesses** in the eastern Delta, near old Avaris, close to the Asian frontier. He built more than any other king: the rock temples of **Abu Simbel** in Nubia, the **Ramesseum** at Thebes, and additions to Karnak and Luxor.

**The Battle of Kadesh, 1274 BC.** Ramesses marched north to retake **Kadesh**, a city on the Orontes river in western Syria, from the Hittite king **Muwatalli II**. Both sides fielded large chariot forces; the Egyptian sources give the Hittites some **2,500 chariots**, a figure that is possible but cannot be checked.

| Phase | What happened, by the Egyptian account |
| --- | --- |
| **The trick** | two captured nomads told Ramesses the Hittite army was far away, in Aleppo. It was in fact **hidden behind Kadesh** |
| **The ambush** | Hittite chariots crossed the river and smashed one Egyptian division (the division of Re) on the march, then attacked Ramesses' camp |
| **The rally** | Ramesses, by his account almost alone, charged again and again; a relief force (the *ne'arin*) arrived in time |
| **The outcome** | the Hittites withdrew into the city; the Egyptians went home |

**Who won? The sources disagree, and here historians largely agree.** Ramesses had the battle carved as a great victory on temples across Egypt, in a long **poem** and a shorter **bulletin**, with reliefs. But **Kadesh stayed Hittite**, Egyptian power in Syria shrank afterwards, and Hittite texts say the Egyptians were beaten back as far as Damascus. **Tactically a draw that Ramesses survived; strategically a Hittite gain.** It is a classic case of a primary source written to persuade.

**The treaty, about 1259 BC.** Sixteen years later, with Assyria rising in the east, Ramesses and the new Hittite king **Hattusili III** made peace. **Both versions survive**: the Egyptian one in hieroglyphs on the walls of Karnak and the Ramesseum, and the Hittite one on a clay tablet in Akkadian from Hattusa. They promise:
- **No more war** between the two kingdoms, for all time.
- **Mutual defence** against attack from outside, and help against rebels.
- **Extradition** of fugitives, who were to be returned unharmed.

Each version presents its own king as the one asked for peace. **A copy of the tablet hangs at the United Nations in New York** as an early example of a peace treaty, though not the first: older treaties are known from Syria.

**The marriage.** About **1245 BC** a Hittite princess came to Egypt as Ramesses' wife, with a great dowry. The peace held for the rest of both empires' lives.

**A note on the Exodus.** Later tradition often places the biblical **Exodus** in Ramesses' reign, because Exodus names a store-city "Raamses". No Egyptian source mentions such an event, and **whether it happened, and when, is a question historians and archaeologists answer very differently.** Its religious meaning belongs to the Theology curriculum.
Minoan Crete and the eruption of Thera:
On Crete, the first civilisation of Europe built palaces without walls, wrote in a script no one can read, and was shaken by one of the largest volcanic eruptions in human history.

**The name.** We do not know what they called themselves. The British archaeologist **Arthur Evans**, who excavated **Knossos** from **1900**, named them **"Minoans"** after **Minos**, the legendary king of Crete in Greek myth. Egyptian tomb paintings call people from the Aegean **Keftiu**, probably the Cretans.

**The palaces.** From about **1950 BC**, great complexes rose at **Knossos, Phaistos, Malia** and later **Zakros**: hundreds of rooms around a central court, with storerooms of huge jars (*pithoi*) for oil and grain, light-wells, drains, staircases and painted walls. Destroyed by earthquakes about **1700 BC**, they were rebuilt larger, the **Neopalatial** peak, about 1700–1450 BC. Strikingly, **the palaces had no fortification walls**.

**What the Minoans left:**

| Thing | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| **Frescoes** | young men and women **leaping over bulls**, processions, dolphins, lilies |
| **Linear A** | a script used for accounts, **still undeciphered**; it does not seem to be Greek |
| **Trade** | Minoan pottery in Egypt, Cyprus and the Levant; Minoan-style frescoes at Avaris in Egypt and at Tel Kabri in Israel |
| **Religion** | peak sanctuaries, double axes, figurines of women holding snakes (some, from Evans's era, are modern fakes) |

**Was Crete a sea empire?** Thucydides, a thousand years later, said Minos had the first navy and ruled the Aegean. Minoan-style towns on other islands support a wide **influence**; whether that was rule, trade or shared culture is debated.

**Thera.** About 110 km north of Crete, the volcanic island of **Thera** (Santorini) blew apart in a huge eruption that buried the Minoan-style town of **Akrotiri** under metres of ash. Akrotiri, excavated from **1967**, is a "Bronze Age Pompeii" with houses two or three storeys high and superb frescoes, though **no bodies**: the people seem to have had warning and left.

**When was the eruption? This is a real dispute.**

| Reading | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| **About 1600 BC** (roughly 1620–1530 BC on recent calibrations) | **radiocarbon** dating, including an olive branch buried alive by the eruption |
| **About 1500 BC** | the **archaeological** sequence: Minoan pottery styles tied to Egyptian history |

Newer radiocarbon work has narrowed the gap but not closed it. What would settle it is a securely dated **tree-ring** or ice-core signal of the eruption.

**The fall.** About **1450 BC**, most palaces were burned. Knossos survived, but its records were now in **Linear B**, an early form of **Greek**. **Mainland Greeks, the Mycenaeans, had taken over Crete.** The Thera eruption probably came too early to be the direct cause, though it may have weakened the island; earthquake, internal conflict and conquest are all candidates.
Mycenaean Greece, Linear B and the quest:
The first Greek-speaking civilisation: warrior kings in stone citadels, bureaucrats counting sheep, and the world that Homer's epics remembered dimly five centuries later.

**When and where.** About **1600–1100 BC**, on the Greek mainland. Its centres were citadels with palaces at **Mycenae** and **Tiryns** in the Argolid, **Pylos** in the south-west, **Thebes** in Boeotia, and others. It is named after Mycenae, the city of **Agamemnon** in Greek legend.

**The Shaft Graves.** In **1876**, the German businessman and excavator **Heinrich Schliemann** dug inside the walls of Mycenae and found royal graves of about **1600 BC** full of gold: cups, swords, and **gold death masks**. He is said to have claimed he had looked on the face of Agamemnon, though the famous telegram may be a legend. **The masks are about 300 years too early for any Trojan War**, but they show a warrior elite suddenly rich.

**The palace age, about 1400–1200 BC:**
- **Cyclopean walls** of huge stones (later Greeks thought only giants could have moved them), and the **Lion Gate** of Mycenae, about 1250 BC.
- **Tholos tombs**, beehive-shaped stone chambers, such as the "Treasury of Atreus".
- A trading reach from Italy and Sardinia to Egypt and the Levant; Mycenaean pottery is found across the eastern Mediterranean.

**Linear B.** Tablets in a script related to Linear A turned up at Knossos and Pylos. In **1952** a young English architect, **Michael Ventris**, working with **John Chadwick**, deciphered it: **the language was Greek**, 500 years older than any Greek writing previously known. The tablets were never meant to last: they are clay **accounts**, baked by chance in the fires that destroyed the palaces. They record sheep, wool, bronze, chariot wheels, rations for women workers, and offerings to gods with familiar names: **Zeus, Hera, Poseidon**, and probably **Dionysus**. At the top stood a king, the ***wanax***.

**The Hittite connection.** Hittite texts of the 1300s–1200s BC mention a powerful kingdom called **Ahhiyawa** to their west, across the sea, whose king the Hittite king once addressed as a "brother". **Most scholars identify Ahhiyawa with Mycenaean Greeks** (Homer's *Achaeans*); a minority doubt it.

**Troy. Did the Trojan War happen?** The site of Troy is **Hisarlik** in north-west Turkey, near the Dardanelles. Its layers named **Troy VI** and **VIIa** were destroyed about **1300–1180 BC**. Hittite texts name a western kingdom **Wilusa**, very probably the Greek *(W)ilios*, Troy, and record trouble there involving Ahhiyawa.

| Reading | Strongest form |
| --- | --- |
| **A real war behind the legend** | a rich city at the mouth of a trade route; Greeks active in the region; a Hittite record of conflict over Wilusa; burnt destruction layers |
| **A legend, not a history** | Troy VI may have fallen to an earthquake; nothing found at Troy names Greek attackers; Homer composed about 750–700 BC and his world mixes many centuries |

Most historians accept **Bronze Age conflict around Troy as plausible** and the *Iliad*'s story as poetry. A text found at Troy naming its enemies would settle it; none has been found.

**The end.** Between about **1200 and 1180 BC**, the palaces were destroyed, Pylos by fire. **Writing vanished from Greece for about four centuries.**
Bronze Age Europe: tin, amber and the Ne:
North of the Alps there were no cities and no writing, but there were long trade routes, master metalworkers, and at least one great battle.

**Why Europe mattered to the whole age.** Bronze needs **tin**, and some of the best sources were in Europe: **Cornwall and Devon** in Britain, **Brittany**, **Iberia**, and the **Ore Mountains** (Erzgebirge) between Saxony and Bohemia. **Amber**, fossil resin from the **Baltic** shores, was prized from Mycenae to Egypt. A 2019 study of tin ingots found off the coast of Israel, from about 1300–1100 BC, traced some of their metal to **Cornwall**, though that result is still being tested.

**Peoples and places:**

| Culture | About | What it is known for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Únětice** (central Europe) | 2300–1600 BC | rich chieftains' graves like **Leubingen** (about 1940 BC), hoards of bronze; control of the Ore Mountain metal |
| **Wessex** (southern England) | 2000–1500 BC | gold-rich burials near Stonehenge, which was by now ancient |
| **Nordic Bronze Age** (Denmark, Sweden) | 1700–500 BC | imported bronze turned into superb objects; rock carvings of ships |
| **Urnfield** (much of Europe) | 1300–750 BC | **cremation**, the ashes buried in urns in large cemeteries |

**The Nebra sky disc.** A bronze disc about 32 cm across, inlaid with gold: a **sun or full moon, a crescent moon, and stars**, including a cluster that looks like the **Pleiades**. Looters found it in **1999** on a hill near Nebra in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany; police recovered it in a sting in **2002**. It is dated, from the swords found with it, to about **1600 BC**, which would make it **the oldest known concrete picture of the sky**. Arcs added later on its edges span about 82 degrees, roughly the angle between the midsummer and midwinter sunsets at that latitude, which suggests it was used to follow the year. In 2020 two scholars argued it was **Iron Age**, centuries younger; most of the specialists who have studied it keep the Bronze Age date.

**The sun chariot.** At **Trundholm** in Denmark, a farmer's plough turned up in 1902 a bronze **horse drawing a disc**, gilded on one side, from about **1400 BC**. It suggests a belief that the sun was carried across the sky, something like later Greek and Norse myths.

**A battle at Tollense.** In the **Tollense** valley in north-east Germany, since 1996 archaeologists have found the bones of **well over a hundred people**, mostly young men, with arrow and club wounds, together with weapons, all from about **1250 BC**. Estimates of how many fought range into the **thousands**, a disputed figure that rests on how much of the site is still unexcavated. It is **the oldest large-scale battlefield known in Europe**, and it shows that organised war on a large scale was not only a thing of the southern kingdoms.

**What Europe shows.** Societies without cities or writing could still be **linked into the Mediterranean world** by trade, and could be wealthy, skilled and violent. Our knowledge comes entirely from **archaeology and science**, and so it changes fast.
Ugarit and the invention of the alphabet:
Almost every alphabet now in use, Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Hebrew, Arabic, descends from one invented in this age by Semitic speakers between Egypt and Canaan. A port in Syria shows it in action.

**Why it was a revolution.** Cuneiform used **hundreds of signs**, and Egyptian hieroglyphs hundreds more; both took years of schooling, so writing belonged to a small class of scribes. **An alphabet needs only twenty or thirty signs, one for each sound**, and can be learned in weeks.

**The first alphabet.** The earliest examples are short inscriptions from two places in Egypt's orbit:

| Site | About | What |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Wadi el-Hol**, in the desert west of Thebes | 1900–1800 BC | two short inscriptions on a rock face along a desert road, found in the 1990s |
| **Serabit el-Khadim**, Sinai | 1850–1500 BC (the date is debated) | graffiti by Semitic-speaking workers at Egyptian **turquoise mines**, near a temple of the goddess Hathor |

This **Proto-Sinaitic** script borrowed the **pictures** of Egyptian hieroglyphs but used them in a new way, called **acrophony**: each picture stood for the **first sound** of its name in the workers' own language. A picture of an ox's head, ***ʾalp*** ("ox"), stood for the sound *ʾ*; a house, ***bayt***, for *b*; water, ***mayim***, for *m*. **That is why our A is an upside-down ox's head**, and *alpha–beta* gives us "alphabet". The script wrote only **consonants**; vowels came later, with the Greeks.

**Ugarit.** A wealthy port on the Syrian coast, at **Ras Shamra** near modern Latakia. A farmer's plough broke into a tomb nearby in **1928**, and French excavations under **Claude Schaeffer** began in **1929**. Ugarit was a **vassal**, first of Egypt, then of the Hittites, and a trading hub between Cyprus, Egypt, Anatolia and Mesopotamia. Its archives contain texts in **Akkadian, Ugaritic, Hurrian, Hittite, Egyptian** and other scripts: a whole international world in one city.

**The Ugaritic alphabet.** In the 1300s–1200s BC, Ugarit's scribes wrote their own Semitic language in **an alphabet of 30 letters made of cuneiform wedges** pressed into clay: alphabetic in principle, Mesopotamian in technique. Schoolboys' **abecedaries** (letter lists) show it had **the same letter order** as the later Phoenician and Hebrew alphabets, a, b, g…, so the order of our ABC is at least 3,300 years old. Ugaritic tablets hold the **Baal cycle**, myths of the storm god **Baal**, his battle with Yam (the sea) and Mot (death), which are essential background for the religion of Canaan and for reading the Hebrew Bible.

**Ugarit's end.** The city was **destroyed about 1185 BC** and never resettled. Among its last tablets is a letter from its king, **Ammurapi**, to the king of **Alashiya** (Cyprus), reporting that enemy ships had come and burned his cities while his troops were away in Hittite service. Tablets were long said to have been found **in a kiln, still being baked** when the city fell; later study suggests they were never in a kiln, so treat that detail as doubtful.

**What came next.** After the collapse, the cities of the Phoenician coast, **Byblos, Tyre and Sidon**, used a **22-letter linear alphabet**, fully formed by about **1050 BC**. Phoenician traders carried it across the Mediterranean, and the **Greeks** adapted it about **800 BC**, adding vowels. That is Stage 4.
The fading of the Indus cities, about 19:
The largest of the first civilisations did not fall in a day. Over a few centuries its great cities emptied, its script fell silent, and its people moved on.

**What there had been.** At its height, about **2600–1900 BC** (Stage 2), the Indus or **Harappan** civilisation covered more ground than Egypt and Mesopotamia together, across modern Pakistan and north-west India. Its cities, **Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Ganweriwala, Rakhigarhi, Dholavira**, had planned streets, brick drains, standard weights and an undeciphered script on stamp seals.

**What changed, about 1900–1700 BC:**

| Sign | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| **The cities shrink** | Mohenjo-daro and Harappa decline and are largely abandoned; buildings are cut up and poorly rebuilt |
| **The shared system ends** | standard weights, the seals and the **script** go out of use; regional pottery styles replace the common one |
| **People move** | settlements multiply in the **east**, in Haryana and the upper Ganges–Yamuna plain, and in **Gujarat** to the south, while the core empties |
| **Trade stops** | Mesopotamian texts stop mentioning **Meluhha**, their name for the Indus, after about 1800 BC |

This later stage, the **Late Harappan**, lasted in places to about **1300 BC**. It was not an end of people or of farming, but an end of **cities**: archaeologists call it **de-urbanisation**.

**Why? The candidates:**

| Cause | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| **A weaker monsoon** | lake and cave records show drier conditions around **2200 BC** (the "4.2-kiloyear event") and after; less rain meant smaller floods for farming |
| **Rivers on the move** | the **Ghaggar-Hakra** river system, on which many sites stood, dwindled; some studies argue it had lost its Himalayan glacier source long before, others that it dried in this period |
| **Lost trade** | the Gulf trade with Mesopotamia faltered as Mesopotamia changed |
| **Disease, flooding, internal breakdown** | proposed; harder to test |

Most specialists now see **several of these together**, with **climate** a leading factor. The causes are still argued over.

**A theory that is dead.** In the 1940s the British archaeologist **Mortimer Wheeler** argued that invading Aryans, led by the war god Indra of the Rigveda, had **sacked Mohenjo-daro**, pointing to skeletons found lying in the streets. Later work, notably by **George Dales** in 1964, showed that those skeletons came **from different periods** and showed no signs of a single massacre. **There is no archaeological evidence of an invasion destroying the Indus cities.** The decline began before any likely arrival of Indo-Aryan speakers.

**What lasted.** Much of the Indus way of life continued in villages: crops, crafts, bangles, perhaps some religious symbols. How much of later Indian culture comes from the Harappans is debated, and cannot be settled while their **script remains unread**.
The Vedic peoples and the Rigveda:
India's oldest text, composed in this age, is a book of hymns to gods of fire, storm and sky, in an Indo-European language. How its language got to India is among the most argued questions in history.

**The Rigveda.** **1,028 hymns** in ten books, in **Vedic Sanskrit**. The oldest books, II to VII, are the "family books" of priestly clans; the tenth is the latest. Most scholars date its composition to roughly **1500–1200 BC**, with a wide margin either way. It was not written down for well over a thousand years, perhaps much longer: **it was preserved by memory**, priests learning it syllable by syllable with checking methods so exact that the text has come down with remarkable fidelity.

**Its world.** The hymns name the rivers of the **Punjab**, the "land of seven rivers", and the **Sarasvati**, the river most praised of all. The people were **herders** more than farmers: wealth was **cattle**; prestige was **horses and chariots**. They lived in tribes (*jana*) under chiefs (*rajan*), and fought each other as much as outsiders: one hymn celebrates the **Battle of the Ten Kings**, won by the Bharata tribe on the Ravi river. Their gods included **Indra** (storm and war), **Agni** (fire), **Varuna** (cosmic order), and the drink **soma** used in ritual. Hymns speak of enemies called **Dasas** or Dasyus. The famous hymn of the four classes, the origin of *varna*, is in the **late tenth book**.

**Later Vedic period, about 1100–500 BC.** Vedic culture moved **east into the Ganges plain**, with farming, iron and growing kingdoms. That is Stage 4.

**How did the language come to India? This is contested, and it matters in Indian politics today.**

| Reading | Strongest form |
| --- | --- |
| **Indo-Aryan migration** (the view of most linguists and geneticists) | Sanskrit is a close sister of the language of the Iranian **Avesta** and belongs to a family spread from the steppe. **Indo-Aryan gods and words appear in Mitanni, in Syria, about 1400 BC.** Horse and chariot vocabulary is inherited, and horses are rare in Harappan sites. Ancient DNA studies (2019) show **steppe-related ancestry arriving in South Asia about 2000–1500 BC**, mostly through men, and absent from a Harappan genome from **Rakhigarhi** |
| **Indigenous origin** ("Out of India" or continuity) | there is **no archaeological sign of an intrusive culture**; farming and crafts show **continuity** from Harappan times; the Rigveda **remembers no migration** and treats the Punjab as home; if the Sarasvati is the Ghaggar-Hakra, which dwindled early, some hymns may be older than the mainstream date. Some go further and identify the Harappans themselves as Vedic |

**Note what is common ground.** The old picture of a violent **"Aryan invasion"** that destroyed the Indus cities is **rejected on both sides**. The mainstream view is of **migrations over centuries**, mixing with the existing population, in which a language spread more than a people replaced another. "Aryan" (*arya*) in the Rigveda is a cultural self-name, not a race.

**What would settle it.** A **decipherment of the Indus script** (if its language is Indo-Aryan, the migration view fails; if Dravidian or another family, it is strengthened); **ancient DNA** from northern India between 2000 and 1000 BC; and secure dates for horse remains and chariots. Finds such as the burials with wheeled vehicles at **Sinauli** (about 2000–1800 BC) have been offered as early chariots; others say they are carts with solid wheels.
The Shang dynasty and the bronze of Anya:
China's first dynasty that can be confirmed by its own writing ruled the middle Yellow River for about five centuries, and cast bronze on a scale no other people matched.

**Before the Shang.** Chinese tradition names a first dynasty, the **Xia**. The **Erlitou** culture, about **1900–1500 BC**, in Henan, with China's first palace complex and first bronze vessels, may be the Xia; but no writing from Erlitou survives, so **whether the Xia existed as tradition describes is debated**.

**The Shang.** Traditionally about **1600–1046 BC** (the dates are approximate before 841 BC). Two capitals are best known:

| Site | About | What |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Zhengzhou** (Erligang phase) | 1600–1400 BC | a city with **rammed-earth walls** about 7 km round, up to 20 metres thick at the base |
| **Anyang** (Yinxu, "the ruins of Yin") | 1250–1046 BC | the last capital, from the reign of **Wu Ding**: palaces, workshops, and a royal cemetery |

**The king.** The Shang king was war leader and **chief priest**. He ruled a core domain directly and a ring of allies and enemies beyond. His power rested on the **ancestors**: dead kings were believed to intercede with the high god **Di**, and the living king alone could reach them, through **sacrifice** and **divination** (the next lesson).

**Bronze.** Shang bronzes are **ritual vessels** for offering food and wine to the ancestors (*ding* cauldrons, *gu* goblets, *jue* pouring cups), decorated with stylised beasts such as the ***taotie*** mask. They were made by **piece-mould casting**, pouring metal into clay moulds made in sections, not by the lost-wax method used in the west. **The Houmuwu ding, found at Anyang, weighs over 800 kg**, the heaviest ancient Chinese bronze vessel known. Casting on this scale needed mines, thousands of workers and tight organisation.

**Lady Fu Hao.** In **1976** archaeologists found an unrobbed tomb at Anyang belonging to **Fu Hao**, one of Wu Ding's consorts. It held **hundreds of bronzes and hundreds of jades**, weapons, and the remains of sacrificed people and dogs. Oracle bones show that Fu Hao **led armies** in war and conducted rituals. She is one of the first women in Chinese history known by name and deeds.

**Sacrifice and chariots.** Shang royal burials included **human sacrifices**, sometimes in hundreds, mostly prisoners of war; foundations of buildings were laid with victims. **Chariots** appear at Anyang about **1200 BC**, buried with horses and drivers, fully developed: they came from the west, via the steppe.

**Not the only bronze culture in China.** At **Sanxingdui** in Sichuan, about **1200–1000 BC**, a quite different people made giant **bronze masks** with protruding eyes and a standing bronze figure over 2.5 metres tall; new pits found from 2019 added more. **Ancient China had several centres**, and the Shang was the one that wrote.

**The end.** About **1046 BC**, **King Wu** of the **Zhou**, a western people, defeated the last Shang king at **Muye**. The Zhou would justify the conquest with a new idea, the **Mandate of Heaven**: Heaven gives the right to rule to the virtuous and takes it from the wicked. That is the next stage.
Oracle bones: China's first writing:
The earliest Chinese writing is not poetry or law but questions put to the dead, scratched on bones and turtle shells and answered by cracks.

**The discovery.** In **1899**, a scholar in Beijing, **Wang Yirong**, is said to have noticed ancient characters on "dragon bones" sold as medicine. Whatever the exact story, collectors traced the bones to farmland near **Anyang**, and excavations there from **1928** to **1937** (and again after 1950) uncovered the last Shang capital. Today about **150,000 inscribed pieces** are known.

**How divination worked:**

| Step | What was done |
| --- | --- |
| **1. Prepare** | an **ox shoulder blade** (scapula) or a **turtle's under-shell** (plastron) was cleaned and smoothed, and rows of hollows were drilled or chiselled into the back |
| **2. Ask** | a diviner, often in the king's presence, put the question as a statement, for example that the king would receive a good millet harvest |
| **3. Heat** | a hot point was pressed into a hollow until the bone **cracked** with a sound, in a ⺊ shape on the front |
| **4. Read** | the **king** read the cracks as auspicious or not |
| **5. Record** | the question, often the king's forecast, and sometimes **the outcome**, were carved beside the cracks |

The character for "divination" today, 卜 (*bu*), still looks like the crack.

**What they asked.** Rain and harvest; war and hunting; whether to make a sacrifice, and to which ancestor; illness, dreams, and **childbirth**. One famous set asks whether Lady **Fu Hao**'s childbirth would be good; the record notes that the king forecast it, and that the child turned out to be a girl, which was judged not good. Such questions show the worries of a court that believed **the dead governed the fortunes of the living**.

**Why they matter so much:**

1. **They confirm a historian.** **Sima Qian**, writing about **100 BC**, gave a list of Shang kings. In **1917**, the scholar **Wang Guowei** showed that the oracle bones name almost the same kings in almost the same order. **A dynasty some had doubted was proved real**, and a later historian's sources proved good.
2. **They are the ancestor of Chinese writing today.** About **4,000** different characters have been found; a large minority can be read with confidence. Many are recognisably the same characters still used. **Chinese is the oldest writing system in continuous use**, over 3,000 years.
3. **They record time.** They date events by a **60-day cycle**, and some note eclipses, which helps date the late Shang.

**What they do not show.** They are a **royal archive**, mostly from about **1250–1046 BC**. Almost nothing of ordinary people's lives is in them, and writing was surely used on bamboo and wood too, which has rotted. So the Shang were probably writing more than survives, and perhaps earlier.
The Olmec, and the Americas around 1200:
Cut off from Eurasia, the Americas made their own Bronze Age equivalents without bronze: Mexico's first great art style, mound cities built by hunter-gatherers, and temples in the Andes.

**The Olmec.** On the hot, wet **Gulf Coast of Mexico**, in southern **Veracruz** and **Tabasco**, a people built the first large ceremonial centres of Mesoamerica. "Olmec" is not their own name but an **Aztec word** for the people of this region, "rubber people", because it was where rubber came from. We do not know what they called themselves.

| Centre | About | What |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **San Lorenzo** | 1400–900 BC (peak about 1200–900 BC) | a plateau partly built up by hand, with drains, houses and monuments |
| **La Venta** | 900–400 BC | a planned centre with a clay pyramid about 30 metres high and buried offerings of jade and serpentine |
| **Tres Zapotes** | later, to about the turn of the era | the Olmec tradition's last major site |

**The colossal heads.** Seventeen giant heads of **basalt** have been found, up to about **3 metres** tall and weighing many tonnes. The stone came from the **Tuxtla Mountains**, some 60 km or more from San Lorenzo, and was moved, probably by rafts and rollers, without draught animals or wheels. Each face is different and wears a helmet-like headdress: they are **probably portraits of rulers**. Some were carved from older thrones.

**What the Olmec made or shared:**
- **Rubber balls**, among the oldest from **El Manatí**, a sacred spring, from about **1600 BC**, and a **ballgame** that lasted to the Aztecs.
- **Jade** carving, and a style with the **"were-jaguar"**, a figure half-baby, half-jaguar.
- Maize farming, and possibly early **calendar** and **writing** ideas; a stone from **Cascajal** with rows of signs, about **900 BC**, has been claimed as the earliest writing in the Americas, but its dating is disputed.

**"Mother culture" or "sister cultures"? Debated.**

| Reading | Strongest form |
| --- | --- |
| **Mother culture** | Olmec motifs appear across Mesoamerica, from central Mexico to El Salvador, earliest and best at San Lorenzo; studies of the clay in pottery (2005) suggested San Lorenzo exported and others imported |
| **Sister cultures** | several regions, such as Oaxaca and central Mexico, were developing at the same time and **shared** a set of symbols by exchange; the clay studies have been challenged |

Better provenance studies of pottery and jade, and firmer dating at the other centres, would settle it.

**North America: Poverty Point.** In north-east **Louisiana**, about **1700–1100 BC**, people built six concentric earth **ridges** in a C-shape over a kilometre across, and great mounds, one of the largest earthworks of its time anywhere. They were **hunter-fisher-gatherers**, not farmers, and they traded for **copper from the Great Lakes** and stone from hundreds of kilometres away. It is a World Heritage Site. **It shows that monumental building did not need farming.**

**The Andes.** In Peru's **Initial Period**, about **1800–900 BC**, coastal valleys built big **U-shaped temple complexes** around plazas, and fine textiles and pottery spread. At **Cerro Sechín**, carved stones show warriors and the dismembered dead. In the highlands, **Chavín de Huántar**, begun about 1200–900 BC (the date is debated), would become the first great shared religious centre of the Andes, in Stage 4.

**Why it matters.** The Americas reached ceremonial centres, art styles, long-distance trade and kingship **independently**. That makes them the best test of which features of civilisation are general to humans and which are local accidents.
The Lapita voyagers of the Pacific:
In a few centuries after about 1300 BC, a people with decorated pottery and outrigger canoes sailed out into the empty Pacific, the first humans ever to reach most of its islands.

**Where they came from.** The Lapita were speakers of **Austronesian** languages. Linguists trace that family to **Taiwan**, from where farmers spread south into the **Philippines** about 2200–2000 BC and on through Indonesia. This is the **"Out of Taiwan"** model, supported by the language evidence and much ancient DNA. Along the way they mixed, more or less, with people already there.

**Where they appear.** About **1350–1300 BC**, a new culture appears in the **Bismarck Archipelago**, north-east of New Guinea, where people had lived for 40,000 years. It is named **Lapita**, after a site in **New Caledonia** where its pottery was excavated in **1952**. Its mark is pottery with **fine stamped patterns**, pressed in with toothed tools (*dentate stamping*), including faces.

**Into Remote Oceania.** Until then no human had gone past the **Solomon Islands**. The Lapita went on:

| Islands | First settled, about |
| --- | --- |
| **Bismarck Archipelago** | 1350–1300 BC (people already present; Lapita culture arrives) |
| **Vanuatu**, **New Caledonia** | 1100–1000 BC |
| **Fiji** | 1000–900 BC |
| **Tonga** | 900–850 BC |
| **Samoa** | about 800 BC |

The gap from Vanuatu to Fiji is about **850 km of open sea**. They crossed it in **outrigger or double-hulled canoes**, sailing **against the prevailing winds**, which meant that if they found nothing, they could run home downwind. They carried a full kit for a new life: **pigs, dogs and chickens**, and **taro, yams, bananas and breadfruit**. **Within perhaps three or four centuries they spread across some 4,500 km.**

**Who they were: what the DNA says.** In **2016**, ancient DNA from the **Teouma** cemetery in Vanuatu (about 1000 BC) and from Tonga showed that the first settlers had **almost entirely East Asian ancestry**, with very little of the Papuan ancestry common in the region today. Papuan ancestry arrived **later**, in following centuries.

**How fast, and how mixed? Debated.**

| Reading | Strongest form |
| --- | --- |
| **"Express train"** | a quick movement of Austronesian farmers out of Taiwan to the Pacific, with little mixing on the way; the early DNA fits |
| **Slower, mixed origin** | Lapita grew up in the **Bismarcks** from a blend of newcomers and local people, through long trade and exchange; local obsidian trade and local styles fit |

Many archaeologists combine them: newcomers who **integrated** with local communities in the Bismarcks before setting out. More dated sites in Island South-East Asia, and more ancient DNA, would settle the balance.

**The long pause.** After Samoa and Tonga, the voyaging **stopped for well over a thousand years**. Here, in the islands of **West Polynesia**, Polynesian culture and languages took shape. The great voyages east to Tahiti, Hawai'i, Rapa Nui and New Zealand came only about **AD 1000–1250** (Stage 7).
The Late Bronze Age collapse and the Sea:
Within about fifty years after 1200 BC, the connected world of the great kings fell apart. Palaces burned from Greece to Syria, empires vanished, and writing stopped in whole regions. Why is one of the great open questions of ancient history.

**What happened, about 1200–1150 BC:**

| Place | What, about |
| --- | --- |
| **Mycenaean Greece** | palaces at Pylos, Mycenae, Tiryns, Thebes destroyed, **1200–1180 BC**; Linear B ends |
| **The Hittite empire** | Hattusa abandoned, about **1185–1180 BC**; the empire ends |
| **Ugarit** | destroyed about **1185 BC**, never reoccupied |
| **Cyprus, Canaan, inland Syria** | many cities destroyed, among them **Emar** (about 1185 BC) and **Hazor** (the date is debated) |
| **Egypt** | survives, but fights off invaders twice and then declines |
| **Assyria, Babylon, Elam** | survive, weakened; Babylon's Kassite dynasty ends about 1155 BC |

**The Sea Peoples.** Egyptian texts name raiders who came by land and sea.
- About **1208 BC**, **Merneptah**, son of Ramesses II, defeated a **Libyan** army allied with northern peoples, among them the **Shekelesh, Lukka, Sherden** and others. His victory stela also contains **the first mention of "Israel"** outside the Bible, as a people in Canaan.
- About **1177 BC**, **Ramesses III** fought a great coalition by land and at sea, at the edge of the Delta. His temple at **Medinet Habu** shows the sea battle and lists the **Peleset, Tjeker, Shekelesh, Denyen** and **Weshesh**. Its text says no land could stand before them, naming Hatti, Carchemish, Cyprus and others as laid waste.

"Sea Peoples" is a **modern label**, popularised by the French Egyptologist **Gaston Maspero** in the late 1800s. Where they came from is uncertain; the Aegean, western Anatolia, Cyprus and Sicily and Sardinia (the Shekelesh and Sherden) have been proposed. The **Peleset** settled on the southern coast of Canaan and are the **Philistines**. Ancient DNA from **Ashkelon**, a Philistine city (2019), showed **European-related ancestry** arriving about this time, which was diluted within two centuries.

**Why did it happen? The main readings:**

| Cause | Strongest form | Weakness |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Invaders** (the Sea Peoples) | Egyptian texts say so plainly; destruction layers fit | the Sea Peoples may be **a symptom**, people already displaced by trouble at home |
| **Drought and famine** | pollen in cores from the Sea of Galilee, Cyprus and Syria show a **dry spell** about 1250–1100 BC; Hittite letters ask Egypt for **grain** shipments | droughts had happened before without collapse |
| **Earthquakes** | a run of quakes over decades (the "earthquake storm" idea) fits some ruins | many destroyed sites show no quake damage, and quakes alone do not explain why cities were never rebuilt |
| **Internal revolt** | heavy palace demands on farmers; some sites look burned from within | hard to show directly |
| **New warfare** (Robert Drews) | infantry with javelins and long swords learned to **beat chariot armies** | the evidence for the tactic is thin |
| **Systems collapse** (Eric Cline and others) | the system was so **interdependent** (tin from one end, grain from another) that several shocks at once broke it all: a "perfect storm" | hard to test, because it can absorb any evidence |

Most historians now lean to some form of **several causes together**, with drought often near the centre. Precise dating of each **destruction layer**, tightly dated **climate records**, and more ancient DNA would decide between them.

**After the collapse.** For two or three centuries the eastern Mediterranean was poorer and mostly illiterate: in Greece, a "**Dark Age**" of about 1100–800 BC. Egypt lost its empire and, after about **1069 BC**, split again. But the collapse also **cleared the ground** for iron, the alphabet and new, smaller peoples.
Connections: the world around 1000 BC:
The stage closes as it opened, with the whole world in view: who had traded with, fought or converted whom, and what survived the collapse into the next age.

**What had joined the Bronze Age world together:**

| Link | What moved, and between whom |
| --- | --- |
| **Metal routes** | **tin** from Central Asia and Europe, **copper** from Cyprus, to every bronze-using kingdom |
| **The great kings' club** | gifts, princesses, envoys and letters in **Akkadian** between Egypt, Babylon, Mitanni, Hatti, Assyria and Cyprus |
| **Luxury trade** | Nubian **gold** to Egypt and on to Asia; Baltic **amber** to Mycenae; lapis lazuli from Afghanistan; Aegean pottery to Egypt, the Levant and Italy |
| **The steppe** | the **horse and chariot**, carried from the Urals to Egypt, Greece, India and China |
| **War and empire** | Egypt ruled Nubia and the Levant; Hatti fought Egypt and destroyed Mitanni; Assyria took Mitanni's place |

**Where everyone stands about 1000 BC:**

| Region | About 1000 BC |
| --- | --- |
| **The Levant** | small new kingdoms: **Phoenician** cities, **Aramean** states, **Philistines**, and **Israel and Judah**, whose early size is debated between those who read the biblical account of David and Solomon closely and those who see small chiefdoms |
| **Anatolia and Syria** | Neo-Hittite states such as **Carchemish**; the Phrygians in the west |
| **Mesopotamia** | **Assyria**, battered but intact, preparing its great expansion |
| **Egypt** | divided, its Third Intermediate Period; **Kush** independent again, soon to rise at **Napata** |
| **Greece** | the Dark Age; small villages; memory of heroes that Homer will shape |
| **South Asia** | Vedic culture moving into the **Ganges plain**; iron coming into use |
| **China** | the **Western Zhou** (from about 1046 BC), ruling by the **Mandate of Heaven** |
| **The steppe** | horsemen beginning to **fight from horseback**, which will replace the chariot |
| **The Americas** | **La Venta** rising among the Olmec; Chavín in the Andes |
| **Oceania** | Lapita settlers reaching **Fiji, Tonga** and soon **Samoa** |
| **Sub-Saharan Africa** | Bantu-speaking farmers spreading out of West-Central Africa towards the Great Lakes; in the far south, hunter-gatherers, ancestors of the San. South Africa's story is kept brief in this survey and told in depth in the South African Politics curriculum |

**Nothing was converted in the modern sense**: religions of this age travelled with people and kings, not with missionaries. But gods did travel. **Egyptian gods went south to Nubia** with Amun's temples; **Mesopotamian gods and myths reached the Hittites**; the **Vedic gods** went with Indo-Aryan speakers to Syria and India.

**What carried into the next stage:**
1. **Iron**, cheap and common enough for ordinary farmers and soldiers.
2. **The alphabet**, soon to reach Greece and Aramaic-speaking scribes across the Near East.
3. **Law and kingship ideas**: Hammurabi's model of the just king, copied for centuries.
4. **Assyria's ambition**, which would build the first empire of the whole Near East.
5. **The Mandate of Heaven** in China, and the **Vedas** in India, both foundations of the axial age.

**Look back at the whole stage:** for nearly a thousand years, powers around the eastern Mediterranean were bound by trade and diplomacy into **the first international system**, and when it broke about 1200 BC, it broke together. Elsewhere, in China, the Americas and the Pacific, peoples built their own worlds on their own lines. Stage 4 begins as the new iron-using kingdoms rise from the wreck.
Map: the world in 800 BC:
Stage 3 ended with the Bronze Age collapse around 1200–1150 BC. By 800 BC the world has rebuilt, and new kinds of power are rising. This is where everyone stands at the start of the age.

**The Near East is recovering, and one power is pulling ahead.** **Assyria**, on the upper Tigris in what is now northern Iraq, has been campaigning every year since the 900s BC and is becoming the first empire to rule the whole Fertile Crescent. Babylon, older and more prestigious, is often under Assyrian control. In the hills of western Iran the **Medes** and **Persians** are still small peoples.

| Region | About 800 BC |
| --- | --- |
| **The Levant** | small kingdoms: **Israel** (capital Samaria) and **Judah** (Jerusalem), Aram-Damascus, the Philistine cities; on the coast the **Phoenician** cities, Tyre the richest |
| **Egypt** | divided among rival dynasties in the Delta; to the south, **Kush** (in today's Sudan) is about to conquer it |
| **The Aegean** | Greece coming out of its "Dark Age": the alphabet is being adopted, and the **polis** (city-state) is forming |
| **Italy** | Villanovan villages in Etruria growing into **Etruscan** cities; huts on the hills of the future Rome |
| **Europe north of the Alps** | the **Hallstatt** culture, using the new metal, **iron** |
| **The steppe** | mounted nomads, among them the ancestors of the **Scythians**, with the first great royal mounds in Siberia |
| **South Asia** | late Vedic chiefdoms on the Ganges plain; no cities yet since the Indus |
| **China** | the **Zhou** kings in the Wei valley; in 771 BC their capital will fall and power will shift east |
| **The Americas** | the **Olmec** at La Venta on Mexico's Gulf coast; the first Maya ceremonial centres; **Chavín de Huántar** rising in the Peruvian Andes |
| **Oceania** | Lapita seafarers have just reached **Fiji, Tonga and Samoa** (about 900–800 BC), the edge of the inhabited Pacific for centuries to come |

**Three changes run through the whole stage:**

1. **Iron.** Iron ore is common where tin and copper are not, so once smelting was mastered iron tools and weapons spread to many more hands. It came into wide use in the Near East after 1200 BC and reached Europe, India, China and parts of Africa during this stage.
2. **Alphabets.** The Phoenician alphabet, about 22 letters, was far easier to learn than cuneiform or hieroglyphs. Greeks, Aramaeans, Israelites and others adapted it, and **Aramaic** became the common language of the Near East.
3. **Bigger states.** From city-states and chiefdoms to empires that ruled millions: Assyria, Babylon, Persia, and by 300 BC Alexander's successors and the Mauryas in India.

**Where the stage ends.** By 300 BC Alexander has come and gone, Rome rules most of central Italy, China is locked in the Warring States, and India is about to be unified. The ideas taught in Athens, in the Ganges valley and in the states of Zhou China in these five centuries are still argued over today, which is why the age has a name of its own.
The axial age: Jaspers's idea and its cr:
Why this stage is called what it is, and why the name is argued over.

**The idea.** In 1949 the German philosopher **Karl Jaspers**, in *The Origin and Goal of History*, pointed to a striking cluster. Between about **800 and 200 BC**, in several regions with little contact, thinkers appeared whose ideas still shape the world:

| Region | Figures (traditional dates) |
| --- | --- |
| **China** | Confucius (551–479 BC), Laozi, Mozi, Mencius, Zhuangzi |
| **India** | the Upanishads; the Buddha and Mahavira (5th century BC) |
| **Iran** | Zarathustra (date much disputed) |
| **Israel and Judah** | the prophets: Amos, Hosea, Isaiah, Jeremiah, the prophets of the exile |
| **Greece** | the philosophers from Thales (about 600 BC) to Socrates, Plato and Aristotle; the historians and tragedians |

Jaspers called it the **"axial age"** (*Achsenzeit*): an axis on which history turned. His claim was that in all these places people began to **reflect on themselves**, to imagine a transcendent order beyond the visible world, to judge kings by moral standards, and to seek salvation or wisdom as individuals.

**The strongest case for it.** The cluster is real: many of the world's lasting traditions of thought do date to these centuries. Sociologists such as **S. N. Eisenstadt** and **Robert Bellah** built on Jaspers, linking the change to bigger states, coinage, cities and literacy, which gave thinkers both leisure and a crisis to think about. A 2015 study by Nicolas Baumard and colleagues argued that the shift tracks **rising affluence**: once enough people lived above subsistence, ascetic and moral teachings appealed.

**The strongest case against it:**

- **The dates are stretched.** Zarathustra may be centuries earlier; much of the Hebrew Bible was edited later; 800–200 BC is wide enough to catch almost anything.
- **It assumes what it should prove.** Earlier societies, like Egypt and Mesopotamia, also had moral gods, laments over injustice, and wisdom literature. Calling them "pre-axial" can make them look more primitive than the evidence shows.
- **The data do not cluster.** A 2018 study using the **Seshat** global history databank found that moralising religion and checks on rulers appeared at different times in different places, tied more to the growth of states than to one age.
- **It is Eurasian.** The Americas and Africa, with their own religious and political change in these centuries, fall outside the scheme.

**What would settle it.** Better dating of the founding texts, and systematic comparisons, like Seshat's, of when such ideas appear everywhere, including societies outside Jaspers's list. This curriculum uses the name as a **convenient label for the centuries**, not as a verdict on the theory.
The Neo-Assyrian empire: Nineveh and the:
The first empire to rule the whole Near East, and the one whose methods every later empire there inherited.

**Where and when.** Assyria's heartland was a triangle of cities on the upper **Tigris**: **Assur**, **Nineveh** and **Kalhu** (Nimrud), near today's Mosul in northern Iraq. The **Neo-Assyrian empire** runs from about **911 to 609 BC**.

**The kings to know:**

| King | Reign | What he did |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Ashurnasirpal II** | 883–859 | yearly campaigns; rebuilt Kalhu as capital, with carved palace reliefs |
| **Shalmaneser III** | 858–824 | fought a coalition including King Ahab of Israel at **Qarqar** (853) |
| **Tiglath-pileser III** | 745–727 | turned raiding into ruling: a standing army, provinces under governors |
| **Sargon II** | 722–705 | took Samaria; built a new capital, Dur-Sharrukin |
| **Sennacherib** | 705–681 | made **Nineveh** the capital; besieged Lachish in Judah (701); destroyed Babylon (689) |
| **Esarhaddon** | 681–669 | conquered **Egypt** (671) |
| **Ashurbanipal** | 668–about 631 | sacked Egyptian Thebes (663); gathered a great library at Nineveh |

**How it worked.** **Tiglath-pileser III's reforms** are the turning point. Conquered lands became **provinces** with Assyrian governors paying regular tribute, a professional army replaced seasonal levies, and a network of roads and relay posts carried royal messages.

**Mass deportation** was the signature policy. Whole populations were moved across the empire to break local loyalties and settle land where labour was needed. **Israel's northern tribes** were deported after Samaria fell in 722–720 BC. How many people were moved over three centuries is debated: one well-known count from the royal inscriptions runs to over four million, but those inscriptions boast, and many scholars think the true figure was lower.

**Terror as propaganda.** Palace reliefs show impalement, flaying and heaps of heads, and royal annals list cities burned. **This was deliberate**: the reliefs were meant to be seen by visiting envoys. Historians debate how far the brutality was routine and how far it was advertised to make surrender cheaper than resistance.

**Ashurbanipal's library.** Excavated at Nineveh from the 1840s and 1850s, its tens of thousands of clay tablets and fragments, now mostly in the **British Museum**, preserved the *Epic of Gilgamesh* and much of what we know of Mesopotamian learning.

**The fall was startlingly fast.** After Ashurbanipal, civil war broke out. **Babylon** under Nabopolassar and the **Medes** under Cyaxares attacked together: **Assur fell in 614**, **Nineveh in 612 BC**, and the last Assyrian king made a final stand at Harran until 609. Within a generation, Assyria as a state was gone, though Assyrian people and their Aramaic language lived on.
The Phoenicians: Tyre, purple and the al:
A string of small cities on a narrow coast that carried trade and the alphabet across the Mediterranean.

**Where.** **Phoenicia** was the coast of today's **Lebanon** and northern Israel and Syria: the cities of **Tyre**, **Sidon**, **Byblos** and **Arwad**, each ruled by its own king. They called themselves Canaanites, or by their city; "Phoenician" is a Greek name, probably from *phoinix*, purple-red.

**What they sold:**
- **Purple dye**, made from the murex sea snail. Thousands of snails gave a few grams of dye, so it was worth more than gold by weight, and "royal purple" became the colour of kings.
- **Cedar** from the Lebanon mountains, for temples and ships.
- **Glass**, ivory carvings, metalwork and fine textiles.
- And their real asset: **ships and sea knowledge**.

**The alphabet.** By about **1050 BC** the Phoenicians wrote with **22 letters**, all consonants. The inscription on the sarcophagus of King **Ahiram** of Byblos is one of the earliest long texts. Around **800 BC** the **Greeks** borrowed it, added vowels, and passed it to the Etruscans and Romans, so the letters you are reading descend from it. The Aramaeans borrowed it too, and from Aramaic came Hebrew square script, Arabic and the scripts of India. **Most of the world's alphabets go back to this one.**

**The colonies.** From the 9th century BC, Tyre founded trading posts across the Mediterranean, mainly for metals:

| Colony | Where | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Kition** | Cyprus | 9th century BC |
| **Carthage** | Tunisia | traditionally 814 BC; archaeology late 9th or 8th century |
| **Gadir** (Cádiz) | Atlantic Spain, near the silver of Tartessos | tradition says about 1100 BC; finds so far point to the 9th century |
| **Motya**, **Utica**, Sardinian ports | Sicily, Tunisia, Sardinia | 8th century BC |

**Under the empires.** The Phoenician cities paid tribute to Assyria, then to Babylon, whose Nebuchadnezzar II besieged Tyre for **thirteen years** (about 586–573 BC), and then to Persia, where Phoenician ships formed the core of the Persian navy in the wars against Greece.

**A voyage around Africa?** Herodotus says that Pharaoh **Necho II** (610–595 BC) sent Phoenicians to sail around Africa, and that they returned after three years reporting that the sun was on their right as they sailed west. Herodotus did not believe that detail, yet it is exactly what sailors rounding southern Africa would see. **Many historians think the voyage possible; others think the story too thin to accept.** No archaeological trace has been found, and only new evidence could decide it.

**The end of independence.** **Alexander** besieged island Tyre for seven months in **332 BC**, built a causeway to it, and sold most of its people into slavery. The Phoenician world lived on in the west, in **Carthage**.
Israel and Judah: two kingdoms between t:
Two small kingdoms in the hills of the southern Levant, whose writings became among the most read in the world. This lesson is their political history. What the texts teach as religion belongs to Theology.

**The setting.** The highlands west of the Jordan, between the great powers of Egypt and Mesopotamia. The name **"Israel"** first appears on an Egyptian victory stela of Pharaoh **Merneptah**, about **1208 BC**, as a people in Canaan.

**The sources, and the problem with them.** The main source is the **Hebrew Bible**, especially the books of Samuel and Kings. They were written and edited over centuries, much of it from the late 7th century BC onwards, by authors with a religious purpose. Archaeology and the inscriptions of neighbours act as a check.

**Where the outside evidence confirms the kings:**

| Evidence | Date | What it shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Kurkh Monolith** (Assyrian) | 853 BC | Ahab of Israel brings 2,000 chariots to the battle of Qarqar |
