| **Mesha Stele** (Moabite) | about 840 BC | Mesha of Moab boasts of throwing off the rule of **Omri, king of Israel** |
| **Tel Dan Stele** (Aramaean) | 9th century BC | most scholars read "**House of David**", the earliest mention of David's dynasty outside the Bible |
| **Black Obelisk** of Shalmaneser III | 841 BC | **Jehu** of Israel bows before the Assyrian king |
| **Sennacherib's Prism** | 701 BC | Sennacherib boasts of shutting Hezekiah of Judah up in Jerusalem like a caged bird |

**Two kingdoms.** **Israel** in the north, larger and richer, capital **Samaria**, built by the Omride dynasty (9th century). **Judah** in the south, smaller, capital **Jerusalem**, ruled by the house of David.

**The north falls.** Israel rebelled against Assyria and **Samaria fell in 722–720 BC**. Its people were partly deported and replaced with settlers from elsewhere.

**Judah survives.** In **701 BC** Sennacherib ravaged Judah and stormed **Lachish**, shown on reliefs in his palace at Nineveh. Hezekiah had cut a water tunnel under Jerusalem, recorded in the **Siloam inscription**, and the city did not fall. A century later **Josiah** (about 640–609 BC) centralised worship in Jerusalem, a reform that many scholars link to the writing of Deuteronomy. He was killed at Megiddo in 609 by Pharaoh Necho II.

**The debate: how much of the earlier story is history?**
- **Maximalists** read the Bible as broadly reliable from David onward, pointing to the Tel Dan Stele and to 10th-century sites such as Khirbet Qeiyafa as signs of an early kingdom.
- **Minimalists** (the "Copenhagen school") argue that the texts are late compositions and that David and Solomon, if real, were local chiefs.
- **The middle ground**, associated with Israel Finkelstein's "low chronology", accepts a real Davidic dynasty but sees 10th-century Judah as small, with a true state only in the 9th–8th centuries.

**What would settle it:** better dating of key buildings in the 10th and 9th centuries, and more inscriptions. **Where they agree:** from about 850 BC the biblical kings are confirmed by outside sources.
Kush: the 25th dynasty and Napata:
For about seventy years, kings from what is now Sudan ruled Egypt as pharaohs.

**Where.** **Kush** lay on the Nile south of Egypt, in **Nubia**, northern Sudan. Its religious centre was **Napata**, at the foot of the sacred mountain **Jebel Barkal**, near the Fourth Cataract. Egypt had ruled Nubia in the New Kingdom (Stage 3) and left behind the cult of the god **Amun**, which the Kushite kings adopted with great devotion.

**The rise.** After the New Kingdom ended about 1070 BC, a new Kushite kingdom grew around Napata. Its kings, **Alara** and **Kashta**, were buried under mounds and then small pyramids at **el-Kurru** and moved north as Egypt fragmented.

**The conquest.** **Piye** (reigned about 744–714 BC) marched north about **728 BC**, took Memphis, and accepted the surrender of the Delta princes. His **victory stela** at Jebel Barkal, one of the longest Egyptian royal inscriptions, tells the campaign in detail: he prays to Amun, scolds a prince for letting horses starve, and presents himself as the restorer of true Egyptian piety. His brother **Shabaka** made Kushite rule over all Egypt permanent.

**The 25th dynasty (about 744–656 BC):**

| King | What to remember |
| --- | --- |
| **Piye** | conquered Egypt; victory stela |
| **Shabaka** | ruled Egypt from Memphis; the "Shabaka Stone", a copy of an old Memphite text |
| **Taharqa** (690–664) | the greatest builder: temples at Karnak and Jebel Barkal; buried in the largest pyramid at **Nuri** |
| **Tantamani** | the last; driven out of Egypt by Assyria |

**The Kushite pharaohs looked back.** They revived Old Kingdom styles in art and texts, building pyramids again for royal burials, centuries after Egypt had stopped.

**Clash with Assyria.** Kush backed the small Levantine kingdoms against Assyria. The Bible names **Tirhakah** (Taharqa), king of Kush, as marching to help Hezekiah in 701 BC. Assyria struck back: **Esarhaddon took Memphis in 671**, and **Ashurbanipal sacked Thebes in 663 BC**. The Kushites withdrew south.

**After.** Egypt was reunited by **Psamtik I** of Sais (664–610 BC), the **26th dynasty**, who used Greek and Carian mercenaries. In **593 BC** his successor Psamtik II raided deep into Kush and burned Napata's statues. Kush endured as a kingdom for nearly a thousand years more, its centre slowly shifting south to **Meroë**.

**A word on the name.** The 25th dynasty is often called the **"Black Pharaohs"**. Egyptian art did show Kushites with darker skin, but Egyptians and Nubians defined each other by land, language and culture more than by colour, and modern racial categories fit the ancient Nile poorly.
Zhou China: the Mandate of Heaven and th:
China's longest dynasty, and the idea it left behind: that a ruler governs only while Heaven approves.

**The Zhou conquest.** The **Zhou** came from the **Wei valley** in the west, near modern Xi'an. Under **King Wu** they overthrew the **Shang** (Stage 3) at the battle of **Muye**, about **1046 BC** (dates for the conquest range over several decades).

**The Mandate of Heaven** (*tianming*). To justify replacing the Shang, Zhou writers argued that **Heaven** gives the right to rule to a virtuous house and **withdraws it from a wicked one**. Disaster, rebellion and defeat were signs the Mandate had passed. **It became the core of Chinese political thought for three thousand years**: every dynasty claimed it, and every successful rebel claimed it had moved to him.

**How the Western Zhou ruled (about 1046–771 BC).** The king granted lands to kinsmen and allies, who ruled them as hereditary lords. Inscriptions cast on **bronze ritual vessels** record these grants and are a key primary source. Whether to call this "feudal", by analogy with medieval Europe, is debated: the analogy helps, but the Zhou system rested on kinship and ritual more than on contracts.

**771 BC: the break.** Raiders allied with rebel nobles killed **King You** and sacked the western capital. The court moved east to **Luoyi** (near modern Luoyang). From here the dynasty is the **Eastern Zhou**, and the kings had prestige but little power.

**The Spring and Autumn period (770–476 BC).** Named after the *Spring and Autumn Annals* of the state of **Lu**, a year-by-year chronicle. Over a hundred lordships fought, merged and swallowed one another until a dozen major states remained.

| Feature | What it meant |
| --- | --- |
| **The hegemons** (*ba*) | the strongest lord led the others in the king's name; the first was **Duke Huan of Qi** (685–643 BC) |
| **Chariot warfare** | battles fought by aristocrats in chariots, with codes of honour |
| **Iron** | cast iron appears from about the 6th century BC, earlier than in the West |
| **Growing states** | rulers taxed land directly and built walls, roads and canals |

**The big states to know:** **Jin** in the north (later split into three), **Qi** on the east coast, **Chu** in the south along the Yangtze, and **Qin** in the far west, on the old Zhou heartland.

**Why it matters.** The decline of royal authority, and the endless wars, created the crisis that Confucius and the other thinkers of the age set out to answer. The period ends in the even harsher **Warring States**.
The Greek polis: colonies, hoplites and:
The Greeks never formed one state. They formed over a thousand small ones, and this is how they worked.

**Out of the Dark Age.** After the Mycenaean palaces fell (Stage 3), Greece had no writing for about four centuries. From the 8th century BC came a revival: the **alphabet**, borrowed from the Phoenicians about **800 BC**; the **Olympic Games**, traditionally first held in **776 BC**; and the epics of **Homer**, the *Iliad* and *Odyssey*, probably written down in the late 8th or 7th century (the date, and whether "Homer" was one poet, are debated).

**The polis.** A city-state: a town and its farmland, with its own laws, gods, army and coins. A modern inventory counts **over a thousand** Greek poleis. Most were tiny; Athens and Sparta were giants. **The polis was its citizens**: Greeks said "the Athenians" decided, never "Athens".

**Colonisation (about 750–550 BC).** Short of land, and eager for trade, cities sent out groups to found new poleis:

| Colony | Where | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Pithekoussai** | island off Naples | about 770 BC, the earliest in the west |
| **Syracuse** | Sicily | 733 BC, founded by Corinth |
| **Byzantion** | the Bosporus | about 660 BC, by Megara |
| **Cyrene** | Libya | about 630 BC, by Thera |
| **Massalia** (Marseille) | southern France | about 600 BC, by Phocaea |

By 550 BC Greeks lived, as Plato later put it, like frogs around a pond, from Spain to the Black Sea. Southern Italy was called "Great Greece".

**The hoplite.** From the 7th century BC the core of every army was the **hoplite**, a citizen in bronze helmet and breastplate with a round shield and a thrusting spear, fighting shoulder to shoulder in the **phalanx**. Each man's shield partly covered his neighbour. Because hoplites bought their own armour, the middle farmers who fought began to claim a share in power. **Whether this "hoplite revolution" drove politics, or followed it, is debated.**

**Tyrants.** In the 7th and 6th centuries many cities were seized by a **tyrant**, a man who took power outside the law, often with popular support against the aristocrats: **Cypselus** of Corinth (about 657 BC), **Pisistratus** of Athens (in power on and off from 561, securely 546–527 BC). The word was not yet an insult; some tyrants built temples, fountains and harbours.

**Lawgivers.** Others wrote down laws to end feuds: **Draco** at Athens (about 621 BC), whose punishments were so harsh that "draconian" still means severe.

**What united the Greeks.** Not a state but a culture: the language, the gods, Homer, the oracle at **Delphi**, and the games at Olympia. They called themselves **Hellenes** and everyone else *barbaroi*, people whose speech sounded like "bar-bar".
The Etruscans:
The people who dominated Italy before Rome, and who taught Rome a great deal.

**Where.** **Etruria**, between the Arno and Tiber rivers: modern **Tuscany** and northern Lazio. Its wealth came from fertile land and **iron, copper and tin**, above all the iron of the island of **Elba**.

**When.** The **Villanovan** culture (from about 900 BC) grew into Etruscan city-states in the 8th and 7th centuries. Their height was about **650–500 BC**.

**The cities.** Never one state, but a league of about **twelve** independent cities that met at a shared shrine: **Tarquinia**, **Caere** (Cerveteri), **Veii**, **Vulci**, Volsinii and others. At their peak they spread north into the Po valley and south into Campania.

**What the Etruscans left:**
- **Tombs.** Their cemeteries are cities of the dead. At **Caere**, family tombs were cut into the rock as houses, with beds and chairs. At **Tarquinia**, painted tomb walls show banquets, dancing, music and games.
- **Trade.** Greek pottery was imported in huge amounts: many of the finest Athenian vases ever found come from Etruscan graves.
- **Religion.** Etruscan priests were famous for **divination**, reading the will of the gods from animal livers and lightning. The Romans kept consulting Etruscan diviners (*haruspices*) for centuries.
- **Women's standing.** Etruscan women dined with men and appear named in inscriptions. Greek writers were shocked; historians caution that the Greek reports are hostile, but the tomb paintings do show couples dining together.

**The language.** Etruscan is written in a version of the **Greek alphabet**, so it can be read aloud, but it is **not an Indo-European language** and is only partly understood. About 13,000 inscriptions survive, most of them short. The **Pyrgi tablets** (about 500 BC), in Etruscan and Phoenician, helped scholars work out some of it.

**The origins debate.** Ancient writers disagreed. **Herodotus** said the Etruscans came from **Lydia** in Anatolia; **Dionysius of Halicarnassus** said they were native to Italy. Their non-Indo-European language and eastern-looking art kept the migration theory alive. **Ancient DNA from 2021** found Etruscans genetically very similar to their Latin neighbours, which supports local origins, and suggests their language is a survival from before Indo-European languages reached Italy. The cultural question is not closed, but the genetics now point clearly one way.

**Decline.** The Etruscans lost a sea battle to **Syracuse off Cumae in 474 BC**, the Celts overran their Po valley lands about 400 BC, and **Rome** took the cities one by one, starting with **Veii in 396 BC**. Rome absorbed their engineering, their symbols of office, the arena games and their gods.
The Scythians: horse archers of the step:
The first steppe nomads whose world we can see in detail, through a Greek historian and the gold in their graves.

**Who.** The **Scythians** were horse-riding pastoralists who spoke an **Iranian language**. The Greeks used the name for the peoples north of the Black Sea; the Persians called nomads further east **Saka**. They were not one empire but many tribes sharing a way of life across the steppe, from the Danube to the Altai mountains.

**When and where.** They appear north of the Black Sea in the **8th and 7th centuries BC**, pushing out an earlier people, the Cimmerians. But their origins were further east: the earliest great mound in "Scythian" style is **Arzhan 1** in **Tuva**, southern Siberia, dated to about **800 BC**.

**How they lived.** They moved with herds of horses, cattle and sheep between pastures, lived in wagons and felt tents, and fought as **mounted archers** with a short, powerful composite bow. This combination, **mobility and missile fire from horseback**, made steppe peoples the most formidable soldiers in Eurasia until gunpowder.

**Their history with the empires:**
- In the 7th century BC Scythian bands raided deep into the Near East, and the Assyrians allied with them by marriage.
- About **513 BC** **Darius I** of Persia crossed the Danube to conquer them. The Scythians retreated, burned the grass and would not fight a battle; Darius withdrew. **The steppe defeated empires by refusing to be found.**
- In **339 BC** their king **Ateas**, said to be about ninety, was killed in battle by **Philip II** of Macedon.

**The sources.** **Herodotus** devoted Book 4 of his *Histories* to them: their burial of kings with horses and servants, their use of enemy skulls as cups, and their **vapour baths with hemp seeds** on hot stones. Archaeology has confirmed much: braziers with burnt hemp seeds were found in the frozen tombs at **Pazyryk** in the Altai (about 4th–3rd centuries BC), where ice preserved felt, carpets, saddles and tattooed bodies.

**The art.** Scythian **"animal style"**: stags, panthers and griffins twisted into gold ornaments. North of the Black Sea, Greek goldsmiths made pieces for Scythian kings, buried in great mounds (*kurgans*).

**Warrior women.** Greek legends of **Amazons** may echo something real: excavations in Scythian cemeteries have found many women buried with bows, arrows and spears, some with battle wounds. How large a share of warriors were women is still debated, but **armed women were a real part of steppe life**.

**Why it matters.** The Scythians began the pattern that runs through Eurasian history to the Mongols: settled empires trading with, paying, fighting and fearing the riders of the grassland.
The Celts: Hallstatt and La Tène:
Iron Age Europe north of the Alps, and the long argument over what the word "Celt" means.

**Hallstatt (about 800–450 BC).** Named after a village on a lake in **Upper Austria**, where **salt mines** made people rich and a cemetery of over a thousand graves was dug from 1846. The salt was preserved in the mines along with leather, wooden tools and textiles. Across central Europe, the Hallstatt culture is marked by **iron swords**, wagons, and **chieftains' burials** under great mounds.

**Contact with the Mediterranean.** After Greeks founded **Massalia** (Marseille) about 600 BC, wine and luxury goods moved up the Rhône:
- The **Hochdorf** grave near Stuttgart (about 530 BC): a chieftain on a bronze couch, with a Greek cauldron and drinking horns.
- The **Vix** grave in Burgundy (about 500 BC): a woman buried with a Greek bronze mixing bowl **1.64 metres tall**, the largest known.
- The **Heuneburg** on the upper Danube: a hillfort with a wall of **sun-dried mud brick** on stone footings, a Mediterranean technique.

**La Tène (from about 450 BC).** Named after a site on **Lake Neuchâtel** in Switzerland, found in 1857, where weapons and ornaments were thrown into the water as offerings. La Tène art is swirling and abstract: curving leaves, spirals and faces on brooches, sword sheaths and gold **torcs** (neck rings). It spread from France and Germany to Britain, Ireland and the Balkans.

**The migrations.** From about **400 BC** Celtic-speaking groups crossed the Alps into the **Po valley**, which the Romans then called "Gaul this side of the Alps". One group, the Senones, defeated a Roman army at the **Allia** and **sacked Rome**, in **390 BC** by the traditional Roman count (about 387 by Polybius). Others served as mercenaries for Syracuse and, after this stage, invaded Greece and settled in Anatolia as the Galatians.

**The name.** Greek writers from about 500 BC speak of the **Keltoi**, living inland from Massalia and near the source of the Danube. Celtic languages, a branch of Indo-European, are first written in **Lepontic** inscriptions in northern Italy from the 6th century BC; Gaulish, Celtiberian, and the ancestors of Irish, Welsh and Breton followed.

**The debate: who were "the Celts"?**
- **The traditional view:** a people with a shared language, art and religion, who spread from a central European homeland with Hallstatt and La Tène.
- **The sceptics** (Simon James, John Collis, around 2000): no ancient writer called the Britons or Irish "Celts"; language, art style and ethnic identity did not travel together; the idea of one Celtic people is largely an invention of the 1700s.
- **"Celtic from the West"** (Barry Cunliffe and John Koch, from 2010): Celtic languages may have formed along the **Atlantic** coast in the Bronze Age, not in central Europe.

**What evidence bears on it.** Ancient DNA is now joining the argument: a large study of Britain published in 2021–22 found a sizeable migration from the continent in the **Late Bronze Age**, which some read as the arrival of Celtic speech. **Where they agree:** Celtic *languages* were spoken across much of Europe by 300 BC; whether their speakers thought of themselves as one people is a separate question.
The Olmec, Monte Albán and the early May:
Mesoamerica in these centuries: the last great age of the Olmec, the first city in Oaxaca, and the beginnings of the Maya.

**The Olmec heartland.** The hot, wet lowlands of Mexico's **Gulf coast**, in Veracruz and Tabasco. The earlier centre, **San Lorenzo** (about 1200–900 BC), was met in Stage 3. By this stage the leading centre was **La Venta** (about **900–400 BC**), on an island in the swamps of Tabasco.

**La Venta.** A planned ceremonial centre laid out on a north–south line, with a **clay pyramid about 30 metres high**, plazas, and offerings buried deep under the ground: tons of green **serpentine** blocks laid as mosaic pavements, then covered over and never meant to be seen again.

**What the Olmec are famous for:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Colossal heads** | 17 known, carved from basalt boulders dragged or rafted from the Tuxtla mountains up to about 100 km away; probably portraits of rulers |
| **Jade** | carved masks and figures; jade became Mesoamerica's most precious material |
| **The "were-jaguar"** | a figure blending human baby and jaguar, a recurring religious image |
| **The ballgame** | rubber balls from about 1600 BC at the bog site of El Manatí; the game lasted until the Spanish conquest |

**"Mother culture" or "sister cultures"?** A long debate.
- **Mother culture:** the Olmec invented the core of Mesoamerican civilisation (the ballgame, the calendar's roots, monumental art, rulership imagery) and spread it. A 2005 study of pottery chemistry found San Lorenzo exported pottery widely, but did not import it, which supports this view.
- **Sister cultures:** many regions, such as Oaxaca and the Mexican highlands, developed together and exchanged ideas; the Olmec were the most spectacular, not the source. Critics disputed the pottery study's method.

The question turns on dating: which region shows each symbol first. **Where they agree:** the Olmec were the most elaborate society in Mesoamerica before about 400 BC, and after La Venta declined the Olmec style faded.

**Monte Albán.** In the **valley of Oaxaca**, the **Zapotec** founded a hilltop city about **500 BC**, levelling a mountaintop for its plazas. Its early carvings, the "**Danzantes**", show sprawled naked men, probably slain or sacrificed captives, with some of the earliest Mesoamerican **glyphs and calendar signs**.

**The early Maya.** In the lowlands of Guatemala and southern Mexico, Maya villages grew into ceremonial centres earlier than once thought. At **Ceibal** a formal plaza was built about **1000–950 BC**. In 2020 laser mapping from the air (lidar) revealed **Aguada Fénix** in Tabasco, a raised platform about **1.4 km long** built about 1000–800 BC, the largest early monument in the Maya area. By the end of this stage, at **Nakbe** and **El Mirador** in northern Guatemala, the Maya were building large pyramids. Their writing and their classic kingdoms come in Stage 5.
Chavín de Huántar and the Andes:
A temple high in the Andes whose religion spread across much of Peru: the first great shared culture of South America.

**Where.** **Chavín de Huántar** stands at about **3,150 metres** in the Andes of north-central Peru, where two rivers meet, on a route between the Pacific coast and the Amazon lowlands.

**When.** The temple was built and rebuilt over several centuries. Dating is debated: one excavator (John Rick) places its main life about **1200–500 BC**; another view (Richard Burger) dates its height to about **900–200 BC**. Either way it is a contemporary of the Olmec, with no contact between them.

**The temple.** An **Old Temple**, U-shaped around a sunken circular plaza, and a later, larger **New Temple**. Inside both run narrow, dark **stone galleries**, with air shafts and water channels.

**The Lanzón.** In the heart of the Old Temple, at a crossing of galleries, stands a **granite blade about 4.5 metres tall**, carved as a fanged being with snakes for hair. It has never been moved, and it was meant to be seen only by the few allowed into the dark.

**The imagery.** Chavín carving shows **jaguars, caimans, harpy eagles and snakes**, animals of the **Amazon rainforest**, not of the highlands. Stone heads once set in the outer walls show a human face changing, step by step, into a fanged creature. Many scholars read this as **priests transformed in trance**, helped by the **San Pedro cactus**, which contains mescaline and is shown in Chavín art.

**Sound and spectacle.** Water channels under the temple may have roared, and in **2001** excavators found **20 conch-shell trumpets** (*pututus*) inside a gallery. The temple seems built to **overwhelm the senses**: darkness, echoes, sudden light, and the transformed priests.

**The Chavín horizon.** Chavín's style, on textiles, gold and pottery, spread across much of Peru. Archaeologists call this the **Early Horizon**, the first time much of the Andes shared one art and probably one religion. Pilgrims brought goods to the temple from far away: **Spondylus** shells from the warm waters off Ecuador, obsidian from the south.

**What it was.** No sign of an army or conquest has been found. **It was a religious centre, not an empire**, and its influence travelled with pilgrims, traders and imitating priests. This is a common pattern in the Andes before the Inca.

**Elsewhere in the Andes:**
- On the south coast, the **Paracas** culture (about 800 BC onwards) began its famous textiles and its practice of shaping the skulls of infants.
- Around **Lake Titicaca**, villages such as Chiripa built sunken temples, the beginning of a tradition that led to Tiwanaku centuries later.

**Why it matters.** Chavín shows that a civilisation could spread **by belief rather than force**, and it established religious images that Andean peoples used for a thousand years.
Nebuchadnezzar's Babylon, 626–539 BC:
Babylon's last great age as the centre of an empire, and the most famous city of the ancient world.

**The rise.** **Nabopolassar**, a Babylonian general, threw off Assyrian rule in **626 BC** and, with the Medes, destroyed Assyria (614–609). His son **Nebuchadnezzar II** (605–562 BC) defeated the Egyptian army at **Carchemish** in **605 BC** and took over Assyria's western lands, from the Euphrates to the borders of Egypt.

**Nebuchadnezzar in the Levant:**
- **Jerusalem** taken in **597 BC**, and King Jehoiachin deported; after a revolt, the city and its temple destroyed in **587 or 586 BC** (the next lesson).
- **Tyre** besieged for about thirteen years (about 586–573 BC), until it accepted Babylonian rule.

**The city.** Babylon on the **Euphrates**, south of modern Baghdad, was rebuilt as the greatest city in western Asia:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The walls** | a double inner wall and an outer wall, with a moat; Greek writers counted them among the wonders of the world |
| **The Ishtar Gate** | glazed blue brick with yellow dragons, bulls and lions; excavated by Germans in 1899–1917 and rebuilt in **Berlin** |
| **The Processional Way** | the road for the New Year festival, lined with glazed lions |
| **Etemenanki** | the ziggurat of Marduk, about 90 metres square at its base; widely taken as the model for the biblical **Tower of Babel** |
| **Esagila** | the great temple of **Marduk**, Babylon's god |

Babylon's population is uncertain; it may have exceeded **100,000**, making it among the largest cities on Earth.

**The Hanging Gardens: a real debate.** Greek writers describe terraced gardens built by a Babylonian king for a homesick wife. But **no Babylonian text mentions them**, Herodotus does not, and excavation has not found them. **Stephanie Dalley** (2013) argues the gardens were at **Nineveh**, built by Sennacherib, whose inscriptions describe water-raising screws and gardens, and that later Greeks confused the two cities. Others think the gardens were at Babylon but are lost, or were legend. A clear Babylonian inscription, or a find under the river-shifted ruins, would decide it.

**Learning.** Babylonian scholars kept the **Astronomical Diaries**, nightly records of the sky, prices and river levels, from about **652 BC to the 1st century BC**: the longest continuous scientific record of the ancient world. The **zodiac** of twelve equal signs was worked out here, probably in the 5th century BC.

**The end.** After Nebuchadnezzar came short reigns and a coup. The last king, **Nabonidus** (556–539 BC), favoured the moon god **Sin** over Marduk and spent about ten years at the oasis of **Tayma** in Arabia, leaving his son **Belshazzar** in charge. Babylon's priests resented him. In **October 539 BC**, **Cyrus of Persia** defeated the Babylonian army at **Opis** and entered Babylon **without a battle**. The city lived on, as one of Persia's capitals, but Babylon never again ruled an empire of its own.
Exile and return: Judah under Babylon an:
How Judah lost its kingdom and temple, and how a community in exile and a small Persian province carried its identity forward.

**The fall of Jerusalem.** Judah rebelled against Babylon twice. In **597 BC** Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem and deported King **Jehoiachin** with the elite. In **587 or 586 BC** (the evidence allows either) the city was taken again, its walls broken and **the temple of Solomon burned**. King Zedekiah was blinded and taken to Babylon.

**Outside confirmation.** Ration tablets found in Babylon list oil issued to **Jehoiachin, king of Judah**, and his sons. Ostraca (inked pottery sherds) from **Lachish** record the last weeks before the Babylonian attack: one officer reports (in paraphrase) that he is watching for Lachish's fire signals because those of Azekah can no longer be seen.

**How many went?** The books of Kings and Jeremiah give different figures, from about **4,600 to over 10,000 people**. Most of the population **stayed** in a ruined Judah. Historians debate how empty the land became: the biblical picture of an empty land may reflect the view of the returning elite more than the archaeology, which shows a sharp fall in population around Jerusalem but continued life north of it.

**Life in exile.** The deportees were settled as farmers in southern Mesopotamia. Over 200 cuneiform tablets from a village called **Al-Yahudu**, "Judah-town" (about 572–477 BC), show Judean families leasing land, paying taxes and giving their children names that honour their God. The exile was **not slavery but resettlement**, and many families prospered and stayed.

**What the exile did.** Without king or temple, the community kept its identity through **written tradition, the Sabbath, circumcision and genealogy**. Many scholars think much of the Hebrew Bible was gathered and edited in these years and in the Persian period that followed. The prophets **Jeremiah** and **Ezekiel** belong to this crisis, as do the later chapters of Isaiah.

**The return.** In **539 BC** Cyrus of Persia took Babylon. The Book of Ezra records his decree allowing exiles to go home and rebuild their temple. Its exact wording may be a later version, but it **fits Persian policy**, shown in the Cyrus Cylinder, of restoring local cults. Returns came in waves.

| Date (BC) | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **515** | the **Second Temple** completed in Jerusalem, in Darius I's sixth year |
| **about 445** | **Nehemiah**, a Jewish official at the Persian court, governor; Jerusalem's walls rebuilt |
| **458 or 398** (debated) | **Ezra**, priest and scribe, brings "the law" from Persia |
| **5th–4th centuries** | **Yehud**, a small Persian province, mints coins inscribed *YHD* |

**A diaspora is born.** Jewish communities stayed in Babylonia and settled in Egypt. On the Nile island of **Elephantine**, a Jewish garrison in Persian service kept its own temple; their Aramaic papyri include a petition of **407 BC** to the governor of Judah to rebuild it after a local riot.

**Why it matters.** From now on most Jews lived **outside** the land, bound by text and practice rather than by a kingdom. That pattern, and the Second Temple, last into Stage 5 and the Roman age.
Cyrus the Great builds the Persian empir:
In about twenty years, a king from south-western Iran built the largest empire the world had yet seen.

**Where it began.** **Persis** (modern **Fars**), in south-west Iran, around the city of **Anshan**. The Persians, like the Medes to their north, spoke an Iranian language and had long been subjects of greater powers. **Cyrus II** became king of Anshan about **559 BC**.

**The conquests:**

| Date (BC) | Conquest |
| --- | --- |
| **about 550** | the **Medes**: King Astyages' army mutinied and handed him over; Cyrus took the Median capital **Ecbatana** |
| **about 547–546** | **Lydia** in western Anatolia: **Croesus**, the proverbially rich king, defeated and his capital **Sardis** taken; the Greek cities of Ionia subdued |
| **540s–530s** | **Eastern Iran and Central Asia**: Parthia, Bactria, Sogdia |
| **539** | **Babylon** taken without a siege, and with it Mesopotamia, Syria and the Levant |

**His death (530 BC)** came on campaign in Central Asia. **Herodotus** says he was killed fighting the **Massagetae**, nomads led by Queen **Tomyris**, who put his head in a skin of blood; other Greek writers tell it differently. His tomb, a simple stone house on a stepped base, still stands at **Pasargadae**, the capital he built.

**How he ruled.** Cyrus kept local elites, temples and customs, and presented himself to each people in their own terms. To the Babylonians he was the chosen of **Marduk**; to the exiles of Judah, the Book of Isaiah calls him the Lord's **"anointed"**. The policy was practical: **cheaper to rule through local habits than against them**.

**The Cyrus Cylinder.** A clay barrel inscribed in Babylonian cuneiform, found at Babylon in **1879** and now in the **British Museum**. Cyrus says that Marduk chose him to replace the impious Nabonidus, that he entered Babylon in peace, and that he returned displaced gods and people to their homes.

**The debate over the Cylinder.** In 1971 the Shah of Iran promoted it as **"the first charter of human rights"**, and a replica stands at the United Nations.
- **For a generous reading:** the policy of return was real and unusual in scale, and Cyrus's reputation for mildness was shared by Greeks, Babylonians and Judeans alike.
- **Against the human-rights label:** it is a standard **Mesopotamian royal building inscription**, modelled on Assyrian ones, written to legitimise a conqueror. It says nothing of rights, and Cyrus also sacked cities that resisted, such as Opis.

Most historians accept the policy and reject the label. Either way, Cyrus became the model of a wise king: the Greek writer **Xenophon** wrote an idealised life of him, the *Cyropaedia*, about 370 BC.

**His son finishes the map.** **Cambyses II** (530–522 BC) conquered **Egypt** in **525 BC**. Herodotus paints him as a mad tyrant who stabbed the sacred Apis bull, but Egyptian evidence, including a carefully honoured Apis burial and the autobiography of the Egyptian official **Udjahorresnet**, shows him working with Egyptian priests. **The Greek picture is hostile, and the Egyptian evidence complicates it.**
Darius I: satrapies, the Royal Road and:
The king who turned Cyrus's conquests into a working state, and left the longest account of his rise in his own words.

**A disputed accession.** In **522 BC** Cambyses died on his way home from Egypt. A man claiming to be his brother **Bardiya** held the throne for some months, until **Darius**, from a different branch of the royal family, killed him with six fellow nobles. Darius said the man was an impostor, a Magus named **Gaumata**.

**Was he?** Darius's own account is the main source, and Herodotus follows a version of it. **Many historians suspect Darius killed the real Bardiya** and invented the impostor to cover a usurpation; others find his account plausible. With no independent source, the question is open.

**The Behistun inscription.** Darius had his version carved on a cliff at **Bisitun** in western Iran, about 100 metres above the road, in **three languages**: Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. It tells of **nineteen battles** in one year against rebels he calls "liars". Copied by **Henry Rawlinson** between 1835 and 1847, it became the key to **deciphering cuneiform**, as the Rosetta Stone was for hieroglyphs.

**The empire Darius ran (522–486 BC).** From the **Aegean to the Indus**, Egypt to Central Asia: the largest empire yet, with perhaps tens of millions of subjects (estimates vary widely).

| Institution | How it worked |
| --- | --- |
| **Satrapies** | provinces under a **satrap** (governor), with separate commanders and secretaries reporting to the king; Herodotus lists twenty tax districts |
| **Tribute** | fixed sums in silver or goods, assessed by district |
| **The Royal Road** | about 2,500 km from **Sardis** to **Susa**, with **111 relay stations**, says Herodotus |
| **Coins** | the gold **daric**, struck from about 500 BC |
| **Aramaic** | the common language of the chancery, from Egypt to Afghanistan |
| **Public works** | a canal from the **Nile to the Red Sea**, completed by Darius |

**The couriers.** Herodotus admired the relay riders, who handed messages from horse to horse so that a letter crossed in about a week what took a traveller three months. His praise, that nothing stops them, neither snow nor rain nor heat nor darkness, is paraphrased in the unofficial motto carved on the New York post office.

**Persepolis.** From about **518 BC** Darius built **Persepolis** (*Parsa*) in Fars, a terrace of palaces for ceremony. The stairs of its audience hall, the **Apadana**, show delegations from **twenty-three peoples** bringing gifts: Ionians with cloth, Indians with gold dust, Ethiopians with an okapi or giraffe. **The image is an empire of willing peoples**, which is how Darius wanted it seen.

**What the clay says.** The **Persepolis Fortification Tablets**, tens of thousands of tablets and fragments in Elamite, mostly from about 509–493 BC, record rations for workers, including women, who were paid and got extra after childbirth. They show a closely administered economy.

**Expansion.** Darius added the **Indus valley** (about 518 BC), campaigned against the **Scythians** (about 513), and took Thrace. The revolt of the Ionian Greeks in **499 BC** led to the Persian Wars, two lessons on.
Zoroastrianism as history:
The religion of the Persian kings' world, one of the oldest living faiths, taught here as history: where it came from, how it spread, and what it touched.

**The founder.** **Zarathustra** (in Greek, Zoroaster) was a priest and poet who preached in eastern Iran or Central Asia. His own words are thought to survive in the **Gathas**, seventeen hymns in an archaic language, **Old Avestan**.

**When did he live? A genuine debate:**
- **Early, about 1500–1000 BC:** the language of the Gathas is very close to the oldest Sanskrit of the Rigveda, and the society they describe is pastoral, with no cities or iron. This was **Mary Boyce's** view and is widely held.
- **Late, about the 6th century BC:** a tradition, preserved in later Zoroastrian and Arab writings, placed him "258 years before Alexander". Most specialists now regard this as a late calculation, but some still prefer a date near the Achaemenids.

Only the dating of the Gathas' language, or a find that fixes it, could settle it. If he is early, he does not belong to Jaspers's axial age at all.

**The core teaching, as history records it.** A supreme wise god, **Ahura Mazda**; a cosmic struggle between **Truth** (*asha*) and **the Lie** (*druj*); every person choosing a side; and a final renewal of the world. Later tradition named an evil spirit, **Angra Mainyu** (Ahriman), as Ahura Mazda's opponent. The detail of the doctrine belongs to the Theology curriculum.

**The Achaemenid kings.** Darius I and his successors say they rule **by the favour of Ahuramazda** and condemn rebels as followers of **the Lie**, the same idea and word (*drauga*, related to *druj*) as in the Gathas. But no Achaemenid inscription names **Zarathustra**. Historians debate whether the kings were Zoroastrian in a later sense, or worshipped Ahura Mazda within a broader Iranian religion that Zoroastrianism later absorbed.

**The Magi.** Herodotus calls the **Magi** a tribe of the Medes who served as priests, interpreted dreams and exposed their dead to birds rather than burying or burning them. That practice became the Zoroastrian custom, later carried out in "towers of silence". The Magi of the Gospel story take their name from them.

**The texts came late.** The Avesta was handed down by memory for over a thousand years and written down only under the **Sasanian** kings, probably in the 5th or 6th century AD. Much was later lost; the oldest surviving manuscripts date from the 13th century AD.

**Influence: the open question.** Zoroastrian ideas of **heaven and hell, a final judgement, resurrection, and armies of angels and demons** resemble ideas that appear in Judaism after the exile, and later in Christianity and Islam.
- **For influence:** the Judeans lived under Persian rule for two centuries, and the ideas appear in Jewish texts after that contact.
- **Against, or uncertain:** the Zoroastrian texts were written down later than the Jewish ones, so the direction of borrowing cannot be proved; the ideas could have grown independently or come through Greek channels.

**Afterwards.** Zoroastrianism was the state faith of Sasanian Iran (Stage 6). After the Arab conquest, communities shrank; some migrated to India from around the 8th–10th centuries AD and became the **Parsis**. Today perhaps 100,000–200,000 people follow the faith.
India's mahajanapadas and the rise of Ma:
After the Indus cities, India's second age of cities, and the kingdom that would unite the subcontinent.

**From tribes to states.** The Vedic peoples of Stage 3 lived in clans (*jana*). By about **600 BC** the clans had settled territories, *janapadas*, and the largest became the **mahajanapadas**, "great realms". Buddhist texts list **sixteen**, from **Gandhara** in today's Pakistan to **Anga** in Bengal; most lay on the **Ganges plain**.

**The second urbanisation (from about 600 BC).** Cities appeared along the Ganges for the first time: **Rajagriha**, **Shravasti**, **Varanasi**, **Kaushambi**, **Ujjain**, **Champa**. What made it possible:
- **Iron** axes to clear the forests of the middle Ganges, and iron ploughs.
- **Wet rice**, which feeds more people per acre than wheat.
- **Trade** along the river and overland, and the first Indian coins, **punch-marked silver**, perhaps from the 5th century BC (the date is debated).
- A glossy pottery archaeologists call **Northern Black Polished Ware** marks the cities' spread.

**Two kinds of state:**

| Kind | Examples | How ruled |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Kingdoms** | Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa, Avanti | a king (*raja*), with Brahmin priests and ministers |
| **Gana-sanghas** ("republics") | the Vajji league with its centre at **Vaishali**; the Shakyas; the Mallas | an assembly of leading clan heads; more an oligarchy than a democracy |

**The Buddha was born among the Shakyas, and Mahavira among the Vajji**, both republics (the next lesson).

**Society.** The **varna** order of four classes, priests (Brahmins), warriors (Kshatriyas), traders and farmers (Vaishyas) and servants (Shudras), was set out in Vedic texts, with people outside it treated as lowest. How rigid it was in practice in these centuries is debated. The earliest **Upanishads**, philosophical texts about the self (*atman*) and ultimate reality (*brahman*), date to about **700–500 BC**.

**The rise of Magadha.** In southern **Bihar**, Magadha had rich farmland, **iron ore** nearby, **elephants** for war, and the Ganges for transport.
- **Bimbisara** and his son **Ajatashatru** (5th century BC) conquered neighbours, including Kosala and the Vajji league.
- The capital moved from Rajagriha to **Pataliputra** (modern **Patna**), on the Ganges.
- The **Nanda** dynasty (about 345–321 BC) ruled most of the Ganges plain, with an army Greek writers reported as enormous, and wealth that made it unpopular.

**The north-west.** **Darius I** made **Gandhara** and the Indus valley Persian provinces about **518 BC**. The city of **Taxila** became a centre of learning, and the great grammarian **Panini**, who fixed the rules of Sanskrit, came from this region (his date is uncertain, probably about the 4th century BC).

**Alexander** reached the Punjab in **326 BC** but turned back before the Ganges. About **321 BC** **Chandragupta Maurya** overthrew the Nandas and founded the **Maurya empire**, which belongs to Stage 5.

**How we know.** Mostly from Buddhist and Jain texts written down centuries later, a few Greek reports, and archaeology. **The outline is secure; most exact dates are not.**
The Buddha and Mahavira: the shramana mo:
Two teachers of the Ganges valley in the 5th century BC whose followers founded Buddhism and Jainism. This lesson is their history; their teachings as religion belong to Theology.

**The shramanas.** In the new cities of the Ganges, many people left home to live as wandering ascetics, **shramanas** ("strivers"). They questioned the authority of the **Vedic sacrifices** run by Brahmin priests and sought release (*moksha*) from the cycle of rebirth through discipline, meditation and insight. Kings and rich merchants gave them food and land. **The Buddha and Mahavira were the most successful of many such teachers.**

**The Buddha.** **Siddhartha Gautama**, of the **Shakya** clan.

| Place | What happened (tradition) |
| --- | --- |
| **Lumbini** (Nepal) | his birth; a pillar set up by the emperor Ashoka about 249 BC records that the Buddha was born here |
| **Kapilavastu** | home of the Shakyas, where he grew up a prince; he left at about 29 |
| **Bodh Gaya** (Bihar) | after years of extreme asceticism, he chose a "middle way" and reached **enlightenment** under a tree, at about 35 |
| **Sarnath** near Varanasi | his **first sermon**, in a deer park |
| **Kushinagar** | his death at about **80** |

He taught for about 45 years, mainly in **Magadha** and **Kosala**, and founded an order of monks, the **sangha**, and later, tradition says, of nuns.

**When? A real debate.** Two traditions disagree by a century or more:
- The **long chronology**, from Sri Lankan chronicles, puts his death about **483 BC** (or 544 BC in Theravada reckoning).
- The **short chronology**, from other Indian sources, puts it about **400–370 BC**. A major conference in 1988 found most specialists leaning towards a death around **400 BC**, give or take a few decades.

**Most scholars accept that he was a real person.**

**Mahavira.** **Vardhamana**, called **Mahavira** ("great hero"), was born near **Vaishali** in the Vajji league, to a warrior family. He left home at about 30, lived as a naked ascetic for twelve years, reached perfect knowledge, and taught until his death at **Pavapuri** in Bihar.
- Jains count him the **24th Tirthankara**, the last of a line of teachers; the 23rd, **Parshvanatha**, may also have been historical, perhaps in the 8th or 7th century BC.
- Jain tradition dates Mahavira's death to **527 BC**, but Buddhist texts name him ("Nigantha Nataputta") as an older contemporary of the Buddha, which points to the 5th century BC.
- Jainism's hallmark is **ahimsa**, non-harming of any living being, carried to great lengths.

**How we know.** The teachings were passed down by memory. The Buddhist **Pali Canon** was written down in **Sri Lanka** in the 1st century BC; Jain scriptures were fixed later still. The earliest firm evidence is **Ashoka's inscriptions** in the 3rd century BC.

**Why it matters.** Under Ashoka (Stage 5) Buddhism began to spread across Asia, and in time it became one of the world's major religions. **Jainism stayed mainly in India**, where it remains influential, especially among merchants.
Confucius and the Hundred Schools:
A minor official of a small Chinese state whose sayings, collected by his students, shaped the government of China for two thousand years.

**Who.** **Kong Qiu**, called **Kongzi**, "Master Kong" (Latinised by Jesuits in the 1600s as Confucius). Traditionally **551–479 BC**. He was born in the state of **Lu**, at Qufu in modern **Shandong**, into a family of the *shi*, the lowest rank of the aristocracy.

**His life (tradition).** He worked as a minor official, perhaps briefly as a minister in Lu, and then, disappointed, travelled for about fourteen years among other states looking for a ruler who would put his ideas into practice. None did. He returned to Lu and taught. Tradition gives him three thousand students, seventy-two of them close disciples.

**The problem he faced.** The Zhou king was powerless (lesson on Zhou China); states fought; ministers usurped their lords. **Confucius thought order could be restored by recovering the moral and ritual ways of the early Zhou**, which he idealised.

**The key ideas:**

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| ***Ren*** | humaneness, goodness towards others |
| ***Li*** | ritual and propriety: the right forms of behaviour, from sacrifices to greetings |
| ***Junzi*** | the "gentleman" or "superior man", **noble by character, not by birth** |
| ***Xiao*** | filial piety: duty to parents and ancestors |
| **Rule by virtue** | a ruler who is good will be followed; punishment alone does not make people good |

**Two passages, in James Legge's translation (first published 1861):**

> "If the people be led by laws, and uniformity sought to be given them by punishments, they will try to avoid the punishment, but have no sense of shame." (*Analects* 2.3)

> "What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others." (*Analects* 15.23)

**The Analects.** The *Lunyu*, "collected sayings", was compiled by his followers and their students, probably over a long period from the 5th century BC into the early Han; how much records his actual words is debated. The traditional claim that he edited the Zhou classics, such as the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, is doubted by most modern scholars.

**The Hundred Schools.** The wars of the following centuries produced a burst of rival thinkers, called the **"Hundred Schools of Thought"**:
- **Mozi** (about 470–391 BC) preached **impartial care** for all people, not just one's family, attacked offensive war and costly rituals, and his followers became experts in defending cities.
- **Mencius** (about 372–289 BC), the second great Confucian, taught that human nature is **good** and that the people may rightfully overthrow a tyrant, who has lost the Mandate of Heaven.
- The **Daoists** and **Legalists**, in the next lesson on the Warring States.

The state of **Qi** supported scholars at the **Jixia** academy in its capital in the 4th century BC.

**After.** Confucius died believing he had failed. Under the **Han** dynasty (Stage 5), Confucianism became the official learning of the state, and for most of the next two thousand years Chinese officials were examined on Confucian texts.
Sparta: helots, the agoge and the Sparta:
The Greek city that turned its citizens into a permanent army, and the problem of seeing it through other people's eyes.

**Where.** **Laconia**, in the south-east of the Peloponnese, in the valley of the Eurotas. Sparta itself was a cluster of villages without walls. The Spartans called themselves **Lacedaemonians**.

**The conquest that shaped everything.** In the **8th and 7th centuries BC** Sparta conquered **Messenia**, the fertile land to its west, over the Taygetus mountains. The Messenians, and many Laconians, became **helots**: state-owned serfs tied to the land, who farmed it and handed over a share of the harvest. **The helots greatly outnumbered the Spartans**: Herodotus says seven helots attended each Spartan at Plataea in 479 BC.

**The Spartan system was built to hold them down.** Every year the officials declared war on the helots, so that killing one was not murder, and young men in the **krypteia** went out at night to murder those who seemed dangerous.

**The citizens.** Full citizens, the **Spartiates** or **homoioi** ("equals"), did no farming or trade. Each lived on an allotment worked by helots and owed a share to his **mess** (*syssition*), where he ate every evening with fifteen or so others. A man who could not pay lost his status.

**The agoge.** From **age seven** boys were taken from their families and raised in groups by the state: hunger, beatings, stealing food (and being punished only if caught), endurance and obedience. At twenty they joined the army and a mess; they lived in barracks until thirty and served until sixty.

**The government:**

| Body | Who |
| --- | --- |
| **Two kings** | from two royal families; led armies |
| **Gerousia** | council of 28 men over sixty, plus the kings |
| **Five ephors** | elected yearly; supervised even the kings |
| **The assembly** | all Spartiates; voted by shouting |

The Spartans credited it all to a lawgiver, **Lycurgus**, who may be legendary.

**Women.** Spartan girls exercised, ate well and married later than other Greeks, and Spartan women **owned property**: Aristotle says about two-fifths of the land in his day.

**Power.** From the 6th century BC Sparta led the **Peloponnesian League** of allied cities, and its hoplites were the best in Greece. Its most famous moment was **Thermopylae** in **480 BC** (lesson on the Persian Wars).

**Decline.** Spartiate numbers shrank: Herodotus gives about **8,000** in 480 BC; by Aristotle's time, the 330s, fewer than a thousand. Inheritance concentrated land in fewer hands, and citizens who fell below the line were never replaced. In **371 BC** **Thebes** crushed the Spartans at **Leuctra**, then freed Messenia. Sparta never recovered its power.

**The Spartan mirage.** This phrase, coined by the French scholar François Ollier in 1933, names the core problem. **Almost everything we know about Sparta was written by outsiders**, mainly Athenians and later writers like Plutarch (about AD 100), who either admired it as a model of discipline or used it to criticise their own cities. The Spartans themselves wrote little. Historians debate how far the classical picture is real and how far it is an idealised image; in Roman times Sparta even staged its old rituals for visitors. **Archaeology**, such as the votive offerings at the sanctuary of **Artemis Orthia**, shows Archaic Sparta richer in art and imports than the austere legend suggests.
Athens invents democracy: Solon to Ephia:
How one Greek city came to be governed by a vote of all its citizens, and who counted as a citizen.

**Where.** **Athens** and its territory, **Attica**, a peninsula of about 2,500 square kilometres in central Greece, with the silver mines of **Laurion** in the south.

**Solon (archon in 594 BC).** Athens was near civil war: poor farmers who borrowed against their own bodies were being sold into slavery. **Solon** was given power to reform. He **cancelled debts and banned debt slavery**, the "shaking off of burdens", and divided citizens into **four classes by wealth**, opening offices by property rather than birth. The poorest class, the **thetes**, could sit in the assembly.

**Tyranny.** **Pisistratus** seized power and, with his sons, ruled from 546 to 510 BC. Sparta helped drive out his son Hippias.

**Cleisthenes (508/7 BC): the founding of democracy.** After a struggle among aristocrats, **Cleisthenes** took the people's side and rebuilt the state:
- **Ten new tribes**, each mixing men from the city, the coast and the inland, to break the power of local clans.
- Some 140 **demes** (villages and city wards) as the basic unit; citizens registered by deme.
- A **Council of 500**, fifty from each tribe, chosen by lot, to prepare business for the assembly.
- **Ostracism**, perhaps his invention, first used in 487 BC: each year the citizens could vote, by scratching names on potsherds (*ostraka*), to exile one man for ten years.

**Ephialtes (462/1 BC)** stripped the old aristocratic council, the **Areopagus**, of most of its powers. Soon afterwards **Pericles** introduced **pay for jurors**, so the poor could serve.

**How it worked at its height:**

| Institution | How |
| --- | --- |
| **The assembly** (*ekklesia*) | all adult male citizens, meeting on the **Pnyx** hill about forty times a year; anyone could speak |
| **The council** | 500 by lot, one year's service |
| **The courts** | juries of hundreds, by lot, from a panel of 6,000 |
| **Officials** | most chosen **by lot**; only the ten **generals** and a few financial posts **elected** |

Lot was the democratic method: Athenians thought elections favoured the rich and famous.

**Who was excluded.** **Women**, **slaves** (perhaps tens of thousands, numbers debated), and **metics**, free foreigners resident in Athens. From **451 BC** a citizen needed an Athenian mother as well as father. Adult male citizens numbered perhaps **30,000 to 60,000** in the 5th century, out of a total population of Attica of perhaps a quarter of a million or more; all these figures are estimates.

**The debate: was it truly a democracy, and what made it possible?**
- **Radical and real:** more direct than any modern democracy; ordinary men decided war and peace and judged their leaders.
- **Built on others' labour:** slavery freed citizens' time, and the tribute of Athens' empire paid for the fleet and the salaries. Moses Finley and others stressed this.
- **The test case:** democracy survived the loss of empire in 404 BC and lasted until 322; pay for attending the assembly was even introduced around 400. That suggests empire helped but was not essential.

Ancient critics, including **Plato**, thought it rule by the ignorant. Its record, the trial of Socrates included, is still argued over.
Carthage: from Tyrian colony to western:
The Phoenician city in North Africa that became the great power of the western Mediterranean, long before its wars with Rome.

**Where.** On a peninsula in the **Gulf of Tunis**, in modern **Tunisia**, with two harbours facing the narrow strait between Africa and Sicily: the chokepoint of the western Mediterranean.

**Founding.** Legend says **Elissa** (Dido to the Romans), a princess of **Tyre**, fled her brother and founded the city in **814 BC**. The earliest archaeological finds date to the **late 9th or 8th century BC**, close enough to make the tradition plausible. The name is Phoenician, *Qart-hadasht*, "new city".

**From colony to leader.** As Tyre fell under Assyria and Babylon, Carthage took over leadership of the western Phoenician world. By the **6th century BC** it controlled or protected the Phoenician settlements of western Sicily, Sardinia, Ibiza, southern Spain and the North African coast.

**Rivals: the Greeks.** Greek colonists wanted the same coasts.

| Date (BC) | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **about 540** | **Alalia**, off Corsica: Carthage and the Etruscans fight Greek settlers from Phocaea, who abandon the island |
| **509?** | first **treaty with Rome**, recorded by Polybius, marking spheres of trade (the date is debated) |
| **480** | **Himera**: Gelon of Syracuse destroys a Carthaginian army in Sicily, by Greek tradition on the same day as Salamis |
| **409–405** | Carthage sacks the Greek cities of Selinous, Himera and Akragas |
| **397** | Dionysius I of Syracuse destroys the Carthaginian island town of **Motya** |
| **310–307** | **Agathocles** of Syracuse invades Africa itself; Carthage survives |

Sicily was a war zone between Carthage and the Greeks for two centuries, and neither could win it outright.

**How Carthage was governed.** Two annual chief magistrates, the **suffetes**, a council of elders, a court of 104 judges and a citizen assembly. **Aristotle**, writing about 330 BC, praised its constitution as one of the best, stable and mixed. Its armies were largely **mercenaries** and Libyan subjects; its citizens manned the fleet.

**Exploration.** A Greek text survives describing the voyage of **Hanno** down the **Atlantic coast of Africa**, perhaps in the 5th century BC, with colonists and a fight with hairy "gorillas". How far he went, to Senegal, Sierra Leone or Cameroon, is debated, and so is how much of the text is literal.

**The tophet: a real controversy.** At Carthage and other Phoenician sites are sanctuaries called **tophets**, with thousands of urns of the **burnt bones of infants** and young animals, from the 8th century BC to Roman times.
- **Child sacrifice:** Greek and Roman writers and the Bible accuse Phoenicians of it; inscriptions on the stones speak of vows fulfilled; the number of infants is very large.
- **A children's cemetery:** a 2010 study of the bones argued many were stillborn or died very young of natural causes, and that the hostile ancient writers were enemies.

The study was challenged in turn. Most specialists now lean towards **at least some sacrifice**, but the debate is not closed, and only more bone studies with agreed methods could close it.

**Where this leads.** In 300 BC Carthage was richer than Rome and the stronger sea power. Their wars, beginning in 264 BC, belong to Stage 5.
The Persian Wars, 499–479 BC:
How a few Greek cities defeated the invasions of the largest empire on Earth, and why the story looks different from Persepolis.

**The spark: the Ionian revolt (499–494 BC).** The Greek cities on the coast of Anatolia, ruled by Persia since Cyrus, rose up, led by **Aristagoras of Miletus**. **Athens** sent twenty ships and **Eretria** five; the rebels burned **Sardis**, the Persian provincial capital, in 498. Persia crushed the revolt at the sea battle of **Lade** and sacked **Miletus** in **494 BC**.

**First invasion: Marathon (490 BC).** Darius sent a fleet under **Datis and Artaphernes** to punish Athens and Eretria. Eretria was burned. The Persians landed at **Marathon**, 40 km from Athens. About 10,000 Athenians and their allies the **Plataeans**, led by **Miltiades**, charged and won. Herodotus counts **6,400 Persian dead to 192 Athenian**. The modern marathon race comes from a later legend of a runner to Athens.

**Between the invasions.** In **483 BC** a rich vein of silver was found at **Laurion**. **Themistocles** persuaded the Athenians to spend it on a fleet of **two hundred triremes**, oared warships, rather than share it out. **It was the decision that saved Greece.**

**Second invasion (480–479 BC).** **Xerxes**, Darius's son, came in person, bridging the Hellespont with boats and digging a canal through the Athos peninsula.

| Date | Battle | What happened |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **August 480** | **Thermopylae** | **Leonidas** and **300 Spartans**, with several thousand allies, held a narrow pass for three days until a local man showed the Persians a path round; the Spartans died fighting |
| **August 480** | **Artemisium** | the Greek fleet fought the Persian navy to a draw nearby |
| **September 480** | **Athens** | evacuated; the Persians burned the Acropolis |
| **September 480** | **Salamis** | in the narrow strait, the Greek fleet, Athenian ships at its heart, destroyed much of the Persian navy; Xerxes went home |
| **August 479** | **Plataea** | the Spartan regent **Pausanias** led the largest Greek army ever fielded and defeated **Mardonius**, who was killed |
| **479** | **Mycale** | the Greeks burned the Persian fleet on the Anatolian coast |

**How big was Xerxes' army?** Herodotus gives **1.7 million** fighting men. **No modern historian accepts this**: Greece could not have fed them. Most modern estimates are in the low hundreds of thousands at most, and some far lower; the fleet, which Herodotus puts at 1,207 warships, is also usually cut down. The honest answer is that **the army was very large and its size is unknown**.

**How many Greeks?** Fewer than one in ten Greek cities fought. After the victory, the allies set up a bronze **Serpent Column** at Delphi naming **thirty-one** states. It survives in **Istanbul**.

**Why did the Greeks win? Two readings:**
- **The Greek reading** (Herodotus, Aeschylus' play *The Persians*, 472 BC): free men fighting for their own cities beat the subjects of a despot.
- **The Persian-centred reading** (historians such as Pierre Briant, using Persian sources): the Greek campaigns were a costly **frontier setback** for an empire whose heart was elsewhere. Narrow seas and passes cancelled Persian numbers, and Persia stayed the greatest power.

Both can be true at once: decisive for Greece, marginal for Persia. Persian records of the war would settle much, and none have yet been found.
Athens' fifth-century empire and the age:
Fifty years in which Athens became an empire and produced much of what later ages called "classical".

**The Delian League (478/7 BC).** After the Persian Wars, Athens led a new alliance of Aegean and Ionian cities to keep fighting Persia. Its treasury was on the sacred island of **Delos**. Members gave ships or, more and more, money.

**From league to empire:**
- About **470 BC** **Naxos** tried to leave and was forced back.
- About **466 BC** the Athenian general **Cimon** crushed a Persian force at the **Eurymedon** river.
- In **454 BC** the treasury was moved to **Athens**. A sixtieth of each year's tribute went to Athena, and the records of those payments, carved on stone, survive as the **Athenian Tribute Lists**.
- Athens imposed garrisons, settlers, courts and, at some point, its coins and measures on members.

**Pericles.** An aristocrat and democratic leader, elected general almost every year from 443 until his death in **429 BC**. Thucydides says Athens was in name a democracy but in fact ruled by its first citizen. His partner, **Aspasia** of Miletus, was famous for her intelligence and attacked for her influence.

**The Acropolis rebuilt.** With league money, over its allies' protests:
- The **Parthenon**, temple of Athena, built **447–432 BC** under the sculptor **Phidias**, with a gold-and-ivory statue of the goddess about 12 metres tall.
- The **Propylaea** gateway, and later the Erechtheion and the temple of Athena Nike.

Much of the Parthenon's sculpture was taken to Britain by Lord Elgin's agents in 1801–12 and is in the **British Museum**; Greece asks for it back.

**A burst of thought and art:**

| Field | Who (5th century BC) |
| --- | --- |
| **Tragedy** | **Aeschylus**, **Sophocles**, **Euripides**, performed at the festival of Dionysus |
| **Comedy** | **Aristophanes**, who mocked Pericles' successors, Socrates and the war |
| **History** | **Herodotus**, who read his work in Athens; **Thucydides** |
| **Philosophy** | the **sophists**, paid teachers of argument such as Protagoras; **Socrates**, who wrote nothing |
| **Medicine** | **Hippocrates** of Kos and his school, explaining disease by natural causes |

**Was the empire good or bad for the allies?** Thucydides presents it as a **tyranny** that the subjects hated. Some modern historians, notably G. E. M. de Ste. Croix, argued that the **ordinary people** of allied cities often favoured Athens, which backed democrats against local oligarchs, and that the hatred was mostly among the rich. The pattern of revolts, who led them and who opposed them, is the evidence each side uses.

**Peace with Persia?** Later writers mention a **Peace of Callias** (about 449 BC) ending the war with Persia. Thucydides does not, and historians still argue over whether it existed.

**The cost.** Sparta and its ally **Corinth** watched Athenian power grow with alarm. A **Thirty Years' Peace** was signed in 446/5 BC. It lasted fifteen.
Primary source: Pericles' Funeral Oratio:
The most famous description of Athenian democracy, delivered by its leader, as written by a historian who may have heard it. Read for what it says and for what kind of evidence it is.

**The setting.** Winter **431/430 BC**, the first year of the Peloponnesian War. Athens held a public funeral for the year's dead, and **Pericles** was chosen to speak. The speech is in **Thucydides**, *History of the Peloponnesian War*, Book 2, chapters 35–46.

**The text** (translated by **Richard Crawley**, 1874):

> "Our constitution does not copy the laws of neighbouring states; we are rather a pattern to others than imitators ourselves. Its administration favours the many instead of the few; this is why it is called a democracy." (2.37)

> "Our public men have, besides politics, their private affairs to attend to, and our ordinary citizens, though occupied with the pursuits of industry, are still fair judges of public matters; for, unlike any other nation, regarding him who takes no part in these duties not as unambitious but as useless, we Athenians are able to judge at all events if we cannot originate, and, instead of looking on discussion as a stumbling-block in the way of action, we think it an indispensable preliminary to any wise action at all." (2.40)

> "In short, I say that as a city we are the school of Hellas" (2.41)

> "Great will be your glory in not falling short of your natural character; and greatest will be hers who is least talked of among the men, whether for good or for bad." (2.45, addressed to the widows)

**Read it closely:**

| Line | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| **"favours the many instead of the few"** | the Greek definition of democracy: rule in the interest of the majority |
| **"not as unambitious but as useless"** | participation as a duty. Greeks called a man who kept to his private affairs an *idiōtēs*, the root of English *idiot* |
| **discussion "an indispensable preliminary"** | debate before action, against the Spartan habit of silence |
| **"the school of Hellas"** | a boast of cultural leadership, made while Athens ruled an empire of other Greeks |
| **the widows' line** | the limits: the ideal woman is the one **never spoken of** |

**What kind of evidence is it?** Thucydides tells us himself, in Book 1:

> "it was in all cases difficult to carry them word for word in one's memory, so my habit has been to make the speakers say what was in my opinion demanded of them by the various occasions, of course adhering as closely as possible to the general sense of what they really said." (1.22)

So the speech is **Thucydides' version**, written years later, of what Pericles said or should have said. Historians debate how close it is: some think it preserves Pericles' real argument, others that it is largely Thucydides' own portrait of Athens at its height.

**What comes next on the page.** The very next chapters describe the **plague** of 430 BC, with bodies piled in the temples and law forgotten. Pericles himself died of it in 429. **Thucydides put the ideal and its collapse side by side**, and that placement is part of what he is saying.

**What to take from it.** A genuine statement of the democratic ideal, a piece of wartime propaganda, and a literary reconstruction, all at once. Reading it well means holding all three.
The Peloponnesian War, 431–404 BC:
Twenty-seven years of war between Athens and Sparta, which ended the Athenian empire and exhausted Greece.

**The sides.** **Athens** and its empire: the strongest navy, the money of the tribute, and the **Long Walls** joining the city to its port at Piraeus. **Sparta** and the **Peloponnesian League**, with Corinth and Thebes: the best army on land.

**The cause: the oldest debate in history-writing.** Thucydides gave the immediate disputes (over Corcyra, Potidaea, and the trade ban Athens imposed on **Megara**), then said the truest cause was something else: **the growth of Athenian power and the fear this caused in Sparta** (1.23, paraphrased).
- **Thucydides' reading:** structural; a rising power and a fearful one made war likely. In 2017 Graham Allison popularised this as the **"Thucydides Trap"**, applied to the United States and China, and classicists have criticised that use.
- **Others blame choices:** Donald Kagan argued the war was **avoidable**, and that Pericles misjudged the Megarian decree; G. E. M. de Ste. Croix argued **Sparta and Corinth** were the aggressors.

**The war in three parts:**

| Phase | Dates (BC) | What happened |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The Archidamian War** | 431–421 | Sparta invades Attica each year; **Pericles' strategy** keeps Athenians behind the walls and uses the fleet. **Plague** (430–426) kills perhaps a quarter to a third of the crowded city, and Pericles (429). At **Pylos** in 425 about 120 Spartiates surrender, shocking Greece. Sparta's **Brasidas** takes **Amphipolis** in 424, and Thucydides, the general responsible, is exiled. The **Peace of Nicias** follows in 421 |
| **The Sicilian disaster** | 415–413 | Athens attacks **Syracuse** with a vast fleet; its leader **Alcibiades**, recalled for trial, defects to Sparta. In **413** the whole force is destroyed and the survivors die in the Syracusan quarries |
| **The Ionian (Decelean) War** | 413–404 | Sparta fortifies **Decelea** in Attica; 20,000 slaves flee, says Thucydides. **Persia** funds a Spartan fleet. An oligarchic coup in Athens (411) fails. The Spartan admiral **Lysander** destroys the Athenian fleet at **Aegospotami** (405). Athens, starved, surrenders in **404** |

**The brutality.** The war hardened behaviour. In **416 BC** Athens besieged neutral **Melos**, killed its men and enslaved its women and children. Thucydides' **Melian Dialogue** puts the logic of power bluntly in the Athenians' mouths: the strong do what they can, the weak suffer what they must (paraphrase).

**After the surrender.** Athens' walls were pulled down and Sparta installed the **Thirty Tyrants**, who killed perhaps 1,500 citizens. Democracy was restored in **403**. In **399 BC** a democratic court condemned **Socrates** to death; his pupil **Plato** spent his life arguing against the city that killed him, and Plato's pupil **Aristotle** came to Athens in 367.

**The 4th century: no one wins for long.**
- Persia's **King's Peace** (387/386 BC) handed the Ionian Greeks back to the Great King.
- **Thebes**, under **Epaminondas**, broke Sparta at **Leuctra** (371) and led Greece until his death at **Mantinea** (362).
- In 401 BC, 10,000 Greek mercenaries marched out of the heart of Persia after a failed revolt, a story told by **Xenophon** in his *Anabasis*. It suggested Persia could be beaten.

**Why it matters.** The Greek cities wore one another out. The power that profited was in the north: **Macedon**.
Laozi, Shang Yang and the Warring States:
China's most violent centuries produced its harshest statecraft and its most mystical philosophy, side by side.

**The Warring States (475–221 BC).** The start date varies by convention (481, 475 or 403 BC). In **453 BC** the great state of **Jin** was split among three of its noble families, recognised in 403 as **Han, Zhao and Wei**. Seven major states remained: **Qin** in the far west, **Chu** on the middle Yangtze (the largest), **Qi** on the east coast, **Han, Zhao and Wei** in the centre and north, and **Yan** around modern Beijing.

**War changed.** The chariot battles of aristocrats gave way to **mass infantry armies of conscripted peasants**, numbering in the hundreds of thousands according to the sources (numbers that are probably inflated, but show the scale).
- **Iron** weapons and tools, and the **crossbow**, with a bronze trigger mechanism, which a peasant could learn quickly.
- **Cavalry**: in **307 BC** King **Wuling of Zhao** made his soldiers adopt nomad trousers and fight as mounted archers, copying the steppe.
- **Long walls** of rammed earth between states and against the nomads, the forerunners of the Great Wall.
- The *Art of War*, attributed to **Sunzi**, probably compiled in these centuries.

**States changed too.** Rulers replaced hereditary lords with **appointed officials** paid in grain, divided land into **counties**, registered households, taxed farmers directly and issued bronze coins shaped like **spades and knives**.

**Shang Yang and Qin.** **Shang Yang** served Duke Xiao of Qin from about **356 to 338 BC**. His reforms:
- Households grouped in fives and tens, **collectively responsible** for each other's crimes, and rewarded for denouncing them.
- **Ranks earned by merit in war** (counted, in principle, in enemy heads) and in farming, not by birth.
- Harsh, published laws applied to all; standard weights and measures; new counties under officials.

When his patron died, his enemies had him executed. **But Qin kept his system**, and it made Qin the most efficient war state in China. The thinking behind it is called **Legalism**: people respond to reward and punishment, not to virtue, so the state should rely on clear law. It is the opposite of Confucius's rule by example.

**Laozi and Daoism.** **Laozi**, "the Old Master", is traditionally an archivist at the Zhou court and an older contemporary of Confucius. But the historian **Sima Qian**, writing about 100 BC, already was not sure who he was, and many scholars doubt he was a single historical person. The book under his name, the *Daodejing*, about 5,000 characters, was probably put together in the 4th century BC. Parts of it were found on **bamboo slips** in a tomb at **Guodian** (sealed about 300 BC, excavated 1993), the oldest copy known.

Its opening, in **James Legge's** translation (1891):

> "The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao. The name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name."

**Daoism**, as history records it, taught following the **Dao**, the way of nature, through *wuwei*, "non-action" or effortless action; it mocked Confucian ritual and Legalist control alike.

**Where it leads.** In the next century **Qin** conquered all the others, and in **221 BC** its king became the First Emperor (Stage 5). The Legalist state won the war, and Confucian and Daoist thought outlasted it.
Early Rome: from kings to the conquest o:
A small town on the Tiber, a list of legendary kings, a republic, and by 300 BC the leading power in Italy.

**Where.** **Rome** grew on hills by the **Tiber**, at the point where the river could be crossed, about 25 km from the sea, in **Latium**, the land of the Latins, between Etruria to the north and the Greek cities to the south.

**The founding: legend and archaeology.** Roman tradition said **Romulus** founded Rome in **753 BC** and that seven kings ruled until 509. Archaeology shows huts on the **Palatine** hill from at least the 10th–9th centuries BC, and by the late 7th century the **Forum** valley was drained and paved, and Rome was becoming a city. The last kings, the **Tarquins**, were of Etruscan origin, and Rome took much from Etruria: temple building, the symbols of office, divination.

**The republic (traditionally 509 BC).** The Romans said they expelled the last king, **Tarquin the Proud**, and replaced him with **two consuls**, elected each year, so that no one man held power. The **Senate**, a council of former officials, advised and in practice guided policy.

**The Struggle of the Orders (494–287 BC).** Rome was divided between **patricians**, a closed group of old families, and **plebeians**, everyone else.

| Date (BC) | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **494** | first "secession": the plebeians walk out; **tribunes of the plebs** created to protect them |
| **451–450** | the **Twelve Tables**, Rome's first written laws |
| **367** | the Licinian–Sextian laws; from **366** one consul may be plebeian |
| **287** | the **Hortensian law**: votes of the plebeian assembly bind all Romans |

The result was not democracy but a new **patrician-plebeian nobility** that shared office.

**Expansion.** Rome took the Etruscan city of **Veii** in **396 BC** after a long war. About 390 the **Gauls** sacked Rome (lesson on the Celts), a humiliation never forgotten. Then:
- The **Latin War** (340–338 BC). Rome's settlement afterwards was its master stroke: some Latins became **Roman citizens**, others got partial rights, and all became allies who **supplied soldiers**. **Rome grew by adding manpower, not only land.**
- The **Samnite Wars** (343–290 BC) against the hill peoples of the central Apennines. A Roman army was humiliated at the **Caudine Forks** (321), but Rome won in the end.
- The **Via Appia**, Rome's first great road, from Rome towards Capua, begun in **312 BC**.

**How much of this is true? A real debate.** Rome's first historians wrote about **200 BC**, and **Livy**, the fullest source, wrote after 30 BC. Livy himself says most records were lost when the Gauls burned the city.
- **Optimists** (such as Tim Cornell, 1995) think the outline, institutions and many names were passed down in family records and official lists, and that archaeology fits it.
- **Sceptics** think much was reconstructed later, shaped by family pride and the politics of the late republic.
