(This is a paraphrase, not a quotation.) *Dhamma* (Sanskrit *dharma*) here means a moral way of life: respect for parents and elders, kindness to servants and animals, generosity to Brahmins and ascetics, and **tolerance of all sects**.

**The edicts.** Ashoka had his messages cut on **rock faces and polished stone pillars** across his empire, from **Kandahar** in Afghanistan to Karnataka in the south. Most are in **Prakrit** in the **Brahmi** script; in the north-west, **Kharosthi**; at Kandahar, in **Greek and Aramaic**. The Thirteenth Edict even names five Greek kings in the West, including Antiochus and Ptolemy, as recipients of his dhamma missions. The script was deciphered by **James Prinsep** in **1837**, and the Ashoka of Buddhist legend was proved to be the "Beloved of the Gods, Piyadasi" of the inscriptions by a find at **Maski** in **1915**.

**Buddhism.** Ashoka became a lay **Buddhist**, built stupas, and, by tradition, sent his son **Mahinda** to bring Buddhism to **Sri Lanka**. His **lion capital** from **Sarnath** is now India's national emblem, and the **wheel** from his pillars is on India's flag.

**How far did dhamma actually govern? A real debate:**
- **One reading** sees a genuine moral revolution in kingship, with officials (*dhamma-mahamattas*) appointed to spread it.
- **Another**, associated with the historian **Romila Thapar**, sees dhamma also as a **policy of unity** for a huge, diverse empire; and notes that Ashoka **did not give Kalinga back** and warned forest peoples that he still had power to punish.

Both readings use the same edicts; the question is how to read a king's words about himself.

**The empire itself** was probably not uniform: a tightly governed core in the Ganges plain, provincial capitals such as **Taxila** and **Ujjain**, and loosely held outer regions.

**The end.** After Ashoka the empire weakened and shrank. In about **185 BC** the last Maurya, Brihadratha, was killed by his general **Pushyamitra**, who founded the **Shunga** dynasty. India would not be so widely united again until the Guptas, and not as widely until the Mughals.
The Kushans, the Indo-Greeks and the nor:
After the Mauryas, north-west India and Afghanistan became a meeting place of peoples: Greek kings, steppe nomads, Parthians, and finally the Kushans, whose empire joined Central Asia to the Ganges.

**The Indo-Greeks** (about **180 BC–AD 10**). Greek kings from Bactria pushed into the Punjab and beyond. We know of over thirty of them, mostly **from their coins**, which carry Greek on one side and an Indian language in Kharosthi script on the other. The most famous is **Menander** (Milinda, mid-100s BC). At **Vidisha** in central India, a pillar set up by **Heliodorus**, a Greek ambassador from Taxila, around **110 BC**, honours the Hindu god **Vasudeva** (Krishna), a Greek describing himself as a devotee of an Indian god.

**The steppe comes south.** The Han Chinese and the Xiongnu set off a chain of migrations. The **Yuezhi**, driven from western China by the Xiongnu in the **170s–160s BC**, moved west and by about **130 BC** had overrun **Bactria**, ending the Greek kingdom. Other nomads, the **Sakas** (Scythians), moved into north-west India, followed by **Indo-Parthian** kings such as **Gondophares** (early first century AD).

**The Kushans.** One of five Yuezhi clans, the Kushans united the others under **Kujula Kadphises** in the first century AD and expanded into India. The empire peaked under **Kanishka I**. **His accession date has been debated for over a century**; the most widely accepted modern date is about **AD 127**, from the work of Harry Falk, but older proposals ranged from 78 to the 140s.

**The Rabatak inscription**, found in northern **Afghanistan** in **1993**, is a key source. Written in **Bactrian** (an Iranian language) in Greek letters, it records Kanishka's genealogy and lists Indian cities under his rule, apparently reaching to the middle Ganges.

**An empire of crossroads.** At its height the Kushan realm ran from **Uzbekistan and Tajikistan** through **Afghanistan and Pakistan** to **Mathura** in northern India, with capitals at **Purushapura** (Peshawar) and Mathura. It controlled the routes where the Silk Roads met the roads to India's ports. A hoard of goods found at **Begram**, north of Kabul, in the 1930s held **Roman glass and bronzes, Indian ivories, and Chinese lacquer** together.

**Gods on coins.** Kushan coins show a crowd of gods: Greek (Helios), Iranian (Mithra, the wind god Oado), Indian (Shiva), and **the Buddha**, labelled in Greek letters *BODDO*. The Kushans seem to have patronised many religions at once.

**Buddhism and the first Buddha images.** Kushan rule saw a great flowering of Buddhist art and the growth of **Mahayana** Buddhism, and tradition makes Kanishka the patron of a Buddhist council in Kashmir. In early Buddhist art the Buddha was shown only by **symbols**, a footprint, an empty throne, a tree. Under the Kushans, **human images of the Buddha** appeared in two schools:

| School | Where | Style |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Gandhara** | around Peshawar and Taxila | Greco-Roman influence: wavy hair, draped robes like a toga |
| **Mathura** | on the Yamuna | Indian traditions: rounder forms, lighter robes |

**Which came first is disputed.** Both appear around the first or second century AD. The answer turns on dating sculptures that are seldom inscribed with clear dates.

**The road to China.** Buddhist monks from Kushan lands carried the faith **north and east** into the Tarim Basin and China. Among the first translators in China was **Lokaksema**, a Kushan monk working at Luoyang in the **late 100s**.

**Decline.** From the **230s**, the Sasanians took over Bactria, where governors called **Kushanshahs** ruled for them, and Kushan power shrank to the Punjab. In the Ganges plain, the space was filled by new Indian dynasties, among them the Guptas.
The Satavahanas, the Tamil kingdoms and:
While the north was ruled by foreign dynasties, peninsular India built its own kingdoms, grew rich on sea trade with Rome, and kept a literature that still survives. At the end of this stage, a new dynasty rose in the old Mauryan heartland.

**The Satavahanas** (also called Andhras) ruled the **Deccan**, the plateau of central India, from about the **first century BC** to the early **third century AD**. When they began is debated, with proposals from the late third century BC to the first century BC. Their capital was **Pratishthana** (Paithan, Maharashtra).

- Their greatest king, **Gautamiputra Satakarni** (early second century AD), defeated the **Western Kshatrapas**, Saka rulers of western India. An inscription by his mother, **Gautami Balashri**, in a Buddhist cave at **Nashik**, records his victories.
- Kings were often named after their **mothers**, an unusual custom among Indian dynasties.
- They supported **Brahmins** and **Buddhist monasteries** alike. The rock-cut halls at **Karla** and **Nashik**, and the earliest caves at **Ajanta**, belong to this era, as does the great stupa at **Amaravati**.

**A Saka king writes in Sanskrit.** The Western Kshatrapa **Rudradaman I** left an inscription on a rock at **Junagadh** (Gujarat) in about **AD 150**. It is one of the earliest long inscriptions in classical **Sanskrit**, and it records the repair of a dam on the **Sudarshana lake**, first built, it says, under **Chandragupta Maurya** more than four centuries before. The same rock carries an edict of Ashoka.

**The Tamil south.** Beyond both empires lay three Tamil kingdoms, already named in Ashoka's edicts as independent neighbours:

| Kingdom | Region |
| --- | --- |
| **Chera** | the Malabar coast (modern Kerala) |
| **Chola** | the Kaveri delta (Tamil Nadu's east coast) |
| **Pandya** | the far south, around **Madurai** |

Their world is known from **Sangam literature**, Tamil poems of love and war, dated very roughly between the first century BC and the third century AD (the dating is debated). They describe ships bringing gold and wine and taking away pepper.

**Rome's trade with India.** After Rome took Egypt in 30 BC, Greek and Egyptian ships sailed from Red Sea ports to India with the **monsoon winds**. Hoards of **Roman gold and silver coins**, many from the first century AD, have been found in south India. At **Arikamedu**, near Pondicherry, Roman wine jars and pottery have been excavated. A papyrus from the second century records a cargo shipped from **Muziris**, on the Kerala coast, worth a great fortune. The Indian Ocean trade is the subject of this stage's connections lesson.

**Sri Lanka.** The island's kings at **Anuradhapura** adopted **Buddhism**, by tradition in the time of Ashoka (third century BC). Its chronicles, the *Dipavamsa* and *Mahavamsa*, written in the fourth to sixth centuries AD, are a major source for Buddhist history across South Asia, though their early sections mix history and legend.

**The Satavahanas fade** in the early third century, splitting into smaller dynasties such as the **Ikshvakus** of the Krishna valley.

**The first Guptas.** In **Magadha**, the Mauryas' old heartland, a minor family rose. Its king **Chandragupta I** (not to be confused with Chandragupta Maurya) came to power around **319–320**; the **Gupta era**, a calendar later used across north India, starts then. He married **Kumaradevi**, a princess of the powerful **Licchavi** clan, and gold coins show the royal couple together. Their son **Samudragupta**, from about 335, would conquer widely. The Gupta age, often called India's classical age, belongs to Stage 6.
Qin Shi Huang unifies China:
In 221 BC the king of Qin finished conquering the last of the Warring States and declared himself the First Emperor. His dynasty lasted fifteen years. The idea of a single Chinese empire lasted until 1912.

**Qin before the conquest.** Qin, in the Wei river valley in the north-west, had been remade in the **350s–340s BC** by the minister **Shang Yang**, along the lines of the school later called **Legalism**: harsh laws applied to all, rewards for farming and fighting, ranks earned by heads taken in battle, and households grouped in fives and tens and held responsible for each other's crimes.

**The conquest.** **Ying Zheng**, born in **259 BC**, became king of Qin in **246** as a boy. Between **230 and 221 BC** his armies destroyed the six other kingdoms one after another: **Han, Zhao, Wei, Chu, Yan, and finally Qi**. He took a new title, **Huangdi**, combining words for the god-like rulers of legend, and called himself **Shi Huangdi**, "First Emperor", meaning his heirs to be numbered for ten thousand generations.

**What he imposed, with his chancellor Li Si:**

| Measure | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| **36 commanderies** (later more) | the old kingdoms abolished; officials appointed and paid by the centre, not hereditary lords |
| **One script** | the small-seal script standardised, so one written Chinese could be read across the empire, whatever the spoken dialect |
| **One currency, one set of weights and measures** | round bronze coins with a square hole, a shape used for 2,000 years |
| **One axle width** | so carts fit the ruts of the new roads |
| **Roads and canals** | thousands of kilometres of roads; the **Lingqu canal** (214 BC) linking the Yangtze and Pearl river systems for the conquest of the south |
| **Walls** | the general **Meng Tian** drove the Xiongnu out of the Ordos (215 BC) and linked older walls along the north. This is **not** the stone Great Wall seen today, which is mostly **Ming**, from the 1400s–1600s |

**The burning of the books.** In **213 BC**, on Li Si's advice, private copies of the **old histories, poetry and philosophy** were ordered burned, except books on medicine, divination and farming, and Qin's own records. In **212**, according to the historian **Sima Qian**, some **460 scholars** were executed. **The story is debated.** Sima Qian wrote under the Han, who had every reason to paint Qin as monstrous; some scholars think the "burying of the scholars" was exaggerated or partly invented later, and that the book ban was narrower than the legend. Others accept the core of the account.

**What new evidence shows.** In **1975**, bamboo slips with **Qin legal texts** were found in a tomb at **Shuihudi** (Hubei), and in **2002** tens of thousands of administrative slips at **Liye** (Hunan). They show a state that was harsh but also **systematic and bureaucratic**: detailed rules, records of grain and labour, appeals and procedures. They complicate the Han picture of pure tyranny.

**The terracotta army.** In **1974**, farmers digging a well near **Xi'an** found pieces of clay soldiers. The pits around the First Emperor's tomb are estimated to hold some **8,000** life-sized warriors, with horses and chariots, each face individually finished. The burial mound itself is **unexcavated**. Sima Qian described rivers of **mercury** inside; soil tests on the mound have found unusually high mercury levels.

**The collapse.** The emperor died on a tour in **210 BC**. Li Si and the eunuch **Zhao Gao** forged his will to put a younger son on the throne. In **209**, two conscripts, **Chen Sheng and Wu Guang**, led a rising; in Sima Qian's story, they had been delayed by rain and faced death for arriving late. (The Qin legal texts suggest lateness was punished by a **fine**, which shows how the Han account may have been sharpened.) Revolt spread; the last Qin ruler surrendered in **207–206 BC**.

**The verdict** in Chinese tradition was long that Qin fell because it **ruled by terror**. Yet every later dynasty kept its central achievement: **one emperor, one bureaucracy, one script**.
The Han dynasty and Emperor Wu:
The Han ruled China for four centuries, with one break, and gave their name to the Chinese people: the Han Chinese. Its most forceful emperor, Wu, doubled its territory.

**The founding.** After Qin fell, two rebel leaders fought for the empire: the aristocratic general **Xiang Yu** and **Liu Bang**, a minor official of peasant birth. Liu Bang won at **Gaixia** in **202 BC** (the dynasty usually dates itself from 206) and became Emperor **Gaozu**, with his capital at **Chang'an** (near Xi'an).

**Qin's system, gentler.** Han kept the centralised state but **cut taxes and softened laws**. At first it gave half the empire to **kings**, many of them Liu relatives. After the **Rebellion of the Seven States** (**154 BC**) was crushed, their power was steadily reduced.

**Han periods:**

| Period | Dates | Capital |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Western (Former) Han** | 206/202 BC–AD 9 | Chang'an |
| **Xin dynasty** of **Wang Mang**, a regent who took the throne | AD 9–23 | Chang'an |
| **Eastern (Later) Han** | AD 25–220 | **Luoyang** |

**Emperor Wu** (*Wudi*, "the Martial Emperor") reigned **141–87 BC**, fifty-four years:

- **Confucianism made state learning.** Influenced by the scholar **Dong Zhongshu**, Wu set up an **Imperial Academy** in **124 BC** to teach the **Confucian classics**, and had local officials recommend men for office for their learning and filial conduct. This was not yet the later examination system, but it began the long marriage of **Confucian learning and government service**. In practice Han rule mixed Confucian ideals with Legalist methods.
- **Monopolies on salt and iron** (from about **119–117 BC**) to pay for war. After Wu's death they were argued over at court, in **81 BC**, in a debate written up as the *Discourses on Salt and Iron*, an early argument over **state control of the economy** versus moral government and light taxes.
- **Wars and expansion:**

| Direction | Conquest |
| --- | --- |
| **North and north-west** | wars against the **Xiongnu** (from 133 BC); the **Hexi corridor** in Gansu taken and garrisoned |
| **Far west** | an army sent to **Ferghana** (Dayuan) in Central Asia for its famous horses (104–101 BC) |
| **South** | the kingdom of **Nanyue** (around Guangzhou and northern Vietnam) conquered, **111 BC** |
| **North-east** | **Gojoseon** in Korea conquered, **108 BC** |

**The costs.** The wars emptied the treasury, and Wu's last years were dark: a **witchcraft scandal** in **91 BC** led to the deaths of the crown prince and thousands of others. An edict in which Wu expresses regret for the burdens of war is recorded in the official history, though some historians doubt it is genuine.

**How big was Han?** A census from **AD 2**, one of the earliest surviving national counts in the world, recorded about **58 million** people. It is among the best population figures of the ancient world, though it counts registered households, not everyone.

**Wang Mang's interlude.** The regent Wang Mang took the throne in **AD 9** and tried radical reforms: **nationalising land**, abolishing the sale of slaves, new coinages. Then, around **AD 11**, the **Yellow River** burst its banks and changed course, flooding the north China plain. Famine bred rebellions, among them the **Red Eyebrows**. Wang Mang was killed in **23**. Historians debate whether he was a usurper whose reforms were doomed, or a reformer undone by a natural disaster beyond anyone's control.

**The Eastern Han** was restored by **Liu Xiu** (Emperor **Guangwu**) in **25**, and ruled from Luoyang. Its general **Ban Chao** reasserted Chinese power in the **Tarim Basin** from the **70s** to **102**.
The Xiongnu and Zhang Qian's journey wes:
On China's northern frontier lived the first great empire of the steppe. To fight it, Emperor Wu sent an envoy into the unknown west. His thirteen-year journey opened the roads later called the Silk Road.

**The Xiongnu.** Herding peoples of the Mongolian steppe, united under a ruler called the **chanyu**. In **209 BC**, the young **Modu** took power by killing his father (Sima Qian tells the story of an archery test with whistling arrows, perhaps legendary). He crushed rival peoples, drove the **Yuezhi** out of Gansu, and built a confederation stretching from Manchuria to the Tarim Basin.

**Why the steppe was dangerous.** Every man was a mounted archer; armies could move far and fast; and nomads could retreat into grasslands where Chinese infantry could not follow or feed itself. What the nomads needed from China was **grain, silk, metal and luxury goods**, by trade or by raid.

**The heqin system.** In **200 BC** Modu surrounded the Han founder **Gaozu** at **Baideng** (near modern Datong) for seven days. Gaozu escaped and made a treaty, the **heqin** ("peace through kinship"): a **Han princess** married to the chanyu, and yearly gifts of **silk, grain and wine**. In effect, China paid tribute, while describing it as generosity.

**Wu's war.** Wu ended the policy. From **133 BC** Han armies under the generals **Wei Qing** and **Huo Qubing** struck deep into the steppe; in **121–119 BC** they drove the Xiongnu north of the Gobi and won the **Hexi corridor**, where Han founded four commanderies, among them **Dunhuang**. The cost in men and horses was enormous on both sides.

**After Wu.** Weakened by war and succession struggles, the Xiongnu split. In **51 BC** one chanyu, **Huhanye**, came to the Han court and accepted vassal status. In **AD 48** the confederation divided into **Southern Xiongnu**, who settled inside the Chinese frontier, and **Northern Xiongnu**, whom Han armies defeated in **89–91**. An inscription that Han's victorious general had carved on a mountain cliff was identified in Mongolia in **2017**.

**Zhang Qian.** Around **139–138 BC**, Wu sent a court officer, **Zhang Qian**, west with about **a hundred men** to find the **Yuezhi** and persuade them to join an alliance against the Xiongnu.

| Stage | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| **Captured** | taken by the Xiongnu almost at once; held about **ten years**; married a Xiongnu wife |
| **Escape west** | reached **Dayuan** (Ferghana valley), then **Kangju** (Sogdiana) |
| **The Yuezhi** | found them settled in **Bactria**, prosperous and with no wish to return and fight |
| **Return** | captured again by the Xiongnu; escaped; home in **126 BC** with only **one** of his companions, his wife with him |

**What he reported.** Zhang Qian described lands no Chinese had seen: **Ferghana's** "heavenly horses", the cities of **Bactria**, **Anxi** (Parthia), and **Shendu** (India). In Bactria's markets he saw **cloth and bamboo canes from Sichuan**, which merchants said came by way of India, proof that Chinese goods already travelled west by routes the court did not know. His report survives in Sima Qian's *Shiji*.

**What followed.** Wu sent embassies west every year; Zhang Qian led a second mission (about **119–115 BC**) to the **Wusun** of the Ili valley. Han garrisons, beacon towers and walls reached to **Dunhuang** and beyond. **Silk** began to flow west in quantity, and grapes and alfalfa came east.

**The name "Silk Road"** is modern: the German geographer **Ferdinand von Richthofen** coined *Seidenstraße* in **1877**. It was never one road but a **network** of routes, and silk was only one of many goods.

**Two debates.**
- **Were the Xiongnu a state?** One reading (Thomas Barfield's) sees an imperial confederation that existed **to extract wealth from China**, rising and falling with it. Others give more weight to the Xiongnu's own institutions, revealed by excavated tombs at sites like **Noin-Ula** in Mongolia.
- **Were the Xiongnu the ancestors of the Huns** who reached Europe in the 370s? The names may be related, and some ancient-DNA studies suggest partial links, but a continuous people across 300 years and 6,000 km has not been shown.
Han inventions, Sima Qian and the fall o:
The Han left two things above all: a set of inventions and techniques that spread across the world, and a way of writing history that every later Chinese dynasty copied. Then, after a long decline, the dynasty broke apart in 220.

**Paper.** The official history credits the court eunuch **Cai Lun** with presenting paper made from bark, hemp, rags and old fishing nets to the emperor in **AD 105**. But archaeologists have found **older paper**, including a fragment with a map from a tomb at **Fangmatan** (Gansu) dated to the second century BC. So Cai Lun probably **improved and promoted** paper rather than inventing it. Paper at first was used for wrapping; writing was still done mostly on **bamboo slips and silk**. Paper reached the Islamic world in the 700s and Europe in the 1100s.

**Other Han achievements:**

| Invention | What and when |
| --- | --- |
| **Cast iron** on a large scale | blast furnaces and state ironworks, already advanced before Han; iron ploughs and tools spread widely |
| **The seismoscope** | **Zhang Heng**'s bronze vessel (**132**) said to detect distant earthquakes, with balls dropping from dragons' mouths |
| **The wheelbarrow**, the **stern-post rudder** (shown on a Han tomb model ship), better **horse collars** | transport and farming |
| **Medicine and mathematics** | the *Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art*, with negative numbers and methods of solving equations |

**Sima Qian** (about **145–86 BC**). Court astrologer and historian to Emperor Wu, he completed his father's project: the ***Shiji***, *Records of the Grand Historian*, a history of the world as the Chinese knew it, from the legendary **Yellow Emperor** to his own day, in **130 chapters**.
- **The form he invented**: annals of rulers, tables, treatises on topics like music and canals, and **biographies** of every kind of person, from kings and generals to assassins, merchants and foreign peoples like the Xiongnu.
- **The cost.** In **99 BC** he defended the general **Li Ling**, who had surrendered to the Xiongnu. Wu sentenced him to death. Sima Qian chose **castration** instead, so that he could finish the book. His letter explaining why, the *Letter to Ren An*, is one of the famous texts of Chinese literature.
- **His method.** He travelled to see places, used court archives, and sometimes recorded conflicting versions side by side.

His successor **Ban Gu** wrote the *Book of Han* (*Hanshu*), finished after his death in 92 by his sister **Ban Zhao**, China's first known woman historian. Every later dynasty would write an official history of the one before it.

**The decline of the Eastern Han:**
- **At court**: child emperors, with power fought over between the families of empresses (the **consort clans**) and palace **eunuchs**. In **166** and after, scholars who protested were purged.
- **In the country**: great **landed families** with private estates and tenants grew powerful, and fewer peasants paid tax.
- **The Yellow Turbans** (**184**): a religious movement led by **Zhang Jue**, promising a new age of "Great Peace", rose across eastern China. It was crushed, but the generals who crushed it became warlords.

**The end.** In **190** the warlord **Dong Zhuo** burned **Luoyang**. The north passed to **Cao Cao**, who controlled the last emperor. At the **Red Cliffs** (**208**) on the Yangtze, an alliance of southern warlords stopped him. In **220** his son **Cao Pi** deposed the Han emperor.

**The Three Kingdoms** (220–280): **Wei** in the north, **Shu** in Sichuan (under **Liu Bei**) and **Wu** in the south-east. The **Jin** dynasty reunited China in **280**, but only briefly. The age was later romanticised in the novel *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*.

**How bad was the collapse?** Registered population fell from about **50–56 million** in the mid-second century to **well under 20 million** in the Three Kingdoms' records. Some of that loss was **real death**, from war, famine and epidemics. Much was **people vanishing from the tax registers**, as they sheltered under great families. How much of each is debated, and the records alone cannot settle it.
Early Korea and Yayoi Japan:
At the eastern edge of Eurasia, Han China's expansion pulled Korea and Japan into the written record. Both first appear in Chinese histories, which means we first see them through Chinese eyes.

**Gojoseon.** The earliest Korean state named in the sources, **Gojoseon** ("Old Joseon"), lay in north-west Korea and southern Manchuria. Around **194 BC** a refugee from China, **Wiman**, seized its throne. In **108 BC** Emperor Wu of Han conquered it and set up **four commanderies**. Three soon lapsed, but **Lelang**, centred near modern **Pyongyang**, lasted until **313**. Its brick tombs, full of Chinese lacquer, bronze mirrors and seals, show a Chinese colonial town that passed on **writing, iron technology and Chinese goods** to the peoples around it.

**The Three Kingdoms of Korea, in tradition and in evidence.** Korea's oldest surviving history, the *Samguk sagi*, compiled in **1145**, gives founding dates of **57 BC** for **Silla**, **37 BC** for **Goguryeo**, and **18 BC** for **Baekje**. Historians treat these dates as traditional:

| Kingdom | Where | What the evidence shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Goguryeo** | the north, astride the Yalu river | a real power by the first century AD, raiding Chinese commanderies; it later took Lelang (313) |
| **Baekje** | the south-west | emerges as a state from the **Mahan** chiefdoms by about the 200s–300s |
| **Silla** | the south-east, around **Gyeongju** | grows from the **Jinhan** chiefdoms; a strong kingdom only from the 300s–400s |

A Chinese history of the third century describes the south as the **Samhan**, three groups of small chiefdoms; one of them, **Byeonhan**, exported **iron** to Lelang and to Japan.

**Japan before this stage.** For over 10,000 years the islands were home to the **Jōmon** hunter-gatherers, makers of some of the world's oldest pottery (met in Stage 1).

**The Yayoi.** Named after a district in **Tokyo** where its pottery was first found in **1884**, the **Yayoi** culture brought **wet-rice farming**, **bronze and iron**, weaving and new pottery from the Korean peninsula into **northern Kyushu**, and then east across the islands.
- **When did it begin? A real dispute.** The traditional date was about **300 BC**. In **2003**, radiocarbon dates from Japan's National Museum of Japanese History pushed the first rice paddies back to about the **tenth century BC**. Many archaeologists accept an earlier start, around 1000–800 BC; others question the samples. More dated sites in Kyushu are what will settle it.
- **Who were they?** Genetics shows that modern Japanese descend from **both** Jōmon people and later **migrants from the continent**, in a mix that varies by region; the **Ainu** of the north and the people of **Okinawa** carry more Jōmon ancestry.
- **Life.** Villages surrounded by **moats and palisades**, such as **Yoshinogari** in Saga; skeletons with arrowheads in them; growing inequality; ritual **bronze bells** (*dōtaku*) and mirrors. Rice farming brought, as so often, more people and more war.

**Japan in Chinese records.** The Chinese called the islands' peoples **Wa**.
- **AD 57**: the *Book of the Later Han* records that a ruler of **Na** in Wa sent an envoy and was given a **seal**. In **1784**, a farmer on the island of **Shikanoshima**, near Fukuoka, dug up a **gold seal** inscribed to the "king of Na of Wa", now generally accepted as the very seal.
- **239**: the *Records of Wei* say that a queen named **Himiko**, ruler of a land called **Yamatai** over many smaller polities, sent an embassy to the Wei court, receiving a title and **a hundred bronze mirrors**. It describes her as unmarried, living secluded, ruling through religious power, with her brother handling affairs. After her death, around **248**, a great mound was built.

**Where was Yamatai?** Japan's most famous historical puzzle. One school puts it in **northern Kyushu**, closest to Korea; the other in the **Kinai** region around **Nara**, where the later Yamato state grew, and points to the large early site of **Makimuku** and the mound tomb **Hashihaka**, which some identify as Himiko's. The Chinese directions, read literally, put Yamatai in the sea south of Japan, so they cannot be read literally. Excavating the imperial tombs, which are closed by the Imperial Household Agency, might help decide it.

**The Kofun period**, named after the huge keyhole-shaped burial mounds, begins in the mid-to-late 200s and belongs to Stage 6.
Meroë and the rise of Aksum:
South of Egypt, along the Nile and in the highlands of Ethiopia, two African kingdoms flourished in these centuries. One fought Rome to a negotiated peace; the other became one of the four great powers of the world in a Persian prophet's eyes.

**Kush moves south.** The kingdom of **Kush**, in modern **Sudan**, had once ruled Egypt as its Twenty-Fifth Dynasty (Stage 4). Its royal centre shifted south from **Napata** to **Meroë**, on the Nile between the fifth and sixth cataracts, and from about **270 BC** the kings were buried there. Historians call the following six centuries the **Meroitic** period.

**Why Meroë.** It lay in the **Butana**, where summer rains allowed cattle and crops away from the river, and it had **iron ore** and wood for fuel. Great heaps of **iron slag** survive. Older books called Meroë "the Birmingham of Africa"; archaeologists now think the scale was real but the comparison overdone.

**What Meroë left:**
- **Pyramids**: about 200 small, steep royal and noble pyramids at Meroë, the largest group in the world. Many had their tops broken off in the **1830s** by an Italian treasure hunter, Giuseppe Ferlini.
- **Temples** to Egyptian gods and to their own, such as the lion-headed war god **Apedemak**, at **Naga** and **Musawwarat es-Sufra**.
- **Meroitic writing**, in hieroglyphic and cursive forms, from about the **second century BC**. The British scholar **Francis Llewellyn Griffith** worked out how to **read** it around **1909–1911**, but the **language is still largely not understood**: we can pronounce the words without knowing most of their meanings. It is one of the oldest written languages of sub-Saharan Africa.
- **Ruling queens.** The title **kandake** (the "Candace" of the New Testament book of Acts) belonged to royal women, several of whom ruled in their own right, such as **Amanirenas** and **Amanishakheto**, shown on reliefs as large, armed and powerful.

**War with Rome.** In about **25 BC**, soon after Rome took Egypt, Kushite forces attacked **Aswan** and **Philae** and carried off **statues of Augustus**. The Roman prefect Petronius struck back and sacked **Napata**. Peace was made on the island of **Samos** in **21–20 BC**, on terms **favourable to Kush**: Augustus dropped his demand for tribute. A bronze **head of Augustus**, found at Meroë in **1910** buried beneath the steps of a temple, perhaps so that people would walk on it, is now in the British Museum.

**Decline.** Meroë weakened in the third and fourth centuries AD, perhaps as trade shifted to the Red Sea, where a new power was rising.

**Aksum.** In the highlands of **northern Ethiopia and Eritrea**, around the city of **Aksum** in **Tigray**, a kingdom grew from about the **first century AD** on earlier farming societies with close links to **South Arabia** across the Red Sea.

| Feature | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| **The port** | **Adulis**, on the Red Sea, trading **ivory**, gold, incense and animals for Mediterranean and Indian goods |
| **Our first look** | the *Periplus of the Erythraean Sea*, a Greek merchant's guide of the mid-first century AD, names Adulis and a ruler it calls **Zoskales**, who it says knew Greek |
| **Coins** | from the late **200s**, Aksum issued its own **gold, silver and bronze** coins with Greek legends, one of very few states in the world to mint gold then |
| **Stelae** | giant granite monuments over royal tombs, carved to look like multi-storey buildings; the largest, about 33 metres, fell and broke, probably while being raised. One stela taken to Rome by Mussolini's forces in **1937** was returned in **2005** |
| **Language** | **Ge'ez**, written in a script derived from South Arabian; still the liturgical language of the Ethiopian Church |

**One of four kingdoms.** A Manichaean text in Coptic, the *Kephalaia*, attributed to the prophet **Mani** (third century), names **four great kingdoms** of the world: **Persia, Rome, Aksum and China**.

**What came next.** In the fourth century Aksum's king **Ezana** campaigned into the Nile valley around Meroë and became a **Christian**. That conversion belongs to Stage 6.
The Bantu expansion:
Over three to four thousand years, farmers speaking Bantu languages spread from a small homeland in West-Central Africa across most of the continent south of the equator. It is one of the largest movements in human history, and almost none of it was written down.

**How we know.** Not from writing but from three other kinds of evidence:
1. **Language.** Today around **500** Bantu languages (counts vary) are spoken by hundreds of millions of people, from Cameroon to Kenya to South Africa: Swahili, Kikongo, Shona, isiZulu, Sesotho and many more. They are **closely related**, as related as the Romance languages, which means they spread quite recently. Linguists, notably **Joseph Greenberg**, traced the homeland to where the most varied and oldest branches are: the **Nigeria–Cameroon borderlands**.
2. **Archaeology.** Pottery styles, villages, iron furnaces and crops, dated by radiocarbon.
3. **Genetics.** Ancient and modern DNA shows that **people moved**, not only languages, and also that they **intermarried** with the hunter-gatherers already living there.

**The outline:**

| When (roughly) | Where |
| --- | --- |
| **from about 3000–2000 BC** | movement out of the homeland south into the **rainforest**, along rivers and the coast |
| **about 1000–500 BC** | Bantu speakers in the **Great Lakes** region of East Africa; **Urewe** pottery and iron-working there by around 500 BC |
| **from about 500 BC** | spread south through **Zambia, Malawi and Angola** |
| **by about AD 200–400** | farming villages in **Mozambique**, **Zimbabwe** and north-east **South Africa** (sites such as Silver Leaves in Limpopo and Matola in Mozambique) |

**What they brought.** **Farming** (yams and oil palm in the forest; **sorghum and millet** in the savanna), **cattle, goats and sheep**, **pottery**, **settled villages**, and, from about the middle of the first millennium BC, **iron**, which made better hoes and axes for clearing land. **Bananas**, a South-East Asian crop, reached Africa at some point, probably by sea; when is debated.

**Who was already there.** The forest **Batwa** (often called "Pygmy" peoples), and in East and southern Africa the ancestors of the **Khoe and San**. Some were absorbed, some pushed into drier lands, some kept their ways side by side with farmers. **Click sounds** in isiZulu and isiXhosa were borrowed from Khoe and San languages, a trace of that meeting.

**Debates:**
- **The route.** An **"early split"** model has eastern and western Bantu branches dividing north of the rainforest; a **"late split"** model has the eastern branch emerging later, from groups who had already passed through the forest to its south. Recent genetic studies have tended to support the **late split**, but the question is still open.
- **"Migration" or "expansion"?** Older accounts imagined great columns of migrants. Most scholars now picture **slow, generational movement** of families and villages, a few dozen kilometres at a time, with language spreading also through marriage and assimilation.
- **Where did African iron come from?** One school argues that West Africans **invented iron-smelting independently**, citing early furnace dates in **Niger** and **Nigeria**; another holds that the knowledge came from North Africa or Meroë. The disputed dates are radiocarbon dates from charcoal, which can be older than the furnace. Securely dated early furnaces would settle it.

**West Africa in the same centuries.** The **Nok** culture of central **Nigeria** (flourishing about **900 BC–AD 1**, roughly) made striking **terracotta** heads and figures and smelted iron. On the inland Niger delta in **Mali**, **Jenne-jeno** was settled about **250 BC** and grew into a town, one of the earliest in sub-Saharan Africa.

**South Africa, briefly.** Bantu-speaking farmers reached what is now **Limpopo and KwaZulu-Natal** in the early first millennium AD, joining Khoe herders and San hunter-gatherers already there. Their descendants include the speakers of today's Nguni and Sotho-Tswana languages. The South African story is followed in depth in the **South African Politics curriculum**.
Teotihuacan, the early Maya and the Hope:
In the Americas, entirely separate from the Old World, these centuries saw the building of one of the largest cities on Earth, the rise of the Maya, and great earthworks in North America.

**Teotihuacan.** In the north-east of the **Basin of Mexico**, about 50 km from modern Mexico City, a city grew from about **100 BC** that by its peak, around **AD 400–550**, may have held **100,000 people or more** (estimates vary), making it among the largest cities in the world. Its real name is unknown: *Teotihuacan*, "place where the gods were born", is what the **Aztecs** called its ruins a thousand years later.

| Feature | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| **The Avenue of the Dead** | a ceremonial avenue over 2 km long, laid out on a grid aligned about 15° east of north |
| **The Pyramid of the Sun** | one of the largest pyramids in the Americas, built mostly in the **first and second centuries AD** |
| **The Pyramid of the Moon** | at the avenue's north end, enlarged in several phases |
| **The Feathered Serpent Pyramid** | built around **AD 200**, with the remains of **well over 100 sacrificed people** found so far (perhaps 200 in all), many dressed as warriors, buried in its foundations. A tunnel beneath it, found in **2003**, held thousands of offerings |
| **Apartment compounds** | some **2,000** walled residential compounds, many with painted murals |

**How it lived.** On farming the valley, and on **obsidian**, volcanic glass for blades, from nearby sources, traded across Mesoamerica. It had **foreign neighbourhoods**: a quarter of people from **Oaxaca** and another with goods from the Gulf coast and the Maya.

**Who ruled?** Unlike the Maya, Teotihuacan left **no clear images or names of kings**. Some archaeologists think it was ruled by a **council or collective** government; others think kings existed but were not portrayed. The question is open, and its limited writing has not answered it.

**The Maya Preclassic.** In the lowlands of **Guatemala, Belize and Mexico's Yucatán**, Maya cities grew large well before the "Classic" age:
- **El Mirador**, in northern Guatemala, at its height around **300 BC–AD 100**, has some of the largest pyramids by volume in the world, joined to other cities by raised **causeways**.
- At **San Bartolo**, murals painted around **100 BC**, found in **2001**, show the **maize god** and sophisticated art, with Maya **writing** from as early as about **300–200 BC**.
- In **2018**, a **LiDAR** survey of northern Guatemala, laser-scanning through the forest canopy, revealed tens of thousands of previously unknown structures, roads and fields: the lowlands were far more densely settled than once thought.

**The Preclassic collapse.** Around **AD 100–250**, El Mirador and other great Preclassic cities declined. **Drought**, deforestation and political change have all been proposed; the evidence does not yet decide between them.

**The Classic begins.** By convention the **Classic period** starts around **AD 250**. The earliest dated Maya monument in the lowlands, **Stela 29 at Tikal**, carries a **Long Count** date equal to **AD 292**. The Long Count, a calendar counting days from a starting point in 3114 BC, used a **zero**; an earlier Long Count date, of **36 BC**, survives at **Chiapa de Corzo** in Chiapas.

**Elsewhere in Mesoamerica**, the Zapotec capital **Monte Albán**, on a levelled mountain top in **Oaxaca**, had been a city since about **500 BC**.

**North America: the Hopewell.** In the **Ohio and Illinois** river valleys, from about **200 BC to AD 500**, the **Hopewell** tradition built great **earthworks** in geometric shapes: circles, squares and octagons. The **Newark Earthworks** in Ohio appear to be aligned with the **18.6-year cycle of the moon**. Hopewell burials hold goods from across the continent: **obsidian** from the Yellowstone region, **copper** from Lake Superior, **shells** and **sharks' teeth** from the Gulf of Mexico, **mica** from the Appalachians. This was a vast **exchange network**, not an empire; the people were farmers of local crops and hunters, before maize became central.
The Nazca and the Moche:
On the coast of Peru, one of the driest deserts on Earth, river valleys running down from the Andes fed two remarkable cultures in these centuries. Neither wrote; we know them from what they built, buried and drew.

**The setting.** Peru's coast gets almost no rain. Life depended on **short rivers** from the mountains, on **irrigation**, and on the rich **fishing** of the cold Pacific current. Every few years, **El Niño** brought warm water, floods and failed fishing.

**Before them: Paracas** (about **800 BC–AD 100**), on the south coast. Its desert cemeteries, excavated by the Peruvian archaeologist **Julio C. Tello** in the **1920s**, held mummy bundles wrapped in some of the finest **textiles** ever made, embroidered in dozens of colours.

**The Nazca** (about **100 BC–AD 600**), in the valleys around the modern town of **Nazca**, on Peru's south coast.
- **Pottery**: bright **polychrome** vessels with up to a dozen colours, painted with animals, plants and mythic beings.
- **Cahuachi**: a ceremonial centre of adobe mounds, perhaps a place of pilgrimage rather than a city.
- **Trophy heads**: many human heads were prepared and carried; whether taken in war or from the community's own dead is debated.
- **Water**: underground channels called **puquios** still bring water to fields. Whether the Nazca built them or they are later is debated.

**The Nazca lines.** On the flat desert between Nazca and Palpa, people cleared the dark surface stones to reveal lighter ground, making **hundreds of straight lines**, trapezoids and spirals, and some **70 or more** animal and plant figures: a **hummingbird**, a **monkey**, a **spider**, a killer whale. Many are only fully visible **from the air**, which is why they became famous in the **1920s and 1930s**. The desert's dryness preserved them; a Japanese team using AI-assisted survey reported hundreds more small figures in **2024**.

**What were they for? A long-running debate:**

| Reading | Evidence for and against |
| --- | --- |
| **An astronomical calendar** (Paul Kosok, **Maria Reiche**, who studied them for decades) | a test by the astronomer Gerald Hawkins in **1968** found no more alignments to stars than chance would give |
| **Ritual pathways**, walked in procession | many figures are drawn as **single continuous lines**, and broken pottery is found along lines |
| **Linked to water and fertility** | some lines point toward water sources and mountains, the sources of rivers |

Most specialists now favour **ritual walking linked to water**, but the readings can overlap, and the lines' builders left no explanation.

**The Moche** (about **AD 100–800**), on Peru's **north coast**, in valleys such as Moche, Chicama and Lambayeque.
- **Monuments**: the **Huaca del Sol** and **Huaca de la Luna** near modern Trujillo, giant platforms of **adobe** bricks, tens of millions of them. The Huaca del Sol is one of the largest adobe structures in the Americas, though Spanish treasure hunters later diverted a river to wash part of it away.
- **Irrigation**: long canals bringing river water to fields across the desert.
- **Ceramics**: **portrait vessels** of individual people, so lifelike that the same man can be recognised at different ages, and scenes of hunting, war, healing and sex.
- **Metalwork**: gold, silver and copper, with ways of **gilding** copper unmatched elsewhere in the Americas.

**The Lord of Sipán.** In **1987**, the Peruvian archaeologist **Walter Alva** excavated an **untouched royal tomb** at **Sipán**, in Lambayeque, of a ruler buried around the **third century AD** with gold, silver, turquoise and sacrificed attendants. It is often called the Tutankhamun of the Americas.

**The Sacrifice Ceremony.** Moche art repeatedly shows a ceremony in which captives' blood is offered to richly dressed figures. Scholars had assumed it was myth. Then tombs at Sipán and **San José de Moro** held people buried in **exactly the costumes** of figures in the scene. The rite was real, and these were the people who performed it.

**One state or many?** The Moche were once seen as a single kingdom ruled from the Huacas del Sol and de la Luna. Most archaeologists now see **at least two** separate regions, northern and southern, sharing a religion and art style rather than a government.

**Their end**, around AD 600–800, has been linked to **droughts and floods** recorded in Andean ice cores in the sixth century; the timing is debated. Meanwhile in the highlands, **Tiwanaku**, by Lake Titicaca, was growing into a power of the next stage.
Connections: the Silk Roads and the Indi:
By AD 300, goods, people, gods and germs moved across Eurasia and Africa further and faster than ever before. No one travelled from Rome to China, but silk did, and so did the knowledge that the other existed.

**Who knew of whom.** Romans called the Chinese the **Seres**, "silk people", and knew almost nothing about them. The Chinese called Rome **Daqin**, "Great Qin", and imagined it as a mirror image of China at the western edge of the world. In between, everyone knew their neighbours.

**The overland routes** ran from Chang'an through the **Hexi corridor** and **Dunhuang**, round the **Taklamakan desert** by its oasis towns, over the Pamirs, and through **Kushan** and **Parthian** lands to Mesopotamia and Syria. Goods passed **hand to hand**: Chinese to Sogdian or Kushan merchants, to Parthians, to Syrian and Greek traders. Cities like **Palmyra** in the Syrian desert and **Petra**, capital of the **Nabataean** Arabs (annexed by Rome in **106**), grew rich on caravans.

**The sea routes** were at least as important, and probably carried more:
- From Egypt's Red Sea ports, **Myos Hormos** and **Berenike**, ships sailed to India on the **monsoon**: south-west winds out in summer, north-east winds home in winter. The geographer **Strabo**, writing under Augustus, says (in paraphrase) that he learned some 120 ships a year were sailing from Myos Hormos to India.
- The ***Periplus of the Erythraean Sea***, a mid-first-century guide by a Greek-speaking merchant from Egypt, lists ports from **Adulis** and the Swahili coast (which it calls **Azania**) to **Barygaza** (Bharuch) and **Muziris** in India, and the goods each wanted.
- Excavations at **Berenike** have found Indian **pepper** in a storage jar, Indian teak, and in **2022** a statue of the **Buddha**.
- Further east, at **Oc Eo**, a port of the kingdom the Chinese called **Funan** in the Mekong delta of southern Vietnam, archaeologists found a Roman **gold medallion of Antoninus Pius** (dated **AD 152**).
- In **166**, the Chinese record that an envoy from **Andun**, king of Daqin, arrived by sea through **Rinan** (central Vietnam) bearing ivory, rhinoceros horn and tortoiseshell. Andun is surely **Marcus Aurelius Antoninus**; the "envoys" were probably **private merchants** claiming official status.

**What moved:**

| From | To | Goods |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **China** | west | **silk**, lacquer, iron, bronze mirrors |
| **India and Sri Lanka** | west and east | **pepper** and spices, cotton cloth, gems, ivory, indigo |
| **Arabia and the Horn of Africa** | Rome, India | **frankincense and myrrh**, ivory, tortoiseshell |
| **Rome** | east | **gold and silver coin**, glass, wine, coral, fine pottery, bronze |
| **Central Asia** | China | **horses**, jade, grapes, alfalfa |

**A worry about the trade.** **Pliny the Elder**, writing in the 70s, complained (in paraphrase) that India, China and Arabia took a hundred million sesterces a year from the empire for luxuries. Whether his figure is a real estimate is debated, but the Roman coin hoards in south India show the flow was real.

**What else travelled:**
- **Religions.** **Buddhism** reached China along these routes: the Parthian monk **An Shigao** was translating Buddhist texts at **Luoyang** from about **148**, and the Kushan **Lokaksema** soon after. **Christianity** spread east into Mesopotamia and Iran. Jewish communities lived from Rome to Babylonia. Manichaeism would soon travel the whole length.
- **Art.** Greek and Roman styles shaped Buddhist sculpture in Gandhara; Indian ivories ended up in Pompeii (a statuette found there in **1938**).
- **Disease, perhaps.** The **Antonine Plague** (from **165**) and severe **epidemics recorded in Han China** in the later second century fell in the same decades. Some historians have suggested a link along the trade routes; it is **unproven**, and ancient DNA would be needed to test it.

**Beyond the main routes.** The **Garamantes** of the Libyan Sahara farmed oases with underground channels and traded with Rome; the **camel** was spreading across North Africa, preparing the trans-Saharan trade of the next stage. **Austronesian** sailors from the islands of South-East Asia were crossing the Indian Ocean; their descendants settled **Madagascar**, whose language is closest to one spoken in **Borneo**, though when they arrived is debated (most estimates fall in the first millennium AD). The **Americas** and most of **Oceania** remained outside these networks altogether.

**What carries into Stage 6:**
1. **Rome and Persia**, the Roman Empire rebuilt by Diocletian and the Sasanians, facing each other across Mesopotamia.
2. **Christianity**, a persecuted minority in 303, about to become the religion of the emperor under **Constantine**.
3. **China divided** after Han, with Buddhism spreading through the divided north and south.
4. **The Guptas**, about to give India its classical age.
5. **Steppe peoples** on the move, among them the **Huns**, who will reach Europe in the 370s.
6. **Aksum**, soon to become Christian; and in the Americas, **Teotihuacan** at its height and the **Classic Maya** beginning.

**The big picture.** In 300 BC most large states knew only their neighbours. By AD 300, a chain of empires and trading peoples stretched from Britain to Japan, and an idea, a coin or a disease could cross it.
Map: the world in AD 300:
Where everyone stands at the start of the age. Seven hundred years later, in AD 1000, almost every name on this map has changed.

**The world in about AD 300 held perhaps 200 million people** (estimates run from about 190 to 260 million). Two empires dominated western Eurasia, a third had just broken up in the east, and most of the world was ruled by no empire at all.

| Region | Who is there, around AD 300 |
| --- | --- |
| **The Mediterranean** | **the Roman Empire** under **Diocletian** (ruled 284–305), split into four commands, the Tetrarchy, to hold the frontiers. Perhaps 50–70 million people. Christians are a persecuted minority, perhaps a tenth of the population |
| **Iran and Mesopotamia** | **the Sasanian Persians** (since 224), ruling from **Ctesiphon** on the Tigris to Afghanistan; Rome's equal and rival |
| **Arabia** | **Himyar** has united Yemen by about 300; the rest is oasis towns and herding tribes |
| **North-East Africa** | **Aksum** in the Ethiopian highlands, minting its own gold coins, trading across the Red Sea; Meroë on the Nile in decline |
| **West Africa** | towns on the middle Niger such as **Jenne-jeno**; farming and iron along the Sahel, no large state yet known |
| **South Asia** | no great empire: the **Kushans** fading in the north-west; the **Guptas** about to rise on the Ganges (from about 320) |
| **China** | **the Jin** reunited China in 280, but civil war from 291 and the sack of Luoyang in **311** split it: northern kingdoms under steppe rulers, a southern court at Jiankang (Nanjing) |
| **Korea and Japan** | three Korean kingdoms, **Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla**; in Japan, great keyhole-shaped burial mounds of the **Kofun** period |
| **The Americas** | the **Classic Maya** beginning (about 250); **Teotihuacan**, near modern Mexico City, one of the world's big cities; the **Moche** on Peru's north coast |
| **Oceania** | Polynesians in **Tonga and Samoa**; the eastern Pacific still empty of people |

**The faiths on the map.** **Christianity** is spread thinly across the Roman cities and beyond, to Armenia and Persia. **Zoroastrianism** is Persia's royal religion. **Buddhism** is moving along the Silk Roads into China. Hindu worship is taking its temple-and-Purana forms in India. **Manichaeism**, founded by the Persian prophet Mani (died about 276), runs from Egypt to Central Asia. **Islam does not yet exist**; its prophet will be born around 570.

**The four big changes of this stage**, to watch for:

1. **The great faiths win whole states.** By 1000, Christianity, Islam and Buddhism are the official or dominant faiths from Ireland to Japan.
2. **Rome splits.** The West breaks into kingdoms; **the East goes on as the Roman Empire** for another thousand years.
3. **A new empire is born in Arabia** and within a century runs from Spain to the Indus.
4. **China reunites** under the Sui and Tang, and its model spreads to Korea and Japan.

**Elsewhere, old patterns go on.** Farming peoples speaking Bantu languages have spread across much of Africa south of the equator (their arrival in what is now South Africa is covered in the South African Politics curriculum). Pacific voyagers wait, for reasons still debated, before the last great push east.
Constantine and Christian Rome, 312–451:
How a persecuted minority became the religion of the Roman state in about eighty years.

**The Great Persecution.** In **303** the emperor Diocletian ordered churches destroyed and scriptures burned, and Christians who refused to sacrifice to the gods were imprisoned or executed. It was the fiercest persecution Rome ever ran, and it failed. In **311** the emperor Galerius, dying, issued an edict of toleration.

**Constantine.** Proclaimed emperor by his father's troops at **York in 306**, Constantine fought his way to power in the civil wars that followed the Tetrarchy. On **28 October 312** he defeated his rival Maxentius at the **Milvian Bridge** outside Rome. Two Christian writers say he had a sign from the Christian God before the battle, though they disagree on what it was: **Lactantius** says a dream told him to mark his soldiers' shields; **Eusebius**, writing decades later from Constantine's own telling, describes a cross of light in the sky.

**The turn, step by step:**

| Year | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| **313** | Constantine and his co-emperor Licinius agree at **Milan** on freedom of worship for all, and return Christian property. Often called the "Edict of Milan", it was really a letter to governors |
| **324** | Constantine defeats Licinius and rules the whole empire |
| **325** | he calls the **Council of Nicaea**, about 250–300 bishops, to settle a dispute over the teachings of **Arius**, a priest of Alexandria |
| **330** | he dedicates **Constantinople**, refounded on the site of Byzantium, as a new capital on the Bosporus |
| **337** | baptised on his deathbed, and dies |

**Was he sincere?** The historian Jacob Burckhardt (1853) saw a cold politician backing a winning movement. Most historians now think he was a genuine, if unconventional, Christian convert, pointing to his letters and his lavish church-building. **What would settle it is evidence of his private belief, which no one can recover**; what is certain is that his patronage changed the Church's position for good.

**The Christian empire.** His nephew **Julian** (361–363) tried to restore the old gods and died on campaign in Persia. In **380** **Theodosius I** declared Nicene Christianity the faith of the empire, and in **391–392** banned pagan sacrifice. Bishops became powerful men: in **390** Bishop Ambrose of Milan made Theodosius do public penance for a massacre at Thessalonica.

**Monks.** In Egypt, **Antony** (died 356) went into the desert alone, and **Pachomius** (about 320s) founded the first communities of monks living under a rule. The idea spread across the empire.

**The first great splits.** Councils kept defining belief, and each definition left some outside. After the **Council of Chalcedon (451)**, much of Egypt, Syria and Armenia, and later Ethiopia, rejected its definition and formed their own churches, which survive today. The Church of the East, in Persia, had gone its own way too. **A single Christian empire produced several Christian churches**, a fact that mattered when Islam arrived two centuries later.
Goths, Huns and the sack of Rome, 376–45:
Eighty years in which peoples from beyond the Danube and the Rhine came inside the Roman frontier, and the western half of the empire began to come apart.

**The Huns arrive.** In the **370s** a horse people from the steppe, the **Huns**, struck the Goths living north of the Black Sea. Where the Huns came from is debated: some historians link them to the **Xiongnu**, China's old steppe enemies, through names and archaeology; others think the link is unproven. They were feared above all as mounted archers.

**The Goths cross the Danube.** In **376** tens of thousands of Goths begged entry into the empire and were let across the Danube. Starved and abused by Roman officials, they revolted. At **Adrianople**, on **9 August 378**, they destroyed a Roman field army and killed the emperor **Valens**. The historian Ammianus Marcellinus, a former officer, says two-thirds of the army fell. Rome had to make peace and settle the Goths inside its borders, as a people under their own leaders.

**The frontier gives way, step by step:**

| Year | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| **31 December 406** (traditional date) | Vandals, Alans and Suebi cross the Rhine into Gaul |
| **about 407–410** | Roman armies leave Britain |
| **24 August 410** | **Alaric** and his Goths **sack Rome** for three days, the first sack of the city by a foreign enemy in 800 years |
| **418** | the Goths (now the Visigoths) are settled in Aquitaine, south-west Gaul |
| **429–439** | the Vandals cross to Africa and take **Carthage** (439), the West's richest province |
| **451** | Attila is checked at the **Catalaunian Plains** in Gaul |
| **455** | the Vandals sack Rome by sea, for two weeks |

**The shock of 410.** Rome was no longer the capital, but the sack stunned the Roman world. In Bethlehem, Jerome wrote that the city which had taken the whole world was itself taken. In North Africa, **Augustine of Hippo** began *The City of God* (413–426), answering pagans who blamed the Christian God for the disaster.

**Attila.** From about **445** **Attila** ruled the Huns alone, from the Hungarian plain, extracting gold from the Eastern Empire. A Roman envoy, **Priscus**, visited his court in **449** and described a wooden palace and a king who ate from a wooden plate while his guests ate from silver. In **451** he invaded Gaul and was fought to a standstill by the Roman general **Aetius** with Visigothic allies; in **452** he ravaged northern Italy and turned back, after meeting an embassy led by **Pope Leo I**. He died in **453**, on his wedding night, and his empire broke up within a year.

**The West loses its last defenders.** The emperor Valentinian III murdered Aetius in 454, and was murdered himself in 455. **By now the western emperors had lost Africa, most of Spain, much of Gaul and Britain**, and with them the taxes that paid for armies.
476: did Rome fall?:
The most famous date in European history, and one of the most argued about.

**What happened.** In **September 476** a general named **Odoacer**, commander of the barbarian troops in Italy, deposed the boy emperor **Romulus Augustulus** and sent the imperial regalia to **Constantinople**, telling the eastern emperor **Zeno** that one emperor was enough. He ruled Italy as king, under nominal eastern authority. No one at the time seems to have treated it as the end of the world. (Another deposed western emperor, Julius Nepos, lived until 480, so even "last emperor" is debatable.)

**The empire did not end in 476.** **The Eastern Roman Empire**, ruled from Constantinople, went on, and its people called themselves **Romans** until 1453. The name "Byzantine" was given to them by Western scholars in the 1500s. What ended in 476 was **Roman government in the West**.

**So the real question is: what happened to the West, and why?**

| Reading | The argument | Its champions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Decline and fall** | internal decay (Gibbon blamed Christianity and barbarism) weakened an empire that then collapsed | Edward Gibbon, 1776–1789 |
| **Pushed from outside** | the empire was strong; the **Huns** drove whole peoples across its frontiers faster than it could absorb them | Peter Heather, 2005 |
| **A real collapse of living standards** | archaeology shows pottery, coins, roof tiles and even cattle size **shrinking** after 400 | Bryan Ward-Perkins, 2005 |
| **Transformation, not fall** | "late antiquity" (about 250–750) was a creative age of new religion, art and law; the barbarians were absorbed into a Roman world | Peter Brown, 1971 |
| **Accommodation** | the Germanic peoples were settled with Roman agreement, perhaps taking a share of the taxes rather than land | Walter Goffart, 1980 (much debated) |
| **Climate and disease** | cooling and plagues weakened the empire from the 160s on | Kyle Harper, 2017 |

**Where they agree.** Almost everyone accepts that **the East survived and the West did not**, and that this comparison is the best test. The East had more cities and taxpayers, a shorter frontier and a capital behind sea walls.

**What would settle it.** Region-by-region archaeology of how ordinary people lived (some areas, such as Britain, crashed hard; others, such as parts of Italy and Spain, changed slowly); better dating of the climate records; and closer study of how the barbarian settlements were actually paid for. Much of the debate is about **which people you look at**: an aristocrat in Gaul keeping his villa, or a potter in Britain losing his market.

**A useful way to hold it.** The **Roman state** in the West ended in the 400s. Roman **law, Latin, the Church and cities** survived it, in the kingdoms that took its place, which is the next lesson.
The Gupta golden age, about 320–550:
The empire under which much of classical Indian science, literature and temple religion took shape, and an argument about what "golden age" should mean.

**The rise.** **Chandragupta I** (no relation to the earlier Maurya) founded the dynasty in the Ganges valley; its era of years begins in **319–320**. His son **Samudragupta** (about 335–375) campaigned across north India and into the south; his conquests are recorded in a Sanskrit poem by the court poet Harishena, carved on an old Ashokan pillar now at Allahabad. **Chandragupta II** (about 375–415) conquered the Shaka kings of Gujarat and western India, opening the ports of the Arabian Sea.

**How it was ruled.** The Gupta heartland was governed directly; beyond it, many kings kept their thrones by paying tribute. Gupta kings followed Hindu gods, especially Vishnu, while patronising Buddhists and Jains too. **Land grants to Brahmins and temples**, recorded on copper plates, became common.

**A visitor's view.** The Chinese monk **Faxian** travelled India from about **399 to 412**, seeking Buddhist texts. He described orderly towns, free hospitals, light punishments, and Buddhist monasteries flourishing, though he noted untouchables living apart.

**What was made in these centuries:**

| Field | Achievement |
| --- | --- |
| **Mathematics** | **Aryabhata** wrote the *Aryabhatiya* in **499**, giving π as about 3.1416 and arguing that the Earth turns on its axis. **Decimal place-value numbers** developed in India in these centuries; **Brahmagupta** set out rules for **zero as a number** in **628**, just after |
| **Literature** | **Kalidasa**, probably of the 400s, wrote the play *Shakuntala*; Sanskrit court poetry reached its classical form |
| **Religion and art** | the first free-standing stone Hindu temples, such as **Deogarh** (about 500); the Sarnath style of Buddha image |
| **Learning** | the great Buddhist monastery-university of **Nalanda** in Bihar, founded in the 400s, later drew students from across Asia |

The painted caves of **Ajanta** are often credited to the Guptas; their famous later phase was in fact made under the neighbouring **Vakataka** kings, Gupta allies by marriage, in the late 400s.

**The end.** From about **455** the **Hunas** (the Alchon "Huns", a Central Asian people) attacked from the north-west. **Skandagupta** held them off, but under **Toramana** and **Mihirakula** (about 500–530s) they overran the Punjab and Malwa. Gupta power faded by the **mid-500s**, and north India broke into regional kingdoms.

**Was it a golden age?** Nineteenth- and twentieth-century historians, British and Indian nationalist alike, called it India's classical peak, a matching piece for Periclean Athens. **Critics**, such as R. S. Sharma and Romila Thapar, point out that the glory belonged to courts and Brahmins: land grants may have weakened central power and tied peasants to landlords, and caste rules hardened. **Both can be true**: an age of high culture for some and harder rules for others. What would settle the economic side is better evidence of ordinary people's lives, which the copper plates and court poems mostly do not give.
Teotihuacan and the Classic Maya kings,:
The two great powers of Mesoamerica in these centuries: a vast city in the highlands, and a world of rival kingdoms in the lowland forests, whose history can now be read in their own writing.

**Teotihuacan.** About 40 km north-east of modern Mexico City stood the largest city of the Americas. Its **Avenue of the Dead** ran past the **Pyramid of the Sun** and **Pyramid of the Moon**; the **Temple of the Feathered Serpent** (about 200) was dedicated with the sacrifice of some two hundred people buried beneath it. **At its height, about 400–550, perhaps 100,000 people or more** lived there, in thousands of walled apartment compounds, some housing migrants from Oaxaca and the Gulf coast. It controlled the green obsidian of Pachuca, the best stone for blades.

**Who ruled it is a puzzle.** Teotihuacan has no royal portraits or boastful inscriptions. Some archaeologists think it was governed by a council or shared rule; others think kings simply chose not to show themselves. Its signs may or may not be a full writing system.

**The Classic Maya.** In the lowlands of southern Mexico, Guatemala and Belize, **from about 250 to 900**, dozens of city-states were ruled by kings called *k'uhul ajaw*, **"holy lord"**. They raised carved stone stelae dated in the **Long Count** calendar, recording births, accessions, wars and rituals. **Maya script was largely deciphered between the 1950s and the 1990s** (the Russian Yuri Knorozov, Tatiana Proskouriakoff in 1960, and many after), so these kingdoms now have a written history with named people.

**The great events:**

| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **January 378** | the **"Arrival"**: a warlord from or tied to Teotihuacan, **Siyaj K'ak'**, reaches **Tikal**; the same day Tikal's king dies, and a new dynasty with Teotihuacan links is installed |
| **562** | **Caracol**, probably allied with Calakmul, defeats Tikal; Tikal raises no dated monuments for over a century |
| **615–683** | **K'inich Janaab Pakal** rules **Palenque**; his tomb inside the Temple of the Inscriptions was found in **1952** |
| **695** | Tikal's king **Jasaw Chan K'awiil** defeats **Calakmul**, the "Snake" kingdom that dominated the 600s |
| **738** | **Copán**'s king, known as 18 Rabbit, is captured and beheaded by his former vassal **Quiriguá** |

**How the 378 "Arrival" is read** is debated: a conquest by Teotihuacan, or a Maya faction using a foreign ally's prestige. The inscriptions call the new king's father "Spearthrower Owl", who may have been a ruler of Teotihuacan itself.

**Teotihuacan's fall.** Around **550** (estimates run to the 600s) the temples and palaces along the Avenue of the Dead were **burned and their statues smashed**. Because the fire targeted the buildings of the elite, many archaeologists suspect a **revolt from within**; others argue for attack from outside, with drought and failing trade weakening the city first. The city shrank but was never quite empty. Seven centuries later the Aztecs revered its ruins as the place where the gods had been born.

**The Maya world had a much larger population than once thought.** Laser scanning from the air (**lidar**), from 2016 on, revealed tens of thousands of hidden houses, causeways and fields around Tikal and other cities.
The Germanic kingdoms: Ostrogoths, Visig:
What replaced the western Roman Empire: kingdoms ruled by small warrior elites over large Roman populations, most of them keeping Roman law, Latin and the Church.

**A minority on top.** The Germanic peoples who took over the West were few: a few tens of thousands of fighters and their families in each kingdom, ruling millions of Romans. Most were Christians of the **Arian** kind (converted in the 300s by the missionary **Ulfilas**, who translated the Bible into Gothic), which set them apart from their Nicene Catholic subjects.

| Kingdom | Where and when | What happened |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Ostrogoths** | **Italy, 493–553** | **Theoderic** (ruled 493–526), raised as a hostage in Constantinople, killed Odoacer and ruled Italy from **Ravenna**; kept the Senate and Roman officials. His minister **Boethius** wrote *The Consolation of Philosophy* in prison before his execution (about 524). Destroyed by Justinian's armies in the Gothic War, 535–554 |
| **Visigoths** | **Gaul, then Spain, 418–711** | ruled from Toulouse until beaten by the Franks at **Vouillé (507)**; then from **Toledo** in Spain. King **Reccared** converted to Catholicism in **587**, confirmed at the Third Council of Toledo (**589**). Ended by the Arab and Berber invasion of **711** |
| **Vandals** | **North Africa, 429–534** | took Carthage in 439, built a fleet and sacked Rome in 455; persecuted Catholic bishops; conquered by Justinian's general **Belisarius** in **533–534** |
| **Lombards** | **Italy, from 568** | invaded after the Gothic War; ruled much of Italy until Charlemagne took their kingdom in 774 |
| **Burgundians** | **the Rhône valley** | absorbed by the Franks in the 530s |
| **Anglo-Saxons** | **eastern Britain, 400s on** | Angles, Saxons and Jutes from across the North Sea settled as Roman Britain broke apart; a patchwork of small kingdoms, pagan until the 600s |

**Britain is the exception.** Elsewhere Latin survived and became Italian, Spanish and French. In lowland Britain the Roman towns, villas and coinage disappeared within a generation or two of 410, Latin did not survive as a spoken language, and English grew from the settlers' speech. **How many Anglo-Saxons came, and whether the Britons were driven out or absorbed**, is long debated; ancient DNA studies (2022) suggest a large migration, with much mixing.

**Two laws for two peoples.** Kings issued written law codes, in Latin, often with separate rules for Goths and for Romans. Over time the distinction faded, and in Spain the **Visigothic Code** (about 654) applied one law to all.

**Their own histories.** Much of what we know comes from writers inside these kingdoms: **Jordanes**' *Getica* (551) on the Goths, **Gregory of Tours** on the Franks, **Isidore of Seville** (died 636) on the Visigoths, and later **Bede** on the English.

**Why it mattered.** These kingdoms are the roots of Europe's later nations. The kings kept the Church, bishops and much Roman administration, and **converting from Arian to Catholic Christianity** (the Visigoths, the Lombards from the late 600s) was how they merged with the people they ruled.
Clovis and the Merovingian Franks, 481–7:
The kingdom that lasted: how a Frankish warlord's conversion created the strongest state in the post-Roman West, the ancestor of France and Germany.

**The Franks.** A group of Germanic peoples on the lower Rhine, long allies and soldiers of Rome. In 1653 workmen at Tournai, in modern Belgium, found the grave of **Childeric**, a Frankish king who died about 481, buried with a Roman general's brooch, a signet ring with his name, and gold and garnet jewellery.

**Clovis** (ruled about 481–511), Childeric's son, made the Franks a great power:

| Year | What he did |
| --- | --- |
| **486** | defeated **Syagrius**, the last Roman ruler in northern Gaul, at Soissons |
| **between 496 and 508** | **baptised a Catholic** at Reims by Bishop **Remigius** |
| **507** | defeated the Visigoths at **Vouillé** near Poitiers and took south-west Gaul |
| **about 507–511** | issued the **Salic law**, the Franks' law code |
| **511** | died in **Paris**, his capital |

**The date of the baptism is disputed.** The traditional date, 496, comes from Gregory of Tours, who tells the story as a copy of Constantine's: Clovis prayed to his Catholic wife **Clotilde**'s God in a losing battle and won. Many historians now date it nearer 508, after Vouillé. What matters is the choice: **Clovis became Catholic, not Arian**, which made him the champion of the Gallo-Roman bishops and their people.

**Gregory of Tours** (about 538–594), bishop of Tours, wrote the *Ten Books of Histories* (often called the *History of the Franks*), our main source. It is vivid, partisan and violent: kings murder brothers and nephews, queens such as **Brunhild** and **Fredegund** feud for decades.

**Partition.** Frankish custom divided a king's lands among his sons. The kingdom split and rejoined many times, into **Neustria** (west), **Austrasia** (east) and **Burgundy**. **Dagobert I** (died 639) was the last king to rule it all with real power.

**The mayors of the palace.** In the 600s and 700s power passed to the king's chief officials, the **mayors of the palace**. Later Carolingian writers mocked the last Merovingians as "do-nothing kings" carried about in ox-carts; much of that is the propaganda of the family that replaced them, though their weakness was real.

**Charles Martel and Poitiers.** The mayor **Charles Martel** defeated an Umayyad army from Spain near **Poitiers** (often called Tours) in **732** (some date it 733). Gibbon imagined that without it the Qur'an might be taught at Oxford. Many historians now see it as the defeat of a large raid, not an invasion, with Muslim expansion already near its limit. **Others still think it ended the danger of conquest north of the Pyrenees.** The Arab sources say little about it, which itself suggests it loomed larger in Frankish memory.

**751: the new dynasty.** Charles's son **Pippin III**, with the Pope's approval, sent the last Merovingian, **Childeric III**, to a monastery and was crowned king. His family, the **Carolingians**, would produce Charlemagne.
Justinian, Theodora and the Roman reconq:
The Roman Empire in the East at its most ambitious: an emperor who rewrote the law, built the greatest church in Christendom and tried to win back the West.

**Rome went on in the East.** In 527 the Roman Empire still ruled the Balkans, Anatolia, Syria, Palestine and Egypt, from **Constantinople**, a city of perhaps half a million behind the land walls built under Theodosius II (about 413). Its people spoke mostly Greek but called themselves **Romans**, and their laws, taxes and army were Roman.

**Justinian and Theodora.** **Justinian** (born about 482, ruled 527–565), a Latin-speaker from the Balkans and nephew of the emperor Justin, married **Theodora**, a former actress, and made her empress with real influence. Our main witness, the historian **Procopius**, praised Justinian's wars and buildings in public and savaged both of them in his *Secret History*, written in secret and not meant to be published in their lifetimes.

**The Nika riot, 532.** In **January 532** the chariot-racing fans of the **Blues** and **Greens** united against the government, shouting "Nika!" ("Conquer!"), burned much of the city and crowned a rival emperor. Procopius says Justinian was ready to flee until Theodora told the council that royalty makes a good burial shroud. The general **Belisarius** trapped the crowd in the Hippodrome and slaughtered it; Procopius gives over **30,000 dead**, a figure no one can check.

**His works:**

| Work | Date | What it was |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The *Corpus Juris Civilis*** | **529–534** | the whole of Roman law gathered and edited: the Code, the Digest of jurists' writings, the Institutes for students. Rediscovered in the West after about 1070, it became **the basis of law in most of continental Europe** |
| **Hagia Sophia** | **532–537** | the "Holy Wisdom" church, by **Anthemius of Tralles** and **Isidore of Miletus**: a dome about 31 metres across. The largest church in the world for nearly a thousand years |
| **Reconquest of Africa** | **533–534** | Belisarius destroyed the Vandal kingdom in one short campaign |
| **Reconquest of Italy** | **535–554** | the Gothic War; Ravenna fell in 540, but the war dragged on twenty years and left Italy ruined |
| **Spain** | **552** | a strip of the south-east coast taken |
