**The plague, 541–542.** Bubonic plague reached Egypt in 541 and Constantinople in **542**; Justinian himself caught it and survived. **Ancient DNA has confirmed that it was *Yersinia pestis***, the same bacterium as the Black Death. It returned in waves for two centuries. **How many died is contested**: older estimates of a quarter to a half of the Mediterranean's people rest on literary accounts; a 2019 study by Mordechai and Eisenberg argued from papyri, coins and laws that the impact was much smaller. Better counts from graves and written records region by region would settle it.

**The cost.** The wars with Persia (Antioch was sacked in 540), the plague and the long Italian war drained the treasury. **Within three years of his death the Lombards invaded Italy**, and much of the West he regained was lost again within a century.
The Sasanian Persian empire, 224–651:
Rome's great rival for four centuries: a Persian empire from the Euphrates to Central Asia, and the model for much of the Islamic state that followed it.

**The founding.** In **224** **Ardashir I**, from a family of Persis (Fars, in south-west Iran), defeated the last Parthian king and founded the **Sasanian** dynasty, named after his ancestor Sasan. His son **Shapur I** (about 240–270) defeated three Roman emperors and in **260** captured the emperor **Valerian**, a scene he had carved in the cliffs of **Naqsh-e Rostam**.

**The empire.** From its capital at **Ctesiphon**, on the Tigris near modern Baghdad, it ruled Mesopotamia (its richest land), Iran, and at times Armenia, the Caucasus, and lands to the Oxus. The king called himself "King of Kings of Iran and non-Iran". Its people were Persians, Aramaic-speaking Mesopotamians, Arabs, Armenians and others; it was **as diverse as Rome**.

**Religion.** **Zoroastrianism** was the faith of the kings, with a powerful priesthood; the priest **Kartir**, in the 270s and 280s, boasted in inscriptions of persecuting Jews, Christians, Buddhists and Manichaeans. Yet large communities of each lived in the empire. **Babylonian Jewry** produced the **Babylonian Talmud** in these centuries, and the **Church of the East** became a great missionary church, later carrying Christianity to India and China.

**The great kings:**

| King | Ruled | Known for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Shapur II** | **309–379** | crowned, tradition says, before he was born; long wars with Rome; recovered Armenian lands after the emperor Julian died on campaign (363) |
| **Peroz** | **459–484** | killed fighting the **Hephthalites** ("White Huns") of Central Asia, who then took tribute from Persia |
| **Kavad I** | **488–531** | backed for a time the **Mazdakite** movement, which preached sharing property, and then crushed it |
| **Khosrow I** (Anushirvan, "of the immortal soul") | **531–579** | reformed taxes on a land survey, built a paid army, sheltered Greek philosophers when Justinian closed the Athens school; remembered as the model just king |
| **Khosrow II** | **590–628** | the last great war with Rome (next lesson) |

**What it left.** The vaulted hall at Ctesiphon, the **Taq Kasra**, with an arch about 35 metres high, still stands in part. Persian administration, court ceremony, the royal hunt, polo, silk weaving and silver plate shaped the **Abbasid caliphate**, and Persian literature kept the Sasanian kings alive in Ferdowsi's *Shahnameh* (finished about 1010).

**The end.** Exhausted by the war of 602–628 and by civil war after it (about ten rulers in four years), the empire met the Arab armies in the 630s. After defeats at **al-Qadisiyya** (about 636) and **Nahavand** (**642**), the last king, **Yazdegerd III**, fled east and was killed near **Merv** in **651**. **Iran became part of the caliphate, but it kept its language**, Persian, which revived as a great literary language in the 900s, written in Arabic script.
The Sui reunite China and the Tang build:
After nearly four hundred years of division, China was rejoined, and for a century and a half the Tang ruled the largest and most open empire in the world.

**The division.** After the Han fell (220), China split. From **311** the north was ruled by a series of kingdoms founded by steppe peoples, the greatest being the **Northern Wei** (386–534), whose kings carved huge Buddhas in the caves of **Yungang** and **Longmen**. The south was ruled by Chinese dynasties from Jiankang (Nanjing). **Buddhism**, arriving from Central Asia, spread across both.

**The Sui (581–618).** **Yang Jian**, a northern general of mixed Chinese and steppe family, seized the throne in **581** as Emperor **Wen**, and in **589** conquered the south: **China was one again**. His son **Yangdi** (604–618) built the **Grand Canal**, linking the Yellow River to the Yangtze (main sections finished about 605–611), with forced labour on a vast scale. Three failed invasions of the Korean kingdom of **Goguryeo** (612–614) cost huge armies; revolts followed, and Yangdi was murdered in 618. **Like the Qin before the Han, a short harsh dynasty built what a longer one used.**

**The Tang (618–907).** **Li Yuan**, a Sui general, founded the Tang in **618**. His son **Li Shimin** killed two brothers at the Xuanwu Gate in **626**, forced his father to abdicate, and ruled as **Taizong** (626–649), remembered as a model emperor.

| What the Tang built | How it worked |
| --- | --- |
| **Government** | three central departments and six ministries; the **Tang Code** (653), the model for law codes in Korea, Japan and Vietnam |
| **Land** | the **equal-field** system, allotting land to households in return for taxes and service |
| **Examinations** | written tests in classics and literature, begun under the Sui, grew in importance, though great families still dominated office |
| **The army and the west** | the Eastern Turks were defeated in **630**, the Western Turks in **657**; Tang garrisons reached the Tarim Basin and beyond |

**Wu Zetian.** A concubine of Taizong and then wife of his son, **Wu Zhao** ruled as empress, then from **690 to 705** as emperor of her own **Zhou** dynasty: **the only woman in Chinese history to rule as emperor in her own name**. Later Confucian historians painted her as a monster; modern historians note that the state ran well under her and that she promoted officials by examination.

**Chang'an.** The capital (modern Xi'an) was a walled grid about **9.7 by 8.6 km**, divided into **108 walled wards** and two great markets, East and West. Perhaps a million people lived in and around it, though the figure is an estimate. **Sogdian** merchants from Central Asia, Persians, Turks, Koreans, Japanese and Arabs lived there; there were Buddhist and Daoist temples, Zoroastrian and Manichaean shrines, and a church of the **Church of the East**, whose stele of **781** records its arrival in **635**. The monk **Xuanzang** returned from India in **645** with hundreds of Buddhist texts and spent the rest of his life translating them.

**The high Tang.** Under **Xuanzong** (712–756) came the age of the poets **Li Bai** and **Du Fu**. It was at its peak in about **750**, five years before it nearly broke apart.
The last war of antiquity: Rome against:
Twenty-six years of total war between the two great empires of western Asia, which ended in a Roman victory and left both too weak to stop what came next.

**The cause.** In **590** the young Persian king **Khosrow II**, overthrown by a general, fled to the Romans; the emperor **Maurice** restored him with a Roman army. In **602** Maurice was overthrown and murdered by a junior officer, **Phocas**. Khosrow declared war, claiming to avenge his benefactor.

**The Persian advance:**

| Year | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| **604–610** | Persian armies break through the Roman frontier in Mesopotamia; Roman civil war as **Heraclius**, son of the governor of Africa, sails on Constantinople and overthrows Phocas (**610**) |
| **613** | Persians take **Antioch** |
| **614** | Persians take **Jerusalem**; many inhabitants killed, and the **True Cross**, Christendom's holiest relic, carried off to Persia |
| **619** | Persians take **Alexandria**; Egypt, the empire's granary, is lost for a decade |
| **626** | Persians on one side of the Bosporus, the **Avars** and their Slav subjects on the other, besiege **Constantinople**; the city holds |

**Heraclius strikes back.** Instead of defending, Heraclius (ruled 610–641) took his army into the Persians' own lands. From **622** he campaigned in Armenia and the Caucasus, allied with the **Turks** of the steppe (a force often identified as Khazar), and in **627** marched into Mesopotamia. At **Nineveh**, in **December 627**, he defeated the Persian army. In **February 628** Khosrow was overthrown and killed by his own son, who made peace and gave back everything Persia had taken. Heraclius **restored the True Cross to Jerusalem in about 630**.

**The cost.** The war was fought as a **religious war** on both sides: the Romans carried icons into battle, the Persians destroyed churches, and the Jews of Palestine were caught between, first backing Persia and then suffering for it. The great cities of Syria and Anatolia were sacked, trade was broken, the Balkans were overrun by Avars and Slavs while the armies were away, and **both treasuries were empty**.

**What happened next.** Persia fell into civil war: about ten rulers in four years. Rome was exhausted. **Within eight years of Nineveh, Arab armies were defeating both empires** at the Yarmuk (636) and al-Qadisiyya (about 636). Historians sometimes call 602–628 the "last great war of antiquity", because after it **the world of Rome-against-Persia that had lasted since the 50s BC was gone**.

**A source to know.** The Qur'an's thirtieth chapter, *Surat al-Rum* ("The Romans"), opens by speaking of the Romans' defeat in a nearby land and their coming victory, which Muslim tradition links to this war. It is one sign of how closely Arabia watched the two empires.
Arabia before Islam and the life of Muha:
The world into which Islam was born, and the life of its prophet as history: what the sources say, and how historians weigh them.

**Arabia around 570.** The peninsula lay between the two empires and was drawn into their rivalry:

| Place | Who ruled |
| --- | --- |
| **Yemen** | the kingdom of **Himyar**, whose last kings converted to **Judaism**; conquered by Christian **Aksum** around **525**, then by **Persia** in the **570s** |
| **The Syrian desert edge** | the **Ghassanids**, Christian Arab allies of Rome |
| **Iraq's desert edge** | the **Lakhmids** of al-Hira, Arab allies of Persia, until Persia ended them about 602 |
| **The Hijaz** (west Arabia) | oasis towns such as **Mecca** and **Yathrib**; herding tribes; no state |

**Religion in Arabia** included many gods, but also Jewish tribes (in Yathrib and elsewhere), Christians, and some who worshipped one God. At **Mecca**, the **Kaaba** shrine drew pilgrims, and the ruling tribe, the **Quraysh**, traded and guarded it.

**The life, as the Muslim tradition records it:**

| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **about 570** | **Muhammad** born in Mecca, of the Quraysh clan of Hashim; orphaned young, raised by his grandfather and his uncle Abu Talib |
| **about 595** | marries **Khadija**, a widowed merchant; works in trade |
| **about 610** | begins to receive revelations, which he recites; these will be gathered as the **Qur'an** |
| **610s** | preaches one God and judgement; wins followers, and hostility from Mecca's leaders. About **615** some followers take refuge with the Christian king of **Aksum** |
| **622** | the **Hijra**: emigration to **Yathrib**, which becomes **Medina** ("the City"). **Year 1 of the Islamic calendar** |
| **624–627** | wars with Mecca: **Badr** (624), **Uhud** (625), **the Trench** (627) |
| **630** | Mecca surrenders; the Kaaba's idols removed |
| **632** | dies at Medina, with much of Arabia allied or submitted to him |

At Medina he was a statesman as well as a prophet: a document known as the **Constitution of Medina** sets out the terms between his followers and the town's clans, including Jewish ones.

**How we know.** The **Qur'an** itself is early: parchment leaves at Birmingham have been radiocarbon-dated to **between about 568 and 645**. But it says little about events. The first full biography, by **Ibn Ishaq** (died about 767), survives only in a later edition by **Ibn Hisham** (died about 833), two centuries after the events. Non-Muslim sources mention Arab conquerors and a prophet from the 630s on.

**The debate.** Most historians accept the outline above. **Sceptical scholars** in the 1970s (John Wansbrough; Patricia Crone and Michael Cook in *Hagarism*, 1977) argued that the late sources were shaped by later needs and should not be trusted. Crone also doubted (1987) that Mecca was a great trading city. **Others** (such as Fred Donner) answer that the early dating of Qur'an manuscripts, the early inscriptions and documents, and the consistency of the tradition support its core. More early documents, inscriptions from Arabian rock faces, and archaeology at Mecca and Medina (not now permitted) would settle more.

**Why it mattered.** In twenty years one man united the tribes of Arabia under a single faith and leadership, which had never happened before, and **created a community ready to expand**.
The Rashidun caliphs and the Arab conque:
In thirty years the community of Medina conquered Persia and half of the Roman Empire, and split over who should lead it.

**The caliphs.** Muhammad left no agreed successor. His companions chose **Abu Bakr**, his father-in-law, as **caliph** (*khalifa*, "successor" or "deputy"). Sunni Muslims call the first four the **Rashidun**, the "rightly guided":

| Caliph | Ruled | Key events |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Abu Bakr** | **632–634** | the **Ridda** ("apostasy") wars bring the Arabian tribes back under Medina |
| **Umar** | **634–644** | the great conquests: Syria, Iraq, Egypt, western Iran; the army registers (*diwan*) and pensions; the Islamic calendar from the Hijra |
| **Uthman** | **644–656** | Iran conquered further; a standard text of the **Qur'an** issued; accused of favouring his **Umayyad** kin; murdered by rebels in Medina |
| **Ali** | **656–661** | Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law; civil war; murdered at Kufa |

**The conquests:**

| Date | Battle or event |
| --- | --- |
| **August 636** | **Yarmuk**, near the Golan: the Roman army in Syria destroyed |
| **about 636** (the date is debated, 636–638) | **al-Qadisiyya**, Iraq: the Persian army defeated; **Ctesiphon** taken |
| **637 or 638** | **Jerusalem** surrenders to Umar in person |
| **639–642** | **Egypt** taken by **Amr ibn al-As**; Alexandria surrenders in 641 or 642 |
| **642** | **Nahavand**: the last great Persian field army defeated |

**Why so fast?** Historians give several reasons, and weigh them differently:
- **Both empires were exhausted** by the war of 602–628 and by plague.
- **The Arab armies** were mobile, experienced, well led (such as **Khalid ibn al-Walid**), and united by faith and the promise of reward.
- **Many subjects did not fight.** Christians whom Constantinople called heretics, in Egypt and Syria, and Jews, had little love for their old rulers. The conquerors offered terms: **protected status** (*dhimma*) and freedom of worship in return for a tax (later called *jizya*).

**Conquest was not conversion.** The Arabs lived at first in **garrison towns** they built, **Basra**, **Kufa** and **Fustat** (by modern Cairo), and ruled through existing officials. For a century or more most people of the conquered lands stayed Christian, Jewish or Zoroastrian. **Majority Muslim populations came only over the next three centuries**, at a pace that is debated (Richard Bulliet's estimate from Persian name lists puts a majority in Iran by about the 800s–900s).

**The First Fitna** (civil war), **656–661.** After Uthman's murder, **Ali** became caliph. He fought Muhammad's widow **Aisha** and her allies at the **Battle of the Camel** (656), and then the governor of Syria, **Mu'awiya**, Uthman's kinsman, at **Siffin** (657), which ended in arbitration. Some of Ali's own followers rejected the arbitration and broke away (the **Kharijites**); one of them killed Ali in **661**. Mu'awiya took power.

**The great division.** Those who held that the leadership belonged to Ali and his descendants became the **Shi'a** ("party" of Ali); the majority, who accepted the caliphs as they came, became known as **Sunni**. **The split began as a dispute about political succession**, and grew over centuries into two traditions of law and devotion (whose beliefs belong to the Theology curriculum).
Monks and missionaries: Ireland, Iona an:
How Christianity reached the peoples beyond the old Roman frontier in north-west Europe: through monks, kings and queens, more than through armies.

**The monastic rule.** **Benedict of Nursia** (about 480–547) founded the monastery of **Monte Cassino**, south of Rome, about 529, and wrote a **Rule** for monks: prayer at fixed hours, manual work, study, obedience to an abbot, and moderation. **The *Rule of Saint Benedict* became the pattern for Western monasteries for a thousand years.** Monasteries kept schools, libraries and the copying of books, which is why most Latin literature survives.

**Ireland**, never part of the Roman Empire, was converted in the 400s. **Patrick**, a Romano-Briton carried off as a slave by Irish raiders, escaped and returned as a missionary; his own *Confession* survives, though his dates (traditionally from 432) are uncertain. Ireland developed a Church centred on great monasteries rather than bishops' cities.

**The Irish go out.** **Columba** founded a monastery on **Iona**, off western Scotland, in **563**, a base for converting the Picts. **Columbanus** crossed to Gaul about 590 and founded monasteries at Luxeuil and, in Italy, Bobbio.

**The mission to the English.** In **597** Pope **Gregory the Great** sent a monk, **Augustine**, with about forty companions to Kent. King **Æthelberht** had a Christian Frankish wife, **Bertha**, and was baptised soon after; Augustine became the first archbishop of **Canterbury**.

| Year | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **627** | **Edwin**, king of **Northumbria**, baptised at York by **Paulinus**, a monk of Augustine's mission |
| **633** | Edwin killed in battle by the pagan **Penda** of Mercia and the Christian British king **Cadwallon**; Northumbria relapses |
| **635** | King **Oswald**, raised in exile on Iona, brings the monk **Aidan**, who founds **Lindisfarne** |
| **664** | **Synod of Whitby**: Northumbria adopts the Roman, not the Irish, way of dating Easter |
| **668** | **Theodore of Tarsus**, a Greek from Asia Minor, becomes archbishop of Canterbury and organises the English Church |

**The golden age of Northumbria.** In the late 600s and early 700s the monasteries of **Wearmouth and Jarrow** and **Lindisfarne** were among the most learned places in Europe. The **Lindisfarne Gospels** were made about 700–720. The monk **Bede** (about 673–735) at Jarrow wrote on time and the calendar, and helped spread the use of **AD dating**, counting from the birth of Christ.

**The English go out.** English missionaries took Christianity back across the North Sea: **Willibrord** to the Frisians (690s), and **Boniface**, who felled a sacred oak of the god Donar at Geismar in Hesse (**723**), organised the Church in Germany with Frankish support, and was killed by pagans in Frisia in **754**.

**How conversion worked.** It usually went **from the top down**: a king accepted baptism, often influenced by a Christian wife or by alliance with a Christian power, and his nobles followed. It was not always lasting, and not always gentle. **For ordinary people, old customs and new faith mixed for generations**: Pope Gregory himself advised Augustine to turn pagan temples into churches and keep the feasts, rather than destroy them.
Primary source: Bede and the sparrow in:
How a king and his council chose a new religion in 627, as told by an English monk about a century later.

**The text** (Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, Book II, chapter 13; finished in **731**; revised translation by **A. M. Sellar, 1907**). King **Edwin** of Northumbria has asked his chief men what they think of the Christian teaching brought by **Paulinus**. First the chief priest, **Coifi**, answers that the old gods have done nothing for him. Then:

> Another of the king’s chief men, approving of his wise words and exhortations, added thereafter: “The present life of man upon earth, O king, seems to me, in comparison with that time which is unknown to us, like to the swift flight of a sparrow through the house wherein you sit at supper in winter, with your ealdormen and thegns, while the fire blazes in the midst, and the hall is warmed, but the wintry storms of rain or snow are raging abroad. The sparrow, flying in at one door and immediately out at another, whilst he is within, is safe from the wintry tempest; but after a short space of fair weather, he immediately vanishes out of your sight, passing from winter into winter again. So this life of man appears for a little while, but of what is to follow or what went before we know nothing at all. If, therefore, this new doctrine tells us something more certain, it seems justly to deserve to be followed.”

**Who and when.** **Bede** (about 673–735) was a monk at **Jarrow** in Northumbria from boyhood. He finished his history in **731**, about **104 years** after the council. He tells us in his preface that he gathered information from written records and from informants in each kingdom.

**Read it closely:**

| Phrase | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **"ealdormen and thegns"** | the king rules with his nobles; the decision is taken **in council**, not alone |
| **"the fire blazes in the midst"** | a real Anglo-Saxon **mead hall**: a long timber hall with a central hearth, like those excavated at **Yeavering**, one of Edwin's own royal sites |
| **"of what is to follow or what went before we know nothing"** | the argument for conversion is **about certainty**: the new faith offers an answer to death |
| **Coifi's speech** (just before) | the chief priest argues the old gods **did not reward him**: a practical, almost transactional reason |

**What to ask of it.**
- **Was it said?** Bede was not there, and the speaker has **no name**. The speech is beautifully shaped, in good Latin, and it may well be Bede's own composition, in the tradition of ancient historians who wrote the speeches they thought fitting. It may also preserve a memory of real arguments.
- **Why does Bede tell it?** His history is the story of how the English became a Christian people under God's providence. **He wants the conversion to look reasonable and freely chosen.**
- **What does it leave out?** That Edwin's conversion followed his marriage to **Æthelburh**, a Christian princess of Kent, and his promise to convert if he won a war (Bede tells both earlier in Book II). Kings had political reasons as well as spiritual ones.
- **What came next?** Bede goes on to tell how Coifi rode out on a stallion with a spear to profane the temple at **Goodmanham**, near York. And in **633**, Edwin was killed and Northumbria returned, for a time, to the old gods.

**Why it matters.** It is one of the very few accounts from anywhere of **a pagan people's council discussing conversion**. Even if the words are Bede's, it shows how an educated Christian of 731 imagined the choice, and it is a model of how to read a source: **who wrote it, when, why, and what they had to gain**.
The Umayyad caliphate from Damascus, 661:
The first Islamic dynasty: Arab kings who ruled from Syria an empire stretching from Spain to the Indus, and built the first great monuments of Islam.

**Mu'awiya** (ruled 661–680), governor of Syria and a member of the Quraysh clan of **Umayya**, became caliph after Ali's death and ruled from **Damascus**. He made the caliphate **hereditary**, naming his son **Yazid** as heir.

**Karbala, 680.** Ali's son **Husayn**, grandson of Muhammad, refused to accept Yazid and set out for Kufa in Iraq, expecting support. At **Karbala**, on **10 October 680** (the tenth of Muharram, 61 in the Islamic calendar), Husayn and a few dozen companions were surrounded by an Umayyad army and killed. **His death became the central event of Shi'i memory**, mourned every year at Ashura.

**Second civil war, 680–692.** A rival caliph, **Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr**, held Mecca for a decade. The caliph **Abd al-Malik** (685–705) finally defeated him in 692 and then remade the state:

| Reform | Date |
| --- | --- |
| **The Dome of the Rock** in Jerusalem, its inscription dated 72 in the Islamic calendar | **691–692** |
| **Arabic** made the language of government, replacing Greek and Persian in the tax offices | **from about 697** |
| **A new coinage** with Qur'anic words and no images | **696–697** |

**The second wave of conquest**, under **al-Walid I** (705–715) and after:

| Where | When |
| --- | --- |
| **North Africa** | completed about **705–710**, after long resistance by the **Berbers** (Amazigh), many of whom then joined the armies |
| **Spain** | invaded **711** (see al-Andalus) |
| **Sindh** (lower Indus) | taken by **Muhammad ibn Qasim**, **711–712** |
| **Transoxiana** | **Bukhara** (709) and **Samarkand** (712) taken by **Qutayba ibn Muslim** |
| **Constantinople** | besieged by land and sea, **717–718**: **failed**, with great losses |

**At its height, about 720–740, the caliphate was among the largest empires the world had yet seen.** Al-Walid built the **Great Mosque of Damascus** (706–715) on the site of a church

**The strains.** The Umayyad state favoured **Arabs**. Non-Arab converts (*mawali*) often paid higher taxes and received less, which bred resentment, especially among the Persian settlers and converts of **Khurasan** in the north-east. Shi'is mourned Husayn; Kharijites rejected the dynasty; the **Berbers** of North Africa rose in a great revolt in **740**. The expansion stopped: defeats at Constantinople (718), against the Khazars in the Caucasus, at Poitiers (732), and against the Turks in Central Asia.

**The fall.** In **747** a movement in Khurasan, led by **Abu Muslim** and calling for a ruler from the Prophet's family, raised **black banners**. It backed the **Abbasids**, descendants of Muhammad's uncle **al-Abbas**. At the **River Zab** in Iraq, in **January 750**, the last Umayyad caliph was defeated; he was killed in Egypt later that year, and most of his family were massacred. **One Umayyad prince escaped**, and reached Spain.

**How it is judged.** Later Abbasid historians, writing under the dynasty that destroyed them, painted the Umayyads as worldly kings rather than true caliphs. Many modern historians see them as **the builders of the Islamic state**: its language, coinage, administration and first great architecture.
Silla's Korea and Japan from Nara to Hei:
How Korea and Japan built states on the Chinese model, and then each made something distinctly its own.

**Korea's Three Kingdoms.** For centuries the peninsula was divided between **Goguryeo** (north, reaching into Manchuria), **Baekje** (south-west) and **Silla** (south-east). **Buddhism** entered from China: Goguryeo in **372**, Baekje soon after, and Silla only in about **528**.

**Silla unifies.** Silla allied with the **Tang**. Together they destroyed **Baekje** in **660**, beating a Japanese fleet sent to help it at the **Battle of Baekgang** in **663**, and **Goguryeo** in **668**. Then Silla fought its ally, and by **676** had driven the Tang armies out. **Unified Silla** (668–935) ruled most of the peninsula from **Gyeongju**, with a society ranked by birth in the strict **"bone rank"** system. In **751**, according to tradition, the minister Kim Dae-seong began the temple of **Bulguksa** and the granite cave shrine of **Seokguram**, whose seated Buddha is one of the masterpieces of East Asian sculpture. In the north, refugees from Goguryeo founded **Balhae** (698–926).

**The end of Silla.** From the 890s, rebels split the peninsula again. In **918** **Wang Geon** founded **Goryeo**, and in **935** the last Silla king surrendered to him. **Goryeo gave Korea its Western name.**

**Japan: the Yamato state.** From the 200s, rulers in the Kinai plain built huge **keyhole tombs** (the Kofun period). **Buddhism** arrived from **Baekje** in **538** or **552** (the sources differ). Prince **Shōtoku** (574–622) is credited with promoting Buddhism and with a **Seventeen-Article Constitution** of 604, though historians debate how much of his legend is real. In **645** a coup destroyed the powerful **Soga** clan and began the **Taika reforms**, which aimed at a Chinese-style state of land allotments and taxes; the **Taihō code** of **701** laid it out in law.

**Nara, 710–784.** The capital **Heijō-kyō** (Nara) was laid out as a small copy of **Chang'an**. Japan's first histories were written here: the ***Kojiki*** (**712**) and ***Nihon shoki*** (**720**). The emperor **Shōmu** built **Tōdai-ji** and its giant bronze Buddha, dedicated in **752**, after a **smallpox epidemic of 735–737** that may have killed a quarter or more of the population (an estimate).

**Heian, 794–1185.** The emperor **Kanmu** moved the capital to **Heian-kyō** (modern **Kyoto**) in **794**. Two monks back from China, **Saichō** and **Kūkai** (805–806), founded the Tendai and Shingon schools of Buddhism. **Real power passed to the Fujiwara family**, who married their daughters to emperors and ruled as regents from the mid-800s. In **894** official embassies to China stopped.

**A court culture of its own.** The **kana** syllabaries let Japanese be written by sound rather than only in Chinese characters, and women of the court, who were less expected to write in Chinese, used them to write some of the world's first great prose. Around **1000**, **Sei Shōnagon** wrote *The Pillow Book* and **Murasaki Shikibu** began *The Tale of Genji*, often called the world's first novel. **The Chinese model was adopted, then made Japanese.**
India after the Guptas: Harsha, the Chal:
Five centuries in which India had no single empire, but many strong regional kingdoms, great temples, and new kinds of devotion.

**Harsha** (ruled **606–647**), from his capital at **Kanauj** on the Ganges, built the last great empire of the north before the 1100s. We know him unusually well from two sources: the *Harshacharita*, a biography by his court poet **Bana**, and the travel account of the Chinese monk **Xuanzang**, who stayed in India from about **630 to 645**, studied at **Nalanda**, and attended Harsha's great religious assemblies. Harsha patronised Buddhists and Hindus alike and wrote plays. **His empire did not outlast him.**

**The Deccan stopped him.** The **Chalukya** king **Pulakeshin II** of Badami defeated Harsha on the **Narmada** river (the date is disputed, from the 610s to the 630s), keeping the north and south apart. His **Aihole inscription** of **634** records his victories.

**The South.** The **Pallavas** of **Kanchipuram** fought the Chalukyas for a century; **Narasimhavarman I** took Badami in **642**. At **Mamallapuram** on the coast they carved temples from boulders and cliffs, and built the **Shore Temple** (about 700). In Tamil country, **bhakti** poet-saints, the **Nayanars** (devotees of Shiva) and **Alvars** (of Vishnu), composed hymns of personal love for God in Tamil rather than Sanskrit, from about the 500s to the 800s. **Bhakti spread north over the following centuries and reshaped Hindu worship.**

**The Arabs in Sindh.** In **711–712** the Umayyad general **Muhammad ibn Qasim** conquered Sindh, the lower Indus. Further advances east were checked in the 700s, in part by the **Gurjara-Pratihara** kings.

**The struggle for Kanauj** (about 750–950). Three great dynasties fought over the old imperial city for two hundred years:

| Dynasty | Base | Known for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Gurjara-Pratiharas** | Rajasthan and the Ganges plain | holding off the Arabs of Sindh |
| **Palas** | **Bengal** | the last great patrons of Buddhism in India: Nalanda, and the monastery of **Vikramashila**, founded by **Dharmapala** (about 800) |
| **Rashtrakutas** | the **Deccan** | the **Kailasa temple at Ellora**, cut from a single hillside under **Krishna I** (about 756–773). Arab merchants of the 800s counted their king among the great kings of the world |

**The Cholas rise.** In about **850** **Vijayalaya** took **Thanjavur** in the Tamil south, founding the imperial **Chola** line. Under **Rajaraja I** (985–1014) the Cholas became the strongest power in south India, with a navy that would reach Sri Lanka and South-East Asia (Stage 7).

**The decline of Buddhism in India.** Buddhism was strong in Gupta times and still had great monasteries in 1000, but it had lost ground to the bhakti movements and to Hindu temple worship, and survived chiefly in the east under the Palas. Its final collapse in India came with the destruction of the monasteries in the late 1100s. **Meanwhile it flourished abroad**, in Sri Lanka, Tibet, China, Korea, Japan and South-East Asia.

**On the threshold.** In **1001** **Mahmud of Ghazni**, a Turkish ruler of Afghanistan, began raiding north India: the opening of the next age.
Al-Andalus: from the conquest of 711 to:
How most of Spain and Portugal became part of the Islamic world, and how an Umayyad refugee founded a state that became western Europe's richest.

**The conquest.** In **711** **Tariq ibn Ziyad**, a Berber commander serving the Umayyad governor of North Africa, crossed the strait at the rock that still bears his name, **Gibraltar** (*Jabal Tariq*, "Tariq's mountain"). The Visigothic king **Roderic** was defeated and killed, probably near the **Guadalete** river. The Visigothic kingdom, divided by a disputed succession, collapsed, and within about seven years most of the peninsula was under Muslim rule. The new province was called **al-Andalus**.

**The Christian north.** In the mountains of **Asturias**, a noble named **Pelayo** defeated a Muslim force at **Covadonga** (about **722**), later remembered as the start of the "Reconquista". Small Christian kingdoms grew in the north: Asturias (later León), Navarre, and the counties of Catalonia, which Charlemagne's armies took around **801** (Barcelona).

**The Umayyads of Córdoba:**

| Ruler | Date | What happened |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Abd al-Rahman I** | **756–788** | the Umayyad prince who escaped the massacre of 750; reached Spain and made himself **emir** at **Córdoba**, independent of Baghdad. Began the **Great Mosque** (about 785) |
| **Abd al-Rahman III** | **912–961** | restored order, and in **929** declared himself **caliph**, rivalling Baghdad and the Fatimids of North Africa; began the palace-city of **Madinat al-Zahra** (936) |
| **al-Mansur** (Almanzor) | **chief minister, about 978–1002** | the real ruler; over fifty raids on the Christian north, including the sack of **Santiago de Compostela** in **997** |

**A wealthy land.** Al-Andalus brought in new crops and irrigation: **rice, sugar cane, citrus fruit, cotton**, many probably arriving through the Islamic world from India and Persia. **Córdoba** in the 900s was the largest city in western Europe, perhaps 100,000 people or more (estimates vary widely).

**Who lived there.** Arabs (a small ruling group), many more **Berbers**, converts called **muwalladun**, Arabic-speaking Christians called **Mozarabs**, and **Jews**. Christians and Jews were *dhimmis*: protected, free to worship, paying a special tax and barred from some roles. Over the 800s and 900s most of the population converted to Islam. Jews rose high: **Hasdai ibn Shaprut** was physician and diplomat to Abd al-Rahman III.

**"Convivencia": how tolerant was it?** The word means "living together".
- **One reading** (María Rosa Menocal and others): al-Andalus was a culture of remarkable coexistence, in which three faiths shared a common Arabic culture of poetry, science and philosophy, far beyond anything in the Christian Europe of the time.
- **The other reading** (Darío Fernández-Morera and others): coexistence was **hierarchical**, with Christians and Jews legally inferior, and with real episodes of violence, such as the execution of the **Martyrs of Córdoba** (850s), Christians who publicly denounced Islam.
- **Both rest on real evidence.** What decides between them is mostly **when and where you look**, and whether "tolerant" is measured against modern standards or against the rest of the world in 950.

**The end of the caliphate.** After al-Mansur's sons, civil war broke out in **1009**; Madinat al-Zahra was sacked, and in **1031** the caliphate was abolished. Al-Andalus split into some twenty small kingdoms, the **taifas**, which the Christian north could now play against each other (Stage 7).
Talas, An Lushan and the fall of the Tan:
How the Tang empire lost Central Asia, nearly fell in a great rebellion, and survived for 150 years as a weaker state before China split again.

**Talas, 751.** In **July 751**, by the **Talas river** in modern Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan, a Tang army under the Korean-born general **Gao Xianzhi** met an Abbasid army sent from Khurasan. When the **Karluk** Turks on the Tang side changed sides, the Tang army was routed. **It is the only battle between the Tang and the Arab caliphate.**

**How much did Talas matter?** It was long told as the battle that decided Central Asia would be Muslim, not Chinese. Many historians now see it as less decisive: the Tang lost Central Asia mainly because of the rebellion that broke out four years later and forced it to withdraw its garrisons. **A famous story** says Chinese prisoners from Talas taught papermaking at **Samarkand**, from where it spread west. It comes from an Arabic writer of the **11th century**, and papermaking may have reached Central Asia earlier; paper certainly spread through the Islamic world in the following decades. One prisoner, **Du Huan**, did travel in the caliphate and returned to China in **762**, writing an account of what he saw.

**The An Lushan rebellion, 755–763.** **An Lushan**, a general of Sogdian and Turkic descent, commanded three frontier armies in the north-east, a favourite of the emperor **Xuanzong** and his consort **Yang Guifei**. In **December 755** he rebelled. He took **Luoyang**, then in **756** **Chang'an**. Xuanzong fled; on the way his soldiers forced him to have Yang Guifei executed. An Lushan was murdered by his own son in 757, but the war went on until **763**, ended only with the help of the **Uyghur** Turks.

**The cost.** The Tang census fell from about **53 million** people in **754** to about **17 million** in **764**. **This drop is not a death toll**: it records the collapse of the government's ability to register people, as well as real deaths. How many actually died is unknown, and claims that it was one of history's deadliest wars rest on the census figure.

**After the rebellion:**

| Change | What it meant |
| --- | --- |
| **Military governors** (*jiedushi*) | ruled their provinces almost independently, collected taxes and passed power to sons |
| **Central Asia lost** | Tibet took the Tarim and the Gansu corridor, and briefly occupied **Chang'an** in **763** |
| **New taxes** | the salt monopoly and the **two-tax system** of **780**, taxing property rather than people; the state became more commercial |

**The great persecution of 842–845.** The emperor **Wuzong** closed thousands of Buddhist monasteries and seized their lands and bronze; Tang records count over **260,000** monks and nuns returned to lay life. Buddhism survived, but never again had the same wealth.

**The fall.** The **Huang Chao** rebellion (**875–884**) swept across China; in **878–879** it sacked the great port of **Guangzhou**, where an Arab account says many thousands of foreign merchants were killed. The Tang never recovered, and in **907** a general, **Zhu Wen**, deposed the last emperor.

**Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms, 907–960.** North China passed through five short dynasties; the south split into about ten kingdoms. In the north-east, the **Khitan** founded the **Liao** empire (from 907/916). In **960** a general, **Zhao Kuangyin**, founded the **Song**, which reunited most of China by 979 (Stage 7). Meanwhile the oldest dated printed book, a copy of the **Diamond Sutra** printed in **868**, survived in a cave library at **Dunhuang**, sealed about 1000 and opened in 1900: China had printing.
The Abbasids, Baghdad and the House of W:
The caliphate's golden century, centred on a new round city in Iraq, and how it broke up into rival states by 1000.

**A new centre.** The **Abbasids** moved the caliphate east, from Syria to Iraq. In **762** the caliph **al-Mansur** founded **Baghdad** on the Tigris, close to the old Sasanian capital Ctesiphon. Its core was a **round city** about two kilometres across, with the caliph's palace and mosque at the centre and four gates facing the four directions. The city soon spread far beyond the walls; by the 800s it may have held several hundred thousand people, among the largest cities in the world.

**A more Persian, more universal empire.** The Abbasids relied on Persians from Khurasan and on **converts of every people**. Under them the distinction between Arab and non-Arab Muslim faded. A chief minister, the **vizier**, ran a bureaucracy on Sasanian lines.

**Harun al-Rashid** (786–809) is the caliph of the much later *Thousand and One Nights* stories. Frankish sources say he sent **Charlemagne** an elephant, **Abul-Abbas**, which reached Aachen in **802**.

**The translation movement.** From the late 700s to the late 900s, scholars in Baghdad translated into Arabic a great body of **Greek** science and philosophy (Aristotle, Galen, Euclid, Ptolemy), along with Persian and Indian works. **Paper**, made in Baghdad by the 790s, made books cheap.

| Scholar | Dates | Work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Hunayn ibn Ishaq** | **809–873** | Christian physician; translated much of Galen |
| **al-Khwarizmi** | **about 780–850** | the book that gave us the word **algebra** (*al-jabr*); his name gives us **algorithm**; spread Indian numerals |
| **al-Kindi** | **died about 870** | the first great Arabic-writing philosopher |
| **al-Razi** (Rhazes) | **died about 925** | physician; distinguished smallpox from measles |

**The House of Wisdom.** The ***Bayt al-Hikma***, associated with the caliph **al-Ma'mun** (813–833), is famous as a great academy of translators. **Historians debate what it was.** Some, such as Dimitri Gutas, argue it was a palace library and archive on the Sasanian model, and that the translation movement was driven by a whole society of patrons (caliphs, viziers, doctors, merchants), not one institution. Others keep a larger role for it. Both agree the translation movement was real and enormous.

**The breakup.** The caliphate's unity lasted barely a century:

| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **756** | al-Andalus independent under the Umayyads |
| **833–848** | the **Mihna**: caliphs try to impose a theological doctrine on scholars, and fail; religious authority passes to the scholars (*ulama*), not the caliph |
| **836–892** | the caliph's Turkish slave soldiers (*mamluks*, *ghulams*) dominate; the capital moved to **Samarra** |
| **869–883** | the **Zanj** revolt: enslaved East Africans working the salt marshes of southern Iraq rise and hold the region for fourteen years |
| **868–905** | Egypt independent under the Tulunids; Persian dynasties (the Samanids in **Bukhara**) rule the east |
| **909** | the **Fatimids**, a Shi'i dynasty, proclaim a rival caliphate in North Africa, and in **969** found **Cairo** |
| **945** | the **Buyids**, Shi'i soldiers from Iran, take Baghdad; the Abbasid caliph keeps his title but loses his power |

**By 1000 there were three caliphs**: Abbasid in Baghdad, Fatimid in Cairo, Umayyad in Córdoba. **The Islamic world was politically divided but culturally one**, joined by Arabic, the pilgrimage to Mecca, trade and learning.
Charlemagne and the Carolingian empire,:
The Frankish king who united most of western Christendom, was crowned emperor in Rome, and gave his name to a revival of learning.

**The family.** Pippin III became king of the Franks in **751** with the Pope's blessing; in **756** he gave the Pope lands in central Italy taken from the Lombards, the beginning of the **Papal States**. His son **Charles**, later **Charlemagne** ("Charles the Great"), born about 748, became king in **768**, and sole king in **771**.

**The wars.** Almost every year he campaigned:

| Against | When | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Lombards** | **774** | took their kingdom; king of the Lombards |
| **Saxons** | **772–804** | thirty years of war and forced conversion; at **Verden** in **782** the *Royal Frankish Annals* say **4,500** Saxons were beheaded (the number and its meaning are debated) |
| **Muslim Spain** | **778** | failed; the rearguard destroyed by Basques at **Roncesvalles**, later the *Song of Roland* |
| **Avars** | **790s** | their ring-fortress and treasure taken in Pannonia |
| **Spanish March** | **801** | Barcelona taken |

**Christmas Day 800.** In St Peter's in Rome, Pope **Leo III**, whom Charlemagne had restored after a rebellion, crowned him **emperor of the Romans**. **Einhard**, his biographer, claims he would not have entered the church had he known. Historians argue over who planned it and why. In Constantinople there was already a Roman emperor (at that moment an empress, **Irene**), and the eastern Romans recognised Charlemagne's title only in **812**, as emperor but not "of the Romans".

**Ruling it.** Charlemagne ruled through counts and through travelling royal envoys (*missi dominici*), held assemblies, issued decrees (**capitularies**), and from the 790s lived mostly at **Aachen**, where his chapel still stands. He set a coinage of **silver pennies** (*deniers*), 240 to the pound: the system Britain kept until 1971.

**The Carolingian renaissance.** Charlemagne brought scholars to his court, above all **Alcuin of York**. The decree known as the *Admonitio generalis* (**789**) called for schools in monasteries and cathedrals. Scribes developed **Carolingian minuscule**, a clear script with lower-case letters, **the ancestor of the letters on this page**. They copied ancient Latin texts on a great scale: **most classical Latin literature that survives does so in Carolingian copies**.

**The division.** Charlemagne died in **814**. His son **Louis the Pious** (814–840) faced revolts by his own sons, who at the **Treaty of Verdun** (**843**) split the empire in three: a **West Frankish** kingdom (the core of France), an **East Frankish** kingdom (the core of Germany), and a **Middle Kingdom** from the Low Countries to Italy, soon divided again. Vikings, Magyars and Arab raiders struck at the weakened kingdoms.

**The empire revived in the east.** The East Frankish king **Otto I** crushed the Magyars at the **Lechfeld** near Augsburg in **955**, and in **962** was crowned emperor in Rome: the beginning of what was later called the **Holy Roman Empire**, which lasted until 1806.
Byzantine Iconoclasm and the Macedonian:
How the Roman Empire in the East survived the Arab conquests, fought over holy images, and recovered to become the strongest power in Europe and the Near East by 1025.

**Survival.** After losing Syria, Egypt and North Africa, the empire held **Anatolia, Constantinople, the Aegean, Sicily and parts of Italy and the Balkans**. It reorganised its army into regional commands called **themes**, whose origins and dating are debated. It beat off Arab attacks on Constantinople, above all the great siege of **717–718**, using its land walls, its fleet and **"Greek fire"**, a liquid fire sprayed from ships, invented by a refugee from Syria named Kallinikos.

**Iconoclasm.** Icons, painted images of Christ and the saints, had become central to devotion. The **iconoclasts** ("image-breakers") held that venerating them was idolatry.

| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **from the 720s–730s** | **Leo III** (717–741), the defender of 717–718, is said to have begun the policy |
| **754** | **Constantine V** (741–775) holds a council at **Hieria** that condemns the veneration of icons; monks who resist are persecuted |
| **787** | the empress **Irene** holds the **Second Council of Nicaea**, which restores icons |
| **815–843** | a second iconoclast period |
| **843** | the empress **Theodora**, regent for her son, restores icons for good, still celebrated as the "Triumph of Orthodoxy" |

**Why did it happen? Historians disagree.** An older view held that emperors were reacting to defeat by Islam, a faith without images, or trying to break the power of the monasteries. **Leslie Brubaker and John Haldon** (2011) argue that the sources for Leo III's iconoclasm were written later by the victors, the icon-lovers, and that the policy really began under Constantine V and was **more about reform and authority than violence**. What would settle it is contemporary evidence from the 720s and 730s, which is very thin.

**The Macedonian dynasty, 867–1056.** **Basil I** (867–886), a peasant from Macedonia (in Thrace) who rose as a groom and murdered his way to the throne, founded the empire's longest-lived dynasty.

| Ruler | Known for |
| --- | --- |
| **Leo VI the Wise** (886–912) | the *Basilika*, a Greek revision of Justinian's law |
| **Nikephoros II Phokas** (963–969) and **John Tzimiskes** (969–976) | soldier-emperors: Crete (**961**) and **Antioch** (**969**) retaken |
| **Basil II** (976–1025) | annexed the **Bulgarian** empire by **1018**; called "the Bulgar-slayer" by later writers |

The chronicler **John Skylitzes**, writing about eighty years later, says Basil blinded **15,000** Bulgarian prisoners after the battle of **Kleidion** (**1014**); historians suspect the number is exaggerated.

**The revival of learning.** Under the patriarch **Photios** (858–867, 877–886), whose *Bibliotheca* summarised hundreds of books, many now lost, scholars recopied ancient Greek texts into the new **minuscule** script. **Much of ancient Greek literature survives only because it was copied in Constantinople in the 800s and 900s.**

**The commonwealth.** Constantinople's missionaries took Christianity to the **Bulgarians** and the **Rus'** (next lessons), and its quarrels with Rome (over the Pope's authority and the wording of the creed) grew. **In 1025 Byzantium was the richest and strongest state in Christendom.**
Srivijaya, Borobudur and the first Angko:
How the lands between India and China built states on the sea trade, adopted Indian religions and scripts, and raised some of the largest monuments in Asia.

**The lands between.** South-East Asia sat on the sea route between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea. Ships waited in its ports for the monsoon winds to change. From early centuries AD, rulers there adopted **Sanskrit**, Indian scripts, **Hindu and Buddhist** religion and Indian ideas of kingship, by choice and through trade, not conquest. Earlier, **Funan** in the Mekong delta (about 100–550) had been the great port kingdom.

**Srivijaya** (about 650–1100s). A Malay maritime kingdom centred at **Palembang** in south-east **Sumatra**, controlling the **Strait of Malacca** and the **Sunda Strait**, the two gates between the oceans.

| Evidence | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| **Old Malay inscriptions** at Palembang and on Bangka island, **682–686** | a ruler's victory, an expedition by boat, and oaths of loyalty with curses on traitors |
| **Yijing**, Chinese monk | stopped at Srivijaya in **671** and later lived there for years (to about **695**), copying Buddhist texts; he advised Chinese pilgrims to study there before going to India |
| **Chinese records** | Srivijaya sent regular tribute missions to the Tang and later the Song, which gave it privileged access to Chinese trade |
| **A copper-plate grant at Nalanda**, about **860** | a Srivijayan king, **Balaputra**, endowed a monastery at the great Indian Buddhist university |

**How it worked.** Srivijaya was less a territorial empire than a **network of ports** held together by the ruler's fleet, alliances with sea peoples, and the wealth of trade in pepper, camphor, spices, gold and Chinese silk and ceramics. **Its power lasted until a Chola naval raid from south India in 1025.**

**Java.** In central Java the **Sailendra** kings, Buddhists, built **Borobudur** (about **780–830**): a stepped stone mountain of nine platforms, with **over 2,600 relief panels** and **504 Buddha statues**, to be walked as a pilgrimage upward toward enlightenment. Nearby, Hindu kings of **Mataram** built the temple complex of **Prambanan** to Shiva, about **850**. Java's centre of power moved to the east of the island in the 900s.

**Angkor.** In what is now Cambodia, the Khmer prince **Jayavarman II** was proclaimed universal monarch on **Mount Kulen** in **802** (as a much later inscription of 1052 tells it), founding the Khmer empire. **Yasovarman I** founded a capital at **Angkor** in the late 800s. Its builders made vast reservoirs (*barays*) and temple-mountains; the greatest, Angkor Wat, came in the 1100s (Stage 7).

**Others on the map:**
- **Champa**, Hindu kingdoms of the Cham on the central coast of Vietnam, with the temple site of **My Son**.
- **Vietnam**, ruled by China for a thousand years, won independence after **Ngô Quyền** defeated a Chinese fleet at the **Bạch Đằng river** in **938**.
- **Pagan** in Burma, founded in the 800s, and the Mon kingdoms of **Dvaravati** in Thailand, both Buddhist.

**A shipwreck tells the trade.** The **Belitung wreck**, found off Sumatra in 1998, was an Arab or Indian-built sewn-plank ship that sank about **830** carrying some **60,000** pieces of Tang Chinese pottery, mostly bowls from Changsha, along with gold and silver: **direct evidence of a sea route from China to the Persian Gulf**.
Ghana and the trans-Saharan gold trade:
The first great West African empire known to written history, built on control of the gold that crossed the Sahara.

**The camel and the desert.** The Sahara was crossed by traders before the camel, but the **dromedary**, common in North Africa by the early centuries AD, made regular caravans possible: it carries about 150 kg and can go many days without water. After the Arab conquest of North Africa (by about **705–710**), Muslim **Berber** and Arab merchants organised the trade, from towns such as **Sijilmasa** in southern Morocco (founded about **757**) and **Tahert** in Algeria.

**What crossed the desert:**

| Going south | Going north |
| --- | --- |
| **salt**, cut in slabs from desert mines such as Ijil | **gold** |
| cloth, copper, horses, glass beads, books | **enslaved people**, ivory, leather, kola nuts |

**Salt was vital in the hot south**, which had little of its own; **gold was what the Mediterranean world wanted**. West African gold was struck into the gold coins of the caliphates and later of Europe.

**Ghana.** The empire of **Wagadu**, which Arab writers called **Ghana** after its king's title, was founded by the **Soninke** people in the Sahel north of the upper Niger and Senegal rivers, in what is now southern **Mauritania** and western **Mali**. It has nothing to do with the modern country of Ghana, which took the name at independence in 1957.

**When it began is not known.** Soninke tradition tells of a founder, Dinga, and of a sacred serpent, Bida, guardian of Wagadu's wealth. Some historians place the state's origins in the 300s–500s, others later. **The written record begins in the late 700s**, when the Arab astronomer **al-Fazari** called it "the land of gold".

**The fullest account** comes from **al-Bakri**, a geographer of Córdoba, writing in **1068** from merchants' reports. In paraphrase: the capital was two towns six miles apart, one of Muslim merchants with twelve mosques, the other the king's town with his palace and the sacred groves of the local religion; the king, not a Muslim, employed Muslims as his ministers and interpreters; **all gold nuggets found in the kingdom belonged to the king**, while gold dust was left to the people, which kept the price high; and **the king taxed every load of salt** entering and leaving.

**The capital** is probably the ruins at **Koumbi Saleh** in southern Mauritania, a stone town of perhaps 15,000–20,000 people at its height (an estimate), though the identification is not certain.

**Where the gold came from.** **Not Ghana itself**: the goldfields of **Bambuk** and **Bure** lay to the south, mined by peoples Ghana did not rule. **Ghana's power came from controlling the trade between the miners and the desert merchants**, and taxing it.

**Others in West Africa by 1000:**
- **Gao** on the Niger, whose king had converted to Islam by about 1000, the forerunner of Songhay.
- **Kanem**, near **Lake Chad**, described by al-Ya'qubi in the 800s.
- **Igbo-Ukwu**, in south-eastern Nigeria: astonishing bronze castings of the **800s–900s**, made by the lost-wax method, buried with tens of thousands of glass beads, some perhaps from far away.

**The end.** Ghana declined in the 1000s–1100s. An old story says the **Almoravids**, Berber reformers from the desert, conquered it in **1076**; many historians now doubt that a conquest happened (Stage 7).
Aksum's decline, Christian Nubia and the:
Three stories from eastern Africa: an old empire fading, Christian kingdoms that held off the caliphate, and a new coastal civilisation beginning.

**Aksum's Christian kings.** King **Ezana** of Aksum converted in the **330s–340s**, under the influence of **Frumentius**, a Syrian Christian captive who became Ethiopia's first bishop. Ezana's coins changed from the old crescent-and-disc to the **cross**: **Aksum was one of the first states in the world to adopt Christianity.** In about **525** King **Kaleb** invaded Yemen to protect its Christians from the Jewish king of Himyar.

**Aksum and Islam.** About **615**, Muhammad's persecuted followers took refuge with the Christian king of Aksum, the *najashi*. **Muslim tradition remembers him with honour**, and Aksum was not attacked in the early conquests.

**The decline.** Aksum's coinage ended in the early **600s**, and the city lost its importance. **The causes are debated**:
- **Trade**: the Persian conquest of Yemen (570s) and then the Islamic conquests shifted the Red Sea trade away from Aksum's port of **Adulis**.
- **Land**: centuries of farming and tree-cutting may have exhausted the soil around the capital.
- **Climate**: changes in rainfall may have added to both.

The Christian kingdom moved its centre south, deeper into the highlands. **Ethiopian Christianity survived**, to rise again under the Zagwe kings (Stage 7).

**Christian Nubia.** On the Nile south of Egypt, three Nubian kingdoms, **Nobadia**, **Makuria** and **Alodia**, accepted Christianity in the **540s–570s**, through rival missions sent by Justinian and by Theodora. When the Arabs of Egypt invaded, the Nubian archers, famous for their aim, beat them back at **Dongola** (**642** and **652**). The two sides made a treaty, the **Baqt** (**652**), an exchange of goods under which Nubia sent enslaved people north each year and Egypt sent grain, cloth and wine south. **It held, with breaks, for about six hundred years**, an unusual peace between a Christian kingdom and the caliphate.

**The Swahili coast.** Along the coast of what is now **Kenya, Tanzania and northern Mozambique**, farming and fishing villages of **Bantu-speaking** people, making a pottery archaeologists call **Tana tradition** (from about the 600s), grew into trading towns.

| Site | What was found |
| --- | --- |
| **Shanga**, Lamu islands, Kenya | a town from about **750**; a sequence of timber mosques, the earliest from the late 700s, later rebuilt in coral stone |
| **Unguja Ukuu**, Zanzibar | a port of the 600s–900s with Persian, Islamic and Chinese pottery |
| **Chibuene**, Mozambique | a southern trading station of the 700s–900s |

**They traded** ivory, mangrove timber, tortoiseshell, gold from the south and enslaved people across the Indian Ocean to Arabia, the Persian Gulf and beyond, for cloth, glass and pottery. Arab geographers called these lands **the land of the Zanj**; the Zanj revolt in Iraq (869–883) was a rising of enslaved East Africans.

**Who built the Swahili towns?** Colonial-era historians assumed they were **Arab or Persian colonies**. Archaeology and linguistics have overturned that: **Swahili is a Bantu language**, the towns grew from local villages, and Islam was adopted gradually by African townspeople, though families with Arabian and Persian ties joined them and later traditions (the "Shirazi" stories) claimed Persian founders. **The consensus now is an African civilisation with deep Indian Ocean connections.**
The Classic Maya collapse, about 750–950:
Why the great kingdoms of the southern Maya lowlands stopped building, stopped writing, and emptied over about two centuries: one of the most debated questions in archaeology.

**What happened.** From about **750**, across the southern lowlands of Guatemala, Belize and southern Mexico, the royal cities stopped raising dated monuments, one after another:

| City | Last dated monument (approximate) |
| --- | --- |
| **Copán** | **822** |
| **Tikal** | **869** |
| **Toniná** | **909**, the last known Long Count date |

The kings disappeared first. Then over the following generations the **population fell sharply**, and the great cities were left to the forest. **By about 950 the southern lowlands held a small fraction of their peak population.**

**What did not happen.** The Maya did not vanish. In the **northern Yucatán** cities flourished in the 800s–900s, such as the Puuc cities like **Uxmal**, and **Chichén Itzá**, which became the great power of the north. **Millions of Maya people live in the region today**, speaking some thirty Maya languages. For this reason many archaeologists dislike the word "collapse" and speak of the end of a political system rather than of a people.

**The explanations, in their strongest forms:**

| Explanation | The evidence |
| --- | --- |
| **Drought** | lake sediments (Lake Chichancanab, 1995) and cave stalagmites (Belize, 2012) show **a series of severe droughts between about 800 and 1000**; one study (2018) estimated rainfall fell by about 40–50% at the worst |
| **Endemic war** | inscriptions record rising warfare; in the **Petexbatún** region, **Dos Pilas** fell about **760** and **Aguateca** was burned and abandoned in haste about **810**, its houses left full of goods |
| **Environmental strain** | dense populations had cut forests and farmed hillsides; soil erosion and shortened fallow could make a drought deadly |
| **Political failure** | divine kings claimed to bring rain and victory; when they could not, people may have stopped supporting them and moved away |
| **Shifting trade** | trade moved from inland rivers to sea routes around the Yucatán coast, favouring northern cities |

**Where historians agree.** Most now think **several of these worked together**: a crowded landscape already under strain, kingdoms at war, and droughts that hit at the wrong time. **The north was drier, yet flourished**, which shows that drought alone does not explain everything.

**What would settle it.** Matching **precisely dated climate records** against **precisely dated abandonments** site by site: if each city emptied during a drought, the climate case is strengthened; if some emptied in wet years, or the order runs the wrong way, other causes come first. Skeletons, which show diet and health, and lidar maps of fields and terraces add more each year.

**Why it matters beyond the Maya.** The collapse is often used as a warning about climate and environment. **That is a fair use, but only if the case is made from the evidence**, which is still being argued.
Tiwanaku and Wari: the Andean empires be:
The two great highland states of the Andes in these centuries, which built roads, colonies and cities at altitudes where few states anywhere have ever thrived.

**The coast first.** On the north coast of Peru, the **Moche** (about **100–800**) built huge adobe pyramids, the **Huacas del Sol and de la Luna**, and made some of the finest pottery in the Americas, modelled with portraits, animals and scenes of sacrifice. The tomb of the **Lord of Sipán**, found intact in **1987**, held gold, silver and turquoise regalia. Moche decline around **600–800** is often linked to severe floods and droughts brought by **El Niño**, though war and politics probably mattered too.

**Tiwanaku** (flourished about **500–1000**). Its city stood near the southern shore of **Lake Titicaca**, in modern **Bolivia**, at about **3,850 metres**.

| Feature | What it was |
| --- | --- |
| **Akapana** | a terraced earth-and-stone platform pyramid |
| **Kalasasaya** | a great walled courtyard |
| **Gateway of the Sun** | a stone gate carved with a figure holding two staffs, the **"Staff God"** |
| **Raised fields** | platforms of earth between water channels, which held heat against the frost and grew potatoes and other crops at high altitude |
| **Llama caravans** | carried goods to colonies in warmer valleys, such as **Moquegua** in southern Peru, and as far as the Atacama in Chile |

**How many people lived there** is debated, with estimates from about 10,000 to several times that. Tiwanaku spread its influence more through religion, trade and colonies than conquest, though historians argue about how much force it used.

**Wari** (about **600–1000**). Its capital, **Huari**, near modern **Ayacucho** in the central highlands of **Peru**, was a dense city of walled compounds. Wari built **administrative centres** across Peru, such as **Pikillacta** near Cusco, a grid of hundreds of rooms, and **roads** between them that the Inca later used. Wari officials used **khipus**, knotted cords for records, centuries before the Inca. In **2013** archaeologists found an untouched royal tomb at **El Castillo de Huarmey** on the coast, holding dozens of noblewomen with gold and fine textiles.

**Were they empires?** **Wari** is often called **the first Andean empire**, because of its planned centres and roads; others think it was a looser network of colonies and alliances. **Tiwanaku** is sometimes seen as more of a religious centre with wide influence. **Both share the Staff God image**, but how they were related, as rivals, partners or offshoots of one religion, is unknown. At **Cerro Baúl** in Moquegua, a Wari outpost with a large brewery stood within sight of Tiwanaku settlements, and the two seem to have coexisted.

**The end.** Wari faded around **1000**, and Tiwanaku around **1000–1150**. Ice cores from the **Quelccaya** ice cap in Peru show **drought** in these centuries, and many link the collapses to it; others stress political breakdown. Their successors, such as the **Chimú** on the coast and, eventually, the **Inca**, inherited their roads, terraces, khipus and gods (Stage 7).

**And in North America**, in these same centuries, maize farming spread up the Mississippi valley, and the **Ancestral Puebloans** began building the great houses of **Chaco Canyon** in New Mexico (from about **850**).
The Viking age, 793–1000:
Two centuries in which Scandinavians raided, traded and settled from Baghdad's markets to the coast of North America.

**Who they were.** "Viking" meant a sea-raider; the people were **Norse** farmers, traders and warriors of Denmark, Norway and Sweden, pagan, speaking Old Norse and writing short inscriptions in **runes**. Their **longships**, light, shallow and fast under oar or sail, could cross open sea and row up rivers.

**The first raid.** In **793** raiders sacked the monastery of **Lindisfarne** in Northumbria. **Alcuin**, at Charlemagne's court, wrote that never before had such terror appeared in Britain. Monasteries were rich, undefended and on the coast.

**Why then? Historians weigh several causes**: better ships and sails; political struggles at home that sent losers abroad; a growing population; the lure of silver from a booming trade with the Islamic world; and, some argue, a reaction to Charlemagne's violent conversion of their Saxon neighbours.

**West: raid, then conquest, then settlement:**

| Where | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| **Ireland** | **Dublin** founded as a Norse base in **841**, Ireland's first town |
| **England** | the **"Great Army"** lands in **865** and conquers every English kingdom but **Wessex**. **Alfred the Great** (871–899) defeats it at **Edington** (**878**); the Danish leader Guthrum is baptised, and the north and east become the **Danelaw**. Alfred's heirs unite England by **927** |
| **France** | **Paris** besieged in **885–886**; in **911** the Viking leader **Rollo** is granted land at the mouth of the Seine: **Normandy**, "land of the Northmen" |
| **Spain** | raids on Seville in **844** |

**Across the Atlantic.** Norse settlers reached **Iceland** around **870**; in **930** they founded the **Althing**, an assembly of free men, one of the oldest of its kind. **Erik the Red** led settlers to **Greenland** about **985**. About **1000** his son **Leif Eriksson** sailed further west, to a land the sagas call **Vinland**. In **1960** a Norse site was found at **L'Anse aux Meadows** in **Newfoundland**, and in **2021** tree rings in its wood showed it was cut with metal tools in **1021**. **This is the first known European presence in the Americas, nearly 500 years before Columbus.** It was a short-lived base.

**East: rivers and silver.** Swedish Norse, called **Rus'** or **Varangians**, travelled down the rivers of what are now Russia and Ukraine, the Dnieper to the Black Sea and Constantinople, the Volga to the Caspian and the markets of the Abbasid caliphate. They sold **furs, wax, honey and slaves** for silver. **Tens of thousands of Islamic silver coins** have been found in hoards in Sweden, especially on the island of **Gotland**. An Arab envoy, **Ibn Fadlan**, met Rus' traders on the Volga in **921–922** and described a ship cremation of a chief. From the late 900s the Byzantine emperors kept a **Varangian Guard** of Norse soldiers.

**Conversion.** The Norse kingdoms became Christian between about **960** and **1100**, from the top down. **Harald Bluetooth** carved on the great runestone at **Jelling** (about **965**) that he had "made the Danes Christian". Iceland's Althing accepted Christianity by vote in about **999 or 1000**, allowing pagan worship in private for a time. **With conversion and settled kingdoms, the Viking age ended**, and the Norse became part of Christian Europe.
Kievan Rus' and the baptism of 988:
How a state grew up on the river road from the Baltic to Constantinople, and how its ruler's baptism tied the East Slavs to Byzantium.

**The Slavs.** By the 600s Slavic-speaking peoples had spread across eastern Europe, from the Baltic to the Balkans. To the south-east, the **Khazars**, a Turkic people, ruled the steppe between the Black Sea and the Caspian from about 650. **Their ruling elite adopted Judaism**, probably in the 700s or 800s; the date and how widely it spread are debated.

**The Byzantine mission to the Slavs.** In **863** two brothers from Thessalonica, **Constantine (Cyril) and Methodius**, went as missionaries to **Moravia**. They created the **Glagolitic alphabet** to write Slavonic, and translated the liturgy. Their followers, driven from Moravia, went to **Bulgaria**, whose khan **Boris** had been baptised about **864–866**; there the **Cyrillic** alphabet, named after Cyril, was developed. **Old Church Slavonic became the written language of Orthodox Slavs.**

**The Rus'.** The main source is the ***Primary Chronicle***, compiled in Kyiv about **1113**. It says that in **862** the quarrelling peoples of the north invited a Varangian, **Rurik**, to rule them at **Novgorod**, and that his kinsman **Oleg** took **Kyiv** in **882**.

**Who were the Rus'?** A long debate. **"Normanists"** hold that the Rus' were Scandinavians who ruled over Slavs, pointing to Norse names in the treaties with Byzantium (911 and 944) and to Scandinavian graves. **"Anti-Normanists"** stressed Slavic origins, and in the Soviet era the question became political. **Most historians now agree** that the ruling Rus' were largely of Scandinavian origin and quickly became **Slavic in speech and culture**: **Igor** (Norse *Ingvar*) and **Olga** (Norse *Helga*) gave their son, Vladimir's father, the Slavic name **Sviatoslav**.

**The rulers of Kyiv:**

| Ruler | Date | Known for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Oleg** | **882–about 912** | trading treaty with Byzantium (**911**) |
| **Olga** | regent, **about 945–960s** | baptised at **Constantinople** about **957**, but her people stayed pagan |
| **Sviatoslav** | **about 960–972** | destroyed the **Khazar** state (about **965**); fought Byzantium in Bulgaria |
| **Vladimir** | **about 980–1015** | the baptism of 988 |

**The baptism of 988.** The *Primary Chronicle* tells that Vladimir sent envoys to examine the faiths of his neighbours: the Muslims of the Volga Bulgars, the Jews of the Khazars, the Latin Christians of Germany, and the Greeks. **His envoys reported that in Hagia Sophia they did not know whether they were in heaven or on earth.** Written a century later, the story is not a record, but it captures the choice.

**The politics.** In **987–988** the emperor **Basil II** faced a rebellion and needed troops. Vladimir sent some **6,000 Varangians**, the start of the Varangian Guard. In return he was promised the emperor's sister **Anna**, a princess born in the purple, and he accepted baptism. When the marriage was delayed, he took the Byzantine city of **Chersonesos** in Crimea. **He was baptised, married Anna, and had the people of Kyiv baptised in the Dnieper** (the dates 987–989 are given in different sources). He threw down the idol of the god **Perun** that he himself had set up.

**What it meant.** **The East Slavs joined the Byzantine, Orthodox world**, not the Latin one: Greek bishops, Slavonic liturgy and Cyrillic letters, Byzantine church architecture and icons. Ukraine, Belarus and Russia all trace their Christian history to this baptism, and **all three claim Kievan Rus' as their own beginning**, a claim at the heart of present politics.
The Polynesian voyages and the Austrones:
The greatest feat of seafaring before the age of European exploration: people who crossed thousands of kilometres of open ocean without instruments, to the last islands on Earth to be settled.

**Who they were.** Polynesians descend from **Austronesian**-speaking peoples who spread by sea from **Taiwan** over thousands of years, into the Philippines and Indonesia, and then out into the Pacific. A people archaeologists call **Lapita**, after their stamped pottery, reached **Tonga** and **Samoa** about **2,800–2,900 years ago** (about 900–800 BC). There, Polynesian culture took shape.

**The long pause.** Then, for well over a thousand years, the voyaging east seems to have stopped. **Why is unknown**: perhaps the winds, perhaps the distances (the next islands east lay much further away), perhaps the need for new canoe designs.

**When did they move east? A debate of dates.**
- **The older, "long" chronology**, built on radiocarbon dates from the 1950s–80s, put the first settlement of the Marquesas or Society Islands in the first millennium AD, perhaps by 300–600.
- **The newer, "short" chronology** (Janet Wilmshurst and colleagues, **2011**) re-dated only the most reliable samples, such as seeds and twigs, and found **settlement of the Society Islands about 1025–1120**, and then **an astonishingly fast spread**, within a century or two, to **Hawaii**, **Rapa Nui** (Easter Island) and **New Zealand** (Aotearoa), the last about **1250–1300**.
- **Most archaeologists now accept the later dates**, at least for the remote islands; some argue a few island groups were reached earlier. More well-dated sites from the first settlements would settle it.

**How they did it.** In **double-hulled sailing canoes**, able to carry families, pigs, dogs, chickens and plants such as taro, breadfruit and coconut. **Navigators read the rising and setting points of stars, the shape of ocean swells, cloud over unseen land, and the flight of birds.** In **1976** the replica canoe **Hōkūleʻa** sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti, about 4,000 km, guided by the Micronesian navigator **Mau Piailug** without instruments: **proof that deliberate voyages, not lucky drift, settled the Pacific.**

**Did they reach America?** **Almost certainly yes.** The **sweet potato**, an American plant, was grown in East Polynesia before Europeans came; carbonised remains in the Cook Islands date to about **1000** (perhaps later). A **2020** DNA study found traces of Native American ancestry in some East Polynesian peoples dating to about **1150–1230**. Whether Polynesians sailed to South America and back, or South Americans sailed west, is still argued.

**West across the Indian Ocean.** Other Austronesians sailed west. **Madagascar**, off Africa's south-east coast, was settled by people whose language, **Malagasy**, is closest to **Ma'anyan**, spoken in southern **Borneo**, nearly 7,000 km away. They arrived at some point in the **first millennium AD** (the dates are debated, from about 500 to later), and mixed with **Bantu-speaking** Africans; modern Malagasy people carry both ancestries. **By 1000, Austronesian languages were spoken from Madagascar to the edge of the eastern Pacific**, more than halfway around the world.

**Australia and New Guinea** were already long settled, by Aboriginal Australians and Papuan peoples, as Stage 1 told.
Connections: the world in AD 1000:
The stage closes in the year 1000: who traded with, fought and converted whom, and what carried over into the next age.

**About 250–300 million people** lived in the world (estimates vary), still mostly farmers. The largest cities were probably **Córdoba**, **Constantinople**, **Baghdad**, **Cairo**, and the great Chinese cities soon to grow under the Song, such as **Kaifeng**.

**The faiths, compared with AD 300:**

| Faith | Where it was established by 1000 |
| --- | --- |
| **Latin Christianity** | western and central Europe, from Iceland and Scandinavia to Poland (**966**) and Hungary (**1000**) |
| **Orthodox Christianity** | Byzantium, Bulgaria, Serbia, Kievan Rus' |
| **Other Christian churches** | the Coptic Church in Egypt, Nubia, Ethiopia, Armenia; the Church of the East in Iraq, Persia and Central Asia |
| **Islam** | from **al-Andalus** to **Sindh** and **Transoxiana**; merchants on the Swahili coast and in the Sahel towns |
| **Buddhism** | China, Korea, Japan, Tibet, Sri Lanka and much of South-East Asia; fading in India |
| **Hinduism** | India, and courts in Java, Cambodia and Champa |

**How the faiths spread.** Three ways, often at once: **conquest** (the Arab armies; Charlemagne's Saxon wars), **kings choosing** (Clovis, Edwin, Boris, Vladimir, Harald Bluetooth), and **merchants and monks** (the Church of the East to China, Buddhism to Japan, Islam along the trade routes of Africa and Asia).

**The great networks:**

| Network | Who and what |
| --- | --- |
| **The Silk Roads** | Sogdians, Persians, Turks and Uyghurs carrying silk, silver, horses and religions between China and the Islamic world |
