| **The Indian Ocean** | Arab, Persian, Indian, Malay and Swahili sailors, carrying Chinese ceramics, spices, cotton, ivory and gold on the monsoon winds |
| **The Sahara** | gold and enslaved people north, salt and goods south |
| **The rivers of Rus'** | Norse and Slav traders, furs and slaves for Islamic silver |
| **The Mediterranean** | Byzantine, Muslim and Italian ships (Venice and Amalfi already rising) |

**Who fought whom.** Byzantium against Bulgaria and the Fatimids; the Song against the Khitan Liao; Danes against the English; and in India, **Mahmud of Ghazni** about to begin his raids (1001).

**What carries over into Stage 7:**
- **The Turks**: the **Seljuks**, converted to Islam, would take Baghdad in **1055** and defeat Byzantium at **Manzikert** in **1071**.
- **East and West**: the quarrels between Rome and Constantinople would break into the **schism of 1054**, and the Turkish advance would bring the **Crusades** (1095).
- **The Song** would build the world's most advanced economy, with printing, paper money and gunpowder.
- **In Africa**, Ghana would give way to **Mali**; on the Swahili coast **Kilwa** would rise; on the Limpopo, **Mapungubwe** and then **Great Zimbabwe** (the South African thread is in the South African Politics curriculum).
- **In the Americas**, **Cahokia** on the Mississippi, the Toltecs and Chichén Itzá, and later the **Aztecs** and **Inca**.

**The shape of the whole stage.** In 300, the world's great states were Rome, Persia and divided China. By 1000, **Rome continued in the East, Persia was part of the Islamic world, and China had been reunited and divided again**. The biggest change was not of empires but of faiths: **most of Eurasia and North Africa now belonged to Christianity, Islam or Buddhism**, and the boundaries drawn between them in these seven centuries are still visible on the map of the world today.
Map: the world in the year 1000:
The stage opens in **the year 1000**, a round number that meant something only to Christians counting from the birth of Christ. Here is where everyone stood. World population was perhaps **250–300 million**, a guess built from tax records and archaeology.

| Region | Around AD 1000 |
| --- | --- |
| **Byzantium** | the Roman Empire in the east, capital **Constantinople**, at a peak under **Basil II** (r. 976–1025), who finished conquering Bulgaria in **1018** |
| **The Islamic world** | split three ways: the Abbasid caliph in **Baghdad**, a figurehead under Iranian Buyid soldiers; the Shi'a **Fatimid** caliphs in **Cairo**, founded **969**; and the Umayyad caliphate of **Córdoba** in Spain, which broke apart after **1009** |
| **Latin Europe** | new Christian kingdoms: **Poland** and **Hungary** (Stephen crowned about **1000**); Otto III ruling the German **Holy Roman Empire**; the Capetian kings of France (from **987**); Kievan Rus', Christian since about **988** |
| **The North Atlantic** | Norse settlers in Iceland and Greenland; a short-lived camp at **L'Anse aux Meadows** in Newfoundland, where tree rings show wood cut in **1021** |
| **South Asia** | the **Chola** kings of the far south, a sea power; **Mahmud of Ghazni** raiding north India from Afghanistan (about 1000–1027) |
| **East Asia** | the **Song** dynasty (from **960**) ruling most of China, paying off the Khitan **Liao** in the north; **Goryeo** in Korea; **Heian** Japan, where Murasaki Shikibu was writing *The Tale of Genji* |
| **South-East Asia** | the Khmer kingdom at **Angkor**; **Srivijaya**, a trading power on Sumatra; **Đại Việt**, independent of China since **939** |
| **Africa** | **Ghana** in the western Sahel, trading gold across the Sahara; **Kanem** near Lake Chad; **Ife**, whose famous brass heads come a little later; early **Swahili** towns on the east coast; **Mapungubwe**'s predecessor at **K2** in the Limpopo valley |
| **The Americas** | **Chichen Itza** at its height in Yucatán; **Tula**, the Toltec city in central Mexico; the great houses of **Chaco Canyon**; **Cahokia** about to grow; **Tiwanaku** and **Wari** in the Andes fading |
| **Oceania** | Polynesian voyagers on the edge of the great push into **eastern Polynesia**; New Zealand still unsettled |

**Three things to carry through the stage:**

1. **No single centre.** The richest and largest cities, Kaifeng in China, Constantinople, Baghdad, Córdoba, were all outside Latin Europe.
2. **The steppe is quiet, but not for long.** The Turks have begun moving west; the Mongols are a scatter of clans.
3. **The Americas and Oceania are on their own.** Their histories ran in parallel with Eurasia's and Africa's, without contact, except for the Norse visit to Newfoundland.

By the stage's end, in **1450**, the Mongols will have joined most of Eurasia and then broken apart, plague will have killed perhaps a third or more of the people in the lands it reached, and Constantinople will be three years from its fall.
The Great Schism of 1054:
In **July 1054**, in the church of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople, a papal envoy laid a document of excommunication on the altar. It is the date usually given for the split between the Catholic West and the Orthodox East. Here it is taught as history; the theology belongs to Theology.

**The people.** **Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida**, sent by **Pope Leo IX**, and **Michael Cerularius**, Patriarch of Constantinople. On **16 July 1054** Humbert placed a bull excommunicating Cerularius on the altar. Days later a synod in Constantinople excommunicated the legates in return.

**A strange detail.** Leo IX had **died in April 1054**, months before. Whether a dead pope's envoy still had authority is doubtful, and the bull excommunicated individuals, not a whole church.

**The quarrels behind it:**

| Issue | East | West |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Authority** | the pope is first in honour among five patriarchs | the pope holds authority over the whole Church |
| **The *filioque*** | the Creed as agreed in 381 | had added "and the Son" to the Creed |
| **Bread at communion** | leavened | unleavened |
| **Language and rite** | Greek | Latin |
| **Clergy** | parish priests may marry | reformers were pressing celibacy |

**Two churches had been drifting apart for centuries.** They spoke different languages, the West had its own emperor since Charlemagne in **800**, and the papacy of the 1050s was a new, reforming, ambitious one.

**The debate: was 1054 the break?**

- **The traditional reading.** 1054 marks the schism: the mutual excommunications set the two churches formally against each other.
- **The gradual reading**, now common among historians. **Contemporaries barely noticed 1054.** Byzantine emperors kept negotiating with popes, crusaders were welcomed in Constantinople in **1096–97**, and there were earlier ruptures (the "Photian schism" of the 860s). On this reading the decisive break was **1204**, when Western crusaders sacked Constantinople and set up Latin bishops (a later lesson).

**What would settle it:** evidence of how ordinary clergy and laity treated each other between 1054 and 1204: whether Greeks and Latins shared communion, married, and accepted each other's priests. The surviving record shows a mixed picture, which is why the argument lasts.

**Attempts at reunion** failed: at **Lyon (1274)** and **Florence (1439)**, emperors agreed to union for political reasons, and their own people rejected it.

**The excommunications were lifted in 1965** by Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras. The churches remain separate.
The Seljuk Turks and the battle of Manzi:
The Turks came out of Central Asia, took over the heart of the Islamic world, and broke Byzantium's hold on Anatolia: the land that is now Turkey.

**Who the Seljuks were.** A clan of the **Oghuz Turks**, steppe horsemen who had converted to Sunni Islam in the late 900s, named after their ancestor **Seljuk**. Under **Tughril Beg** they took Khurasan in eastern Iran (battle of **Dandanaqan, 1040**) and entered **Baghdad in 1055**. The Abbasid caliph kept his title and religious standing; Tughril took the title **sultan**, "holder of power." **The caliph reigned; the sultan ruled.**

**The battle.** On **26 August 1071**, near **Manzikert** (Malazgirt) north of Lake Van in eastern Anatolia, the Seljuk sultan **Alp Arslan** defeated the Byzantine emperor **Romanos IV Diogenes**.

- Part of the Byzantine army, under **Andronikos Doukas**, a rival family's man, withdrew during the fighting; many historians read it as betrayal.
- **Romanos was captured.** Alp Arslan treated him with honour and released him within about a week on terms.
- Back home, Romanos found he had been deposed. He was defeated in civil war, blinded, and died in 1072.

**What happened next mattered more than the battle.** Byzantium fell into **ten years of civil war**. Rival generals hired Turkish bands to fight each other. Turkish groups spread across Anatolia almost unopposed, and by about **1080** a Seljuk prince, **Süleyman**, had a state centred on **Nicaea**, near Constantinople itself. It became the **Sultanate of Rum** ("Rome"), later based at **Konya**.

**The debate: how decisive was Manzikert?**

- **Catastrophe.** Byzantine writers such as Michael Attaleiates, who was there, saw it as a disaster. It opened Anatolia, the empire's main source of soldiers and taxes, to the Turks.
- **Not the battle but the aftermath.** Casualties seem to have been fairly light and the peace terms mild. Turks were already raiding before 1071. **The empire lost Anatolia through its own civil wars**, not one afternoon's fighting.

**What would settle it:** a clearer count of the losses and a better timeline of Turkish settlement in the 1070s. Both readings agree that **by 1081, when Alexios I Komnenos took the throne, most of Anatolia was gone.**

**Why it matters for the next lesson.** Alexios needed soldiers. In **1095** his envoys asked the pope for Western help. The answer was the First Crusade.

**The Great Seljuks themselves** fragmented after the death of the vizier **Nizam al-Mulk** and sultan **Malik Shah** in **1092**. Nizam al-Mulk founded the **Nizamiyya** colleges (Baghdad, **1067**), which spread a model of the madrasa across the Sunni world.
The First Crusade and the crusader state:
In **November 1095**, at **Clermont** in France, **Pope Urban II** preached an armed pilgrimage to help the Christians of the East and free Jerusalem. Four years later a Western army took the city.

**The call.** Alexios I Komnenos had asked for mercenaries against the Turks. Urban asked for something new: **a war that counted as penance**, earning the fighters remission of their sins. The crowd's reported cry, *Deus vult*, "God wills it," appears in later accounts of the speech, which survive only in versions written after the crusade had succeeded.

**What happened:**

| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **1096** | the "People's Crusade" under **Peter the Hermit**, mostly poor pilgrims, is destroyed by the Turks in Anatolia. Bands in the **Rhineland massacre Jews** at Speyer, Worms and Mainz |
| **1097** | the princes' armies, perhaps 50,000–70,000 people with non-combatants (estimates vary), cross to Asia; **Nicaea** is taken and handed to the Byzantines |
| **1098** | **Antioch** falls after an eight-month siege |
| **15 July 1099** | **Jerusalem** taken by storm, followed by a **massacre of Muslims and Jews** described by both Christian and Muslim writers; the death toll is debated |

**Why did it succeed?** Largely because **the Muslim Near East was divided**: Seljuk princes fought each other, and the Fatimids of Egypt, who had just retaken Jerusalem from the Turks in 1098, were rivals of the Seljuks. No united response came for a generation.

**The four crusader states**, called *Outremer*, "overseas": the **County of Edessa** (1098), the **Principality of Antioch** (1098), the **Kingdom of Jerusalem** (1099) and the **County of Tripoli** (1109). A thin Frankish elite ruled a mostly Muslim and Eastern Christian population, helped by military orders such as the **Templars** and **Hospitallers**, and by Italian merchants.

**The turn.** In **1144** **Zengi**, ruler of Mosul and Aleppo, took **Edessa**. The **Second Crusade** (1147–49), led by the kings of France and Germany, failed before **Damascus** in 1148.

**The debate: why did people go?**

| Reading | The argument |
| --- | --- |
| **Land and loot** | an older view: landless younger sons seeking fortunes |
| **Faith** | Jonathan Riley-Smith and others, from charters: crusaders **sold or mortgaged land** to pay their way, and many came home poorer. Penance and pilgrimage best explain the cost they accepted |
| **Politics and pressure** | the papacy's reform programme, the Byzantine appeal, and lords bringing their followers |

**What would settle it:** the evidence of thousands of charters made by departing crusaders, which is why the faith reading has gained ground; but motives were mixed, and charters were written by clergy.

**Crusading spread beyond the Holy Land**: to Spain, where **Toledo** had fallen to Castile in **1085**, and to the pagan Baltic from the 1140s.
Saladin, the Third Crusade and the end o:
The Muslim answer to the crusades came from Syria and Egypt, and its most famous leader was a Kurdish soldier remembered by friends and enemies alike: **Saladin**.

**Who.** **Salah al-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub** (about 1137–1193), from a Kurdish family serving Zengi's son **Nur al-Din**. Sent to Egypt, he became vizier in **1169** and in **1171** ended the Shi'a **Fatimid** caliphate, returning Egypt to the Sunni Abbasid fold. After Nur al-Din died in 1174 he united **Egypt and Syria**: for the first time, the crusader states faced one power on both sides. His dynasty is called the **Ayyubids**.

**Hattin and Jerusalem.** On **4 July 1187**, at the **Horns of Hattin** west of the Sea of Galilee, Saladin destroyed the army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, drawing it away from water in summer heat. **Jerusalem surrendered on 2 October 1187.** Unlike 1099 there was no massacre; inhabitants were allowed to ransom themselves, though many who could not pay were enslaved.

**The Third Crusade, 1189–92**, the "Kings' Crusade":

| Leader | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| **Frederick Barbarossa**, German emperor | **drowned** crossing a river in Anatolia, **June 1190**; most of his army went home |
| **Philip II** of France | helped take **Acre** (**July 1191**), then returned home |
| **Richard I** of England | won at **Arsuf** (1191), came within sight of Jerusalem twice, and turned back |

The **Treaty of Jaffa (1192)** left Jerusalem with Saladin, a coastal strip with the Franks, and **Christian pilgrims free to visit**. Saladin died in Damascus in **1193**.

**The later crusades**, briefly. The Fifth (1217–21) attacked Egypt and failed. Emperor **Frederick II** got Jerusalem **by treaty in 1229**, without a battle; it was lost for good in **1244**. **Louis IX** of France was captured in Egypt in **1250** and died on crusade at **Tunis in 1270**.

**The Mamluks.** In **1250** the Ayyubids' own slave soldiers, the **Mamluks**, took power in Egypt. Their sultan **Baybars** (r. 1260–77) took crusader castles one by one, and **Acre fell in May 1291**. That was the end of the crusader states.

**How the two sides remembered it.** In Europe the crusades became a romance of chivalry. In Arabic writing of the time they were one danger among several, the "Franks", and later the Mongols looked worse. The idea of "the Crusades" as a central Muslim grievance grew strongly in the 19th and 20th centuries.

**Saladin's reputation** is unusual: Western writers soon turned him into a model of chivalry, and his own biographer, **Baha al-Din ibn Shaddad**, who served him, presents a pious, generous ruler. Both are flattering sources, and historians weigh them against Saladin's ruthlessness when needed, such as his execution of captured Templars and Hospitallers after Hattin.
The Fourth Crusade and the sack of Const:
A crusade called to retake Jerusalem ended by sacking the greatest Christian city in the world. It did more than 1054 to make the split between East and West lasting.

**The call.** **Pope Innocent III** called a new crusade in **1198**, aimed at Egypt. The leaders contracted **Venice** to build a fleet for about **33,500 men** and their horses (the treaty of **1201**).

**The chain of events:**

| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **1202** | far fewer crusaders arrive than planned, and they **cannot pay Venice**. The doge, **Enrico Dandolo**, old and nearly blind, proposes that they work off the debt by retaking **Zara** (Zadar) on the Adriatic for Venice. A Christian city, under the king of Hungary, who was himself a crusader. **Innocent excommunicated the crusaders** for it |
| **1203** | a Byzantine prince, **Alexios Angelos**, whose father had been deposed and blinded, offers money, troops and church union if they restore him. The fleet sails to **Constantinople**, and he is crowned as **Alexios IV** |
| **early 1204** | Alexios IV cannot pay. He is overthrown and **murdered** by a Byzantine rival, Alexios V. The crusaders, camped outside, decide to take the city for themselves |
| **12–13 April 1204** | **Constantinople is stormed and sacked for three days**: churches looted, relics carried off to the West, nuns and citizens assaulted. The historian **Niketas Choniates**, who lived through it, wrote that the Muslims had treated Jerusalem better |

**The bronze horses** now in St Mark's, Venice, came from the sack.

**The results:**

- A **Latin Empire of Constantinople** (1204–1261), with a Latin patriarch. **Venice** took **three-eighths** of the empire, including key ports and islands such as Crete.
- Byzantine successor states: the **Empire of Nicaea**, **Epirus** and **Trebizond**. **Michael VIII Palaiologos** of Nicaea retook Constantinople in **1261**, but the restored empire was small and poor.
- **A lasting Greek bitterness toward the Latin West.** Pope **John Paul II** expressed regret for the sack in **2001** and **2004**.

**The debate: accident or plot?**

- **A chain of accidents.** Donald Queller and Thomas Madden: each step followed from the one before, from debt, from Alexios's promises, from the murder of Alexios IV. Nobody set out to take Constantinople in 1202.
- **A plot, or at least an agenda.** Venice had commercial grievances against Byzantium (its merchants were arrested in 1171); Philip of Swabia, Alexios's brother-in-law, wanted the Byzantine throne in friendly hands; some leaders may have planned the diversion early.

**What would settle it:** evidence of meetings and agreements before 1202. The main Western witnesses, **Villehardouin** (a leader) and **Robert of Clari** (a knight), disagree on motives, and none of the key private agreements survive.

**What it meant later.** A weakened Byzantium could not hold back the **Ottomans**, who are the end of this stage.
Lords, vassals and peasants: the argumen:
Textbooks used to say that medieval Europe was "feudal". Many historians now think the word does more harm than good. This lesson teaches what actually happened, and then the argument.

**What happened, which nobody disputes.** In Latin Europe from about **900 to 1300**, power was local. Kings were weak; real authority lay with men who held **castles** and armed horsemen. Around them:

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Lord and vassal** | a free man swore loyalty (**homage** and **fealty**) to a lord, promising military service and counsel; the lord promised protection |
| **Fief** (Latin *feodum*) | land or income granted in return for service, from which the word "feudal" comes |
| **Manor** | an estate worked by peasants for a lord, with the lord's own land (the demesne) and the peasants' strips |
| **Serf** | a peasant bound to the land: owing labour days, dues and fees, unable to leave or marry outside without permission; not a slave, who could be sold as a person |

**Most people were peasants**, perhaps nine in ten. Bishop **Adalbero of Laon**, about **1025**, described society as **those who pray, those who fight, and those who work**: a clergyman's ideal, not a census.

**The "-ism" is not medieval.** No one in the Middle Ages spoke of "feudalism". The word was made by lawyers and writers of the **17th and 18th centuries**, and Montesquieu (1748) popularised the "feudal laws". The French revolutionaries **abolished "feudalism" in August 1789**, meaning the lords' remaining rights.

**The argument:**

- **Keep the word.** **Marc Bloch** (*Feudal Society*, 1939–40) used it for a whole society bound by personal ties of dependence. **François-Louis Ganshof** (*Feudalism*, 1944) used it narrowly for the lord–vassal–fief bond. Marxist historians use the **"feudal mode of production"** for lords taking surplus from peasants by force or law. All three find it useful for comparing societies, including Japan's.
- **Drop the word.** **Elizabeth A. R. Brown** ("The Tyranny of a Construct", **1974**) argued that "feudalism" forces very different arrangements into one false model. **Susan Reynolds** (*Fiefs and Vassals*, **1994**) went further: the neat fief-for-service bond is largely a creation of **later lawyers**, especially the 12th-century Lombard *Libri feudorum*, read back into earlier centuries. Earlier documents show many kinds of landholding and loyalty.

**A related argument: was there a "feudal revolution" about 1000?** Georges Duby and others argued that around **1000** public order collapsed in France and castle lords seized power violently. Dominique Barthélemy answered that the change was slower and the "anarchy" partly an illusion of new kinds of documents.

**What would settle it:** systematic study of charters region by region: how land was actually held and what was owed for it. That work has mostly supported the critics on the narrow fief model, and left the wider question of lordship over peasants still debated.

**How this curriculum uses the words:** "lord", "vassal", "fief", "manor" and "serf" for the specific things; "feudal" only with care, and never as if it describes all of Europe at once.
Towns, merchants and guilds in medieval:
Between about **1000 and 1300**, Latin Europe grew: more people, more land farmed, more towns, more trade. It was the background to everything else in the European lessons.

**More people.** Europe's population roughly **doubled or more** over these three centuries; all estimates rest on thin evidence. Forests were cleared, marshes drained, and settlers moved east beyond the Elbe. A warmer climate (the **Medieval Climate Anomaly**, roughly 950–1250) helped in the north. So did the heavy plough, the horse collar and three-field rotation, though how new these were is debated.

**The towns.** Few were large by Chinese or Islamic standards. Around **1300**, **Paris**, **Venice**, **Milan**, **Florence** and **Genoa** were the giants, each perhaps around **100,000**, give or take. But towns had something new: **self-government**.

| Kind | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **Italian communes** | cities ruling themselves through elected councils, by the 1100s: **Venice**, **Genoa**, **Pisa**, **Florence**, **Milan** |
| **Charters** | lords and kings granted towns rights in writing: freedom from many dues, their own courts. A serf who lived in a chartered town for a year and a day was often free: "**town air makes free**", a later German maxim |
| **Leagues** | the **Hanseatic League** of German trading towns, led by **Lübeck**, dominating the Baltic and North Sea trade from the 1200s; the **Lombard League** defeating Emperor Frederick Barbarossa at **Legnano in 1176** |

**Trade.** Italian ships carried spices, silk and sugar from the eastern Mediterranean, much of it through Egypt, the crusader ports and Constantinople. **Flanders** wove English wool into fine cloth. The two met at the **fairs of Champagne**, in north-eastern France, the hub of European trade in the **12th and 13th centuries**.

**New tools of business,** many learned from the Islamic world: **Hindu-Arabic numerals**, introduced to Italian merchants by **Leonardo of Pisa (Fibonacci)** in **1202**; **bills of exchange**, so a merchant did not have to carry coin; **double-entry bookkeeping**; partnership contracts. Florence minted the gold **florin** from **1252**.

**Guilds.** Merchants and craftsmen formed associations: weavers, goldsmiths, bakers. A **guild** set prices and quality, limited competition, trained **apprentices**, who became **journeymen** and then **masters**, and looked after members' widows. Critics then and since saw them as closed shops; defenders, as a guarantee of quality and a safety net.

**Building.** Towns and bishops raised **Gothic cathedrals**, beginning with Abbot Suger's rebuilt choir at **Saint-Denis**, near Paris, in the **1140s**: pointed arches and flying buttresses carrying walls of glass.

**The limit.** The boom ended around **1300**. The **Great Famine of 1315–17** killed perhaps 5–10 per cent of northern Europeans, and the Black Death followed in **1347**.
Popes against kings: from Canossa to Avi:
For three centuries, popes and kings fought over who ruled the Church, and sometimes who ruled Christendom. The struggle shaped Europe's idea that church and state are separate powers.

**The reform papacy.** In the 11th century reformers wanted the clergy free of lay control: no buying of church offices (**simony**), no married priests, and **no kings appointing bishops**. Bishops were also great landholders, so kings needed them.

**Canossa.** **Pope Gregory VII** (1073–85) declared the papacy's powers in the ***Dictatus papae*** (**1075**), including that a pope may depose emperors. The German king **Henry IV** refused to give up appointing bishops. Gregory excommunicated him and released his subjects from their oaths. In **January 1077** Henry stood in the snow outside the castle of **Canossa**, in northern Italy, for three days as a penitent until Gregory lifted the ban. The war resumed; Henry drove Gregory out of Rome, and he died in exile in **1085**.

**The compromise.** The **Concordat of Worms (1122)**: the Church elected and invested bishops with ring and staff, the symbols of spiritual office; the emperor could attend and invest them with their lands.

**The height of papal power.** **Innocent III** (1198–1216): he forced King John of England to accept his archbishop, called the Fourth Crusade and the **Albigensian Crusade** (from **1209**) against the Cathars of southern France, and held the **Fourth Lateran Council** (**1215**), which required yearly confession. The friars arose in his time: **Franciscans** (from about **1209**) and **Dominicans** (approved **1216**), preaching in the towns. From the **1230s** popes appointed **inquisitors** against heresy.

**The kings strike back.** **Philip IV** of France taxed his clergy. **Boniface VIII** answered in ***Unam sanctam*** (**1302**): submission to the pope is necessary for salvation. In **1303** Philip's men seized Boniface at **Anagni**; he died weeks later.

**Avignon, 1309–77.** Pope **Clement V**, a Frenchman, settled at **Avignon**, on the Rhône. Seven popes lived there, all French. Critics such as the poet **Petrarch** called it a "Babylonian captivity".

**The Western Schism, 1378–1417.** A disputed election produced **two popes**, one in Rome and one in Avignon, and from **1409 three**. The **Council of Constance** (1414–18) ended it, and claimed that a general council stood above the pope. It also burned the Czech reformer **Jan Hus** in **1415**, despite a safe-conduct.

**England's side of the story.** **Magna Carta** (**1215**): barons forced King John to accept that the king was under the law. Innocent III annulled it within weeks, but it was reissued and became a foundation of English law.

**Why it mattered.** No single power ever ruled Latin Christendom. Kings, popes, councils, towns and nobles all had **claims against each other**, written down and argued by lawyers, a pattern unlike that of Byzantium, China or the caliphates.
The first universities and the recovery:
The university, a self-governing corporation of teachers and students granting degrees, was invented in Latin Europe around **1200**. It grew out of cathedral schools and a flood of new learning translated from Arabic and Greek.

**The word.** *Universitas* meant any **corporation** or guild, not "universe". A university was a guild of masters or students.

**The first ones:**

| University | Beginnings |
| --- | --- |
| **Bologna** | famous for **law** by the 1100s; the traditional date **1088** is a later claim. Run by its **students**, who hired the professors |
| **Paris** | grew from the schools around Notre-Dame in the 1100s; royal privileges in **1200**, statutes in **1215**. Run by its **masters**; the centre for **theology** |
| **Oxford** | teaching by the late 1100s; grew after **1167**, when English students were barred from Paris. **Cambridge** from **1209**, after a quarrel at Oxford |
| **Salamanca, Montpellier, Padua** | the 1200s; by **1500** Europe had perhaps around 60 |

**How they worked.** Everyone began in the **arts**: grammar, logic and rhetoric, then arithmetic, geometry, music and astronomy, in Latin. Then the higher faculties: **law**, **medicine** or **theology**. Degrees were a **licence to teach**. Teaching was by **lecture** (reading a text with commentary) and **disputation** (arguing a question both ways in public).

**The translation movement.** From the 1100s Western scholars went to **Toledo**, retaken by Castile in **1085**, and to Sicily, where Arabic, Greek and Latin met. **Gerard of Cremona** (died **1187**) translated dozens of works from Arabic, including Ptolemy's astronomy and Ibn Sina's (Avicenna's) **Canon of Medicine**. Translators worked directly from Greek too, in Sicily and in Constantinople. **Most of Aristotle**, lost to the Latin West for centuries, arrived in the 1100s and 1200s, with the commentaries of **Ibn Rushd (Averroes, died 1198)** of Córdoba.

**Scholasticism.** The method of the schools: set reason and authorities against each other to resolve questions. **Peter Abelard** (died **1142**) in *Sic et Non* lined up authorities that disagreed. **Thomas Aquinas** (about 1225–74), a Dominican at Paris, wrote the ***Summa Theologiae*** (from **1265**), reconciling Aristotle with Christian teaching. In **1277** the bishop of Paris condemned 219 propositions, many of them Aristotelian, showing how unsettling the new learning was.

**The debate: where did the university come from?**

- **A European invention.** The legal corporation, with charters and self-government and degrees, has no exact earlier parallel. Islamic **madrasas** were usually endowed by a single founder and taught chiefly religious law.
- **A borrowed model.** **George Makdisi** (*The Rise of Colleges*, **1981**) argued that the licence to teach, the disputation and the college all have close parallels in the madrasa, and may have come through Spain and Sicily. Some point to older centres such as **al-Qarawiyyin** in Fez (a mosque founded in **859**).

**What would settle it:** a clear line of transmission: a Western text or teacher who copied a madrasa practice. Parallels are clear; the line has not been shown, so the question remains open.
The Hundred Years' War, 1337–1453:
Not one war and not a hundred years: a series of wars, with long truces, between the kings of England and France, fought almost entirely on French soil. It ended in the same year Constantinople fell.

**Why.** The English kings were also **dukes of Aquitaine (Gascony)** in south-western France, and so vassals of the French king: an impossible position for a king. When the last direct Capetian died in **1328**, **Edward III** of England claimed the French crown through his mother **Isabella**. The French nobility chose **Philip VI of Valois**. In **1337** Philip confiscated Gascony, and Edward declared himself king of France. Trade mattered too: the Flemish cloth towns depended on English wool.

**The war in four phases:**

| Phase | Key events |
| --- | --- |
| **English victories, 1337–60** | the sea battle of **Sluys (1340)**; **Crécy (26 August 1346)**, where English **longbowmen** cut down French knights; **Calais** taken (**1347**); **Poitiers (1356)**, where Edward's son, the **Black Prince**, captured King **John II**. The **Treaty of Brétigny (1360)** gave England about a third of France |
| **French recovery, 1369–89** | **Charles V** and his commander **Bertrand du Guesclin** avoided pitched battles and won back most of the land |
| **Henry V, 1415–29** | **Agincourt (25 October 1415)**; the **Treaty of Troyes (1420)** made Henry heir to France. He died in **1422**, and his baby son Henry VI was claimed as king of both realms |
| **French victory, 1429–53** | **Joan of Arc** relieved **Orléans (May 1429)** and saw **Charles VII** crowned at **Reims (July 1429)**. She was captured, tried by a church court under English control, and **burned at Rouen on 30 May 1431**. French armies with **cannon** won at **Formigny (1450)** and **Castillon (17 July 1453)**. England kept only **Calais**, until **1558** |

**How it was fought.** Not mainly in battles but in **chevauchées**: mounted raids that burned villages and crops to ruin the enemy's revenue. Free companies of unpaid soldiers plundered in the truces. For French peasants the war meant decades of devastation, on top of the **Black Death (1348)** and the **Jacquerie** revolt (**1358**).

**Joan of Arc** is unusually well documented: the **transcripts of her trial (1431)** and of the **retrial (1456)** that cleared her survive. She was canonised in **1920**.

**What it changed:**

- **Kings got taxes and standing armies.** Charles VII founded permanent companies of soldiers in **1445**, paid by regular taxes.
- **National feeling grew** on both sides, and English displaced French as the language of England's government and law over the 14th and 15th centuries.
- **The infantry and the gun** rose; the mounted knight's day as the master of battle waned.

Historians argue over how far a "war" with such long pauses was one event at all. The name was coined in the **19th century**.
Song China: the richest state on earth,:
While Latin Europe was building its first towns, China under the **Song dynasty** had cities of perhaps a million people, paper money and a civil service chosen by examination.

**Founding.** In **960** the general **Zhao Kuangyin** (Emperor **Taizu**) seized power and reunited most of China after the half-century of division that followed the Tang. His capital was **Kaifeng**, on the Yellow River and the Grand Canal.

**The neighbours were strong.** The Khitan **Liao** held the north-east, including the region of modern Beijing; the Song bought peace with them by the **Treaty of Chanyuan (1005)**, paying silver and silk each year. The Tangut **Western Xia** held the north-west. Then the **Jurchen**, from Manchuria, destroyed the Liao and founded the **Jin**, and in **1127** took **Kaifeng**, capturing the retired emperor and the emperor himself (the **Jingkang incident**). The court fled south and rebuilt at **Hangzhou** (then called Lin'an). Historians divide the dynasty into the **Northern Song (960–1127)** and the **Southern Song (1127–1279)**.

**The economy, which is the reason to study it:**

| Change | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| **Rice** | a fast-ripening, drought-hardy rice from **Champa** (in today's Vietnam) was spread by the government from **1012**; the south, wetter and warmer, became the heart of the economy |
| **People** | registers suggest the population passed **100 million** around 1100, perhaps the first state to do so |
| **Money** | merchants in Sichuan used paper certificates; the state took over issuing them in the **1020s**, the **world's first government paper money**. Later issues brought inflation |
| **Iron and coal** | output of iron rose steeply: Robert Hartwell estimated about **125,000 tonnes in 1078**, a figure others think too high; coal fuelled the furnaces near Kaifeng |
| **Trade** | ocean junks with watertight bulkheads sailed to South-East Asia and the Indian Ocean from ports like **Quanzhou**, where Arab and Persian merchants lived |

**Government by scholars.** The **examinations**, begun under the Sui and Tang, became the main road to office. Candidates in their tens of thousands studied the Confucian classics. The reformer **Wang Anshi** (from **1069**) pushed state loans to farmers and new taxes; his opponents, led by **Sima Guang**, called it meddling, and the fight split the court for decades.

**Thought and art.** **Zhu Xi** (1130–1200) shaped **Neo-Confucianism**, which became the basis of the exams from the 14th century until 1905. Landscape painting, porcelain and poetry flourished. **Footbinding** of girls, beginning among elite women, spread in the Song.

**The debate: a "medieval economic revolution"?**

- **Yes.** Mark Elvin (1973) and others: Song China had markets, money, technology and output that Europe matched only centuries later. Why it did not go on to an industrial revolution is one of history's great questions.
- **Overstated.** The figures rest on official records of uncertain meaning; much of the growth was the settling of the south, not new kinds of production; and output per person may have grown far less than totals.

**What would settle it:** better estimates of income per person, which economic historians have attempted with mixed results.

**The end.** The Southern Song held out against the **Mongols** for four decades, longer than any other large state. It fell in **1279**, at the sea battle of **Yamen**, where a minister reportedly leapt into the sea holding the last boy emperor.
Printing, gunpowder and the compass in S:
Three Chinese inventions changed the world. All three came to full use in the Song, and all three later reached Europe, by routes that are still partly unclear.

**Printing.**

| Step | When and where |
| --- | --- |
| **Woodblock printing** | a whole page carved in reverse on a block. The oldest dated printed book is a **Diamond Sutra of 868**, found at Dunhuang |
| **Mass printing** | under the Song the state printed the Confucian classics, histories, medical texts and the whole Buddhist canon; private printers sold books for exam candidates |
| **Movable type** | the scholar **Shen Kuo**, in his *Dream Pool Essays* (**1088**), records that a commoner named **Bi Sheng** made type from **baked clay** in the **1040s** |
| **Metal type** | developed in **Korea**; the ***Jikji***, a Buddhist text printed in **1377**, is the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type |

**Why movable type mattered less in China than in Europe.** Chinese writing needs thousands of different characters, so carving a whole block was often as cheap and easier. Woodblocks stayed the main method in China until the 19th century.

**Gunpowder.** Saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal. Daoist alchemists searching for elixirs seem to have found the mixture by the **9th century**. The first written formulas are in the ***Wujing Zongyao***, a military manual compiled in **1044**. Then a sequence:

1. **Fire arrows** and incendiary bombs, flung by catapult.
2. The **fire lance**, a bamboo or paper tube on a spear that shot flame, used against the Jin in the **1130s**.
3. **Exploding bombs** with iron casings, used in the Jin-Mongol wars of the **1230s**.
4. **True guns** with metal barrels. The oldest securely dated one, a bronze hand cannon found in **Heilongjiang**, is from about **1288**.

**Europe.** Roger Bacon described a powder in the **1260s**, and cannon appear in an English manuscript of **1326**. Whether gunpowder came west through the **Mongols** or along trade routes is debated, but that it came from China is generally agreed.

**The compass.** Chinese writers knew a magnetised needle points south (as they put it) by the 11th century; **Shen Kuo** described it. A text of **1119** (Zhu Yu's) records sailors using it in cloudy weather off Guangzhou. It appears in European writing around **1190**. Whether Europe learned it from China or found it independently is unresolved.

**What would settle the transmission questions:** a document or object tracing each step west. For paper the route is clear (through the Islamic world from the 8th century). For the compass and printing it is not. The early European press, **Gutenberg's**, of about **1450**, shows no proven debt to China, though the idea may have travelled.

**Why these three mattered.** In 1620 Francis Bacon named **printing, gunpowder and the compass** as the three inventions that had changed the world, in learning, war and navigation, without knowing all three were Chinese.
Japan's shoguns: Kamakura and Ashikaga,:
In these centuries Japan passed from rule by court aristocrats in Kyoto to rule by warriors: the **samurai** and their chief, the **shogun**. The emperor remained, as the source of legitimacy, but rarely as the ruler.

**From court to warriors.** In the **Heian** period (794–1185), the **Fujiwara** family ruled through the emperors. Warrior clans grew strong in the provinces. The **Genpei War** (**1180–85**) between the **Taira** and the **Minamoto** ended at the sea battle of **Dan-no-ura** (**1185**), where the Taira were destroyed and the child emperor Antoku drowned. The story became *The Tale of the Heike*, sung by blind monks.

**The Kamakura shogunate.** **Minamoto no Yoritomo** set up a warrior government (the *bakufu*, "tent government") at **Kamakura**, in the east, far from the court. The emperor named him **shogun** in **1192**. Historians date the start to **1185** or **1192**, depending on whether they count real power or the title. After Yoritomo's death the **Hōjō** family ruled as regents for puppet shoguns: a regent for a figurehead for a figurehead.

**The Mongol invasions.** Kublai Khan, ruler of China, demanded Japan's submission. The Hōjō refused.

| Invasion | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| **1274** | a Mongol-Korean force landed at **Hakata Bay** in Kyushu, fought one day, and withdrew; a storm wrecked part of the fleet |
| **1281** | a much larger force, from Korea and southern China, was held at the beach by a **defensive wall**, then destroyed by a **typhoon** |

The Japanese called the storms ***kamikaze***, "divine wind". **The debate:** how much credit goes to the storms and how much to the samurai. Underwater archaeology at **Takashima** has found the wrecks; some studies suggest many ships were badly built river boats, hurriedly made, which would make the fleet's loss less surprising. The defenders' wall and fighting clearly mattered too.

**Ashikaga.** The invasions brought no plunder to reward the warriors, and the Hōjō weakened. Emperor **Go-Daigo** overthrew them in **1333** and tried to rule himself (the **Kenmu Restoration**). His general **Ashikaga Takauji** turned on him, and became shogun in **1338**, ruling from the **Muromachi** district of Kyoto. Go-Daigo fled south: Japan had **two rival imperial courts** from **1336 to 1392**.

**The height of Ashikaga power.** **Ashikaga Yoshimitsu** reunited the courts in **1392**, built the **Golden Pavilion (Kinkaku-ji)** in **1397**, and accepted the title "King of Japan" from the Ming emperor in order to trade with China, a choice later Japanese writers resented. After him the shoguns weakened; the **Ōnin War (1467–77)** began a century of civil war, in the next stage.

**Religion and culture.** New Buddhist movements reached ordinary people: **Pure Land** (calling on Amida Buddha), **Nichiren** (the Lotus Sutra) and **Zen**, which the warriors favoured. Nō theatre, ink painting and the tea ceremony took shape under Ashikaga patronage.

**Feudal?** Japan's lords and retainers are often compared with Europe's, which raises the same question as the "feudalism" lesson: a useful comparison, or a European label?
The Khmer Empire and the city of Angkor:
In what is now Cambodia, the Khmer kings built the largest religious monument on earth and a city whose full size was revealed only in the 2010s.

**The kingdom.** Tradition dates it to **802**, when **Jayavarman II** declared himself a universal king, a *chakravartin*. Its centre, **Angkor**, lay north of the great lake **Tonlé Sap**, whose seasonal flood fed rice fields. At its height in the **12th and early 13th centuries** the Khmer ruled much of mainland South-East Asia: today's Cambodia, Thailand, Laos and southern Vietnam.

**Angkor Wat.** Built under **Suryavarman II** (r. **1113–about 1150**), dedicated to the Hindu god **Vishnu**. Its five towers stand for **Mount Meru**, the centre of the universe in Hindu and Buddhist thought; the moat stands for the ocean around it. Its walls carry nearly a kilometre of carved reliefs, including the churning of the ocean of milk and the king's own army on the march.

**A Buddhist king.** In **1177** the **Cham**, from what is now central Vietnam, sacked Angkor. **Jayavarman VII** (r. **1181–about 1218**) drove them out and rebuilt the capital as **Angkor Thom**, centred on the **Bayon**, a temple with over 200 huge carved faces. He was a **Mahayana Buddhist**, and his inscriptions claim he built **102 hospitals** and rest houses along the roads.

**An eyewitness.** **Zhou Daguan**, a Chinese envoy, lived at Angkor in **1296–97** and wrote *A Record of Cambodia*: the only detailed outside account. He describes markets run by women, slaves from the hill peoples, and a golden-towered city.

**The size, revealed.** In **2012–13** **lidar**, a laser scanner flown in a helicopter, saw through the forest and mapped streets, ponds and house mounds: a low-density urban landscape of perhaps **1,000 square kilometres**, with water channels and huge reservoirs (*barays*).

**The debate: what were the barays for?**

- **A "hydraulic city"**: Bernard-Philippe Groslier (**1979**) argued the reservoirs irrigated rice fields and so fed the city: the water system was the base of Khmer power.
- **Mainly religious and symbolic**: others answered that the barays could not have watered enough land to matter, and that rice depended on rain and the lake's flood.

Recent fieldwork finds the network did move water on a large scale, which favours a middle position.

**The decline.** Angkor's kings moved south toward **Phnom Penh** in the 15th century. The traditional date, **1431**, is a sack by the Thai kingdom of **Ayutthaya**. The causes are debated:

| Reading | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| **War** | Ayutthaya's rise and repeated attacks |
| **Climate** | tree rings show **long droughts** broken by intense monsoons in the 14th and 15th centuries, which could have wrecked the water system |
| **Religion** | the shift to **Theravada Buddhism** ended the giant royal temple-building |
| **Trade** | sea trade with Ming China favoured a capital near the Mekong and the coast |

Most historians now see several working together. **Angkor was never wholly abandoned**: Angkor Wat stayed a Buddhist monastery, and it is on Cambodia's flag.
The Delhi Sultanate, 1206–1398:
For three centuries north India was ruled by Muslim sultans of Turkish and Afghan descent from **Delhi**. The south went its own way, under the **Cholas** and then **Vijayanagara**.

**Before the sultanate.** **Mahmud of Ghazni**, from Afghanistan, raided north India some 17 times between about **1000 and 1027**, plundering temple treasuries, including **Somnath** in Gujarat (**1025**). He did not stay. **Muhammad of Ghor** came to conquer: beaten by the Rajput king **Prithviraj Chauhan** at **Tarain** in **1191**, he won there in **1192** and took Delhi.

**The sultanate.** When Muhammad was murdered in **1206**, his general **Qutb al-Din Aibak**, a former slave, became the first **sultan of Delhi**. Five dynasties followed, to **1526**:

| Dynasty | Key ruler and events |
| --- | --- |
| **Mamluk ("Slave"), 1206–90** | **Iltutmish** (r. 1211–36) consolidated the state and finished the **Qutb Minar**; his daughter **Raziya** (r. 1236–40) ruled in her own right, and was overthrown |
| **Khalji, 1290–1320** | **Alauddin Khalji** (r. 1296–1316) **beat off Mongol invasions** several times, fixed prices in Delhi's markets, and sent armies deep into the south |
| **Tughluq, 1320–1414** | **Muhammad bin Tughluq** (r. 1325–51) moved much of Delhi's elite to **Daulatabad** in the Deccan (**1327**), then back; issued a **token copper currency** that was forged everywhere. **Ibn Battuta** served him as a judge |
| **Sayyid and Lodi, 1414–1526** | a much smaller state; ended by the Mughal Babur at **Panipat (1526)** |

**Timur.** In **December 1398** **Timur** (Tamerlane), a Turko-Mongol conqueror from Samarkand, sacked **Delhi** and massacred much of its population. The sultanate never recovered its reach.

**The south.** The **Cholas** of Tamil Nadu were at their height around 1000: **Rajaraja I** built the **Brihadisvara temple** at Thanjavur (**1010**), and his son **Rajendra I** sent a fleet against **Srivijaya** in **1025**. In **1336** the Hindu kingdom of **Vijayanagara** was founded in the Deccan, and the **Bahmani** sultanate in **1347**; they fought each other into the 16th century.

**The debate: religion and conquest.**

- **A religious war.** Older nationalist and colonial histories, using the sultans' own court chronicles, presented the conquest as a long war of Islam against Hinduism, marked by temple destruction and forced conversion.
- **Politics first.** **Richard Eaton** counted about **80** securely documented temple desecrations between **1192 and 1760**. He argued they were real and deliberate, but targeted at **royal temples tied to enemy kings**, as a political act; and that most conversion came slowly, through Sufi shrines and the settling of new farmland, not the sword.

**What would settle it:** inscriptions, surviving buildings and local records, which are thin, set against court chronicles that boasted of piety. Both readings accept that temples were destroyed and that sultans also employed Hindus and ruled Hindu majorities.

**What the sultanate built.** The **Qutb Minar**, a new **Indo-Islamic architecture**, and the language that became **Hindustani** (Urdu and Hindi), mixing Persian and local speech. The poet **Amir Khusrau** (1253–1325) wrote in both.
Temüjin becomes Genghis Khan, 1162–1227:
A boy abandoned on the Mongolian steppe became the founder of the largest land empire in history. Most of what we know of his early life comes from one source, so this lesson says where the evidence is thin.

**The source.** ***The Secret History of the Mongols***, written in Mongolian for the Mongol court some years after his death (dates proposed range from **1228** to the 1250s). It is a family epic, not a neutral chronicle. Persian historians who served the Mongols, **Juvaini** (1260) and **Rashid al-Din** (about 1307), and hostile writers such as **Ibn al-Athir**, add the conquests.

**The steppe in the 1100s.** The grasslands of Mongolia held many rival peoples: **Mongols**, **Tatars**, **Kereits**, **Naimans**, **Merkits**. They lived by herding horses, sheep and goats, and moved with the seasons. China's Jin dynasty kept them divided by playing one against another.

**Early life.** **Temüjin** was born on the **Onon River**, in a year given variously from **1155 to 1167**; **1162** is the usual choice. His father **Yesügei**, a minor chief, was **poisoned by Tatars** when Temüjin was about nine. The clan abandoned the widow **Hö'elün** and her children, who lived by fishing and gathering. Temüjin killed his half-brother in a quarrel over food, was captured and enslaved by a rival clan, and escaped.

**The rise.** He married **Börte**; when the Merkits kidnapped her, he won her back with the help of **Toghrul**, khan of the Kereits, and his own blood-brother **Jamukha**. Over twenty years of wars he defeated the Tatars, broke with Toghrul and destroyed the Kereits, and finally beat and executed Jamukha.

**1206.** A great assembly, a **kurultai**, on the Onon proclaimed him **Chinggis Khan**, usually spelled Genghis. The title's meaning is uncertain; "fierce" or "oceanic" ruler are common guesses.

**What he built:**

| Change | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| **Decimal army** | units of **10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000**, mixing tribes so loyalty went to the khan, not the clan |
| **The guard** | a personal guard of about **10,000**, drawn from the sons of commanders, which was also a training school and a hostage system |
| **Promotion by merit and loyalty** | many top generals, such as **Jebe** and **Subutai**, were of humble birth |
| **Writing** | the Uyghur script adopted for Mongolian |
| **Law** | a body of rulings later called the ***Yasa***; whether it was ever a written code is debated |

**The conquests he began:**

- **Western Xia** forced to submit (**1209–10**).
- The **Jin** in north China: their capital **Zhongdu**, now Beijing, taken in **1215**.
- **Khwarazm**, the empire of Central Asia and Iran. In **1218** its governor at **Otrar** killed a Mongol trade caravan, and the shah killed or insulted Genghis's envoys. The invasion of **1219–21** destroyed **Bukhara**, **Samarkand**, **Merv**, **Nishapur** and **Urgench**. The death tolls in the sources (over a million at Merv) are not credible as counts, but the devastation was real and Iran's cities and irrigation took generations to recover.

**Death.** Genghis died in **August 1227**, during a final campaign against Western Xia. His burial place is unknown.

**How to judge him** is itself an argument. To Mongolians he is the father of the nation. To the people of Merv or Nishapur he was destruction itself. Both are true in their own frame, and the lesson on Pax Mongolica takes up whether the empire he founded did more to connect or to destroy.
The Mongol conquests and the four khanat:
Genghis's sons and grandsons carried the conquests from Korea to Hungary. Then, in a single generation, the empire split into four.

**Ögedei (r. 1229–41)**, Genghis's third son, was chosen as Great Khan. He built a capital at **Karakorum** in Mongolia (walls about **1235**) and finished off the **Jin** in **1234**.

**The western campaign, 1236–42**, led by **Batu**, a grandson, and **Subutai**:

| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **1236–37** | the **Volga Bulgars** and the **Kipchak** (Cuman) steppe peoples conquered |
| **1237–38** | the Rus' cities of **Ryazan**, **Vladimir** and others destroyed |
| **December 1240** | **Kiev** taken and sacked |
| **9 April 1241** | Polish and German knights beaten at **Legnica** in Silesia |
| **11 April 1241** | the Hungarian army destroyed at **Mohi** |
| **1242** | the Mongols **withdraw** from Hungary |

**The debate: why did they turn back?**

- **Succession.** Ögedei died in **December 1241**; princes went home to choose a successor. The traditional reading, though the news may have arrived too late to explain the timing.
- **Grass and weather.** Horse armies needed pasture. A **2016** study of tree rings by Ulf Büntgen and Nicola Di Cosmo found a **cold, wet spring of 1242** that turned the Hungarian plain to marsh.
- **Losses and strategy.** Mongol losses at Mohi were heavy, and Hungary may have been a raid rather than a conquest from the start.

**What would settle it:** a Mongol source on the decision. None survives, so the readings are weighed against each other, and several may be true together.

**Möngke (r. 1251–59)** sent two great campaigns: his brother **Hülegü** west against Iran, the Assassins and Baghdad (the next lesson), and his brother **Kublai**, with Möngke himself, against the Song in China. Möngke died in **1259** at the siege of a Song fortress in Sichuan.

**The split.** Kublai and his younger brother **Ariq Böke** both claimed the throne, and fought from **1260 to 1264**. Kublai won, but the western khans never fully accepted him. **The empire became four states:**

| Khanate | Founded from | Ruled | Capital |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Yuan** | Kublai | China, Mongolia, Korea as a vassal | **Dadu** (Beijing) |
| **Ilkhanate** | Hülegü | Iran, Iraq, much of Anatolia | **Tabriz**, later Sultaniyya |
| **Chagatai Khanate** | Genghis's son Chagatai | Central Asia | the Ili valley, near today's Kazakhstan-China border |
| **Golden Horde** (the Ulus of Jochi) | Batu, Jochi's son | the western steppe and the Rus' princes | **Sarai** on the Volga |

**They fought each other.** The Golden Horde, newly Muslim under **Berke**, went to war with the Ilkhanate from **1262**, and allied with the Mamluks of Egypt against fellow Mongols.

**How big?** At its peak the Mongol empire covered perhaps **23–24 million square kilometres**: the largest contiguous land empire there has ever been, though such figures depend on how one draws borders on the steppe.

**Why the Mongols won so often:** mobility (each rider had several horses), the composite bow, discipline, intelligence gathered from merchants, the use of **Chinese and Muslim engineers** for sieges, and a deliberate use of **terror**: cities that surrendered were usually spared, and those that resisted were often destroyed, so that the next city would surrender.
The sack of Baghdad, 1258, and Ain Jalut:
In **February 1258** the Mongols took **Baghdad**, the seat of the Abbasid caliphs for five centuries, and killed the last caliph there. Two years later they suffered their first great defeat in the Islamic lands.

**The campaign.** Möngke sent his brother **Hülegü** west in **1253**. First he destroyed the Nizari Ismailis, known in the West as the **Assassins**, whose castle **Alamut** in northern Iran surrendered in **1256**. Then he summoned the caliph, **al-Musta'sim**, to submit. The caliph refused, apparently trusting that the Muslim world would rise to defend him. It did not.

**The siege.** The Mongols, with Georgian and Armenian Christian allies and Chinese siege engineers, surrounded the city in **January 1258**. They breached the walls, and Baghdad surrendered on **10 February**. A week of slaughter and looting followed.

**The caliph.** Al-Musta'sim was executed. The most famous account says he was **rolled in a carpet and trampled by horses**, because the Mongols avoided shedding royal blood; this appears in several sources, and is plausible, but details vary.

**How many died?** Sources give figures from about **200,000 to over a million**. No city of the time could be counted that way, and such figures are not reliable. **The true number is unknown**, but the killing was enormous. Christians, who sheltered in a church, were largely spared, as were some notables who surrendered early.

**The books in the Tigris.** A later story says the river ran **black with ink** from the libraries thrown into it. Libraries were certainly destroyed, but the vivid detail comes from writers well after the event and should be held loosely.

**Ain Jalut.** Hülegü went on into Syria, taking **Aleppo** and **Damascus** in **1260**. Then news came of Möngke's death and he withdrew east with most of his army. The **Mamluks** of Egypt, under **Sultan Qutuz** and the general **Baybars**, marched out and destroyed the remaining Mongol force under **Kitbuqa** at **Ain Jalut**, in Galilee, on **3 September 1260**. Baybars murdered Qutuz on the way home and became sultan.

**Why Ain Jalut mattered.** It stopped Mongol expansion toward Egypt and North Africa, and made the **Mamluk Sultanate** the leading power of the Arab world until **1517**. The Mamluks set up a member of the Abbasid family in **Cairo** as a figurehead caliph in **1261**.

**The debate: did 1258 end the Islamic "golden age"?**

| Reading | The argument |
| --- | --- |
| **Yes, a catastrophe** | the centre of Arabic learning and the caliphate were destroyed at a blow; Iraq's irrigation and population declined for centuries |
| **No, a turning point within a continuing story** | the Abbasid caliphs had lost real power by about **945**; learning had many centres (Cairo, Damascus, Córdoba, Samarkand); and Hülegü himself founded the **observatory at Maragha (1259)** for the astronomer **Nasir al-Din al-Tusi**, whose models were later echoed by Copernicus |

**What would settle it:** measures of scholarly output and economic life across the whole Islamic world before and after 1258. The work done so far supports a shift of centres, to Cairo, Iran and later the Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal lands, more than an ending.

**The Ilkhans converted.** In **1295** the Ilkhan **Ghazan** became a Muslim. Within two generations of sacking Baghdad, the Mongol rulers of Iran were patrons of Islam.
Pax Mongolica: roads, relay posts and a:
"Pax Mongolica", the Mongol peace, is a modern term, modelled on *Pax Romana*. It means the century from about **1250 to 1350** when one family's rule made travel across Eurasia easier than ever before. Whether "peace" is the right word is the question.

**What made travel possible:**

| Institution | What it did |
| --- | --- |
| **The *yam*** | a relay network of **post stations**, a day's ride apart, with fresh horses and supplies for official messengers; Marco Polo described it in China |
| **The *paiza*** | a tablet of gold, silver or wood, carried as a passport, ordering officials to help the bearer |
| **Merchant partnerships** | Mongol princes invested in merchant ventures (*ortogh*) and protected trade roads |
| **Religious tolerance** | the khans patronised Buddhist, Muslim, Christian and Daoist clergy, wanting all their prayers, and exempted them from taxes |

**Who travelled:**

- **Franciscan friars** sent by popes and kings: **John of Plano Carpini** to the Great Khan's camp in **1245–47**, and **William of Rubruck** to Karakorum in **1253–55**. Rubruck found a Paris goldsmith there and held a public debate between Christians, Muslims and Buddhists.
- **Rabban Sauma**, a Turkic Christian monk from near Beijing, went the other way: to Constantinople, Rome and Paris in **1287–88**, as an envoy of the Ilkhan seeking an alliance against the Mamluks.
- **Merchants**, above all Italians: the Florentine **Pegolotti**, about **1340**, wrote a merchant's handbook saying the road from the Black Sea to China was perfectly safe by day and night (paraphrased).
- Ideas and goods: Chinese medicine and paper money in Iran; Persian astronomers in China; **gunpowder** spreading west.

**The debate:**

- **A real peace and a real connection.** Historians such as **Thomas Allsen** showed how much the Mongols moved people, goods and knowledge on purpose, gathering craftsmen, doctors and scholars and exchanging them between khanates. Jack Weatherford's popular *Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern World* (2004) goes further, presenting the Mongols as founders of a globalised world.
- **The peace of the graveyard.** The connections were bought with **conquest on a vast scale**: the population of north China and Iran fell steeply (how far is debated, since Chinese census figures partly reflect fleeing and uncounted people). The khanates **fought each other** for decades. Merchants travelled at the khans' pleasure, under heavy taxes.

**What would settle it:** firmer population figures, and trade volumes over time. Neither exists in a reliable form for most regions. Both sides agree on the core facts: huge destruction, then a century of unusually open roads.

**The dark side of connection.** The same roads, caravans and armies may have carried the **Black Death**, which ancient DNA traces to Central Asia in the **1330s**, west to the Black Sea by **1346**.

**The end.** By the **1350s** the khanates were breaking down: the Ilkhanate collapsed after **1335**, the Yuan fell in **1368**, the Golden Horde was at war with itself. The roads became dangerous again, and Europeans began to look for routes to Asia **by sea**.
Kublai Khan and Yuan China, 1271–1368:
Genghis's grandson **Kublai** conquered all of China and ruled it as a Chinese emperor, while staying a Mongol khan. His dynasty, the **Yuan**, lasted less than a century.

**The founding.** Kublai (1215–94) won the succession war in **1264** and moved his capital from Mongolia into China: a new city, **Dadu** ("great capital"), called **Khanbaliq** by Turks and Persians, on the site of modern **Beijing**. He also kept a summer capital at **Shangdu**, the "Xanadu" of Coleridge's poem. In **1271** he took a Chinese dynastic name, **Yuan**, "origin".

**The conquest of the Song.** The key was **Xiangyang**, on the Han River, besieged from **1268 to 1273**. It fell when two Muslim engineers from Iran built **counterweight trebuchets** that hurled huge stones. **Hangzhou** surrendered in **1276**, and the last Song loyalists died at **Yamen** in **1279**. For the first time **all of China was ruled by a foreign people**.

**Failures abroad.** Kublai's fleets failed against **Japan (1274, 1281)**. His armies were driven out of **Đại Việt**, today's northern Vietnam, whose general **Trần Hưng Đạo** destroyed a Mongol fleet on the **Bạch Đằng River** in **1288**, on stakes hidden at high tide. An expedition to **Java (1293)** ended in withdrawal.

**How the Yuan ruled:**

| Feature | What it meant |
| --- | --- |
| **A ranked population** | Mongols first; then *semu* ("various kinds": Central Asians, Persians, Arabs); then northern Chinese; and **southern Chinese** last. How rigidly this worked in practice is debated |
| **Foreigners in office** | Muslims, Uyghurs and others often served as tax officials and governors, distrusting Chinese scholars |
| **The exams** | **suspended** until **1315**, then restored with quotas favouring Mongols |
| **Paper money** | issued on a large scale, valid across the empire, and over time **printed to excess** |
| **Tibetan Buddhism** | the Tibetan lama **Phagpa** was imperial preceptor and designed a new script, the Phags-pa, for all the empire's languages |
| **The Grand Canal** | extended north to Dadu, to bring southern rice to the capital |

**Culture under the Mongols.** Chinese scholars shut out of office turned to painting, and to drama: Yuan **zaju** plays are a high point of Chinese theatre. Foreign visitors, among them Marco Polo, were dazzled by Dadu.

**The fall.** After Kublai's death in **1294**, emperors came and went quickly, with succession struggles. In the **1340s** the Yellow River broke its banks and changed course, causing famine. The paper money lost value. Rebels, some inspired by a Buddhist movement awaiting the future Buddha **Maitreya**, rose as the **Red Turbans** from **1351**. One of their commanders, **Zhu Yuanzhang**, a former monk of peasant birth, took **Dadu in 1368**. The last Yuan emperor fled north to Mongolia, where Mongol khans went on ruling as the "Northern Yuan".

**How to read the Yuan.** Chinese historians long treated it as an occupation. Others stress how much it connected China with the rest of Eurasia, and that the shape of modern China, including its capital at Beijing and the inclusion of Yunnan and Tibet's link to the court, owes something to the Yuan.
The Golden Horde and the rise of Moscow:
For two centuries the Rus' principalities paid tribute to the Mongol khans of the **Golden Horde**. Out of that subjection rose a small town that became the capital of Russia: **Moscow**.

**The Horde.** After the western campaign of **1236–42**, **Batu** built his capital at **Sarai**, on the lower **Volga**. His people were called the **Ulus of Jochi**, after Batu's father; the name **Golden Horde** is a later Russian one. Most of its people were **Kipchak Turks**, ruled by a Mongol elite who soon spoke Turkic. Khan **Özbeg** (r. **1313–41**) made **Islam** the court religion.

**How it ruled the Rus'.** It did not occupy the forest lands. It demanded:

- **Tribute**, assessed by census, at first collected by the Horde's own officials.
- **Submission**: each Rus' prince had to travel to Sarai, sometimes to Karakorum, to receive a ***yarlyk***, a patent to rule. Several who displeased the khan were executed.
- **Soldiers** when called for.

**The khans exempted the Orthodox Church from tax**, and it prospered.

**Alexander Nevsky.** Prince of Novgorod, he beat the Swedes on the **Neva** (**1240**) and the crusading **Teutonic Knights** on the ice of **Lake Peipus** (**1242**). Yet he cooperated with the Horde and helped crush revolts against its tax collectors. He was later made a saint and a national hero. Whether he was a realist or a collaborator is an old Russian argument.

**Moscow's rise.** A minor town in **1250**. Its princes rose by **serving the khan**:

| Prince | What he did |
| --- | --- |
| **Ivan I "Kalita"** ("moneybag", r. about 1325–40) | won the right to **collect the tribute** for the khan from other princes, and kept some; the head of the Rus' Church, the **metropolitan**, settled in Moscow in the **1320s** |
| **Dmitry Donskoy** (r. 1359–89) | defeated a Horde army at **Kulikovo**, on the Don, in **1380**. Two years later Khan **Tokhtamysh** burned Moscow, and tribute resumed |

**The Horde breaks.** **Timur** smashed Tokhtamysh's armies in **1391** and **1395**, and destroyed Sarai. In the 15th century the Horde split into the khanates of **Kazan**, **Astrakhan**, **Crimea** and others. In **1480** a Horde army and Moscow's **Ivan III** faced each other across the **Ugra River** and the Horde withdrew; this "stand on the Ugra" is the traditional end of the "Tatar yoke" (next stage).

**West of Moscow.** Much of the old Rus' lands, including **Kiev**, passed to the **Grand Duchy of Lithuania**, Europe's last pagan state, which joined **Poland** by royal marriage in **1386** and turned Catholic. Their armies beat the Teutonic Knights at **Grunwald (Tannenberg) in 1410**.

**The debate: what did the "Tatar yoke" do to Russia?**

- **A catastrophe that held Russia back.** The classic 19th-century Russian view (Karamzin, Solovyov): devastation, tribute, and two centuries cut off from Europe.
- **A shaping force.** The "Eurasianists" (George Vernadsky) argued that Moscow borrowed Mongol institutions of taxation, census, post and autocracy, which built the Russian state.
- **Charles Halperin** (*Russia and the Golden Horde*, **1985**) showed how Russian chroniclers kept an "ideology of silence", writing as if the khans were merely bad weather, so the degree of borrowing is hard to measure.

**What would settle it:** tracing particular Muscovite institutions, such as the post, the words for treasury and customs (Russian *kazna* and *tamozhnya* came into Russian through Turkic and Mongol) and the tax system, back to Horde models in documents. Some borrowing is clear; how much it shaped Russian autocracy remains argued.
Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta: two travelle:
Two men crossed the medieval world and left books about it: a Venetian merchant and a Moroccan judge. Each book is precious evidence, and each must be read with care.

**Marco Polo (about 1254–1324).**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The journey** | left **Venice in 1271** with his father **Niccolò** and uncle **Maffeo**, merchants who had already been to Kublai's court; reached Kublai about **1275**; claimed to serve him for some **17 years**, including as an official on missions in China; returned by sea, escorting a Mongol princess to Iran, reaching Venice in **1295** |
| **The book** | taken prisoner in a war between Venice and **Genoa**, he told his story in prison (about **1298**) to **Rustichello of Pisa**, a writer of romances, who wrote it up in French. Known as *Le Devisement du monde* ("The Description of the World") or *Il Milione* |
| **The text** | survives in about **150 manuscripts**, all differing; no original exists |

**Did Marco Polo go to China?**

- **The sceptics.** Frances Wood (*Did Marco Polo Go to China?*, **1995**): he never mentions the **Great Wall**, **tea**, **chopsticks**, **footbinding** or written Chinese characters, and no Chinese record names him. Perhaps he drew on Persian merchants' reports.
- **The defenders.** Hans Ulrich Vogel (*Marco Polo Was in China*, **2013**) showed that his descriptions of **paper money**, **salt production** and revenues are detailed and accurate in ways found in no other Western or Persian source. The Great Wall as we know it is mostly **Ming**, built later; foreigners in Yuan service often lived in a non-Chinese world of Mongols and Persians.

Most specialists now accept that **he went**, while noting that the book exaggerates his importance.

**Ibn Battuta (1304–between about 1368 and 1377).**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The journey** | left **Tangier in 1325** for the pilgrimage to Mecca, aged 21, and kept going for some **29 years**: Egypt, Syria, Arabia, the **Swahili coast** (1331), Anatolia, the **Golden Horde**, Central Asia, **Delhi** (where he served Muhammad bin Tughluq as a judge for several years), the **Maldives**, Sri Lanka, and by his account **China**. Then home, and a last journey across the Sahara to **Mali (1352–53)** |
| **The distance** | often given as about **117,000 km**, a modern estimate |
| **The book** | the **Rihla** ("journey"), dictated at Fez in **1355–56** on the order of the Marinid sultan **Abu Inan**, to a scholar, **Ibn Juzayy**, who polished it |

**How reliable is the Rihla?** Ibn Juzayy copied some passages from earlier travellers, notably **Ibn Jubayr** (1180s). Parts of the itinerary are impossible to fit to the dates, and some historians doubt he reached **China** or the far Volga. But much is confirmed independently, and his descriptions of **Delhi**, the **Maldives** and **Mali** are unique evidence.

**Why read them together.** Polo, a Christian outsider at a Mongol court, and Ibn Battuta, a Muslim scholar welcome wherever Islamic law ran, show **two networks**: the Mongol roads and the world of Islam, which stretched from Morocco to the Indian Ocean. Ibn Battuta could travel for decades because **a qualified judge was useful in any Muslim city**.

Both books were **dictated, edited, and partly borrowed**. Neither is a diary. The next primary-source lesson reads Ibn Battuta on Mali.
Mali: Sundiata and Mansa Musa:
In the 1200s and 1300s the empire of **Mali** ruled the western Sahel from the Atlantic coast to beyond the Niger bend. It was rich in gold, Muslim at court, and famous as far as Cairo and Catalonia.

**Before Mali.** **Ghana** (in today's Mauritania and Mali, not modern Ghana) had controlled the gold trade across the Sahara since before 800. It declined in the late 1000s and 1100s. A story that the Berber **Almoravids** conquered it in **1076** comes from later writers and is doubted by many historians. Among its successors was the **Sosso** kingdom under **Sumanguru** (Soumaoro Kanté).

**Sundiata.** The founder of Mali, a prince of the **Malinke** (Mandinka) people, won a battle at **Kirina**, about **1235**, that broke Sosso. His story survives in two ways:

| Source | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **The *Epic of Sundiata*** | an oral epic kept by **griots**, hereditary bards, and performed to this day. Sundiata is born lame, mocked, rises to walk, goes into exile, and returns to defeat the sorcerer-king Sumanguru. The best-known version was written down by **D. T. Niane** from the griot **Mamadou Kouyaté** and published in **1960** |
| **Ibn Khaldun** | the North African historian, writing about **1380s**, names a king **Mari Jata** who conquered Sosso: an independent written confirmation that the conqueror existed |

The **Kurukan Fuga**, a charter said to have been agreed at Sundiata's founding assembly, was reconstructed from oral tradition in the 20th century; how much is truly 13th-century is debated.

**The empire's wealth.**

- **Gold** from the fields of **Bambuk** and **Bure**, near the upper Senegal and Niger rivers. Much of the gold in the Mediterranean world in these centuries came from West Africa.
- **Salt** from the Sahara, at mines such as **Taghaza**, carried south by camel and traded for gold.
- **Copper**, **cloth**, horses, and slaves, who were also traded north across the desert.
- **Cities**: **Timbuktu**, **Djenné** and **Gao** on the Niger.

**Mansa Musa.** *Mansa* means king. Musa ruled from about **1312 to 1337** (the dates are uncertain by some years). In **1324** he made the **pilgrimage to Mecca**, passing through **Cairo** with thousands of followers and a great deal of gold.

**What the sources say.** The Damascus writer **al-Umari**, who visited Cairo about twelve years later, reported that Musa's spending had **lowered the value of gold** there, and that it had not recovered. Musa also told Cairo officials that his predecessor had sent a fleet into the Atlantic and then gone himself, never returning. That story rests on this single report, and nothing confirms the voyage.

**What Musa brought home.** Scholars and an architect, **Abu Ishaq al-Sahili**, credited with the **Djinguereber mosque** in **Timbuktu** (about **1327**). Timbuktu became a centre of Islamic learning and books, at its height in the 15th and 16th centuries.

**Famous in Europe.** The **Catalan Atlas** of **1375**, made in Majorca, shows a king of Mali on a throne holding a **gold nugget**.

**The "richest man who ever lived".** A modern internet claim. **His wealth cannot be measured**, and there is no way to compare it with modern fortunes. What the sources show is that he was very rich and very generous, and remembered so.

**Not known:** **the site of Mali's capital.** Niani, in Guinea, was long proposed; the archaeology there does not clearly fit.

**Decline.** In the 15th century Mali lost its northern cities to the Tuareg and then to **Songhay**, whose king **Sunni Ali** took Timbuktu in **1468** (next stage).
Primary source: Ibn Battuta judges Mali,:
Ibn Battuta reached the capital of Mali on **28 June 1352**, by the date he gives, and stayed about eight months. His account is the only eyewitness description of the Mali court. Read it slowly, as evidence about Mali and about the man writing.

**The text** (Ibn Battuta, *Rihla*, dictated 1355–56; translated by H. A. R. Gibb, *Travels in Asia and Africa 1325–1354*, London, **1929**, as given in the Internet Medieval Sourcebook. Gibb uses the words of his day for black Africans, "negroes" and "blacks", where Ibn Battuta wrote *Sudan*, "the blacks"):

> "The negroes possess some admirable qualities. They are seldom unjust, and have a greater abhorrence of injustice than any other people. Their sultan shows no mercy to anyone who is guilty of the least act of it. There is complete security in their country. Neither traveller nor inhabitant in it has anything to fear from robbers or men of violence. They do not confiscate the property of any white man who dies in their country, even if it be uncounted wealth. On the contrary, they give it into the charge of some trustworthy person among the whites, until the rightful heir takes possession of it."

**Who.** A judge trained in **Maliki** Islamic law, from Tangier, about **48** years old, at the end of his travels. **The king** was **Mansa Sulayman**, Musa's brother, who ruled from about **1341 to 1360**. The "whites" are the **North African and Arab merchants** living in their own quarter of the city.

**Read it phrase by phrase:**

| Phrase | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **"abhorrence of injustice"** | praise in the terms that matter most to a judge: **justice** |
| **"complete security"** | the roads were safe: the mark of a strong state, and what a merchant or traveller valued above all |
| **"they do not confiscate the property"** | the dead foreign merchant's goods are held for his heirs: a state that **protects trade** and respects Islamic inheritance law. Many rulers did seize such property |
