| **"the whites"** | a community of foreign Muslims, living under the king's protection: evidence of the trans-Saharan trade network |

**Read it against the rest of the account.** On the same pages Ibn Battuta is scornful:

- He calls Sulayman **"a miserly king"**, and describes the king's welcome gift arriving: **"three cakes of bread, and a piece of beef fried in native oil, and a calabash of sour curds."** He "burst out laughing". Later, after he complained, the king gave him a house and an allowance, and he softened.
- He praises their **zeal for Friday prayer** and learning the Qur'an by heart.
- Among their "bad qualities" he lists that **women servants and young girls went about uncovered**, and that people sprinkled dust on their heads before the king, a court custom he found degrading.

**What the passage is good evidence for:** the **safety of roads**, the **protection of foreign merchants**, the **public practice of Islam**, and the elaborate **court ceremony** of Mali, all of which fit other sources.

**What to be careful about:** he judges Mali **by the standards of Moroccan Islamic law**. What he calls bad, uncovered women, older court customs he notes are "prior to the introduction of Islam", is evidence of a **Mande culture keeping its own ways alongside Islam**, seen by an outsider who disapproved. And the text was **dictated three years later** and polished by an editor.

**The lesson in method.** One source can be **both praise and prejudice**, and both are evidence: of Mali, and of how a learned Muslim of the 14th century saw a Muslim kingdom unlike his own.
Mapungubwe and Great Zimbabwe:
On the plateau between the **Limpopo** and **Zambezi** rivers, African states built in stone and traded gold to the Indian Ocean. They are the ancestors of the region's later kingdoms. South Africa is touched on briefly here; the South African Politics curriculum covers its history in depth.

**Mapungubwe, about 1220–1290.** A flat-topped hill at the meeting of the **Limpopo and Shashe** rivers, where South Africa, Botswana and Zimbabwe now meet. Its people grew out of an earlier town nearby, **K2** (about 1000–1220).

- **The elite lived on the hilltop**, commoners below: an early sign of a **class-divided society** with a sacred king set apart.
- Graves on the hill held gold objects, including the famous **golden rhinoceros**, found in **1933**, made of gold foil over a wooden core.
- **Glass beads** from the Indian Ocean trade, and ivory and gold going the other way.
- It was abandoned around **1290**, perhaps because of a drier climate, and power moved north.

**Great Zimbabwe, about 1200/1300–1450.** In the south of today's **Zimbabwe**. **"Zimbabwe" comes from the Shona for "houses of stone"**, and gave its name to the country in **1980**.

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **The Hill Complex** | stone enclosures on a granite hill, the oldest part |
| **The Great Enclosure** | a curving wall about **250 metres** long and up to about **11 metres** high, built of shaped granite blocks **without mortar**, with a solid **conical tower** inside |
| **The valley** | many smaller enclosures and dwellings |

Its people were **ancestors of the Shona**. The population is estimated at around **10,000 to 18,000** at its height, a figure with wide uncertainty. Its wealth came from **cattle** and from controlling **gold** traded to the coast through **Sofala** and on to **Kilwa**. Finds there include Chinese **celadon** porcelain, Persian pottery, glass beads, and a **coin from Kilwa**. Carved **soapstone birds** from the site are on Zimbabwe's flag.

**Decline.** The site was largely abandoned by about **1450**. Possible reasons, not settled: exhaustion of grazing, wood and soil around a large town; a shift of the gold trade north to the Zambezi, where the **Mutapa** state rose; and the rise of **Khami** (the Torwa state) to the west.

**The fight over who built it.** When Europeans saw it in the **1870s–90s**, many refused to believe Africans had built it, and credited Phoenicians, Arabs or the Queen of Sheba. **David Randall-MacIver** (**1905**) and **Gertrude Caton-Thompson** (**1929**) showed from the excavated objects that it was **medieval and African**. White-minority Rhodesia in the **1970s** still pressured officials and writers to avoid saying so.

**This is not a live debate among archaeologists.** The evidence for African builders is overwhelming, and the episode is now taught as a case study in **how politics can distort the reading of evidence**.

**Mapungubwe today** is a South African national park and a UNESCO World Heritage Site (**2003**); the golden rhinoceros is a national symbol. For how this past was suppressed and recovered in South Africa, see the South African Politics curriculum.
The Swahili coast: Kilwa and the monsoon:
Along some **3,000 kilometres** of the East African coast, from Somalia to Mozambique, stood a chain of Muslim trading towns built of coral stone. Their people spoke **Swahili**, and their wealth came from the winds.

**The monsoon.** From about November to March the winds blow from the north-east, carrying ships from Arabia and India to Africa. From about April to September they blow from the south-west, carrying them back. **A merchant could sail out and home in one year**, as long as he waited for the wind.

**The towns:**

| Town | What it was known for |
| --- | --- |
| **Mogadishu** | the north; textiles. Ibn Battuta visited in **1331** |
| **Lamu, Malindi, Mombasa** | in today's Kenya; Malindi sent envoys to Ming China in the **1410s** |
| **Zanzibar, Pemba** | islands off Tanzania |
| **Kilwa Kisiwani** | an island off southern Tanzania; at its height in the **1300s**, because it controlled the **gold** shipped north from **Sofala** |

**Kilwa.** Its rulers minted their own **copper coins**, and one has been found at Great Zimbabwe and another, famously, in northern Australia (how it got there is unknown). The **Great Mosque** was enlarged with domes and vaults in the early 1300s. The sultan **al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman** built **Husuni Kubwa** on a cliff above the sea, about the **1320s–30s**: a palace with courtyards and a bathing pool, one of the largest buildings in sub-Saharan Africa at the time. Ibn Battuta, visiting in **1331**, praised this sultan's generosity.

**What was traded:**

- **Out of Africa:** gold, ivory, iron, timber (mangrove poles), ambergris, and enslaved people.
- **Into Africa:** cotton cloth from India, glass beads, Chinese porcelain, Persian and Arab pottery.

**The language.** **Swahili is a Bantu language**, related to the languages of the African interior, with many words borrowed from **Arabic**, and later Persian, Portuguese and English. The name comes from the Arabic *sawahil*, "coasts".

**Islam** arrived early: at **Shanga** in the Lamu islands, Mark Horton excavated a series of mosques, the earliest wooden, from about the **late 700s or 800s**. By 1300 the coast was Muslim and part of the wider Indian Ocean world of Islamic law and learning.

**The debate: African or Arab?**

- **The colonial-era reading.** The towns were **Arab and Persian colonies** on an African shore, built by foreigners. The towns' own traditions supported it in part: the **Kilwa Chronicle** tells of a founder from **Shiraz** in Persia.
- **The archaeological reading**, from the **1980s**. Excavations showed the towns grew from **local African villages**, with local pottery and building in an unbroken line; the language is African; the people were Africans who joined the Indian Ocean world.
- **Ancient DNA (2023).** A study of medieval Swahili burials (Brielle and others, in *Nature*) found ancestry roughly **half African and half Asian**, mostly **Persian** with some Indian, mixing from about **1000**. The African ancestry came mainly from **women**, the Asian mainly from **men**: incoming men marrying into African families.

**What it settles.** Both older readings were partly right: **an African society, African in language and roots, that absorbed Persian and Arab newcomers**, whose descendants then remembered Shiraz as a founding story.

**What comes next.** In **1498** Vasco da Gama reached Malindi, and in **1505** the Portuguese sacked Kilwa (next stage).
Ethiopia: Lalibela's churches and the So:
In the highlands of north-east Africa, a Christian kingdom with roots in ancient Aksum carved churches out of solid rock and later claimed descent from King Solomon. Here it is taught as history; the theology belongs to Theology.

**The background.** **Aksum** (Stage 5 and 6) had become Christian in the **4th century**. After it declined, by about the 10th century, the Christian state moved south into the highlands. Its church, using the **Ge'ez** language in worship, received its head bishop (the *abuna*) from the **Coptic patriarch of Alexandria** in Egypt.

**The Zagwe dynasty, about 1137–1270.** Both dates are uncertain; some lists start earlier. They were Agaw people, not of the old Aksumite line.

**Lalibela.** The most famous Zagwe king, **Lalibela**, ruled around the **1180s–1220s**. At his capital, **Roha**, later renamed **Lalibela** after him, are **eleven churches cut downward from the living rock**: carved as single blocks, with their windows, doors and columns, standing in trenches. The best known is **Bete Giyorgis** (St George's), shaped as a cross from above.

**The debate: when and why were they built?**

- **The tradition.** Lalibela built all eleven, with angels' help, as a **"New Jerusalem"**, perhaps after Saladin took the real Jerusalem in **1187**: a river on the site is called the Jordan, and features are named after places in the Holy Land.
- **The archaeology.** David Phillipson and others argue that the complex was cut over **a longer period**, some parts **before** Lalibela's time, and that some carved spaces may first have been fortifications or palaces, later turned into churches.

**What would settle it:** firm dating of the rock-cutting and of the plaster and paintings inside. Rock-cut monuments are hard to date, so the argument rests on style and sequence.

**The Solomonic dynasty, from 1270.** **Yekuno Amlak** overthrew the Zagwe in **1270**. His line claimed descent from **King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba**, through their son **Menelik I**, said to have brought the **Ark of the Covenant** to Aksum. The claim was set out in the ***Kebra Nagast*** ("Glory of the Kings"), compiled in Ge'ez in the early **14th century**. This line, with breaks, ruled until **Haile Selassie** was deposed in **1974**.

**Expansion and conflict.**

| King | What he did |
| --- | --- |
| **Amda Seyon** (r. 1314–44) | defeated the Muslim sultanate of **Ifat** to the east and extended the kingdom; his wars are told in a royal chronicle |
| **Zara Yaqob** (r. 1434–68) | reformed the Church, enforced religious conformity harshly, and built a capital at Debre Berhan; Ethiopian monks attended the **Council of Florence** (**1441**) |

**Christians and Muslims.** The highlands were Christian; the lowlands toward the Red Sea and the Somali coast were Muslim sultanates, trading through **Zeila**. Wars alternated with trade. The struggle came to a climax in the 1500s (next stage).

**The neighbours to the north.** The Christian kingdoms of **Nubia**, in today's Sudan, were weakening under **Mamluk** pressure; the kingdom of **Makuria** had a Muslim king by **1317**, and its Christianity faded over the following two centuries.

**Why it matters.** Ethiopia is one of the **oldest continuous Christian states**, and one of the few African states never colonised (apart from Italy's occupation, 1936–41).
Cahokia and the peoples of North America:
North of Mexico, the largest town in the Americas before European contact rose beside the Mississippi around **1050**. In the dry south-west, other peoples built great stone houses and roads. None of them wrote, so everything here comes from archaeology and from the traditions of their descendants.

**Cahokia.** Across the Mississippi from today's **St Louis**, in Illinois.

| Feature | What it was |
| --- | --- |
| **The growth** | a sudden expansion around **1050**, which archaeologists call the "Big Bang": villages were cleared and a planned town laid out |
| **The people** | perhaps **10,000–20,000** at the peak around **1050–1200**, with estimates running lower and higher; others lived in the surrounding farmland |
| **Monks Mound** | an earthen platform about **30 metres** high, the **largest earthwork in the Americas north of Mexico**, built from millions of basket-loads of soil; a great building stood on top |
| **The plaza** | a huge levelled square in front of it, for gatherings and the stick-and-stone game *chunkey* |
| **"Woodhenge"** | circles of tall posts, apparently aligned with the sunrise at the solstices and equinoxes |
| **Mound 72** | burials of a high-status man laid on a bed of thousands of **shell beads**, with mass graves of many young women and others who were evidently **sacrificed** |

Cahokia's people farmed **maize**, with squash and native seed crops. Its style of mounds, plazas, symbols and chiefdoms spread widely: archaeologists call it the **Mississippian** culture, with later centres at **Moundville** (Alabama), **Etowah** (Georgia) and **Spiro** (Oklahoma).

**The decline.** A wooden **palisade** went up around the centre after about **1175**, suggesting conflict. Population fell after **1200**, and the site was largely empty by about **1350**. The causes are debated: **floods** (lake sediments show a major one about 1200), **drought**, political breakdown, and **deforestation**, though a 2020 study of soils found no evidence of the erosion that deforestation should have caused.

**The south-west: Chaco and Mesa Verde.** In what is now New Mexico and Colorado, the **Ancestral Puebloans** built:

- At **Chaco Canyon**, about **850–1150**, multi-storey "great houses" such as **Pueblo Bonito**, with hundreds of rooms, linked by straight **roads**. Chaco imported **macaw feathers** and **cacao** from Mexico, over 2,000 km away.
- At **Mesa Verde**, from the **1190s**, the famous **cliff dwellings**.

Tree rings record a **"Great Drought" from 1276 to 1299**. By **1300** the Four Corners region was emptied, and people moved south and east to the **Rio Grande**, **Hopi** and **Zuni** areas, where their descendants, the Pueblo peoples, live today. "Abandonment" is the archaeologists' word; the Pueblo peoples speak of **migration**.

**The north-east: the Haudenosaunee.** The **Iroquois Confederacy** of five nations (Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca) united under the **Great Law of Peace**. **When is debated**: Barbara Mann and Jerry Fields (1997) argued for **1142**, linking an eclipse in the oral tradition to a known eclipse; most others favour the **15th or 16th century**, from archaeology of village fortifications and alliance patterns. **What would settle it:** firm dating of the shift from warring villages to allied ones in the archaeological record.

**The far north.** The **Thule**, ancestors of the Inuit, spread east across Arctic Canada to Greenland from about **1200**, meeting the Norse there.
Tenochtitlan and the rise of the Inca:
By **1450** two peoples who had been minor newcomers two centuries earlier were building the largest states in the Americas: the **Mexica** (Aztecs) in Mexico and the **Inca** in the Andes. Most of their expansion came after 1450; this lesson is their rise.

**The Mexica.** A people speaking **Nahuatl**, who by their own tradition migrated from a northern homeland, **Aztlan**, into the **Valley of Mexico**, then a basin of lakes ruled by rival city-states.

| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **about 1325** | traditional founding of **Tenochtitlan** on an island in **Lake Texcoco**, where, in their story, their god showed an **eagle on a cactus**, now on Mexico's flag. Other dates, such as 1345, are given |
| **to 1428** | the Mexica are tributaries and mercenaries of the **Tepanec** city of **Azcapotzalco** |
| **1428** | under **Itzcoatl**, they overthrow the Tepanecs and form the **Triple Alliance** with **Texcoco** (whose poet-king **Nezahualcoyotl** became famous) and **Tlacopan**: the "Aztec Empire" |
| **1440–69** | **Moctezuma I** expands the alliance's tribute empire south and east |

**The city.** Built out into the lake on **chinampas**, raised fields of mud and reeds, very productive, crossed by canals and joined to the shore by causeways. At its centre, the **Templo Mayor**, a pyramid with twin shrines to **Huitzilopochtli**, god of war and the sun, and **Tlaloc**, god of rain. By **1519** Tenochtitlan had perhaps **200,000** people, an estimate with a wide range.

**Sacrifice.** Human sacrifice was central to the Mexica state religion: feeding the sun with blood. **The scale is debated.** Spanish and later figures, such as **80,400** victims at the temple's rededication in **1487**, are not credible as counts. But excavations from **2015** of the skull rack (**tzompantli**) near the Templo Mayor have uncovered hundreds of skulls, including women and children, confirming it was large.

**The Maya**, meanwhile, were no longer building their old southern cities. In Yucatán, **Mayapan** (about **1220–1440s**) was the last great Maya capital, until it was destroyed in civil war.

**The Andes.** After the fall of **Wari** and **Tiwanaku** around **1000**, the Andes were divided among regional states. The strongest was **Chimú**, on the north coast of Peru, with its capital **Chan Chan**, a vast city of adobe.

**The Inca.** A small kingdom around **Cusco** in the southern highlands, from about the **1200s**. By their own history, the turning point came when a prince, **Pachacuti** ("earth-shaker" or "turner of the world"), defended Cusco against the **Chanka** people and took the throne, about **1438**. He rebuilt Cusco in stone and began the conquests that made **Tawantinsuyu**, "the four parts together".

**The debate on dates.** The **1438** date comes from Spanish chroniclers' reckonings of Inca king lists, organised by John Rowe in **1945**. **Radiocarbon dates** from Inca sites suggest expansion began **decades earlier**, perhaps around **1400**. **What would settle it:** more securely dated Inca buildings across the empire. The question matters because it changes how fast the empire grew.

**How the Inca governed** came mostly later, but its tools were older Andean ones: the **quipu**, knotted cords for recording numbers; **labour tax** (*mit'a*); terraces and storehouses.

**The Amazon** was not empty. Lidar surveys in Bolivia (**2022**) mapped towns of the **Casarabe** culture, about **500–1400**, with platform mounds, causeways and reservoirs.
The Black Death, 1346–1353:
The worst recorded disaster in human history, measured by the share of people killed. In about seven years, plague killed perhaps **a third to a half or more** of the people of Europe and the Middle East.

**The disease.** **Plague**, caused by the bacterium ***Yersinia pestis***, carried by fleas on rodents. In its **bubonic** form it causes swollen lymph nodes (*buboes*) and kills perhaps half of those infected; in its **pneumonic** form, spread by breath, it is almost always fatal.

**Where it came from.** Ancient DNA from a cemetery near **Lake Issyk-Kul**, in today's **Kyrgyzstan**, where gravestones record deaths from "pestilence" in **1338–39**, matched the strain that caused the Black Death (Spyrou and others, *Nature*, **2022**). It travelled west along the routes of the Mongol world.

**How it spread:**

| Date | Where |
| --- | --- |
| **1346** | the Golden Horde besieging **Caffa**, a Genoese port in Crimea. The story that they **catapulted corpses** over the walls comes from one writer, **Gabriele de' Mussis**, who was not there |
| **1347** | **Constantinople**; **Alexandria**; Genoese galleys bring it to **Messina** in Sicily in **October** |
| **1348** | Italy, France, Spain, England; **Cairo**, **Damascus** (where Ibn Battuta saw it), Tunis |
| **1349–51** | Germany, Scandinavia, Scotland, Poland |
| **1352–53** | **Russia** |

**How many died?** Records are patchy. Estimates for Europe range from about **30 per cent to 60 per cent** (Ole Benedictow argues for the high end), perhaps **25–50 million** people. Egypt and Syria lost a similar share. Whether the same plague struck **China** and **sub-Saharan Africa** in these years is uncertain, and argued.

**How people responded:**

- **Explanations**: God's punishment; a conjunction of planets (the Paris medical faculty, **1348**); bad air, "miasma".
- **Flagellants** walked from town to town whipping themselves in penance, until the pope condemned them in **1349**.
- **Massacres of Jews**, accused of poisoning wells: at **Strasbourg** in **February 1349**, and in hundreds of towns. **Pope Clement VI** issued bulls in **1348** saying Jews were dying too, and forbidding the killings. Many cities ignored him.
- **Quarantine** began: **Ragusa** (Dubrovnik) isolated arrivals in **1377**, later for forty days, *quaranta giorni*.
- **Writing**: **Boccaccio**'s *Decameron* opens with the plague in Florence. **Ibn Khaldun** lost both parents to it in Tunis.

**Was it really plague?** In the 1980s and 1990s some scholars argued it spread too fast to be plague, and proposed other diseases. **Ancient DNA settled it**: *Yersinia pestis* has been found in the teeth of victims across Europe, including the **East Smithfield** plague pit in London. **How** it spread so fast is still argued: through rats and their fleas, or also through **human fleas and lice** passing it person to person.

**What it changed:**

- **Labour became scarce.** In England wages rose despite the **Statute of Labourers (1351)**, which tried to freeze them. Serfdom in western Europe weakened. Revolts followed: the **Jacquerie** in France (**1358**), the **Peasants' Revolt** in England (**1381**).
- **Plague returned** every decade or two for centuries.

**The debate on the long run.** One reading: the Black Death **raised wages and living standards** for survivors in north-west Europe, a step toward its later economic divergence. Another: in **eastern Europe** lords responded by tying peasants down harder, so the same shock led to opposite results, and **institutions**, not plague itself, decided the outcome.
The Ming dynasty and the voyages of Zhen:
The dynasty that drove out the Mongols in **1368** sent the greatest fleets the world had yet seen across the Indian Ocean, and then stopped.

**The founder.** **Zhu Yuanzhang** (1328–98), an orphan of peasant birth and former Buddhist monk, rose through the Red Turban rebellion, took **Dadu** in **1368**, and ruled as the **Hongwu** emperor from **Nanjing**. He was suspicious and cruel: from **1380**, after executing his chancellor and abolishing the office, his purges killed tens of thousands. In **1371** he **banned private sea trade** (the *haijin*, "sea ban").

**Yongle.** His son **Zhu Di** rebelled against his nephew, the Jianwen emperor, and took the throne in **1402** as the **Yongle** emperor (r. 1402–24). He:

- moved the capital to **Beijing** (formally **1421**) and built the **Forbidden City** (about **1406–20**);
- commissioned the ***Yongle Encyclopedia*** (**1408**), over 11,000 volumes;
- occupied **Đại Việt** (Vietnam) in **1407**; the Vietnamese leader **Lê Lợi** drove the Ming out in **1427**;
- and sent out the fleets.

**Zheng He (1371–1433).** Born **Ma He** to a **Muslim** family in **Yunnan**, he was captured as a boy when Ming armies took the province, castrated, and became a **eunuch** in Zhu Di's household, rising as a commander in his rebellion.

**The seven voyages, 1405–1433:**

| Voyage | Reach |
| --- | --- |
| **1–3 (1405–11)** | South-East Asia, Sri Lanka and **Calicut** in India. In **1411** Zheng He's troops captured a king of Sri Lanka and took him to China |
| **4 (1413–15)** | **Hormuz**, at the mouth of the Persian Gulf |
| **5–7 (1417–33)** | **Aden**, the Red Sea, and the Swahili coast at **Mogadishu** and **Malindi**. Envoys sent with the fleet reached **Mecca** |

The first voyage, by Chinese records, carried about **27,000 men** in more than **60 large "treasure ships"** and many smaller vessels. The records give the biggest ships lengths of about **120–140 metres**. **Many naval historians doubt this**, since wooden ships that size would barely hold together; perhaps half that is more likely. The size of the fleet, however, is not in doubt.

**What they were for.** Not conquest or settlement but **display and tribute**: to show the Ming's power, bring foreign rulers into the **tribute system**, and trade luxury goods. Envoys from dozens of states came to Beijing. A **giraffe**, sent from Bengal in **1414**, was hailed at court as a *qilin*, an auspicious beast. A stone the fleet set up at **Galle**, in Sri Lanka (**1409**), honours the Buddha, Allah and a Hindu god in **Chinese, Persian and Tamil**.

**Why did they stop?** The voyages ended after **1433**, and Zheng He probably died at sea on the last one.

- **Cost**: huge, while the treasury was also building Beijing and fighting the Mongols.
- **Court politics**: Confucian officials distrusted the eunuchs who ran the fleets, and the fleets were a eunuch enterprise.
- **The north**: the real danger was the steppe. In **1449**, at **Tumu**, the Oirat Mongols **captured the emperor himself**. The great Ming wall-building came afterwards.

**The debate: did China "turn inward"?** One reading: after 1433 the Ming chose isolation, leaving the oceans to Europeans. The other: **private Chinese trade** with South-East Asia went on, often smuggled, and the Ming remained deeply engaged with the world; the sea ban was eased in **1567**. **What would settle it:** trade volumes from Chinese, South-East Asian and later European records, which favour continued engagement.

**A false claim.** Gavin Menzies's *1421* (2002), saying the fleets reached America, is **rejected by historians** for lack of evidence.
The rise of the Ottomans, 1300–1450:
A small Turkish principality in north-western Anatolia, one of a dozen, grew in a century and a half into an empire that ruled the Balkans and surrounded Constantinople.

**The setting.** After the Mongols defeated the Seljuk sultanate of Rum at **Köse Dağ** (**1243**), Anatolia broke into small Turkish principalities, the **beyliks**. One, on the Byzantine frontier near Bursa, was led by **Osman** (died about **1323–24**). His followers were called the *Osmanlı*, and in Europe the **Ottomans**. The traditional founding date, **1299**, is symbolic; the first securely dated event is a victory over the Byzantines at **Bapheus** in **1302**.

**The rise:**

| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **1326** | Osman's son **Orhan** takes **Bursa**, the first capital |
| **1331, 1337** | **Nicaea** and **Nicomedia** taken from Byzantium |
| **1346** | Orhan marries **Theodora**, daughter of the Byzantine claimant **John VI Kantakouzenos**, and fights for him in Byzantium's civil war |
| **1354** | an **earthquake** wrecks the walls of **Gallipoli**, on the European side of the Dardanelles; the Ottomans occupy it. **The Ottomans are in Europe** |
| **about 1369** | **Adrianople** (Edirne) taken, becoming the capital; the date is debated, between about 1361 and 1371 |
| **15 June 1389** | **Kosovo**: Murad I defeats the Serbs under Prince **Lazar**; both die. The battle became the centre of Serbian national memory |
| **1396** | **Bayezid I** destroys a crusade of French, Hungarian and other knights at **Nicopolis**, on the Danube |

**Disaster.** **Timur**, the Turko-Mongol conqueror from Samarkand who had sacked Delhi in 1398, invaded Anatolia. On **28 July 1402**, at **Ankara**, he destroyed the Ottoman army and **captured Bayezid**, who died in captivity in **1403**. Bayezid's sons fought each other for eleven years, the **Interregnum** (1402–13). The state could have vanished. Timur died in **1405**, and **Mehmed I** reunited it by **1413**.

**Recovery.** **Murad II** (r. 1421–51) beat off a last crusade at **Varna** (**1444**), where the young king of Poland and Hungary, **Władysław III**, was killed, and won a second battle of **Kosovo** (**1448**).

**What made the Ottomans strong:**

- **The Janissaries**: infantry recruited through the ***devshirme***, the levy of Christian boys from Balkan villages, converted to Islam and trained as the sultan's own slave soldiers, from the late **14th century**.
- **The *timar***: grants of the revenue of land to cavalrymen in return for service.
- **Flexible rule**: Christian vassal princes, Christian soldiers, and local customs kept where they paid.
- **One heir**: from the 15th century, the winning son often killed his brothers, which kept the state from being divided.

**The debate: who were the first Ottomans?**

- **Holy warriors.** **Paul Wittek** (**1938**): the *gazi* thesis. The Ottomans were frontier fighters for the faith, whose religious zeal drew warriors to them.
- **Pragmatic frontier lords.** Rudi Lindner and Heath Lowry: the early Ottomans had **Christian allies and commanders**, married Byzantine princesses, and behaved like a tribal or plunder confederation. *Gaza* language appears mostly in later writings.
- **A synthesis.** Cemal Kafadar (*Between Two Worlds*, **1995**): *gaza* was a real ideal, but in a frontier culture where it was compatible with alliances across religious lines.

**What would settle it:** contemporary sources from the 1300s, which are very few: an inscription at Bursa of **1337** that calls Orhan a *gazi* is itself disputed in reading and date. Hence the long argument.
The fall of Constantinople, 1453:
On **29 May 1453** the Ottoman sultan **Mehmed II** took **Constantinople**. The Roman Empire, which had ruled from that city since 330, came to an end.

**The empire in 1450** was little more than the city, some islands and the **Morea** in southern Greece. Its emperor, **Constantine XI Palaiologos**, had about **50,000** subjects in a city that had once held perhaps half a million. His predecessor had accepted **union with Rome** at the **Council of Florence** (**1439**) to win Western help. Many of his own people rejected it; one official was reported to say he would rather see the Turkish turban in the city than the Latin mitre.

**Mehmed II** (born **1432**) became sultan for the second time in **1451**, at eighteen. In **1452** he built the fortress of **Rumeli Hisarı** on the Bosporus, cutting the city off from the Black Sea.

**The siege, 6 April – 29 May 1453:**

| Element | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| **The armies** | defenders about **7,000–8,000**, including Genoese and Venetians; the Ottoman army perhaps **50,000–80,000** fighting men, with far higher figures in the sources |
| **The guns** | the founder **Urban**, a Hungarian, had first offered his services to the emperor, who could not pay. He cast for Mehmed a giant bronze cannon that fired stones of about half a tonne |
| **The walls** | the **Theodosian Walls**, a triple line from the 5th century, unbroken by any army for a thousand years |
| **The chain** | a boom across the **Golden Horn**, the city's harbour. On **22 April** Mehmed had about **70 ships dragged overland** on greased rollers behind the Genoese colony of **Galata** into the Horn |
| **The end** | the final assault on **29 May**. The Genoese commander **Giovanni Giustiniani** was badly wounded and carried off, and the defence broke. **Constantine XI died fighting**; his body was never certainly identified |

The story that a small gate, the **Kerkoporta**, was left open comes from one Greek historian, **Doukas**, and is not confirmed.

**The sack** lasted a day or more; by the custom of the time a city that refused to surrender could be plundered for three days. **Hagia Sophia** became a **mosque**, and Mehmed prayed there within days. He made the city his capital, repopulated it with Muslims, Christians and Jews, and in **1454** appointed **Gennadios Scholarios**, an opponent of union with Rome, as **Orthodox patriarch**. He styled himself ***Kayser-i Rum***, "Caesar of Rome".

**The rest of Byzantium** followed: the Morea in **1460**, **Trebizond** in **1461**.

**The debate: what did 1453 change?**

| Older reading | The objection |
| --- | --- |
| it **ended the Middle Ages** | a teaching convention; for most people nothing changed that year |
| it sent **Greek scholars to Italy**, starting the Renaissance | the flow began earlier: **Manuel Chrysoloras** taught Greek in Florence from **1397**, and **Bessarion** came for the Council in **1439** |
| it **closed the trade routes**, so Europeans sought a sea route to Asia | the Ottomans welcomed trade and taxed it; Portugal's voyages down Africa began in the **1410s–30s** |

**What is agreed:** the Ottomans now held the straits between Europe and Asia and the Black Sea and the Aegean, and had become a great power. The city, as **Istanbul**, became the capital of an empire that lasted until **1922**.
Connections: the world in 1450:
The stage closes in **1450**. Look across the world and see what linked it, and what was about to change.

**What linked the world: the circuits.** The sociologist Janet Abu-Lughod (*Before European Hegemony*, **1989**) described the world of about **1250–1350** as eight overlapping trade circuits, from Flanders to China, with no single centre. Europe was one region among many, and far from the richest.

| Link | Who it joined |
| --- | --- |
| **The Mongol roads** | China, Iran, Russia and the Black Sea, in the century after 1250 |
| **The Indian Ocean** | the Swahili coast, Arabia, India, South-East Asia and China, on the monsoon |
| **The Sahara** | Mali and West Africa with North Africa and the Mediterranean, by camel caravan |
| **The Mediterranean** | Venice, Genoa, the Mamluks, Byzantium and the Ottomans |

**What was carried:**

- **Faiths.** **Islam** spread into Anatolia and the Balkans with the Turks, among the Golden Horde, and through merchants into **South-East Asia**: **Samudra Pasai** in Sumatra had a Muslim king by the **1290s**, and **Malacca**'s ruler converted in the early **1400s**. **Theravada Buddhism** spread across mainland South-East Asia. **Lithuania**, Europe's last pagan state, became Catholic in **1387**.
- **Technologies.** **Gunpowder** and the **compass** went west from China; Europe took up **Hindu-Arabic numerals**.
- **Disease.** The **Black Death** travelled the same roads as the silk.

**Oceania.** **Polynesian** voyagers settled **Aotearoa (New Zealand)** about **1250–1300**, the last large land on earth to be settled. A 2020 DNA study (Ioannidis and others, *Nature*) found that some **eastern Polynesians** carry **Native American** ancestry from a contact around **1200**, and the South American **sweet potato** was already grown across Polynesia.

**The world in 1450:**

| Region | Where things stood |
| --- | --- |
| **Ottomans** | three years from taking Constantinople |
| **Mamluk Egypt** | the leading Arab state; Cairo, one of the largest cities west of China |
| **The Timurids** | Timur's heirs in Samarkand and Herat; his grandson **Ulugh Beg** built an observatory at **Samarkand** in the **1420s** |
| **India** | the Delhi Sultanate shrunken; **Vijayanagara** and the **Bahmanis** strong in the south |
| **China** | the Ming, after the voyages and after **Tumu (1449)**, facing north |
| **Korea** | the **Joseon** dynasty (from **1392**); King **Sejong**'s **hangul** alphabet, promulgated **1446** |
| **Africa** | Mali waning, **Songhay** rising; Kilwa rich; Great Zimbabwe emptying; Ethiopia under Zara Yaqob |
| **Europe** | the Hundred Years' War almost over; **Gutenberg** printing with movable type at **Mainz**, about **1450**; Portugal on the African coast |
| **The Americas** | the **Triple Alliance** expanding in Mexico; **Pachacuti** building the Inca state |

**What carries over into Stage 8.** **Portugal** had taken **Ceuta** in Morocco (**1415**), settled **Madeira** and the **Azores**, passed **Cape Bojador** (**1434**), and in **1444** brought captured Africans to **Lagos** in Portugal for sale: the opening of the Atlantic slave trade. **Printing**, **gunpowder** and **ocean ships** were about to join the world's separate regions into one. The **Little Ice Age** was cooling the north.

**Look back at the whole stage:** **the Mongols joined Eurasia and the plague followed them**; Africa's states traded gold to three continents; the Americas built their largest cities on their own. In 1450 no one could have known that Eurasia's small western kingdoms would be the ones to cross the oceans.
Map: the world in 1450:
In 1450 the world's great regions still mostly knew each other through middlemen. Within a century, ships and silver would tie them all together. This is the starting line.

**Where everyone is, about 1450:**

| Region | Who holds it |
| --- | --- |
| **East Asia** | **Ming China**, the largest state on earth. In 1449 the emperor was captured by the Oirat Mongols at Tumu; the great fleets of Zheng He had stopped sailing in 1433. **Joseon Korea** under King Sejong, whose new alphabet, hangul, was announced in 1446. **Japan** under a weak Ashikaga shogun, about to fall into a century of civil war |
| **South-East Asia** | **Malacca**, a Muslim sultanate on the strait that every ship between India and China passed; **Ayutthaya** in Siam; **Đại Việt** in the north of Vietnam |
| **South Asia** | the shrunken **Delhi Sultanate** in the north (the Lodi family took it in 1451); the Hindu empire of **Vijayanagara** in the south; the **Bahmani** sultanate in the Deccan |
| **The Near East** | the **Ottomans**, who would take Constantinople in **1453**; the **Mamluks** in Egypt and Syria; Iran split among Turkmen clans after the heirs of Timur |
| **Europe** | the Hundred Years' War ending (1453); Italian city-states rich from trade; Castile and Aragon still facing Muslim **Granada**; **Muscovy** a growing principality under Tatar overlordship |
| **Africa** | **Mali** fading and **Songhai** rising on the Niger bend; **Benin** in the forest under Oba Ewuare; **Kongo** south of the Congo River; Christian **Ethiopia** under Zara Yaqob; the Swahili ports of the east coast; **Great Zimbabwe** declining as the **Mutapa** state rose to its north |
| **The Americas** | the **Aztec** Triple Alliance (formed 1428) ruling central Mexico; the **Inca**, just beginning their great conquests under **Pachacuti** (ruled about 1438–1471); many peoples of North America, the Amazon and the Caribbean |
| **Oceania** | Polynesians settled across the Pacific, as far as Aotearoa (New Zealand) by about 1300; Aboriginal Australians on their continent for some 50,000 years or more |

**Three things true in 1450 that will not be true in 1750:**

1. **The Americas and Afro-Eurasia have no regular contact.** The Norse visit to Newfoundland around AD 1000 left no lasting link.
2. **No European state holds land outside Europe**, except Portugal's toeholds on the African coast and Atlantic islands (Ceuta, 1415; Madeira and the Azores).
3. **The richest economies are in Asia.** China and India together held perhaps half the world's people and most of its manufacturing.

**World population** was probably somewhere around **400 to 500 million**. Estimates for this period are rough, especially for the Americas, and that uncertainty becomes a lesson of its own.

**What drives this stage.** Better ships and guns, a European hunger for Asian spices and gold, and a Chinese hunger for silver. By 1750, the oceans have become highways, and every region in this table has been changed by the others.
The Italian Renaissance and the humanist:
**The Renaissance** ("rebirth") was a movement among Italian scholars and artists, from about 1350 to 1550, to recover and imitate the learning and art of ancient Greece and Rome. It began in the city-states of northern Italy, above all **Florence**.

**Why Italy?** Its cities were rich from banking and the Mediterranean trade. They were full of Roman ruins and Latin manuscripts. And they were small republics and princedoms that competed for prestige by paying artists and scholars. The **Medici** banking family ran Florence for most of the 1400s: Cosimo (died 1464), then **Lorenzo "the Magnificent"** (1449–1492).

**Humanism** was the scholarly heart of it. The humanists studied grammar, rhetoric, history, poetry and moral philosophy (the *studia humanitatis*) from classical texts. Their method was **going back to the sources** (*ad fontes*) and checking them carefully:

- **Petrarch** (1304–1374) hunted lost Latin manuscripts and called the centuries after Rome a "dark" age. The idea of a "Middle Ages" comes from humanists like him.
- **Lorenzo Valla** showed in **1440**, from its Latin, that the *Donation of Constantine*, a document granting the popes power over the West, was a forgery written centuries after Constantine.
- Greek scholars from Byzantium taught in Italy, and more came after 1453, bringing Plato and the Greek fathers.

**The artists** studied Roman ruins and the human body, and worked out **linear perspective**, the geometry of making a flat picture look deep:

| Who | Dates | Known for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Brunelleschi** | 1377–1446 | the dome of Florence cathedral, finished 1436 |
| **Leonardo da Vinci** | 1452–1519 | the *Last Supper*, the *Mona Lisa*, notebooks of engineering and anatomy |
| **Michelangelo** | 1475–1564 | *David* (1504), the Sistine Chapel ceiling (1508–1512) |
| **Raphael** | 1483–1520 | the *School of Athens* in the Vatican |

**Politics** got its own humanist: **Niccolò Machiavelli** wrote *The Prince* in **1513**, advising rulers to act as things are, not as they ought to be. It was printed in 1532.

**North of the Alps**, the movement took a more religious turn. **Erasmus** of Rotterdam (about 1466–1536) printed a new Greek New Testament in 1516 and mocked church abuses in *The Praise of Folly* (1511).

**Contested: was it really a rebirth?** The Swiss historian **Jacob Burckhardt** (1860) saw the Renaissance as the birth of the modern individual and a sharp break with the Middle Ages. Medievalists answered that there had been earlier revivals (Charles Homer Haskins's *Renaissance of the Twelfth Century*, 1927) and that much Greek learning had reached Europe through Arabic scholarship. Many historians now speak of a long continuity with real changes inside it. The test is a concrete one: compare what was read, taught and painted in 1300 and in 1500, and see how much is truly new.
Gutenberg and the printing press:
**Around 1450, in Mainz, Germany, Johannes Gutenberg built a printing press with movable metal type.** Within fifty years it had spread across Europe, and it changed how ideas travelled for good.

**What he actually invented.** Printing itself was not new. China printed from carved wooden blocks by the 700s; **Bi Sheng** made movable type of baked clay in the 1040s; Korea printed with **movable metal type** by the 1200s, and the oldest surviving metal-type book, the Buddhist *Jikji*, dates from **1377**. Gutenberg's achievement was a *system* suited to an alphabet of a few dozen letters:

- a hand mould for casting thousands of identical metal letters quickly;
- an alloy of lead, tin and antimony that cast cleanly;
- an oil-based ink that stuck to metal;
- a screw press adapted from wine and paper presses.

**The Gutenberg Bible**, finished about **1454–1455**, ran to perhaps 160–180 copies. Around fifty survive, whole or in part.

**How fast it spread:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| 1465 | first press in Italy, near Rome |
| 1470 | Paris |
| 1476 | **William Caxton** at Westminster, England |
| 1500 | presses in well over 200 European towns |

Books printed before 1501 are called *incunabula* ("cradle books"). Something like **27,000–30,000 editions** survive from those fifty years, which means millions of copies; estimates of the total vary widely. A book that took a scribe months now took a print shop weeks, and its copies were identical.

**What changed:**

1. **Cheaper books, more readers.** Literacy grew slowly, but print gave readers far more to read.
2. **Fixed texts.** Every copy said the same thing, so scholars could cite page and line, and correct errors in the next edition.
3. **Speed of argument.** In 1517–1520 Martin Luther's pamphlets sold in the hundreds of thousands. The Reformation was the first great movement carried by print.
4. **Vernacular languages.** Printers sold in German, French and English, which helped fix national languages.

**Elsewhere.** In the Ottoman Empire, Jewish refugees from Spain printed in Hebrew in Istanbul from 1493, and Armenians and Greeks also printed, but a press for Turkish in Arabic script came only in **1727**, under **İbrahim Müteferrika**. Why so late is debated: calligraphers' guilds, religious caution about printing sacred script, the difficulty of joined Arabic letters, or simply a manuscript market that already worked. In China, woodblock printing stayed dominant, because for thousands of characters carved blocks were cheaper than metal type.

**Contested: a revolution, or a slow change?** **Elizabeth Eisenstein** (*The Printing Press as an Agent of Change*, 1979) argued that print transformed European thought: it made the Reformation and the scientific revolution possible. **Adrian Johns** (*The Nature of the Book*, 1998) answered that early print was full of piracy and error, and trust in printed books had to be built over centuries. What would settle it is evidence of how readers actually used books: annotations, library lists and letters.
Ming China after the treasure fleets:
**After the voyages of Zheng He ended in 1433, Ming China turned its energy to its northern frontier and its own vast economy.** It was still, through most of this stage, the largest and richest state on earth.

**The northern danger.** In **1449**, at **Tumu**, the Oirat Mongols destroyed a Ming army and captured the Zhengtong emperor himself. The court's answer, over the next century and a half, was walls. **Most of the Great Wall that tourists see today, in brick and stone, was built by the Ming**, especially from the late 1400s into the 1500s. It was not one continuous line but a system of walls, forts and watchtowers.

**The sea ban.** The Ming restricted private overseas trade (the *haijin*, "sea ban"). The ban bred smuggling and piracy along the coast: the *wokou*, "Japanese pirates", who were in fact often Chinese. In **1567** the court opened a port in Fujian to licensed private trade. Around the same time the Portuguese were allowed to settle at **Macau** (from about **1557**).

**A silver economy.** The Ming's paper money had collapsed in the 1400s, and the economy turned to **silver**, weighed out in lumps. In the **1570s–1580s** the chief minister **Zhang Juzheng** pushed the **Single Whip reform**, which merged taxes and labour duties into **one payment in silver**. China, with perhaps a quarter of the world's people, now needed huge amounts of a metal it did not mine in quantity. That demand is one end of the global silver trade.

**Culture.** Ming cities supported a lively commercial culture: printed novels such as *Journey to the West* (published 1592), blue-and-white porcelain shipped all over the world, and the philosophy of **Wang Yangming** (1472–1529), who taught that moral knowledge is found by looking inward and acting on it.

**Contact.** The Jesuit **Matteo Ricci** reached Macau in 1582 and Beijing in **1601**, where he lived until his death in 1610. He dressed as a Confucian scholar, translated Euclid with the scholar Xu Guangqi, and drew a world map for Chinese readers.

**War in Korea.** In **1592** the Japanese warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi invaded **Korea**, intending to go on to China. Ming armies came to Korea's aid, and the Korean admiral **Yi Sun-sin** wrecked Japanese supply fleets. The Japanese withdrew in **1598** after Hideyoshi died. The war devastated Korea and drained the Ming treasury.

**The long reign.** The **Wanli Emperor** (ruled 1572–1620) withdrew from government for years at a time in a quarrel with his officials. Factional fights, costly wars and later famines weakened the dynasty in the decades before its fall in 1644.

**Contested: did China "turn inward"?** The old story says the Ming chose isolation after Zheng He, and so fell behind Europe. Others answer that China was simply not short of anything it needed by sea, that its private trade grew enormously in the 1500s, and that Chinese merchants and goods filled South-East Asia. The evidence that bears on it is the volume of private trade, ships and silver, which was large, set against official policy, which was restrictive.
The Portuguese round Africa:
**Between 1415 and 1498, Portugal felt its way down the coast of Africa, round the Cape of Good Hope, and across to India.** It was a small, poor kingdom on the Atlantic, and that is part of why it went.

**Why Portugal?** It faced the open ocean, had no Mediterranean trade to speak of, and was shut out of the spice trade by Venice and the Mamluks. Its kings wanted **West African gold** without going through Muslim middlemen, a Christian ally against Islam (the legend of **Prester John**), and in time direct access to Asian spices.

**The steps:**

| Year | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **1415** | Portugal seizes **Ceuta** in Morocco |
| 1420s–1430s | Madeira and the Azores settled; Madeira later grows sugar |
| **1434** | Gil Eanes passes **Cape Bojador**, long feared as the edge of safe sailing |
| **1444** | enslaved Africans landed and sold at Lagos, in Portugal; the Atlantic slave trade's first step |
| 1460 | death of **Prince Henry "the Navigator"**, the expeditions' patron |
| **1482** | the fort of **São Jorge da Mina (Elmina)** built on the Gold Coast; Diogo Cão reaches the Congo River |
| **1488** | **Bartolomeu Dias** rounds the Cape of Good Hope and lands at Mossel Bay |
| **1497–1499** | **Vasco da Gama** sails to **Calicut** in India and back |

**The tools.** The **caravel** was a small, light ship whose triangular sails could work against the wind. Portuguese pilots learned the **volta do mar**, swinging far out into the Atlantic to catch the westerlies home. Henry's famous "school of navigation" at Sagres is mostly a later legend.

**Da Gama's voyage.** He left Lisbon in **July 1497**, rounded the Cape in November, and sailed up the Swahili coast. At **Malindi** he took on a pilot who knew the monsoon route, and he reached **Calicut in May 1498**. The ruler there, the Zamorin, was unimpressed by his gifts. But the spices he brought home paid for the voyage many times over. More than half his men died on the way, many of scurvy.

**Then came force.** The Indian Ocean was a rich, crowded trading world of Gujaratis, Arabs, Malays, Chinese and Swahili, and the Portuguese could not outsell them. They used **guns on ships** instead:

- **1505**: the Swahili ports of Kilwa and Mombasa are sacked.
- **1509**: off **Diu**, a Portuguese fleet defeats a Mamluk and Gujarati fleet.
- **1510**: **Afonso de Albuquerque** takes **Goa**, which becomes Portugal's capital in Asia; **1511**: he takes **Malacca**; **1515**: **Hormuz**.

They built a chain of forts, the *Estado da Índia*, and tried to make other ships buy a pass (a *cartaz*). They never controlled the ocean's trade; they taxed a slice of it.

**Ethiopia.** In 1541 a small Portuguese force under Cristóvão da Gama, Vasco's son, helped Christian Ethiopia against the Muslim sultanate of Adal, whose leader Ahmad ibn Ibrahim (called Grañ, "the left-handed") had overrun much of the highlands. Ahmad was killed in 1543.

**Brazil, by accident.** In 1500 a fleet bound for India under **Pedro Álvares Cabral** swung so far west that it reached **Brazil**, which Portugal claimed. The **Treaty of Tordesillas** (1494) had already split the non-European world between Spain and Portugal along a line west of the Cape Verde islands.
Columbus and 1492:
**On 12 October 1492, three Spanish ships under Christopher Columbus reached an island in the Bahamas.** It was the start of lasting contact between the Americas and the rest of the world, after perhaps 15,000 years apart.

**Who he was.** Columbus was born in **Genoa** in 1451 and sailed for years in the Portuguese Atlantic. **He did not need to prove the earth was round**; educated Europeans had known that since antiquity. His idea was that **Asia lay a short way west**, and here he was badly wrong. He shrank the size of the earth and stretched Asia, and put Japan roughly where the Caribbean is. Portugal's experts turned him down. So, at first, did Spain's.

**Spain in 1492.** In **January 1492**, **Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile** took **Granada**, the last Muslim state in Iberia. In March they ordered every Jew to convert or leave (the **Alhambra Decree**). In April they agreed to back Columbus. Victory, religious zeal and a hunger for gold came together in the same few months.

**The first voyage.** He sailed from **Palos on 3 August 1492** with the *Niña*, the *Pinta* and the *Santa María*, about ninety men. After a stop in the Canaries, the crossing took five weeks. The landfall was an island the **Taíno** people called **Guanahani**; Columbus named it San Salvador. Which modern island it was is still argued. He went on to **Cuba** and **Hispaniola**, where the *Santa María* ran aground on Christmas Day, and he left 39 men there in a fort. On his return none of them were alive.

**What he saw and wanted.** His own journal (known through a summary by Bartolomé de las Casas) describes the Taíno as generous and unarmed, and in the same pages considers how easily they could be made to serve. **The search for gold** drove everything after.

**Four voyages, 1492–1504.** On the second (1493) he brought 17 ships and over a thousand settlers, and Hispaniola's conquest began: forced tribute in gold, enslavement, and disease. As governor he ruled so badly that in **1500** he was arrested and sent home in chains. He died in **1506** at Valladolid, still insisting he had reached Asia.

**Others followed fast.** **John Cabot**, sailing for England, reached Newfoundland in **1497**. **Amerigo Vespucci**'s accounts argued that this was a "New World", and a 1507 map by **Martin Waldseemüller** named it **America** after him.

**Contested: how to judge Columbus.** One reading stresses the seamanship and the world-changing result: he crossed an ocean no one in Europe had crossed on purpose and come back. Another stresses what followed on Hispaniola, where the Taíno, perhaps hundreds of thousands of people, were nearly destroyed within a generation. These are not exactly rival facts; both are documented. The dispute is over what weight to give each, and over how far Columbus personally, rather than the colonial system after him, is to blame. The evidence for his own conduct is in his letters and the 1500 inquiry into his rule, rediscovered in 2006.
The conquest of Mexico, 1519–1521:
**Between 1519 and 1521 the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan was conquered by a few hundred Spaniards and, crucially, tens of thousands of Indigenous allies.**

**The Aztec Empire.** Its centre was **Tenochtitlan**, an island city in Lake Texcoco, with a population usually estimated at **150,000 to 200,000** or more, larger than any city in Spain. The Mexica and their partners in the Triple Alliance ruled much of central Mexico by tribute, not by direct government. Many subject peoples resented them, and the **Tlaxcalans**, never conquered, were their sworn enemies.

**The expedition.** **Hernán Cortés** left Cuba in February 1519, defying the governor who had sent him, with about **500 soldiers**, horses, and some small cannon. Two interpreters made everything possible: a shipwrecked Spaniard who had learned Maya, and **Malintzin** (called **Doña Marina** or **La Malinche**), a Nahua woman given to the Spaniards as a slave, who spoke Nahuatl and Maya and soon Spanish.

**The march:**

| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| 1519 | landing on the Gulf coast; Veracruz founded |
| September 1519 | after hard fighting, **alliance with Tlaxcala** |
| October 1519 | massacre at **Cholula** |
| **8 November 1519** | Cortés enters Tenochtitlan; **Moctezuma II** receives him, and is soon held hostage |
| May 1520 | while Cortés is away, **Pedro de Alvarado** massacres nobles at a festival in the main temple |
| **30 June – 1 July 1520** | the Spaniards flee the city by night with heavy losses (**La Noche Triste**). Moctezuma is dead, whether killed by his own people's stones or by the Spaniards, the sources disagree |
| 1520 | **smallpox** reaches the city and kills many, including the new ruler Cuitláhuac |
| **May–August 1521** | siege, with boats on the lake and huge Indigenous armies; the city falls on **13 August 1521**; the last ruler, **Cuauhtémoc**, is captured |

**Why did it fall?** Several causes worked together:

1. **Allies.** Tlaxcala, Texcoco and other cities supplied most of the fighters. For them it was a war against the Mexica, with the Spaniards as useful partners.
2. **Disease.** Smallpox struck in the middle of the war.
3. **Steel, horses and ships** gave the Spaniards an edge in particular fights, but could not have taken a city of that size alone.
4. **Politics.** Holding Moctezuma hostage paralysed the government for months.

**Contested: who conquered Mexico?** The traditional account, from Cortés's own letters and Bernal Díaz's memoir, tells a story of Spanish daring. Historians such as **Matthew Restall** (*Seven Myths of the Spanish Conquest*, 2003) argue that it was largely an Indigenous war won by Indigenous armies, and that the story that the Mexica took Cortés for the returning god Quetzalcoatl was invented after the conquest. Others reply that the Spaniards' leadership and the alliances they built were the decisive new element. The Nahua side survives in accounts gathered decades later, such as the **Florentine Codex** compiled under Bernardino de Sahagún, and in Tlaxcalan pictorial histories, which show their own warriors doing most of the fighting.

**After.** Mexico City was built on the ruins. The new colony was called **New Spain**, and in 1535 it got the first viceroy in the Americas.
The conquest of the Inca, 1532–1572:
**The Inca Empire, the largest state in the Americas, was seized by a small Spanish force in 1532–1533, but Inca resistance went on until 1572.**

**The empire.** The Inca called it **Tawantinsuyu**, "the four parts together". In barely a century it had stretched some **4,000 km** along the Andes, from modern Ecuador to central Chile, with perhaps **10 million** people (estimates vary widely). It had no writing in the usual sense, but kept records on **khipu**, knotted cords. It had about 40,000 km of roads, storehouses, and a labour tax called **mit'a**.

**A civil war.** Around **1528** the ruler **Huayna Capac** died, possibly of a European disease (smallpox is the usual guess) that had travelled ahead of the Europeans themselves. His sons **Huáscar** and **Atahualpa** fought for the throne. When the Spaniards arrived, Atahualpa had just won, and his generals had captured Huáscar.

**Cajamarca.** **Francisco Pizarro** reached the highland town of **Cajamarca** with about **168 men** in **November 1532**. Atahualpa came to meet them in the main square with thousands of attendants, mostly unarmed. On **16 November 1532** the Spaniards attacked from hiding with guns, horses and steel, killed thousands, and **captured Atahualpa**.

**The ransom.** Atahualpa offered to fill a room with gold, and twice over with silver. The treasure was brought and melted down. Meanwhile Huáscar was killed on his orders. In **1533** the Spaniards executed Atahualpa anyway, and in November they took the capital, **Cusco**, with the help of Huáscar's supporters, who saw them as allies against Atahualpa's party.

**Resistance.**

| Year | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **1536** | **Manco Inca**, installed as a puppet, rebels and besieges Cusco for months |
| 1537 onward | Manco withdraws to **Vilcabamba** in the forest and keeps an independent Inca state |
| 1541 | Pizarro killed in Lima by rival Spaniards; the conquerors fight their own civil wars |
| **1572** | Viceroy Francisco de Toledo's forces take Vilcabamba; the last ruler, **Túpac Amaru**, is beheaded in Cusco |

**Why such a small force won.** The same factors as in Mexico, in a different mix: an empire already split by civil war, **epidemics** that killed leaders and soldiers, **steel and horses**, and many Andean peoples, recently conquered by the Inca, who joined the Spaniards. Capturing the ruler in a state built around him was devastating.

**After.** **Lima** was founded in 1535 and became the capital of the **Viceroyalty of Peru** (1542). Toledo reorganised the Andes in the 1570s, moving Indigenous people into new towns and turning the Inca *mit'a* into forced labour for the silver mines.

**The sources.** Spanish chroniclers wrote most of the accounts. Two Andean writers give other views: **Garcilaso de la Vega, "El Inca"** (1539–1616), son of a conquistador and an Inca princess, and **Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala**, whose illustrated letter to the king of Spain, finished about 1615, shows colonial abuses in nearly 400 drawings.
The Columbian Exchange:
**The Columbian Exchange** is the swap of plants, animals and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world that began in 1492. The historian **Alfred Crosby** gave it the name in **1972**. It may be the most important single consequence of the voyages.

**What crossed:**

| From the Americas | To the Americas |
| --- | --- |
| **maize**, **potatoes**, **cassava**, **sweet potatoes** | **wheat**, **rice**, barley |
| tomatoes, **chilli peppers**, beans, squash, peanuts | **sugar cane**, coffee, bananas, citrus |
| cacao, vanilla, **tobacco**, rubber | **horses**, **cattle**, **pigs**, sheep, goats, chickens |
| (disease: possibly **syphilis**; debated) | (disease: **smallpox**, **measles**, influenza; and with enslaved Africans, **malaria** and **yellow fever**) |

**The crops changed diets across the world:**

- **Potatoes** grew well in cold, poor soils and fed northern Europe, from Ireland to Russia, by the 1700s.
- **Maize and sweet potatoes** let Chinese farmers plant hills that rice could not use. They helped the population of Qing China grow to roughly **300 million by 1800**.
- **Maize and cassava** became staples across much of Africa.
- **Chilli peppers** became central to the food of India, Sichuan, Korea and Thailand. Cuisines that seem ancient are often only a few centuries old.

How much of the Old World's population growth after 1700 is owed to American crops is debated; one economic study (Nunn and Qian, 2011) credits the potato alone with roughly a quarter of it, a figure others consider too high.

**The animals changed the Americas.** Horses escaped and spread north. By the 1700s the **Comanche**, **Lakota** and other Plains peoples had built new mounted ways of life around hunting bison. Cattle and sheep turned great areas of Mexico and the pampas of Argentina into pasture, often trampling Indigenous fields.

**Sugar** changed the most lives of all. Cane, brought from the Atlantic islands, needed heavy labour and was grown on plantations in Brazil and the Caribbean. That demand drove the Atlantic slave trade.

**Disease** was the most terrible part of the exchange. Peoples of the Americas had no prior exposure to the crowd diseases of Afro-Eurasia, and epidemics killed huge numbers. That catastrophe has its own lesson.

**Syphilis, contested.** A severe new form of syphilis swept Europe from **1495**, starting among the armies at Naples. The "Columbian" view is that sailors brought it from the Americas. The alternative is that related diseases were already present in the Old World and were only newly recognised. Skeletal evidence from before 1492 has been claimed on both sides of the Atlantic, and the evidence that would settle it is secure, well-dated pre-1492 Old World skeletons with the disease, or ancient DNA of the bacterium. Studies so far point both ways.

**Why it matters for the rest of this curriculum.** Population growth in Asia and Europe, the plantation economy, and the Plains wars of the 1800s all rest partly on this exchange.
The great dying in the Americas:
**After 1492 the Indigenous population of the Americas collapsed, probably by around 90 per cent within roughly a century.** Historians agree it was among the largest population losses in human history. They disagree on how many people there were to begin with, and on how much of the loss was caused by disease, by violence and by the colonial system.

**How many?** No one counted the people of the Americas in 1492, so every estimate is a reconstruction from later tribute lists, missionary reports, and the carrying capacity of farmland:

| Estimate of the Americas' population in 1492 | By |
| --- | --- |
| about **8 million** | Alfred Kroeber, 1939 (now seen as far too low) |
| about **54 million** | William Denevan, 1976, revised 1992 |
| **90–112 million** | Henry Dobyns, 1966 (seen by many as too high) |
| about **60 million**, falling to about **6 million** by 1600 | Koch and colleagues, 2019, reviewing the regional studies |

Central Mexico alone has been put at anywhere from about 5 to 25 million in 1519; the high figure, from **Sherburne Cook and Woodrow Borah**, is now widely thought too large.

**What killed them?**

**Disease** is the core of every account. **Smallpox** reached Hispaniola by 1518 and Mexico in 1520; **measles**, **influenza**, typhus and others followed in waves. Populations with no prior exposure suffered very high death rates, and epidemics often hit before Europeans arrived in person. In Mexico two great epidemics called ***cocoliztli*** (in **1545** and **1576**) killed huge numbers. What caused them is debated; a 2018 study found DNA of a *Salmonella* bacterium (a form of enteric fever) in victims at one site.

**Conquest and the colonial system** made the epidemics deadlier. War, massacre, **enslavement**, forced labour in mines and fields, the seizure of food, and the breaking-up of families and farms left people hungry and unable to recover. On Hispaniola the Taíno were all but gone by the 1540s, from a mix of all of these.

**Contested: the balance of causes.** The **"virgin soil" reading**, associated with Alfred Crosby, stresses disease, which would have caused a disaster even if the newcomers had been gentle. The other reading, argued by historians such as **Andrés Reséndez** (*The Other Slavery*, 2016) and **Massimo Livi Bacci**, holds that disease alone does not explain such a deep and lasting fall, since Old World populations recovered from their own plagues within generations; enslavement, overwork and dislocation kept them from recovering. The evidence that weighs between them is regional: whether places with lighter colonial pressure lost less.

**Contested: was it genocide?** Some historians and Indigenous scholars apply the term, especially to particular campaigns and to the system as a whole. Others reserve it for intent to destroy a people, which they argue the documents show for some episodes and not for the epidemics, which no one at the time understood or could control. The facts of the deaths are not in dispute; the dispute is over intent and definition.

**A trace in the climate.** One suggestion (Lewis and Maslin, 2015; Koch, 2019) is that so much farmland went back to forest that it drew down carbon dioxide, which shows as a dip in Antarctic ice cores around **1610**, and helped cool the climate during the Little Ice Age. The dip is measured; how much it was caused by reforestation is debated.
Spain's American empire and Las Casas:
**By the 1550s Spain ruled the largest empire in the world, from California to Chile.** How to govern it, and whether its conquests were just, was argued inside Spain itself.

**The structure.** From 1524 the **Council of the Indies** in Spain made the laws. Two **viceroyalties** governed in the king's name: **New Spain** (from 1535, capital Mexico City) and **Peru** (from 1542, capital Lima). Royal courts called *audiencias* heard cases. **The Catholic Church**, given control of the mission by the pope, built churches, schools and, by **1551**, universities in Mexico City and Lima.

**The encomienda.** Conquerors were rewarded with *encomiendas*: grants of the labour and tribute of a group of Indigenous people, in return for "protecting" them and teaching them Christianity. In practice it was often forced labour close to slavery.

**The protest.** In **1511**, on Hispaniola, the Dominican friar **Antonio de Montesinos** preached to the settlers: by what right did they hold these people in such servitude? The crown answered with the **Laws of Burgos** (1512), which regulated the encomienda but did not end it.

**Bartolomé de las Casas** (1484–1566) had come to the Caribbean in 1502 and held an encomienda himself. In **1514** he gave it up and spent the next fifty years campaigning for Indigenous people's rights. He became a Dominican friar and a bishop, and wrote the **Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies** (written **1542**, printed 1552), a list of atrocities meant to shock the king.

**His campaign had effects:**

| Year | Event |
| --- | --- |
| 1537 | Pope Paul III's bull *Sublimis Deus* declares the peoples of the Americas rational and not to be enslaved |
| **1542** | the **New Laws** forbid enslaving Indigenous people and order encomiendas to end with their holders. Settlers in Peru rebelled, and the crown softened the laws |
| **1550–1551** | the **Valladolid debate**: Las Casas against **Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda**, who argued from Aristotle that some peoples were "natural slaves" and could rightly be conquered |

The debate had no formal winner, but it is one of the first great public arguments in Europe about the rights of conquered peoples.

**Las Casas and Africa.** Early on, Las Casas suggested that enslaved Africans be brought to spare the Indigenous people. He later wrote that he deeply regretted this, judging the enslavement of Africans just as unjust. The Atlantic slave trade had other, larger causes, but the episode shows how narrowly even reformers then drew the circle.

**A new society.** Spaniards, Indigenous people and Africans mixed, and colonial society ranked people by ancestry: **mestizos** (Spanish and Indigenous), **mulattos** (Spanish and African), and others. Indigenous communities kept their languages and many customs, and Nahuatl was written in the Latin alphabet in town records for centuries.

**Contested: the "Black Legend".** Spain's enemies, especially Protestant England and the Netherlands, reprinted Las Casas to paint Spain as uniquely cruel. The phrase ***leyenda negra*** was coined by the Spanish writer **Julián Juderías** in **1914** to describe that propaganda. One reading holds that Spain was no worse than other colonisers, and unusual in debating its own conduct at all. The other answers that the abuses Las Casas listed were real and documented, whatever use enemies made of them. The two claims can both be true, which is why the argument goes on.
The Ottoman Empire under Suleiman the Ma:
**Under Suleiman I, who ruled from 1520 to 1566, the Ottoman Empire was the most powerful state in Europe and the Middle East.** It stretched from Hungary to the Persian Gulf and from Algeria to the Caspian.

**The ground his father won.** Mehmed II had taken Constantinople in 1453 and made it the capital, **Istanbul**. **Selim I** (ruled 1512–1520) then doubled the empire: he beat the Safavids of Iran at **Chaldiran** in **1514**, where Ottoman cannon and muskets broke the Safavid cavalry, and conquered the **Mamluk** sultanate in **1516–1517**. That brought **Syria, Egypt** and the holy cities of **Mecca and Medina** under Ottoman rule, and gave the sultans the prestige of guardians of Sunni Islam.

**Suleiman's campaigns:**

| Year | Event |
| --- | --- |
| 1521 | takes **Belgrade** |
| 1522 | takes **Rhodes** from the Knights of St John |
| **1526** | **Battle of Mohács**: the Hungarian army is destroyed and King Louis II dies in the retreat |
| **1529** | **first siege of Vienna**, abandoned as winter came |
| 1534 | takes **Baghdad** from the Safavids |
| 1538 | the admiral **Hayreddin Barbarossa** wins at **Preveza**; Ottoman fleets dominate the eastern Mediterranean |
| 1541 | central Hungary annexed |
| **1566** | Suleiman dies in his tent during the siege of **Szigetvár** in Hungary |

**How the empire worked:**

- **The *devshirme*.** Christian boys from the Balkans were taken as a levy, converted to Islam, and trained for the sultan's service. The best became governors and grand viziers; others joined the **Janissaries**, a standing infantry corps armed with guns, one of the first of its kind in Europe.
- **The *timar*.** Cavalrymen were paid with the revenue of a piece of land, not with ownership of it.
- **Law.** The Turks call Suleiman ***Kanuni***, "the Lawgiver", for the *kanun* codes his officials issued alongside religious law (*sharia*).
- **Religious communities.** Christians and Jews paid a special tax and kept their own religious courts and leaders. Many Jews expelled from Spain in 1492 settled in Ottoman cities such as Salonica and Istanbul.

**The capital.** The architect **Mimar Sinan** (about 1490–1588) built hundreds of buildings, including the **Süleymaniye Mosque** (1550–1557). Suleiman married **Hürrem Sultan** (known in Europe as Roxelana), a former slave from what is now Ukraine, who became a major political figure in her own right.

**Rivals.** In Europe, Suleiman fought the Habsburg emperor **Charles V**, and he allied with Charles's other enemy, **Francis I of France**: a Muslim–Christian alliance that shocked Europe. To the east, the Safavids. On the seas, the Portuguese in the Indian Ocean, where Ottoman fleets fought them from the Red Sea and the Gulf.

**After Suleiman.** A Spanish, Venetian and papal fleet beat the Ottoman navy at **Lepanto** in **1571**, but the Ottomans rebuilt it within a year. A **second siege of Vienna failed in 1683**, and by the **Treaty of Karlowitz** (1699) the empire gave up most of Hungary.

**Contested: Ottoman "decline".** The older view, partly drawn from Ottoman writers themselves, held that the empire declined after Suleiman. Many historians now reject this: the empire lasted another 350 years, and its government adapted, with power shifting from the sultan to viziers, households and provincial elites (Baki Tezcan called this *The Second Ottoman Empire*, 2010). The other side points out that the empire did lose wars and territory to European powers from 1683 on. The question is what you measure: military position against Europe, or the state's ability to govern and survive.
Safavid Iran: Ismail and Shah Abbas:
**The Safavids ruled Iran from 1501 to 1722, and made it a Shi'a country**, which it remains today.

**Origins.** The Safavids began as a **Sufi order** based at Ardabil in north-west Iran. By the late 1400s its followers among the Turkmen tribes were fierce warriors, called ***Qizilbash***, "red heads", for their red caps. In **1501** the order's young leader **Ismail**, about fourteen years old, took **Tabriz** and was proclaimed **shah**. Within a decade he ruled most of Iran.

**A Shi'a state.** Ismail declared **Twelver Shi'ism** the official religion of a population that was then mostly Sunni. Shi'a scholars were brought from Lebanon and Iraq, and over the following two centuries most Iranians became Shi'a. This made the border with the Sunni Ottomans a religious frontier as well as a political one.

**War with the Ottomans.** At **Chaldiran** in **1514**, Ottoman guns beat Ismail's cavalry, and Tabriz was lost for a time. The two empires fought on and off for over a century over **Iraq**, **eastern Anatolia** and the **Caucasus**. The **Treaty of Zuhab** (**1639**) left Baghdad with the Ottomans and drew a border close to the modern line between Iran and Iraq.

**Shah Abbas I** (ruled **1588–1629**) was the dynasty's greatest ruler:

| Reform | What it did |
| --- | --- |
| **A slave army** | Georgian, Armenian and Circassian converts (*ghulams*) trained with guns, loyal to the shah rather than to the Qizilbash chiefs |
| **A new capital** | **Isfahan**, from **1598**, built around the vast **Naqsh-e Jahan square**, with its mosques and palace |
| **Trade** | Armenian silk merchants resettled at **New Julfa** outside Isfahan (1605) and given privileges; Iranian silk sold across Europe and Asia |
| **War** | regained land from the Ottomans and Uzbeks; took **Hormuz** from the Portuguese in **1622** with English East India Company ships |

Isfahan became one of the great cities of the world. European visitors such as Jean Chardin described a court of poets, painters, carpets and tiles.

**Shelter for a Mughal.** In the 1540s Shah Tahmasp (ruled 1524–1576) sheltered **Humayun**, the exiled Mughal emperor, and helped him regain India. Persian art and language shaped the Mughal court for two centuries.

**The fall.** By the early 1700s the dynasty was weak. In **1722** Afghan rebels under **Mahmud Hotaki** besieged and took **Isfahan**. A general, **Nadir**, drove the Afghans out and in **1736** made himself shah. In **1739** **Nadir Shah** invaded Mughal India, sacked **Delhi**, and carried home the **Peacock Throne**: a blow that the Mughals never recovered from.

**What lasted.** A Shi'a Iran with roughly its modern borders, Persian as the high language of courts from Istanbul to Delhi, and a Sunni–Shi'a political divide between Iran and its neighbours that runs through later Middle Eastern history.

**Contested: why Shi'ism?** One reading stresses religious conviction, rooted in the order's own beliefs. Another stresses statecraft: a distinct faith set Iran apart from the Ottomans and bound subjects to the dynasty. These are not exclusive, and the sources, chiefly the dynasty's own chronicles, do not let historians weigh the motives exactly.
The Mughals from Babur to Akbar:
**The Mughal Empire, founded in 1526, came to rule most of the Indian subcontinent.** At its height around 1700 it ruled perhaps 100 to 150 million people, one of the largest populations under one government anywhere.

**Babur** (1483–1530) was a prince from Central Asia descended from both **Timur** and **Chinggis Khan**. Driven from his home in the Fergana valley, he took **Kabul** in 1504, then turned to India. At the **First Battle of Panipat** (**1526**) his small army, using **field guns** and a line of carts, beat the much larger army of **Ibrahim Lodi**, sultan of Delhi. In **1527** at **Khanwa** he beat the Rajput confederacy under Rana Sanga. His memoir, the ***Baburnama***, written in Chaghatai Turkish, is one of the great autobiographies: frank about his battles, his drinking, his gardens, and his homesickness for melons.

**A false start.** His son **Humayun** lost India to the Afghan general **Sher Shah Suri** in **1540**. Sher Shah's short reign left lasting reforms: a silver coin called the **rupiya**, and roads including the Grand Trunk Road. Humayun came back with Persian help in **1555** and died a year later.

**Akbar** (ruled **1556–1605**) came to the throne at thirteen. His regent won the **Second Battle of Panipat** (**1556**), and Akbar went on to conquer Gujarat (1573), Bengal (1576), Kashmir and much more.

**How Akbar built a lasting state:**

| Policy | What it did |
| --- | --- |
