| **The *mansabdari* system** | every officer held a rank (*mansab*) fixing his pay and how many cavalry he kept; most were paid with the revenue of land (*jagir*), moved often so no one built a local base |
| **Revenue** | his minister **Todar Mal** surveyed the land and set taxes by average yields, paid in cash |
| **The Rajputs** | Hindu warrior kings were made partners: Akbar married Rajput princesses and gave Rajputs high rank |
| **Tolerance** | he abolished the pilgrim tax (1563) and the ***jizya***, the tax on non-Muslims (1564) |

**Ideas.** At his new city of **Fatehpur Sikri** (built from 1571), Akbar held debates in a "house of worship" (from **1575**) among Sunni and Shi'a scholars, Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians and Jesuit priests from Goa. His policy was ***sulh-i kul***, "peace with all". He also gathered close followers into a discipleship called the ***Din-i Ilahi***. Whether that was meant as a new religion or a personal order of loyalty to the emperor is debated; it had few members and died with him. His friend **Abu'l Fazl** wrote the official history, the ***Akbarnama***.

**Akbar's India** was also the India of **Guru Nanak** (1469–1539), founder of the **Sikh** tradition in the Punjab, and of devotional poets such as **Kabir** and **Mirabai**, who sang across Hindu and Muslim lines.

**Why it mattered.** Akbar's settlement, with its alliance with Hindu elites, a common court culture in Persian, and a cash revenue system, made the empire both strong and Indian rather than a foreign occupation. Its loosening under his great-grandson is a later lesson.

**Contested: how tolerant was Akbar?** One reading sees a genuine pluralist, ahead of his age. Another sees a ruler doing what any ruler of a Hindu-majority land had to do to rule it, while still fighting brutal wars (he massacred the defenders of **Chittor** in 1568). Abu'l Fazl's flattering history is the main source, and the critical Muslim historian **Badauni**'s private chronicle offers the counterweight.
Luther and the Protestant Reformation:
**In 1517 a German monk, Martin Luther, challenged the sale of indulgences, and within a generation the Western Church had split for good.** This lesson treats the Reformation as history: what happened, why it spread, and what it did. Its theology belongs to the Theology curriculum.

**The background.** The Western (Latin) Church was the one church of western and central Europe. Many complained of its wealth, of clergy who were absent or ignorant, and of the papacy's politics. Earlier reformers, **John Wyclif** in England (died 1384) and **Jan Hus** in Bohemia (burned **1415**), had been condemned.

**The spark.** An **indulgence** was a grant by the Church reducing the punishment owed for sins, which could be obtained, among other ways, by a donation. In 1517 the friar **Johann Tetzel** was preaching one near Wittenberg in Saxony to raise money, partly for rebuilding **St Peter's in Rome**. Luther, a professor of theology at the university of **Wittenberg**, wrote **Ninety-five Theses** against the abuse, dated **31 October 1517**.

**The break:**

| Year | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **1517** | the *Ninety-five Theses*; printed copies spread across Germany in weeks |
| 1519 | debate at Leipzig: Luther denies that popes and councils cannot err |
| **1520** | three pamphlets set out his programme; he burns the papal bull threatening him |
| **1521** | excommunicated in January; at the **Diet of Worms** in April he refuses to recant before the emperor **Charles V**, and is outlawed |
| 1521–1522 | hidden in the **Wartburg** castle by his prince, **Frederick the Wise**, he translates the New Testament into German |
| **1524–1525** | the **Peasants' War**: tens of thousands of peasants rise, partly inspired by his ideas. Luther condemns them, and princes crush the revolt, with perhaps 70,000 to 100,000 dead |
| **1530** | the **Augsburg Confession** sets out the Lutheran position |
| **1555** | the **Peace of Augsburg**: each prince chooses Lutheran or Catholic for his lands (later summed up as *cuius regio, eius religio*, "whose realm, his religion") |

**Luther's core claims**, as historical facts about what he taught: that people are saved by **faith** through God's grace, not by works or purchases; that **scripture** is the final authority, above popes and councils; and that **all believers** share in the priesthood. He also allowed clergy to marry, and married the former nun **Katharina von Bora** in 1525.

**Why it spread, when Hus's movement had been contained:**

1. **Print.** Luther was the best-selling author in Europe. His pamphlets, with woodcuts by Lucas Cranach, reached a mass audience.
2. **Princes.** German princes and city councils could take church lands and control their own churches. Frederick protected Luther.
3. **The emperor was busy.** Charles V was fighting France and the Ottomans (who were at Vienna in 1529), and could not crush the Lutherans for decades.
4. **Long-held grievances** against Rome's taxes and clergy.

**Contested: religion or interest?** One reading holds that the Reformation was, at heart, a religious movement driven by real spiritual hunger. Another stresses the politics: princes and towns adopted it when it served them. A third question is whether the late-medieval Church was in decline at all. **Eamon Duffy** (*The Stripping of the Altars*, 1992) showed lively, popular Catholic devotion in England right up to the break. The evidence lies in local records, such as wills, parish accounts and town council decisions, which show who changed and when.

**Did he nail the theses to the door?** The story comes from Luther's colleague Melanchthon, writing after Luther's death. In **1961** the Catholic historian **Erwin Iserloh** questioned it; others defend it. What is certain is that Luther sent the theses to the Archbishop of Mainz on 31 October 1517.
Calvin, Henry VIII and the spread of Pro:
**Within forty years of 1517, Protestant churches of several kinds ruled much of northern Europe.** They disagreed with Rome, and also with each other.

**Zurich.** In Switzerland, **Huldrych Zwingli** began a reform in Zurich from **1519**, stricter than Luther's: images removed from churches, the Mass abolished. He and Luther met at **Marburg** in 1529 and failed to agree about communion. Zwingli was killed in battle against Catholic cantons at **Kappel** in **1531**.

**The radicals.** The **Anabaptists** (from 1525, in Zurich) baptised only adult believers and wanted a church separate from the state. Catholics and Protestants alike persecuted them. In **1534–1535** radicals seized the city of **Münster** and were crushed. The peaceful Anabaptist tradition survives in the **Mennonites** and **Amish**.

**Geneva.** **John Calvin** (1509–1564), a French lawyer turned theologian, published his ***Institutes of the Christian Religion*** in **1536** and from **1541** led the church in **Geneva**. Calvin's churches were run by elected elders and ministers, and Geneva trained preachers for all of Europe. His form of Protestantism became the most international:

| Where | Name |
| --- | --- |
| France | **Huguenots** |
| the Netherlands | the **Dutch Reformed** Church |
| Scotland | **Presbyterians**, led by **John Knox** from 1560 |
| England | the **Puritans**, within and against the Church of England |
| Hungary, parts of Germany, Poland | Reformed churches |

**England.** Here the break came from the top. **Henry VIII** (ruled 1509–1547) wanted his marriage to Catherine of Aragon annulled so he could marry Anne Boleyn and have a male heir. When the pope refused, Parliament's **Act of Supremacy** (**1534**) made the king head of the Church in England. Between **1536 and 1541** the monasteries were dissolved and their lands sold. Henry kept much traditional doctrine; England's religion then swung with each ruler:

- **Edward VI** (1547–1553): firmly Protestant; the *Book of Common Prayer*, 1549.
- **Mary I** (1553–1558): restored Catholicism and burned about 280 Protestants.
- **Elizabeth I** (1558–1603): a Protestant settlement (**1559**) with a church that kept bishops and some old forms.

**Scandinavia.** The kings of **Sweden** (from 1527) and **Denmark–Norway** (from 1536) made their churches Lutheran, taking church lands at the same time.

**Poland–Lithuania.** By the **Warsaw Confederation** of **1573**, its nobles agreed to keep peace among the religions, an unusual guarantee for the age.

**The map by about 1600.** Lutheran: much of Germany and all of Scandinavia. Reformed: Scotland, the northern Netherlands, Swiss cities, parts of Germany and Hungary. Anglican: England. Catholic: Italy, Spain, Portugal, most of France, Poland, Austria, Bavaria and Ireland, where the population stayed Catholic under Protestant English rule.

**Contested: did Protestantism make capitalism?** The sociologist **Max Weber** (*The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism*, 1905) argued that Calvinist ideas of work and calling helped create modern capitalism. Critics point to rich Catholic Italy and Flanders, and say that Protestant regions' later wealth came from other causes. One economic study (Becker and Woessmann, 2009) argues that the difference in Prussia came mostly from Protestants learning to read the Bible, not from a work ethic. The evidence is the comparison of similar Catholic and Protestant regions over time.
The Catholic Reformation: Trent and the:
**The Catholic Church answered the Protestant challenge with its own reform**, which also had roots older than Luther. Historians call it the **Counter-Reformation**, the **Catholic Reformation**, or simply **early modern Catholicism**, and the choice of name is itself an argument.

**The Council of Trent** met in the north Italian city of Trent in three sessions between **1545 and 1563**. It did two things:

1. **Defined doctrine against the Protestants**: it held that scripture and the Church's tradition together carry authority, kept the seven sacraments, and affirmed the Mass and the Latin Vulgate Bible.
2. **Reformed discipline**: bishops had to live in their dioceses, **seminaries** were founded to train priests, and the sale of offices and abuses of indulgences were curbed.

Its decisions shaped Catholic life until the Second Vatican Council of the 1960s.

**The Jesuits.** **Ignatius of Loyola** (1491–1556), a Basque soldier wounded in 1521, turned to religion and wrote the *Spiritual Exercises*. With a few companions he founded the **Society of Jesus**, approved by the pope in **1540**. The Jesuits became the Church's teachers and missionaries:

| Field | What they did |
| --- | --- |
| **Schools** | hundreds of colleges across Europe, free to pupils; Descartes was taught by them |
| **Asia** | **Francis Xavier** to Goa (1542) and Japan (1549); **Matteo Ricci** to Beijing (1601) |
| **The Americas** | missions in Brazil, Mexico, New France, and the **reductions** of Paraguay, settlements of Guaraní people |
| **Politics** | confessors to kings; leaders of the Catholic recovery in Poland, Austria and Bavaria |

**Other new orders and figures.** The **Capuchins**, a reformed branch of the Franciscans (1520s). **Teresa of Ávila** (1515–1582) reformed the Carmelite nuns and wrote on prayer. **Charles Borromeo**, archbishop of Milan, became the model of a reforming bishop.

**Control and enforcement.** The **Roman Inquisition** was reorganised in **1542** to pursue heresy in Italy. The first papal **Index of Forbidden Books** appeared in **1559**. (The separate **Spanish Inquisition**, founded in **1478**, was a royal court whose first targets were converted Jews.) Their records show many thousands tried; most were not executed, and the number put to death is far lower than legend claims, though it was real.

**Art.** The Church backed an art meant to move the faithful: the **Baroque**, with the sculpture of **Gian Lorenzo Bernini** and the paintings of **Caravaggio** in Rome.

**The calendar.** Pope **Gregory XIII** reformed the calendar in **1582**, dropping ten days. Catholic countries took it at once; Protestant Britain only in 1752 and Orthodox Russia in 1918. (That calendar is the one counted in Stage 1.)

**The results.** By 1600, Catholicism had won back Poland, much of Austria, Bavaria and parts of Hungary. And through Spanish, Portuguese and French missions it became a world religion, with more Catholics outside Europe in time than in it.

**Contested: what to call it.** "**Counter-Reformation**" stresses reaction to Protestants. "**Catholic Reformation**" stresses reform that began earlier, as with Spain's Cardinal Cisneros in the 1490s. The historian **John O'Malley** (*Trent and All That*, 2000) proposed "**early modern Catholicism**" to cover both, along with the missions. Each name fits part of the evidence.
Muscovy and Ivan the Terrible:
**Between 1462 and 1613, the principality of Moscow grew into a great power, through a terrible reign and a near-collapse.**

**Ivan III, "the Great"** (ruled **1462–1505**), gathered the Russian lands around Moscow. He annexed the merchant republic of **Novgorod** in **1478**. In **1480** he faced down a Tatar army on the **Ugra River**; neither side attacked, and the two-century overlordship of the Golden Horde's successors was over. He married **Sophia Palaiologina**, niece of the last Byzantine emperor, in 1472, and used the double-headed eagle. Around the 1510s–1520s a monk wrote that Moscow was the **"Third Rome"**: Rome and Constantinople had fallen, and Moscow was the last true Christian empire.

**Ivan IV** (born 1530, ruled **1533–1584**) came to the throne at three. In **1547** he was crowned **tsar** (from *Caesar*), the first Muscovite ruler to take the title formally. His reign split into two halves.

**The good years:**

- **1552**: he took **Kazan**, the Tatar khanate on the middle Volga. **St Basil's Cathedral** in Red Square commemorates it.
- **1556**: he took **Astrakhan**, opening the whole Volga to the Caspian.
- A new law code (1550), and an assembly of the land (*zemsky sobor*).

**The terrible years.** From **1558** he fought the long **Livonian War** for the Baltic coast, and lost it (1583). After his wife Anastasia died in 1560 he grew suspicious and violent. In **1565** he created the ***oprichnina***: a private state inside the state, policed by black-clad horsemen, the *oprichniki*, who killed and robbed nobles and peasants. In **1570** they massacred thousands in **Novgorod**. In **1581**, in a rage, he struck and killed his own son and heir, Ivan.

**His Russian nickname, *Grozny***, means "formidable" or "awe-inspiring" as much as "terrible".

**Siberia.** Around **1582**, the Cossack **Yermak**, paid by the Stroganov merchant family, crossed the Urals and defeated the khanate of Sibir. Russians then pushed east through the forests for furs, reaching the **Pacific** at Okhotsk by **1639**. In **1689** the **Treaty of Nerchinsk** with Qing China fixed the border on the Amur, China's first treaty with a European state.

**The Time of Troubles** (**1598–1613**). Ivan's line died out with his son Fyodor in 1598. Famine (1601–1603), pretenders claiming to be a dead son of Ivan, and civil war followed. **Polish troops held Moscow** from 1610 to 1612, until a militia led by the merchant **Kuzma Minin** and Prince **Dmitry Pozharsky** drove them out. In **1613** an assembly elected **Michael Romanov** tsar. His family ruled until 1917.

**The Romanov century.** In **1649** a new law code bound the peasants fully to the land: **serfdom** became law, just as it was fading in western Europe. In **1654** Cossacks of Ukraine, who had risen against Poland under **Bohdan Khmelnytsky** in **1648**, accepted the tsar's protection, which led to Russian rule of eastern Ukraine. Church reforms by Patriarch **Nikon** in the 1650s split off the **Old Believers**, who still exist.

**Contested: how mad was Ivan?** One reading sees a ruler deranged by illness and grief (mercury has been found in his remains, but so it was in many people who took it as medicine). Another sees a calculated campaign of terror to break the old nobility and make the tsar absolute. The oprichnina's records are fragmentary, and much of what is told comes from hostile foreign writers and the exiled Prince Kurbsky's letters, so motive is hard to prove.
Songhai and the Moroccan invasion of 159:
**Songhai was the largest of the great West African empires, and it fell in a single battle in 1591**, to a Moroccan army that had crossed the Sahara with guns.

**The rise.** Songhai's heartland was around **Gao** on the middle Niger. As Mali weakened, **Sunni Ali** (ruled **1464–1492**) built an empire by constant war, with a river fleet on the Niger. He took **Timbuktu** in **1468** and **Djenné** a few years later. Timbuktu's Muslim scholars remembered him as a harsh ruler and a doubtful Muslim, which colours the sources.

**Askia Muhammad** (ruled **1493–1528**), one of Sunni Ali's generals, seized power in 1493. He made Islam the basis of the state:

- He made the **hajj** to Mecca in **1496–1497**, and was named the caliph's deputy for West Africa.
- He organised provinces under governors, a standing army, and a fleet.
- He backed the scholars of **Timbuktu**, whose libraries and teaching made the city a famous centre of Islamic learning. Many of its manuscripts survive today.

The traveller known in Europe as **Leo Africanus** visited Timbuktu around **1510** and described its rich court, its many judges and scholars, and the high price of books.

**The wealth.** Songhai controlled the Niger trade and the southern end of the routes across the Sahara: **gold** from the forest regions to the south, **salt** from mines in the desert at **Taghaza**, slaves, cloth and books. Under **Askia Dawud** (ruled 1549–1582) the empire was at its peak.

**The invasion.** **Ahmad al-Mansur**, sultan of **Morocco** (ruled **1578–1603**), was flush with ransom money after crushing a Portuguese invasion at the **Battle of the Three Kings** in 1578. He wanted the Saharan salt mines and, above all, Songhai's **gold**. He sent about **4,000 men**, many of them Spanish-born converts and renegades, under the eunuch commander **Judar Pasha**, with **muskets** and some cannon. They crossed the Sahara, a march of months in which many died.

**Tondibi.** In **March 1591**, near Gao, the Moroccans met the army of **Askia Ishaq II**, which was far larger but fought mainly with spears, bows and cavalry. The guns broke it. The Moroccans took **Gao and Timbuktu**.

**After the battle:**

1. **No Moroccan empire.** The occupiers, called the ***Arma***, held the river towns but never controlled the countryside. Within decades they were a local ruling caste only loosely tied to Morocco.
2. **Scholars exiled.** In **1593–1594** leading Timbuktu scholars, including the jurist **Ahmad Baba**, were arrested and taken to Marrakesh.
3. **Fragmentation.** Songhai survived as a smaller state to the south, in **Dendi**, and the Niger region broke into smaller powers, such as the **Bambara** kingdoms of **Ségou** in the 1700s.

**The sources.** Two chronicles written in Arabic in Timbuktu in the 1600s, the ***Tarikh al-Sudan*** of **al-Sa'di** and the ***Tarikh al-Fattash***, are the main histories. They are written by and for the scholarly elite.

**Contested: did 1591 end West Africa's golden age?** One reading holds that the invasion broke the last great Sahelian empire and its security, and the trade and scholarship that depended on it. The other holds that the decline was already under way: since the late 1400s the Portuguese had been buying gold on the **Atlantic coast**, pulling trade south to the forest kingdoms and away from the Sahara. The evidence is in trade volumes along the desert routes and on the coast before and after 1591, which are hard to measure.
Potosí and the silver that circled the w:
**Between the 1540s and 1800, the mines of Spanish America produced most of the world's silver, and much of it ended up in China.** That flow tied every inhabited continent into one economy for the first time.

**The mountain.** In **1545** silver was found at **Potosí**, a peak called the **Cerro Rico** ("rich hill"), at over 4,000 metres in what is now Bolivia. Within a few decades Potosí was one of the largest cities in the Americas, with perhaps **100,000 to 160,000** people by about 1600; the figures are contemporary estimates. Mexico's **Zacatecas** mines were found in **1546**.

**How it was mined:**

- **Mercury amalgamation.** Crushed ore was mixed with **mercury**, which binds silver. The method, worked out in Mexico in the **1550s** (the "patio process"), reached Potosí in the **1570s**. The mercury came from **Huancavelica** in Peru, and from Almadén in Spain. Both were poisonous to work.
- **The *mita*.** In the 1570s Viceroy Toledo turned the Inca labour tax into a draft: Andean villages sent a share of their men, thousands a year, to work in Potosí for months. Many never came back. African slaves also worked in the mints and processing.

**Across the Pacific.** Spain reached the Pacific through **Ferdinand Magellan**'s voyage (**1519–1522**). Magellan was killed on **Mactan** in the Philippines in **1521**; **Juan Sebastián Elcano** brought one ship and 18 men home, the first voyage around the world. In **1565** the friar-navigator **Andrés de Urdaneta** found the eastward return route across the North Pacific. In **1571** the Spaniards founded **Manila**.

**The Manila galleons** then sailed once or twice a year between **Acapulco** in Mexico and Manila, from **1565 until 1815**:

| Going west | Coming east |
| --- | --- |
| **American silver** | Chinese **silk** and **porcelain** |
| | Asian spices, cotton cloth, lacquer, ivory |

At Manila, Chinese merchants from Fujian bought the silver. Manila's Chinese quarter, the Parián, grew to tens of thousands of people.

**Why China?** After the **Single Whip reform**, Ming taxes were paid in silver, and China valued silver much more highly against gold than Europe did, so silver bought more there. Silver flowed east by every route: across the Pacific, and across the Atlantic to Seville and then out through Europe, the Ottoman lands and India. Japan, then the world's other great producer, also shipped silver to China. Estimates of how much of the world's silver ended up in China range from about a third to a half.

**The Spanish dollar**, the *peso de ocho* ("piece of eight"), became the first world currency, used from China to North America.

**What it did:**

1. **Spain's power.** Silver paid for Philip II's armies, yet the crown still went bankrupt repeatedly, first in **1557**.
2. **The price revolution.** Prices in Europe rose roughly fourfold over the 1500s.
3. **Asia.** Silver fed Ming commerce, and its supply troubles in the 1630s–1640s may have hurt the Ming in their last years.

**Contested: what caused Europe's price revolution?** **Earl Hamilton** (1934) blamed American silver: more money, higher prices. Others point out that prices began rising before much silver arrived, and blame Europe's population recovering after the Black Death. Most now combine both. And the historians **Dennis Flynn and Arturo Giráldez** (1995) argued that **world trade was "born" in 1571**, with Manila, because only then were all the populated continents linked by direct, lasting trade. Critics answer that older networks were already global in effect. The test is whether prices on different continents start to move together after 1571.
The Wars of Religion in France and the N:
**From the 1560s to 1598, France tore itself apart in civil wars between Catholics and Protestants, and the Netherlands rose against Spain.** Religion and politics were tangled together in both.

**France.** By 1560 perhaps a tenth of the French were **Huguenots** (Calvinists), including great noble families such as the Bourbons. The crown was weak: Henry II died in 1559 after a jousting accident, leaving young sons and their mother **Catherine de' Medici** as regent.

| Year | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **1562** | the Duke of Guise's men kill Huguenots at worship at **Wassy**; war begins |
| **1572** | the **St Bartholomew's Day massacre**, from **24 August**: after an attempt on the Huguenot leader Coligny, he and other leaders are killed in Paris, and mobs kill Protestants across France. Some thousands died in Paris and more in the provinces; estimates for the whole country run from about 5,000 to over 10,000 |
| 1576 | the Catholic League forms |
| **1589** | Henry III is assassinated; the heir is the Protestant **Henry of Navarre** |
| **1593** | Henry converts to Catholicism to win Paris. "Paris is well worth a Mass" is attributed to him but is probably a later invention |
| **1598** | the **Edict of Nantes** gives Huguenots freedom of worship in many places and fortified towns |

**Henry IV** was assassinated in **1610** by a Catholic fanatic. His grandson Louis XIV revoked the Edict in **1685**, and some 200,000 Huguenots fled abroad, some of them to the Cape (pointing across to the South African Politics curriculum).

**The Dutch Revolt.** The seventeen provinces of the Netherlands belonged to **Philip II** of Spain, the most powerful Catholic king in Europe. Their towns were rich, and Calvinism had spread. In **1566** crowds smashed images in churches (the "iconoclastic fury"). Philip sent the **Duke of Alba** with an army in 1567; his "Council of Troubles" executed over a thousand people.

- **1568**: revolt under **William of Orange**, the start of what the Dutch call the **Eighty Years' War**.
- **1579**: the northern provinces join in the **Union of Utrecht**; the southern ones (roughly modern Belgium) return to Spain.
- **1581**: the north formally renounces Philip.
- **1584**: William is assassinated.
- **1648**: Spain recognises the **Dutch Republic** at the Peace of Westphalia.

The new republic, Protestant but unusually tolerant, became the richest trading nation of the 1600s.

**England and the Armada.** Elizabeth I helped the Dutch rebels, and Philip resolved to invade England. In **1588** the **Spanish Armada**, about 130 ships, was beaten off by English fireships at Calais and wrecked by storms off Scotland and Ireland.

**Contested: were these really religious wars?** One reading holds that religion was the driving force: the historian **Natalie Zemon Davis** ("The Rites of Violence", 1973) showed that crowds in France killed in ritual ways, purging what they saw as pollution. Another holds that nobles, kings and towns used religion to pursue power, and that "religious violence" is a modern category projected backwards (argued by **William Cavanaugh**, 2009). Both readings fit some episodes. The evidence is in who fought on which side and whether they switched when interests changed.
Tokugawa Japan:
**After more than a century of civil war, Japan was united around 1600 and ruled by the Tokugawa shoguns for over 250 years of peace.**

**The warring states.** The **Ōnin War** (**1467–1477**) wrecked the Ashikaga shogunate, and Japan broke into the domains of warlords (*daimyō*), the **Sengoku** ("warring states") period. In **1543** Portuguese traders landed on **Tanegashima** island with **arquebuses**; Japanese smiths copied them within a few years. In **1549** the Jesuit **Francis Xavier** arrived, and over the next decades perhaps **300,000** Japanese became Christians, especially in Kyushu.

**The three unifiers:**

| Who | Dates | What he did |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Oda Nobunaga** | 1534–1582 | took Kyoto in 1568; at **Nagashino** in **1575** his massed musketeers beat a cavalry army. Betrayed by a general and killed at **Honnō-ji** temple in **1582** |
| **Toyotomi Hideyoshi** | 1537–1598 | a man of low birth who finished unifying Japan by 1590; the **"sword hunt"** of **1588** disarmed peasants; he fixed the line between samurai and farmers; **invaded Korea in 1592 and 1597** |
| **Tokugawa Ieyasu** | 1543–1616 | won the **Battle of Sekigahara** in **1600**, named **shogun** in **1603**, ruled from **Edo** (Tokyo); destroyed Hideyoshi's heirs at **Osaka** in **1615** |

**How the Tokugawa kept peace:**

- **Daimyō were controlled.** Under *sankin-kōtai*, formalised in **1635**, each lord spent alternate years in Edo and left his family there when he went home. The cost and the hostages kept them loyal.
- **Fixed status.** Society was ordered as samurai, farmers, artisans and merchants, with the emperor in Kyoto as a revered figure without power. Samurai became salaried administrators.
- **Neo-Confucian** ideas of loyalty and order were the official philosophy.

**Christianity banned.** Hideyoshi first ordered missionaries out in 1587. The Tokugawa **banned Christianity** in **1614**. After the **Shimabara Rebellion** (**1637–1638**), a rising of mostly Christian peasants in Kyushu, crushed with tens of thousands killed, the Portuguese were expelled (**1639**). Christians were made to tread on holy images to prove they had given up the faith; some kept it secretly for centuries.

**The "closed country".** From **1641** the only Europeans allowed were the **Dutch**, confined to the small artificial island of **Dejima** in Nagasaki harbour. Japanese were forbidden to go abroad on pain of death.

**Contested: how closed was Japan?** The word ***sakoku***, "closed country", was coined only in **1801**, by a translator. The historian **Ronald Toby** (1984) argued that Japan was not isolated but managed foreign relations through **four gates**: the Dutch and Chinese at **Nagasaki**, **Korea** through the island of **Tsushima**, the **Ryukyu** kingdom (Okinawa) through Satsuma, and the **Ainu** of the north through Matsumae. Trade with China and Korea went on. The other view stresses how much was shut: no Christianity, no travel, and European contact through one tiny island. Both are true; the question is which you emphasise.

**Edo culture.** The peace brought growth. **Edo** may have had about **a million** people by the 1700s, one of the largest cities in the world. Merchants grew rich, and towns enjoyed **kabuki** theatre, the puppet plays of **Chikamatsu**, the haiku of **Matsuo Bashō** (1644–1694), and woodblock prints of the "floating world" (*ukiyo-e*). Scholars of **"Dutch learning"** (*rangaku*) studied European medicine and science from books brought to Dejima.
The Thirty Years' War and the Peace of W:
**From 1618 to 1648 a war that began as a Bohemian revolt drew in most of Europe and devastated Germany.** It was the last great war in which religion was a central cause, and the first in which France openly fought beside Protestants against Catholics.

**The setting.** The Holy Roman Empire was a patchwork of hundreds of states, Catholic, Lutheran and Calvinist, under an elected emperor, by now always a Habsburg. The **Peace of Augsburg** (1555) had not recognised Calvinists, and both sides accused the other of breaking it.

**The phases:**

| Phase | Years | What happened |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Bohemian** | 1618–1620 | on **23 May 1618** Protestant nobles throw two imperial officials out of a window of Prague castle (the **Defenestration of Prague**); they survive. Bohemia elects a Calvinist king, Frederick of the Palatinate. The Catholic armies crush the revolt at the **White Mountain** (**1620**) |
| **Danish** | 1625–1629 | Christian IV of Denmark intervenes for the Protestants and is beaten by the imperial general **Albrecht von Wallenstein**. In **1629** the **Edict of Restitution** orders church lands taken since 1552 returned |
| **Swedish** | 1630–1635 | **Gustavus Adolphus** of Sweden lands in Germany. **Magdeburg** is stormed by imperial troops in **1631**, and some 20,000 of its people die. Gustavus wins at **Breitenfeld** (1631) and is killed winning at **Lützen** (**1632**). Wallenstein, suspected of treason, is murdered on the emperor's orders in 1634 |
| **French** | 1635–1648 | Catholic **France**, led by **Cardinal Richelieu**, declares war on Spain and fights the Habsburgs alongside Protestant Sweden. The war becomes a contest of great powers |

**The cost.** Armies lived off the land: they took food, burned villages, and spread typhus and plague. **Germany may have lost about a fifth to a third of its population**, with some regions losing far more and others little. Older estimates of over half are now thought too high. It was the worst European catastrophe between the Black Death and the twentieth century.

**The Peace of Westphalia** (**1648**), negotiated at **Münster** and **Osnabrück**:

- **Calvinism** recognised alongside Lutheranism and Catholicism; the religious map fixed as of 1624.
- **The Dutch Republic** and the **Swiss Confederation** recognised as independent.
- **France** and **Sweden** gained territory; the German princes gained power against the emperor.

**The same crisis elsewhere.** In **Britain**, the **civil wars** (1642–1651) between Charles I and Parliament ended with the king's execution in **1649** and a republic under **Oliver Cromwell**, until the monarchy returned in 1660. Spain faced revolts in Catalonia and Portugal (1640); France the **Fronde** (1648–1653); and in China the Ming fell (1644).

**Contested: a "general crisis"?** In **1954** the historian **Eric Hobsbawm** argued that the 1600s saw a general crisis across Europe. **Geoffrey Parker** (*Global Crisis*, 2013) extended it to the world and pointed to the **Little Ice Age**: cold, failed harvests and famine from China to Ireland, which made wars and revolts more likely. Critics answer that each revolt had its own local causes and that a common climate cannot explain particular events. The evidence is in harvest records, tree rings and ice cores, set against the timing of each revolt.

**Contested: the "Westphalian system".** Westphalia is often said to have founded the modern system of sovereign states that do not interfere in each other's affairs. Historians such as **Andreas Osiander** (2001) answer that the treaties said nothing of the kind: they kept the Empire, and gave outside powers a guarantee to intervene in it. The idea of a "Westphalian order" is a later reading back. The test is to read the treaty texts, which are short on sovereignty and long on the Empire's constitution.
The fall of the Ming and the Qing conque:
**In 1644 the Ming dynasty fell to rebels, and the Manchus from the north-east took Beijing and founded the Qing, China's last dynasty.** The Qing went on to rule the largest Chinese state in history.

**The Ming's last decades.** The 1620s–1640s brought cold, drought, locusts and famine, part of the Little Ice Age. The treasury was empty after wars in Korea and the north. Unpaid soldiers deserted, and peasant rebel armies grew in the north-west. The greatest rebel, **Li Zicheng**, took **Beijing in April 1644**. The last Ming emperor, **Chongzhen**, hanged himself on a hill behind the palace.

**The Manchus.** North of the Great Wall, the **Jurchen** chief **Nurhaci** (1559–1626) had united the Jurchen tribes and organised them into the **Eight Banners**: military and social units that also took in Mongols and Chinese. In 1616 he declared a new state. His son **Hong Taiji** renamed his people **Manchus** and the dynasty **Qing** ("pure") in **1636**.

**1644.** The Ming general **Wu Sangui**, holding the **Shanhai Pass** where the Great Wall meets the sea, chose to let the Manchus in to fight Li Zicheng. Together they routed the rebels, and in **June 1644** the Qing entered Beijing and declared their child emperor ruler of China.

**The conquest of the south** took nearly forty years:

| Year | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **1645** | all Chinese men ordered to shave the front of the head and wear the Manchu **queue** (braid) on pain of death; resistance is crushed, as at **Yangzhou**, where a massacre lasted days |
| 1644–1662 | Ming princes hold out in the south |
| **1662** | **Zheng Chenggong** (Koxinga), a Ming loyalist commander, drives the **Dutch** from **Taiwan** |
| **1673–1681** | **Revolt of the Three Feudatories**: Wu Sangui and two other generals rebel and are defeated |
| **1683** | Taiwan taken by the Qing |

**The great emperors:**

- **Kangxi** (ruled **1661–1722**), the longest-reigning Chinese emperor: crushed the revolts, signed the **Treaty of Nerchinsk** with Russia (1689), fought the Zunghar Mongols, and patronised Jesuit astronomers.
- **Yongzheng** (1722–1735): reformed finances.
- **Qianlong** (1735–1796): conquered **Xinjiang** after destroying the Zunghars in the 1750s, and ruled Tibet and Mongolia as well.

**How the Qing ruled.** A few hundred thousand Manchus ruled well over 100 million Chinese. They kept the Ming system of examinations and officials and adopted Confucian kingship, but kept the Banners as a separate garrison caste, kept Manchu as a language of state, and ruled Mongols, Tibetans and Muslims of the west through different institutions, as khan and patron of Tibetan Buddhism as well as emperor.

**Peace and growth.** With peace and the new American crops, China's population grew to roughly **300 million by 1800**. Trade with Europeans was confined to Canton (Guangzhou) from **1757**, a matter for the next stage.

**Contested: did the Manchus become Chinese?** The older view, put by **Ho Ping-ti** (1967), held that the Qing succeeded because they **sinicised**: they adopted Chinese ways. Historians of the **"New Qing History"**, such as **Evelyn Rawski** (1996), using Manchu-language archives, argued that the Qing kept a distinct Manchu identity and ran a multi-ethnic Inner Asian empire of which China was the largest part. The evidence is in the Manchu documents, which earlier historians did not read, and how the Qing presented themselves to different subjects.
The Atlantic slave trade: scale and the:
**Between about 1500 and 1866, some 12.5 million Africans were forced onto ships bound for the Americas, and about 10.7 million survived the crossing.** It was the largest forced migration in history before the twentieth century. This lesson gives the facts plainly.

**The numbers.** They come chiefly from the **Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database** (SlaveVoyages), built by historians from the records of some 36,000 voyages. Its estimates, with an uncertainty historians accept as modest for the totals:

| Destination | Enslaved people landed (rough) |
| --- | --- |
| **Brazil** | about 4.8 million, the largest single destination |
| British Caribbean (Jamaica, Barbados…) | about 2.3 million |
| Spanish Americas | about 1.3 million |
| French Caribbean (Saint-Domingue…) | about 1.1 million |
| Dutch, Danish Caribbean and the Guianas | about 0.5 million |
| **Mainland North America** (the future USA) | about 0.4 million |

The largest carriers were **Portuguese and Brazilian** ships (nearly half of all), then **British**, then **French**. **Most of the trade happened after 1700**; its peak came in the late 1700s and early 1800s.

**Why it grew.** The Americas had land and a collapsing Indigenous population. **Sugar**, then tobacco, rice, cotton and coffee, needed gangs of labourers. European indentured servants came in smaller numbers and could not be held for life. Africans were bought, and their children were born enslaved. **Slavery in the Americas became hereditary and tied to race**, unlike most older forms of slavery.

**How people were taken.** Most were captured in **wars**, **raids** and **kidnappings**, or enslaved as **punishment** or for **debt**, by African states and traders who sold them at the coast. Many died on the march to the coast or in forts and pens waiting for ships; how many is not known.

**The Middle Passage** was the voyage across the Atlantic, the middle leg of the route Europe–Africa–Americas–Europe:

- The crossing took from about **one to three months**, depending on the route.
- People were chained below decks in spaces often too low to sit upright, in heat, filth and darkness.
- **Death rates** at sea averaged roughly **12 to 15 per cent**, higher in the early centuries and on long voyages, from dysentery ("the flux"), smallpox, and despair. Crews also died at high rates.
- There were **revolts** on perhaps one voyage in ten, almost all crushed; some captives jumped overboard rather than live enslaved.
- About two in three of the enslaved were men and boys, because planters bought them for field labour; the share of children rose over time.

**The routes were not one triangle.** Many ships sailed straight between **Brazil and Angola**, trading Brazilian tobacco and rum for captives. "Triangular trade" describes the British and French pattern best.

**Who profited.** Ship-owners and merchants in Lisbon, Liverpool, Bristol, Nantes, Amsterdam and Rhode Island; planters; the governments that taxed sugar; and African rulers and merchants who sold captives for cloth, guns, iron, alcohol and **cowrie shells** from the Maldives.

**Contested: what did it do to Africa?** **Walter Rodney** (*How Europe Underdeveloped Africa*, 1972) argued that the trade drained Africa of people and set it on a path of dependence. **John Thornton** (*Africa and Africans in the Making of the Atlantic World*, 1992) stressed that Africans controlled the trade on their own coast and that Europeans could not dictate terms there. These are not quite opposites: one concerns effects, the other control. Economic studies such as **Nathan Nunn** (2008) find that regions that lost the most people to the trade are poorer and less trusting today. Critics question how cleanly such long chains of cause can be traced.
Kongo, Benin, Dahomey and Asante:
**The Atlantic trade was carried on through African states that had their own politics, interests and limits.** Four kingdoms show the range, from refusal to deep involvement. The aim is to understand them, not to shift blame: the trade's demand came from the Americas, and its violence fell on Africans.

**Kongo**, south of the Congo River mouth, met the Portuguese in **1483**. Its king, Nzinga a Nkuwu, was baptised as **João I** in **1491**. His son **Afonso I** (ruled about **1509–1542**) made Kongo a Christian kingdom, sent sons to study in Lisbon, and wrote letters in Portuguese to the king of Portugal. In **1526** he complained that Portuguese traders were kidnapping his subjects, even nobles, and asked that the trade be controlled. It was not. Portugal founded **Luanda** to the south in **1576**, the base of its colony of **Angola**, and the slave trade from there was enormous. In **1665** a Portuguese army defeated Kongo at **Mbwila** and killed its king. Kongo broke into civil wars for decades, which themselves produced captives for sale. In **1706** a young woman prophet, **Kimpa Vita** (Dona Beatriz), who preached a Kongolese Christianity and the reunion of the kingdom, was burned as a heretic. To Kongo's south-east, **Queen Njinga** of Ndongo and Matamba (about 1583–1663) fought and negotiated with the Portuguese for decades.

**Benin**, in the forest of what is now southern Nigeria, was an old kingdom ruled by the **oba** from Benin City. The Portuguese arrived about **1485**. Benin traded **pepper**, **ivory**, cloth and some captives for brass, coral and cloth. **For long stretches, from the early 1500s to the late 1600s, the obas restricted or banned the sale of men out of the kingdom**, and Benin was never among the largest exporters. Its craftsmen cast the famous **brass plaques** of the 1500s and 1600s, many showing Portuguese soldiers. (Most were looted by a British force in **1897**, a story for a later stage.)

**Dahomey**, a kingdom of the **Fon** people inland from the "Slave Coast" (now Benin Republic), grew in the 1700s. King **Agaja** (ruled about 1718–1740) conquered the coastal kingdoms of **Allada** (**1724**) and **Whydah** (Ouidah, **1727**), the busiest slave port in the region. Dahomey became a highly organised military state, known later for its **women soldiers**, and itself paid tribute to the larger **Oyo** empire to its north-east from about 1730.

**Asante**, in the forest of modern Ghana, rose around **1700**. Its founder **Osei Tutu** (died about 1717), with the priest **Okomfo Anokye**, united Akan states around the **Golden Stool**, believed to hold the soul of the nation, and defeated its overlord Denkyira about **1701**. From **Kumasi** it ruled a gold-rich empire and sold both **gold** and **captives** taken in its wars to Dutch and English forts on the coast, including **Elmina**, which the Dutch took from Portugal in **1637**.

**What these cases show:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **African states controlled the coast** | Europeans held forts by permission and paid rent and customs; they could not march inland in this period |
| **Rulers had reasons to sell** | captives from wars were a source of guns, cloth and revenue, and guns helped win more wars |
| **Some resisted** | Afonso's letters; Benin's restrictions |
| **The trade reshaped politics** | military states such as Dahomey and Asante rose; others, such as Kongo, were torn apart |

**Contested: did Agaja try to stop the trade?** An English slave trader, William Snelgrave, wrote that Agaja's conquests aimed to stop it, and the historian **I. A. Akinjogbin** (1967) argued this. **Robin Law** and others argue that Agaja wanted to **control** the trade and its revenue, and that Dahomey's exports soon rose again. The evidence is in shipping figures from Whydah before and after 1727, which point toward Law's reading, and in Agaja's own messages to Europeans, which are known only through European reports.
Primary source: Olaudah Equiano on the s:
The best-known first-hand account of the Middle Passage, written by a man who said he had survived it.

**The text.** Olaudah Equiano, *The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, or Gustavus Vassa, the African, Written by Himself*, first published in London in **1789**. He wrote in English, so there is no translator. Quoted from the Project Gutenberg text:

> "The first object which saluted my eyes when I arrived on the coast was the sea, and a slave ship, which was then riding at anchor, and waiting for its cargo. These filled me with astonishment, which was soon converted into terror when I was carried on board."

And, once the ship was loaded:

> "The closeness of the place, and the heat of the climate, added to the number in the ship, which was so crowded that each had scarcely room to turn himself, almost suffocated us. This produced copious perspirations, so that the air soon became unfit for respiration, from a variety of loathsome smells, and brought on a sickness among the slaves, of which many died, thus falling victims to the improvident avarice, as I may call it, of their purchasers."

**Who.** By his own account Equiano was born about **1745** in an **Igbo** village in what is now south-eastern Nigeria, kidnapped at about eleven, sold from hand to hand to the coast, and shipped to **Barbados** and then **Virginia**. He was bought by a British naval officer, renamed **Gustavus Vassa**, served at sea in the Seven Years' War, and **bought his own freedom in 1766**. In London he became a leader of the campaign to abolish the slave trade. He died in **1797**.

**Read it closely:**

| Phrase | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **"waiting for its cargo"** | he uses the traders' own word for the people, himself included. The irony is deliberate |
| **"astonishment… soon converted into terror"** | the order of feeling: he had never seen the sea or such a ship. Elsewhere he says he thought the white crew meant to eat him |
| **"scarcely room to turn himself"** | the same fact the abolitionists' famous plan of the ship *Brookes* (1788) showed in a diagram |
| **"the improvident avarice… of their purchasers"** | his argument: crowding killed people, so it was wicked and also foolish, even on the traders' own terms. He is writing to persuade a British public and Parliament |

**Why he wrote it.** The book appeared in **1789**, the year Parliament first debated abolition. It was sold by subscription, with names of supporters printed at the front, and went through nine editions in his lifetime. It is a work of evidence and of argument at once.

**Contested: was Equiano born in Africa?** In 2005 the literary historian **Vincent Carretta** published two records, a **1759 baptism** register in London and a **1773 naval muster roll**, both giving his birthplace as **South Carolina**. If they are right, his account of Africa and the crossing may be drawn from the stories of others he knew, written with great skill. Others, notably the historian **Paul Lovejoy** (2006), answer that such records were often wrong or written by others, and that the details of Igbo life in the book are too accurate to be secondhand. Neither side has a decisive document. **Either way, the book stands as testimony to the trade**, since every detail of the ship matches the evidence of many voyages. What would settle the question is another record from his early life.
The East India companies and the Dutch a:
**In the early 1600s the English and Dutch formed trading companies to break the Portuguese hold on Asian trade.** They became the most powerful businesses in the world, with their own armies, forts and fleets.

**Two companies:**

| | **English East India Company (EIC)** | **Dutch East India Company (VOC)** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Founded | royal charter of **31 December 1600** | **20 March 1602** |
| Model | at first a fresh subscription for each voyage | permanent capital, shares traded on the **Amsterdam** exchange: often called the first true joint-stock company |
| Main base | **Surat** (from about 1613), then **Madras** (1639), **Bombay** (1668), **Calcutta** (1690) | **Batavia** (Jakarta), from **1619** |
| Main trade | Indian **cotton cloth**, then tea | **spices**: nutmeg, cloves, pepper, cinnamon |

**The VOC's methods.** It was given the right to make war and treaties in Asia, and used them. **Jan Pieterszoon Coen** seized Jakarta in **1619** and renamed it Batavia. In **1621** he conquered the **Banda Islands**, the world's only source of nutmeg, and most of their people were killed, enslaved or driven away; the islands were then worked by enslaved labourers. The VOC took **Malacca** from the Portuguese in **1641** and coastal **Sri Lanka** in the 1650s, and from **1641** held the only European foothold in Japan, at Dejima. In **1623** at **Amboina** it executed English traders, pushing the EIC to concentrate on India.

**The EIC in India** was, in this period, a trader by permission. Sir **Thomas Roe** went to the Mughal emperor Jahangir's court as English ambassador (**1615–1619**). The company's forts were coastal and small. Its turn to conquest at **Plassey** (1757) belongs to the next stage.

**Others.** The **French** company was founded in **1664**, with its base at Pondicherry; the Danes held Tranquebar. In South-East Asia, local powers stayed strong: **Aceh** in Sumatra, **Mataram** in Java, **Ayutthaya** in Siam, which expelled the French in 1688.

**Into the Pacific.** VOC ships charted the coasts of Australia. **Willem Janszoon** reached Cape York in **1606**, the first recorded European landing. **Abel Tasman** in **1642** sighted **Tasmania** and the coast of **New Zealand**, where a clash with **Māori** in Golden Bay killed four of his men. Neither place was settled by Europeans for over a century.

**The Cape, in brief.** VOC ships sailing to Batavia needed fresh water, meat and vegetables on the long voyage. On **6 April 1652** **Jan van Riebeeck** landed at Table Bay to build a fort and garden as a **refreshment station**. The land was the home of **Khoikhoi** herders and **San** hunter-gatherers. In **1657** the company released some employees as **free burghers** to farm; from **1658** it brought enslaved people, from Africa, Madagascar, India and the East Indies; and the first war with the Khoikhoi came in **1659–1660**. The settlement grew slowly, and its long history is taught in depth in **the South African Politics curriculum**.

**Why it mattered.** The companies joined Asian production to European capital. They pioneered shares, stock exchanges and limited liability on a large scale, and they showed that a private company could act like a state. Indian cotton cloth, bought by the EIC, became a mass fashion in Europe, which later spurred British industry to copy it by machine.

**Contested: how much did the companies change Asia before 1750?** One reading holds that they were still small players in a huge Asian trade dominated by Asian merchants, rulers and ships. Another stresses that in specific places, such as the Banda Islands, Ceylon and Java, the VOC already ruled by force. Both hold, in different places, and the evidence is in the share of Asian trade carried in company ships, which grew over the period but stayed modest outside the spice islands.
The colonies of the Americas to 1750:
**By 1750 most of the Americas was claimed by European empires**, and their colonies had become societies of their own, built from European settlers, Indigenous peoples and enslaved Africans in very different mixes.

**Portuguese Brazil.** The first export was brazilwood, used for dye. From the 1530s–1550s **sugar** plantations grew in **Pernambuco** and **Bahia**, worked first by enslaved Indigenous people and then by Africans. The **Dutch** held north-eastern Brazil from **1630 to 1654**. In the **1690s** gold was found in **Minas Gerais**, setting off a gold rush and a new surge in the slave trade. Escaped slaves built settlements called *quilombos*; the largest, **Palmares**, lasted most of the 1600s and fell in **1694**.

**The Caribbean sugar revolution.** In the **1640s** English planters on **Barbados** switched from tobacco to sugar, with Dutch know-how from Brazil, and within a generation the island's labour force was mostly enslaved Africans. England took **Jamaica** from Spain in **1655**. France held **Martinique**, **Guadeloupe**, and from **1697** the western part of Hispaniola, **Saint-Domingue**, which by the late 1700s was the richest colony in the world. Death rates in the cane fields were so high that the islands depended on constant new arrivals from Africa.

**English North America:**

| Year | Colony |
| --- | --- |
| **1607** | **Jamestown**, Virginia; saved financially by **tobacco**, planted from 1612 |
| **1619** | the first Africans recorded in English Virginia, landed at Point Comfort; Virginia's first elected assembly meets |
| **1620** | **Plymouth**, founded by Puritan separatists from the *Mayflower* |
| **1630** | **Massachusetts Bay**, a larger Puritan colony |
| 1664 | the Dutch colony of **New Netherland** (founded 1624, capital New Amsterdam) taken by England and renamed **New York** |
| 1681 | **Pennsylvania**, a Quaker colony |

By 1750 the British mainland colonies held well over a million people, about a fifth of them enslaved. In the southern colonies, slavery became the base of the economy, and laws made it hereditary and racial.

**New France.** **Samuel de Champlain** founded **Quebec** in **1608**. New France had few settlers, but its **fur trade** depended on alliances with the **Huron-Wendat**, Algonquin and others. Jesuits lived among them. Explorers followed the rivers: **La Salle** reached the mouth of the Mississippi in **1682** and claimed **Louisiana**; New Orleans was founded in **1718**.

**Indigenous power.** Indigenous nations were not bystanders. The **Haudenosaunee** (Iroquois) Confederacy of five, later six, nations fought the **Beaver Wars** in the mid-1600s for control of the fur trade. In New England, **King Philip's War** (**1675–1676**), led by the Wampanoag leader Metacom, was proportionally one of the deadliest wars in American history. In New Mexico, the **Pueblo Revolt** of **1680**, led by **Popé**, drove the Spanish out for twelve years.

**Spanish America** kept its old centres. **Mexico City** and **Lima** were the great cities of the Americas, with cathedrals, universities and printing presses. Spain also pushed north into Florida (**St Augustine**, **1565**, the oldest continuously settled European town in the United States), New Mexico (**Santa Fe**, about 1610), and Texas.

**Three kinds of colony** had emerged:

1. **Plantation colonies** (Brazil, the Caribbean, the American South): an enslaved African majority or large minority, producing crops for export.
2. **Settler colonies** (New England, Pennsylvania, Quebec): European families farming, with Indigenous people pushed out.
3. **Conquest colonies** (Mexico, Peru): a European elite ruling a large Indigenous population.

These differences shaped the Americas' later history, including its revolutions, which open the next stage.
The Mughals from Jahangir to Aurangzeb:
**From 1605 to 1707 the Mughal Empire reached its greatest wealth and size, and began to come apart.**

**Jahangir** (ruled **1605–1627**), Akbar's son, loved painting and nature and kept a frank diary. His empress **Nur Jahan** was the real power at court for years, issuing orders and coins in her own name. English ambassador **Thomas Roe** came to his court (1615–1619). In **1606** Jahangir had the fifth Sikh Guru, **Arjan**, executed, a turning point after which the Sikh community began to arm.

**Shah Jahan** (ruled **1628–1658**) built on a scale that still defines India's image:

| Building | Date |
| --- | --- |
| the **Taj Mahal** at Agra, tomb of his wife **Mumtaz Mahal**, who died in childbirth in **1631** | built about **1632–1653** |
| **Shahjahanabad**, a new capital at Delhi, and its **Red Fort** | 1639–1648 |
| the jewelled **Peacock Throne** | 1630s |

The court was dazzling, and European travellers such as **François Bernier**, a French doctor at the court, described its wealth. But the cost was huge, and campaigns in Central Asia and the Deccan were expensive failures or slow gains.

**The war of succession** (**1657–1659**). When Shah Jahan fell ill, his four sons fought for the throne. The eldest, **Dara Shikoh**, a scholar who translated the Hindu **Upanishads** into Persian, was defeated by his brother **Aurangzeb**, captured and executed in **1659**. Aurangzeb kept his father prisoner in Agra fort until his death in 1666.

**Aurangzeb** (ruled **1658–1707**) was an able and austere ruler who spent most of his reign at war:

- **Expansion.** He conquered the Deccan sultanates of **Bijapur** (**1686**) and **Golconda** (**1687**), and the empire reached its **greatest extent**, almost the whole subcontinent.
- **Religious policy.** He ruled more strictly by Islamic law, **reimposed the *jizya*** on non-Muslims in **1679**, destroyed some major temples (as at Varanasi and Mathura, 1669–1670), and had the ninth Sikh Guru, **Tegh Bahadur**, executed in **1675**. He also employed many Hindu officers and gave grants to other temples.
- **The Marathas.** In the western Deccan, **Shivaji** (1630–1680) built a **Maratha** kingdom by guerrilla war, escaped Mughal captivity, and was crowned in **1674**. Aurangzeb spent his last 25 years in the Deccan fighting the Marathas and never defeated them.

**After 1707.** Aurangzeb died at nearly ninety. Wars among his heirs, the rise of regional powers (the Marathas, the Nizam of Hyderabad, Bengal, Awadh, the Sikhs) and Nadir Shah's **sack of Delhi** in **1739** left the emperor a figure with prestige and little power. That fragmentation opened the way for the East India Company in the next stage.

**Contested: why did the empire weaken?** Three readings:

1. **Religion.** **Jadunath Sarkar** (early 1900s) blamed Aurangzeb's bigotry for turning Hindus, Rajputs, Sikhs and Marathas against the empire.
2. **The system.** Historians of the **Aligarh school**, such as **Irfan Habib** (1963) and **M. Athar Ali**, pointed to a crisis of land revenue: too many nobles chasing too little good *jagir* land, squeezing peasants into revolt.
3. **Regional growth.** Others, such as **Muzaffar Alam** and **C. A. Bayly**, argued that the provinces grew richer and more confident, so the centre lost power without the economy collapsing.

**Audrey Truschke** (2017) argued that Aurangzeb's religious policy has been exaggerated by later writers; critics answer that his own orders show it. The evidence is in revenue records, temple grants and destructions, and the careers of Hindu nobles under him, which researchers continue to count.
Peter the Great and the Russian Empire:
**Peter I** (born **1672**, ruled **1682–1725**) turned Muscovy into the **Russian Empire**, a European great power with a new capital on the Baltic. He did it at enormous cost.

**Early life.** Peter became co-tsar at ten with his half-brother Ivan V, under the regency of his half-sister Sophia, and grew up partly in the foreign quarter of Moscow, among Dutch, German and Scottish soldiers and craftsmen. He was about two metres tall, restless, and fascinated by ships. He took full power in 1689 and ruled alone from 1696.

**The Grand Embassy** (**1697–1698**). Peter travelled through Europe, partly incognito, working as a shipwright in **Amsterdam** and studying shipyards in **England**. He came home to put down a revolt of the old musketeer regiments, the **streltsy**, and had hundreds executed.

**The Great Northern War** (**1700–1721**), against **Sweden**, the Baltic's great power under **Charles XII**:

| Year | Event |
| --- | --- |
| 1700 | Peter's army routed at **Narva** |
| **1703** | Peter founds **St Petersburg** on land taken from Sweden at the mouth of the Neva |
| **1709** | **Battle of Poltava** in Ukraine: Charles XII's army destroyed; Charles flees to the Ottomans |
| **1721** | **Treaty of Nystad**: Russia gains the Baltic coast (modern Estonia and part of Latvia). Peter takes the title **Emperor** |

**The reforms:**

- **Army and navy.** A conscript army on European lines, recruited by levies of peasant households; a Baltic navy built from nothing.
- **Government.** A **Senate** (1711) and **colleges** (ministries) on Swedish models; the **Table of Ranks** (**1722**), which ranked officials and officers in fourteen grades and let commoners rise into the nobility by service.
- **The Church.** When the patriarch died in 1700 Peter left the post empty, and in **1721** replaced it with a **Holy Synod** of bishops supervised by a lay official: the Church became a branch of the state.
- **Customs.** Nobles were ordered to shave their beards (or pay a beard tax) and wear Western dress. Schools of navigation, mathematics and medicine; the first Russian newspaper (1703); an Academy of Sciences planned and opened after his death.
- **The capital.** St Petersburg was built on marshland by forced labour; tens of thousands of workers died, though the figures are disputed. It became the capital in **1712**.

**The price.** Taxes were raised again and again, with a **poll tax** on every male peasant from **1724**. **Serfdom deepened**: the reforms rested on peasants bound to landlords and the state. Peter suspected his son and heir **Alexei** of plotting with his opponents; Alexei died in prison in **1718** after torture.

**The empire in 1725** stretched from the Baltic to the Pacific. Russia was now a permanent player in European wars. Peter's successors, above all **Catherine the Great** (ruled 1762–1796), carried his work further, in the next stage.

**Contested: a revolution from above, or a continuation?** One reading, already that of Russians in the 1800s (the "Westernisers"), sees Peter as a sharp break that brought Russia into Europe. The **Slavophiles** answered that he cut the elite off from Russian tradition and people. Many historians now stress continuity: Western soldiers, officers and ideas had been coming into Muscovy for decades before him, and his reforms built on 1600s foundations. The evidence is how much of the army and state of 1725 already existed in some form in 1680.
The scientific revolution:
**Between Copernicus in 1543 and Newton in 1687, European thinkers overturned the ancient picture of the heavens and the body, and built a new method of knowing nature by experiment and mathematics.**

**The old picture.** Universities taught the natural philosophy of **Aristotle** and the astronomy of **Ptolemy**: an Earth at rest at the centre of the universe, crystalline spheres carrying the planets, and heavens made of a different, perfect substance. In medicine, the Roman doctor **Galen**.

**The steps:**

| Year | Who | What |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1543** | **Nicolaus Copernicus** (Poland) | *On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres*: the **Sun at the centre**, the Earth moving |
| **1543** | **Andreas Vesalius** (Padua) | *On the Fabric of the Human Body*: anatomy from dissection, correcting Galen |
| 1570s–1590s | **Tycho Brahe** (Denmark) | the most accurate naked-eye observations ever made |
| **1609, 1619** | **Johannes Kepler** | planets move in **ellipses**, at speeds governed by mathematical laws |
| **1609–1610** | **Galileo Galilei** (Italy) | turns a **telescope** on the sky: mountains on the Moon, moons of Jupiter, phases of Venus. *The Starry Messenger*, 1610 |
| 1620 | **Francis Bacon** (England) | *Novum Organum*: knowledge built by organised experiment |
| **1628** | **William Harvey** (England) | the **circulation of the blood** |
| 1637 | **René Descartes** (France) | *Discourse on Method*: begin from doubt; nature as matter in motion |
| 1660s–1670s | Boyle, Hooke, **Leeuwenhoek** | gas laws; the microscope; Leeuwenhoek sees bacteria and sperm cells |
| **1687** | **Isaac Newton** (England) | *Principia*: three laws of motion and **universal gravitation**, one set of laws for the heavens and the Earth |

**Galileo and the Church.** In **1616** the Church declared the Sun-centred view contrary to scripture, and Galileo was warned not to hold it. His *Dialogue* of 1632 seemed to mock the pope's position. In **1633** the Roman Inquisition tried him; he recanted and spent the rest of his life under house arrest near Florence. He died in 1642. The case is often told as science against religion. Historians add that many leading scientists were devout, that Jesuit astronomers confirmed Galileo's observations, and that the trial turned also on politics and personal offence.

**New institutions.** The **Royal Society** of London (**1660**) and the French **Academy of Sciences** (**1666**) met to test experiments and published journals. Results were to be repeated and witnessed.

**Elsewhere.** Ideas travelled. Jesuit astronomers such as **Adam Schall** and **Ferdinand Verbiest** ran the Qing astronomical bureau in Beijing and built instruments there; Japanese scholars studied Dutch medical books. Islamic astronomy had a long tradition of its own: the observatory of **Ulugh Beg** at Samarkand (1420s) and the models of **Ibn al-Shatir** of Damascus (died about 1375), which use the same geometric devices Copernicus later used.

**Contested: was there a "revolution"?** The phrase became standard in the 1940s. **Steven Shapin** opened his book *The Scientific Revolution* (1996) with the line that there was no such thing, meaning there was no single, coherent event. Others answer that between 1543 and 1687 the picture of the cosmos really did change completely, which is revolution enough. **Contested also: why Europe?** Joseph Needham asked why modern science arose in Europe and not in China, which led in many technologies. Answers stress universities, printing, competing states, or the accidents of particular discoveries. Whether Copernicus knew of Ibn al-Shatir's work, through Byzantine or other channels, is debated: the match in geometry is clear, but no document proving transmission has been found.
Connections: the world joined by 1750:
**In 1450 the regions of the world mostly knew each other through middlemen. By 1750 ships, silver, sugar, enslaved people, crops and germs had joined them into one system.** This lesson pulls the threads together and points ahead.

**Who traded with whom:**

| Flow | Route |
| --- | --- |
| **Silver** | Potosí and Mexico → Seville and Manila → China and India |
| **Silk, porcelain, tea** | China → Manila, Europe, the Americas |
| **Cotton cloth** | India → Europe, Africa, South-East Asia |
| **Spices** | the Moluccas and Banda → Batavia → Amsterdam |
| **Enslaved Africans** | West and West-Central Africa → Brazil and the Caribbean; also across the Sahara and the Indian Ocean, older trades that continued |
| **Sugar, tobacco, gold** | the Americas → Europe |
| **Furs** | North America and Siberia → Europe and China |

**Who fought whom.** The **gunpowder empires**, as the historians Marshall Hodgson and William McNeill called them, the Ottomans, Safavids and Mughals, fought each other and the Habsburgs. Spain fought the Dutch and the English; England and France were fighting in every ocean by the 1740s. Morocco's guns broke Songhai. Russia beat Sweden and met China on the Amur. In the Americas and Africa, Indigenous and African states fought newcomers and each other, often with newcomers' guns.

**Who converted whom:**

- **Catholicism** spread through the Americas, the Philippines, parts of Africa (Kongo) and India (Goa); it was crushed in Japan.
- **Protestantism** split northern Europe from the south and crossed to North America.
- **Shi'ism** became Iran's faith; **Sunni** Islam spread further in South-East Asia and West Africa.
- **Sikhism** grew in the Punjab.

**What changed for everyone:**

1. **Demography.** The Americas lost most of their Indigenous people; Africa lost millions to the slave trades; China, India and Europe grew, fed partly by American crops. World population rose to perhaps **700–800 million** by 1750.
2. **Power at sea.** European fleets ruled the oceans, but on land in Asia and Africa European power was still small. In 1750 the Qing, the Mughal remnants, the Ottomans and the African kingdoms still held their own territories.
3. **Knowledge.** Print and the new science spread, and Europe's thinkers were turning the same methods on society: the **Enlightenment**.

**Carried into the next stage:**

- **Britain and France** were about to fight the **Seven Years' War** (1756–1763), the first war fought across the globe.
- The **East India Company** stood ready to step into the Mughal collapse, at **Plassey** in **1757**.
- The plantation colonies, slave societies with free settler minorities, were heading for revolutions: in **America**, **Haiti** (Saint-Domingue) and **Latin America**.
- **Britain**, with Atlantic trade, coal and Indian cloth to copy, was close to the **Industrial Revolution**.
- At the Cape, the VOC's station was growing into a colony (followed in **the South African Politics curriculum**).

**Contested: the Great Divergence.** Why did north-western Europe, and not China or India, go on to industrialise and dominate the world? **Kenneth Pomeranz** (*The Great Divergence*, 2000) argued that the richest parts of China, such as the Yangtze delta, were about as prosperous as England until about **1750–1800**, and that Britain pulled ahead thanks to **coal** near the surface and the land and resources of its **colonies**. Others, using wage and price data (for example **Robert Allen** and **Stephen Broadberry**), find that north-western Europe was already ahead in wages and output by the 1600s, which points to older causes, such as institutions, markets or culture. The question is what Europe's and Asia's living standards really were around 1700, and the wage and price data are still being argued over. It is the hinge of the next stage.
Map: the world in 1750:
In 1750 the world held perhaps **750 to 800 million people**. Most were farmers, and the greatest states on earth were in Asia. Nobody alive could have guessed that within 150 years a handful of European countries would rule most of the globe.

| Region | Where things stood about 1750 |
| --- | --- |
| **China** | the **Qing** under the Qianlong emperor (r. 1735–1796), at the height of their power; between 1755 and 1759 they destroyed the Dzungar state and took Xinjiang. Probably over 200 million people |
| **Japan and Korea** | **Tokugawa** Japan, at peace and closed to most foreigners; Joseon Korea |
| **South Asia** | the **Mughal** empire broken up after Aurangzeb's death (1707) and Nadir Shah's sack of Delhi (1739). The **Marathas** were the rising power; the British and French East India Companies held trading posts |
| **Iran and Central Asia** | the Safavids gone (1722); Iran divided after Nadir Shah's murder (1747); **Ahmad Shah Durrani** founding Afghanistan (1747) |
| **The Ottoman Empire** | still vast, from the Balkans to Iraq, Egypt and North Africa |
| **Europe** | rival monarchies: Britain, France, Habsburg Austria, Prussia under Frederick II, Russia under Empress Elizabeth |
| **Africa** | **Asante**, **Dahomey** and **Oyo** in the west, deep in the Atlantic slave trade; Ethiopia, soon to split in its "Era of the Princes" (from 1769); the Dutch at the Cape since 1652 |
| **The Americas** | Spain from California to Chile; Portuguese Brazil in a gold boom; British colonies on the Atlantic coast with about **1.2 million people, a fifth of them enslaved**; French Canada and Louisiana; the **Comanche** a rising power on the southern plains |
| **South-East Asia and Oceania** | the Konbaung dynasty founded in Burma (1752); Ayutthaya Siam, destroyed by Burma in 1767; Aboriginal Australia and Polynesia not yet reached by Cook (voyages 1768–1779) |

**The Atlantic slave trade was at its peak.** In the eighteenth century, more than six million Africans were carried across the Atlantic, more than in any other century.

**Three forces were about to remake this map:**

1. **Revolutions of a new kind**, claiming that power came from the people and that rights belonged to everyone, beginning in North America, France and Haiti.
2. **Industry**: machines driven by coal, first in Britain, which would give their owners wealth and weapons no one had had before.
3. **Nations and empires**: the idea that each people should have its own state, and the use of industrial power to conquer others.

**Hold the starting picture.** In 1750 China and India together produced, on most estimates, a larger share of the world's manufactured goods than all of Europe. By 1914 that had reversed. Why it reversed is one of the great questions of this stage.
The Enlightenment: reason, rights and th:
**The Enlightenment** was an eighteenth-century movement of writers and thinkers, centred in France, Britain, the German lands and Scotland, who held that **reason and evidence, not tradition or revelation alone, should guide how people live and are governed**.

**Its roots** lay in the scientific revolution of Stage 8 (Newton's *Principia*, 1687) and in John Locke, whose *Two Treatises of Government* (1689) argued that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property, and that government rests on consent.

| Thinker | Place and date | The idea |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Montesquieu** | France, *The Spirit of the Laws*, 1748 | liberty needs the **separation of powers**: law-making, enforcing and judging in different hands |
| **Voltaire** | France, 1694–1778 | religious **toleration**, free speech, mockery of persecution |
| **Diderot and d'Alembert** | Paris, the *Encyclopédie*, 1751–1772 | all knowledge gathered for public use |
| **Rousseau** | Geneva and France, *The Social Contract*, 1762 | legitimate power comes from the **general will** of the people |
| **Beccaria** | Milan, *On Crimes and Punishments*, 1764 | against torture and the death penalty |
| **Adam Smith** | Scotland, *The Wealth of Nations*, 1776 | markets and the division of labour create wealth |
| **Kant** | Königsberg, "What is Enlightenment?", 1784 | his motto, from Horace: *Sapere aude*, "dare to know" |
| **Mary Wollstonecraft** | London, 1792 | women's rights and education |

**How it spread.** Through print, salons (often hosted by women), coffee houses, learned societies and Masonic lodges: a new **public sphere** where private people argued about public affairs.

**Kings used it too.** The "enlightened despots" — Frederick II of Prussia, Catherine II of Russia, Joseph II of Austria — reformed laws and schools while keeping absolute power.

**Its limits were real.** Most Enlightenment writers excluded women from politics. Some of its leading figures wrote theories of race: **David Hume** added a footnote in 1753 claiming non-white peoples were naturally inferior, and Kant wrote on race in similar terms. Yet the same ideas of natural rights were used by abolitionists and, as the coming lessons show, by enslaved people themselves.

**Contested: what was the Enlightenment's legacy?**

| Reading | The argument |
| --- | --- |
| **The root of modern freedom** (e.g. Jonathan Israel) | a "radical Enlightenment" gave us democracy, equality and secular government |
| **The critique** (Horkheimer and Adorno, 1944; many postcolonial writers) | its faith in reason and control also fed racial science, empire and the bureaucratic state |
| **Many Enlightenments** (e.g. J. G. A. Pocock) | Scottish, French, German, Catholic and Protestant versions differed too much to have one legacy |

What would decide it is close tracing of who read what, and what they did with it.
The Seven Years' War, 1756–1763: a war o:
The **Seven Years' War** set Britain and Prussia against France, Austria, Russia (until 1762) and later Spain. It was fought in Europe, North America, the Caribbean, West Africa, India and the Philippines, and it has been called the first world war.

**It began in North America.** In 1754 Virginian militia under a young **George Washington** clashed with the French in the Ohio valley. Formal war in Europe followed in 1756.

| Theatre | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| **Europe** | **Frederick II** of Prussia fought off much larger armies. He was saved in 1762 when Empress Elizabeth of Russia died and her successor Peter III, an admirer, made peace |
| **North America** | Britain took **Quebec** (1759) and Montreal (1760) — the end of French Canada |
| **India** | at **Plassey** (23 June 1757) **Robert Clive** of the East India Company beat the Nawab of Bengal, Siraj ud-Daulah, after the Nawab's commander Mir Jafar was bought off. The French were defeated at Wandiwash (1760) |
| **West Africa** | Britain took the French slaving posts of Senegal (1758) |
| **Caribbean and Pacific** | Britain captured Guadeloupe, Martinique, **Havana** and **Manila** (1762) |

**The peace.** By the **Treaty of Paris** (February 1763) France gave Canada and the lands east of the Mississippi to Britain, and Louisiana west of it to Spain. Havana and Manila went back to Spain, which gave Britain Florida.

**Why it matters so much:**

1. **Britain emerged the leading world power** at sea and in trade.
2. **Plassey began British rule in India.** In 1765 the Company won the right to collect Bengal's revenue (the *diwani*).
3. **The war's cost set off revolutions.** Britain's national debt nearly doubled, to about £130 million. Trying to tax the American colonists to pay for their defence led to 1776. France's debts, made worse by its later aid to the Americans, led to 1789.
4. **Native Americans lost a counterweight.** With France gone, Native nations could no longer play one empire off another. **Pontiac's War** (1763) followed, and Britain's Proclamation of 1763 tried to bar settlers beyond the Appalachians, which angered colonists.

**The lesson in one line:** a European dynastic quarrel was now fought worldwide, and its bills came due in revolution.
The American Revolution, 1763–1791:
