Argentina, Brazil, Canada and Australia drew millions more. Many went back: a large share of Italian migrants returned home, some crossing many times.

**Indentured labour.** When slavery ended in the British Empire, planters looked to Asia. From 1834 well over a million Indians signed **indentures** — contracts for usually five years — to work in **Mauritius**, British Guiana, Trinidad, **Natal** (from 1860), **Fiji** (from 1879) and elsewhere. Conditions could be harsh, and critics called it a new form of slavery, though it differed in law and in its end date. India ended the system in 1917. Chinese contract workers, called "coolies" by Europeans, went to **Cuba** and **Peru** in conditions often close to slavery, about a hundred thousand or more to each, from the 1840s to the 1870s.

**Chinese migration** spread across Southeast Asia — to the tin mines of Malaya, the plantations of Sumatra, the trade of Singapore and Bangkok — and to California's gold rush (1849) and its railways.

**Closing doors.** Settler countries soon shut out Asians: the **Chinese Exclusion Act** of the United States (1882), the head tax in Canada (1885), the **White Australia** policy (1901). Europeans moved freely; Asians increasingly could not.

**Why they went.** Push and pull together: population growth, land shortage and famine at home; wages perhaps several times higher abroad; letters and money sent back by those who had gone first, which pulled whole villages after them. **Remittances** sustained families from Sicily to Guangdong.

**What it made.** The populations of the Americas, Australia and South Africa; the Indian communities of the Caribbean, East and South Africa and Fiji; the Chinese of Southeast Asia — and arguments over who belonged, which ran into the next century.
Darwin, germ theory and the science of t:
The nineteenth century changed what people knew about life, disease and matter more than any before it, and science became tied to industry, medicine and the state.

**Evolution.** **Charles Darwin** sailed round the world on HMS *Beagle* (1831–1836), studying fossils and the animals of places like the Galápagos islands. Over twenty years he worked out **natural selection**: individuals vary, more are born than survive, and those whose variations suit their surroundings leave more offspring, so species change. In 1858 **Alfred Russel Wallace**, working in the Malay archipelago, reached the same idea, and their papers were read together in London that July. *On the Origin of Species* appeared in **November 1859**; *The Descent of Man* (1871) applied the theory to humans. The monk **Gregor Mendel**'s experiments on pea plants (1866), ignored until 1900, later supplied the mechanism of inheritance.

**Darwin and religion.** The theory sparked fierce argument, as at Oxford in 1860 between Thomas Huxley and Bishop Samuel Wilberforce. But the old story of a constant "war between science and religion", popularised in books of the 1870s–1890s, is **rejected by most historians of science today**: many Christians accepted evolution, and the real relations were complicated.

**Misused.** The philosopher Herbert Spencer coined "survival of the fittest" (1864); "**Social Darwinism**" applied it to races and nations, and Darwin's cousin **Francis Galton** founded **eugenics** (he named it in 1883). These ideas fed racism and empire, and later the crimes of Stage 10.

**Medicine and germs:**

| Date | Discovery |
| --- | --- |
| **1796** | **Edward Jenner**, in England, vaccinates against smallpox using cowpox |
| **1846** | ether **anaesthesia** demonstrated in Boston |
| **1847** | **Ignaz Semmelweis** cuts deaths in a Vienna maternity ward by making doctors wash their hands |
| **1854** | **John Snow** traces a London cholera outbreak to the Broad Street water pump |
| **1860s** | **Louis Pasteur**, in Paris, shows that microbes cause fermentation and decay: **germ theory** |
| **1867** | **Joseph Lister** in Glasgow uses carbolic acid as an antiseptic in surgery |
| **1876–1884** | **Robert Koch** in Germany identifies the germs of anthrax, **tuberculosis** (1882) and cholera |
| **1885** | Pasteur's rabies vaccine |
| **1890** | **Kitasato Shibasaburō** and Emil von Behring develop antitoxins against tetanus and diphtheria |
| **1897** | Ronald Ross, in India, shows mosquitoes carry malaria |

Clean water and sewers did even more than doctors: cities that built them saw deaths from cholera and typhoid collapse.

**Physics and chemistry.** **Michael Faraday** showed electromagnetic induction (1831), the basis of the dynamo; **Dmitri Mendeleev** drew up the **periodic table** (1869); Marie and Pierre Curie's work on **radioactivity** (1898) opened the atom.

**The effect on lives.** Life expectancy rose fastest where these discoveries and clean water arrived: in Britain to around 50 by 1914, while the world average, on Our World in Data's figures, was still only around 30–35.
Connections: the world in 1914:
In 1750 Asia's empires were the world's greatest powers. In 1914 a few industrial states ruled most of the planet, and the world was more tightly joined than ever.

**Who ruled whom.** By an often-quoted estimate, Europeans and their offshoots controlled about four-fifths of the world's land by 1914. The states that kept their independence outside Europe and the Americas were few: **Japan**, the new Chinese republic, the Ottoman Empire, Iran, Siam, Afghanistan, **Ethiopia** and Liberia.

**What joined the world:**

| Link | How |
| --- | --- |
| **Steam** | steamships cut the Atlantic crossing to about a week; railways crossed continents |
| **Canals** | **Suez** (1869) and **Panama** (August 1914) |
| **Cables** | the telegraph linked London to India (1870) and across the Pacific (1902): news in minutes, not months |
| **Money** | the gold standard and London's banks financed trade worldwide |
| **People** | tens of millions of migrants from Europe, India and China |
| **Ideas** | nationalism, liberalism, socialism and Christian missions spread to every continent; so did resistance to them |

**Who traded with, fought or converted whom:**
- **Britain and India**: Indian cotton, tea and jute, Indian taxes and Indian soldiers, used from China to East Africa.
- **Europe and Africa**: rubber, palm oil, gold and diamonds out; conquest, missions, borders and taxes in.
- **The Atlantic**: grain, beef and coffee from the Americas to Europe's cities.
- **Japan** fought China and Russia and colonised Taiwan and Korea; it was now a power in its own right.
- **Christian missions** grew fast in Africa, Korea and the Pacific; **Islam** spread in West and East Africa, often faster under colonial rule than before.

**What carried over into Stage 10:**

| From this stage | Into the next |
| --- | --- |
| Germany unified and industrialised; France resentful over Alsace-Lorraine | the **alliances**: Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy (1882); France, Russia and Britain (by 1907) |
| Nationalism in the Balkans and the Ottoman retreat | the **Balkan Wars** (1912–1913) and the assassination at **Sarajevo** (28 June 1914) |
| Industrial weapons — machine guns, artillery, railways | a war of mass killing |
| Russia's 1905 revolution and unrest | the Russian revolutions of 1917 |
| Colonial empires | millions of soldiers and labourers from India, Africa and Indochina in Europe's war |
| China's 1911 revolution, Mexico's 1910 revolution | civil wars and new states |
| Socialist parties, unions and women's suffrage campaigns | mass politics, the vote for women in many countries after the war |

**Look back at the whole stage.** Three revolutions — political (America, France, Haiti, Latin America), industrial (Britain and then the world), and national — gave a handful of states the will and the means to rule the rest. The people they ruled took up those same ideas of rights and nationhood to resist them. That contest, fought out through two world wars and decolonisation, is the story of the stages to come.
Map: the world in the summer of 1914:
In June 1914 about 1.8 billion people lived on Earth, and most of them were ruled, directly or indirectly, by a handful of empires. This is the map the next thirty-one years tore up.

**Europe was the centre of the world's power, and it was split into two armed camps.**

| Camp | Members | Bound by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Triple Entente** | France, Russia, Britain | the Franco-Russian alliance (1894) and British understandings with France (1904) and Russia (1907) |
| **Triple Alliance** | Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy | a defensive treaty of 1882; Italy would in fact switch sides in 1915 |

**The empires, region by region:**

- **Europe and the Near East.** Five great land empires: the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman, plus Britain and France with their overseas empires. **All four of the land empires would be gone by 1923.** The Ottomans still held Anatolia, Syria, Iraq, Palestine and Arabia's coastal holy cities, but had lost almost all of Europe in the Balkan Wars of 1912–13.
- **Africa.** Partitioned among Britain, France, Germany, Belgium, Portugal, Italy and Spain. **Only Ethiopia and Liberia were independent.** South Africa had become a self-governing British dominion in 1910 (its own story is in the South African Politics curriculum).
- **South Asia.** India, then including today's Pakistan and Bangladesh, was ruled by Britain as the Raj: about 300 million people.
- **East Asia.** China had become a republic in 1912 after the Qing dynasty fell, but was weak and fracturing. **Japan was the one non-Western great power**, holding Taiwan (since 1895) and Korea (annexed 1910).
- **The steppe and Central Asia** lay inside the Russian Empire and western China.
- **The Americas.** The United States was the world's largest industrial economy but stood outside European alliances. Latin America was independent; **Mexico was four years into a revolution** (1910–1920) that would kill perhaps a million people or more.
- **Oceania.** Australia (federated 1901) and New Zealand were British dominions; Germany held north-eastern New Guinea, Samoa and Micronesian islands.
- **Persia** was nominally independent but divided into Russian and British spheres of influence in 1907.

**Three things to hold while reading this stage:**

1. **Empires fought with their colonies' manpower.** Indian, African, Australian, Canadian and Vietnamese men fought in both wars.
2. **The wars were global but began in Europe and East Asia.** The second war had two starting points: China in 1937 and Poland in 1939.
3. **New ideologies arrived:** communism in power (1917), fascism (1922), Nazism (1933). Each claimed to be the future.

By 1945, the European empires would be exhausted, the United States and the Soviet Union would be the two great powers, and the new map would be drawn by them.
The July Crisis of 1914 and the argument:
On **28 June 1914**, in **Sarajevo**, Bosnia, a 19-year-old Bosnian Serb named **Gavrilo Princip** shot dead **Archduke Franz Ferdinand**, heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, and his wife Sophie. Within six weeks, five great powers were at war.

**The five weeks, step by step:**

| Date (1914) | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **5–6 July** | Germany promises Austria-Hungary unconditional support against Serbia: the **"blank cheque"** |
| **23 July** | Austria-Hungary sends Serbia an ultimatum designed to be refused |
| **28 July** | Austria-Hungary declares war on Serbia |
| **30 July** | Russia orders general mobilisation in support of Serbia |
| **1 and 3 August** | Germany declares war on Russia, then France |
| **4 August** | Germany invades **Belgium** to reach France; **Britain declares war** |

**Why one shooting became a world war.** Germany's war plan (associated with Alfred von Schlieffen) assumed a two-front war and required knocking out France fast, through neutral Belgium, before Russia's slow armies were ready. Once Russia mobilised, Germany's generals felt they had days, not weeks. **Alliances, railway timetables and the cult of the offensive** made a local war hard to contain. Behind them lay naval rivalry between Britain and Germany, nationalism in the Balkans, and Austria-Hungary's fear that Serbian nationalism would break up its multi-national empire.

**Who was to blame is one of history's great arguments.** The Treaty of Versailles (Article 231, 1919) put the responsibility on Germany and its allies. Historians since have argued it out:

- **Fischer: Germany chose war.** In 1961 the German historian **Fritz Fischer** (*Germany's Aims in the First World War*) used German archives to show that Berlin pushed Vienna to act, accepted the risk of a general war, and drew up sweeping annexation plans (the **September Programme** of 1914). His strongest evidence is the blank cheque and German pressure throughout July. His case caused uproar in West Germany because it suggested continuity with 1939.
- **Clark: sleepwalkers, not a single culprit.** In 2012 **Christopher Clark** (*The Sleepwalkers*) argued that responsibility was shared: Serbian officials' links to the assassins, Russia's early mobilisation, France's encouragement of Russia, and Britain's ambiguity all mattered. **No one government planned the general war; each took risks expecting the others to back down.**
- **Others** stress Vienna's own determination, or deeper forces: imperial rivalry (Lenin's reading), or the "unspoken assumptions" of a whole generation that war was normal and short (James Joll).

**What would settle it.** The documents are mostly known; the argument is over **weight and intent**: whether Berlin wanted a European war or only a local one it would risk widening. Records of what German leaders privately expected Russia to do in early July are the crux, and they are ambiguous.
The Western Front, 1914–1917: the Marne,:
In August 1914 German armies swept through **Belgium** and northern France. Everyone expected a short war. It lasted four years and three months.

**1914: the plan fails.** The invasion of Belgium was brutal: German troops killed **about 6,500 Belgian and French civilians** in the first weeks, burning the university town of Louvain. On **5–12 September 1914**, French and British armies stopped the Germans on the **Marne**, east of Paris. Both sides then tried to outflank each other northward (the "race to the sea"). By the end of 1914 a line of trenches ran about **700 kilometres from the Channel coast to Switzerland**, and it barely moved for three years.

**Why the front froze.** Defence was stronger than attack. **Machine guns, barbed wire and above all artillery** could destroy an attack in the open. Railways brought defending reserves faster than attackers could walk across shell-torn ground. Radios were too heavy to carry forward, so generals lost contact with their men the moment an attack began.

**The great battles:**

| Battle | When | What it meant |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Second Ypres** | April 1915 | first large-scale use of poison gas (chlorine) on the Western Front, by Germany |
| **Verdun** | Feb–Dec 1916 | Germany attacked a French fortress city to bleed France white; **roughly 300,000 dead** on both sides, about 700,000 casualties in all (estimates vary) |
| **The Somme** | July–Nov 1916 | a British-French offensive; on **1 July 1916** the British Army suffered about **57,000 casualties, some 19,000 of them dead**, its worst day ever. Over a million casualties on all sides by November. First tanks used, September 1916 |
| **Nivelle offensive** | April 1917 | a failed French attack followed by **mutinies** in much of the French army, May–June 1917 |
| **Passchendaele (Third Ypres)** | July–Nov 1917 | a British offensive in Flanders, remembered for mud deep enough to drown in |

**Life in the trenches** was long stretches of boredom, rats, lice and shelling, broken by terror. Most deaths came from **artillery**, not bullets. Men served in rotation; few spent more than days at a time in the front line.

**Were the generals fools? The historians disagree.**

- **"Lions led by donkeys."** The view of many war poets and of Alan Clark's *The Donkeys* (1961): generals such as Britain's **Douglas Haig** wasted lives in hopeless frontal attacks out of stubbornness and lack of imagination. The Somme's first day is its strongest evidence.
- **The "learning curve."** Historians such as **Gary Sheffield** argue the generals faced a genuinely new problem, with no technology yet able to solve it, and learned: by 1918 the British and French were using **combined arms** (creeping artillery barrages, tanks, aircraft, infantry tactics) that won the war.

**What would settle it** is comparison: whether any army found a cheaper way to break trench lines earlier. None did, which supports the learning-curve case; whether the costly lessons could have been learned faster is still argued.
The Eastern Front, Italy and the Balkans:
The war in the east was larger in space, more mobile and, for civilians, often worse than the war in the west. It is less remembered in the English-speaking world because few British or American soldiers fought there.

**1914: Russia attacks early.** Russia invaded East Prussia faster than Germany expected, and was crushed at **Tannenberg (26–30 August 1914)** by Generals **Hindenburg and Ludendorff**, who became Germany's heroes and later its effective rulers. Further south, Russia beat Austria-Hungary in **Galicia**, taking Lemberg (Lviv) in September 1914. **Austria-Hungary's army lost much of its trained officer corps in the first year and never fully recovered.**

**1915: the Great Retreat.** A German-Austrian breakthrough at **Gorlice–Tarnów (May 1915)** drove Russia out of Poland, Lithuania and much of Galicia. Millions of refugees fled east. The Russian army, short of rifles and shells, **deported hundreds of thousands of Jews and Germans** from front-line areas as supposed spies.

**1916: Brusilov.** In **June 1916** the Russian general **Aleksei Brusilov** attacked on a wide front with careful preparation and nearly broke Austria-Hungary. It was the Entente's most successful offensive of the war, but Russia's losses were vast and morale at home sank.

**The Balkans.** Serbia threw back two Austrian invasions in 1914. In autumn 1915, after **Bulgaria** joined the Central Powers (October 1915), Serbia was overrun; its army and government retreated through the Albanian mountains in winter, and tens of thousands died on the way. An Allied force sat at **Salonika** in Greece for most of the war. **Romania** joined the Entente in August 1916 and was largely conquered by December; Bucharest fell on 6 December 1916.

**Italy.** Italy stayed neutral in 1914, then joined the Entente in **May 1915**, after the secret **Treaty of London** promised it Austrian lands. It fought **eleven battles on the Isonzo river** against Austria-Hungary in the mountains, with little gain, then was routed at **Caporetto (October–November 1917)**, losing about 300,000 men, most as prisoners. Italy held on the Piave river with British and French help.

| Front | Character |
| --- | --- |
| **West** | static trenches, dense firepower, high casualties per kilometre |
| **East** | long fronts, great advances and retreats, mass refugees and deportations |
| **Italy** | mountain warfare, avalanches as deadly as shells |
| **Balkans** | small states overrun; disease and hunger |

**Why it mattered.** The eastern war broke three empires. **Russia's defeats fed the revolution of 1917**; Austria-Hungary became dependent on Germany; and the movement of armies and peoples across Poland, Ukraine and the Baltic laid down the grievances and borders fought over again in 1918–21 and 1939–45.
The Ottoman war: Gallipoli, the Arab Rev:
The Ottoman Empire entered the war on Germany's side in **late October–November 1914**, after its warships, with German crews, bombarded Russian Black Sea ports. Its government was run by the **Committee of Union and Progress** (the "Young Turks"), led by a triumvirate: **Enver, Talat and Cemal Pashas**.

**The fronts the Ottomans fought on:**

| Front | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| **Caucasus** | Enver's winter offensive against Russia ended in disaster at **Sarıkamış** (December 1914–January 1915); much of his army froze or was killed |
| **Gallipoli** | Britain and France tried to force the **Dardanelles** strait, take Constantinople and open a sea route to Russia |
| **Mesopotamia** | a British-Indian army advanced up the Tigris towards Baghdad; besieged at **Kut**, about 13,000 men surrendered in **April 1916**. Britain took Baghdad in March 1917 |
| **Sinai and Palestine** | British forces from Egypt took Jerusalem in **December 1917** and Damascus in **October 1918** |

**Gallipoli.** After a naval attack failed in March 1915, Allied troops landed on the Gallipoli peninsula on **25 April 1915**: British, French, Indian, and the **Australian and New Zealand Army Corps (ANZAC)**. They never got off the beaches and ridges. A young Ottoman officer, **Mustafa Kemal**, held the heights above Anzac Cove and became famous. The Allies withdrew by **January 1916**; each side lost roughly a quarter of a million casualties. **For Australia and New Zealand, 25 April (Anzac Day) became a founding national memory; for Turks, the defence of Çanakkale became one too.**

**The Arab Revolt.** In **June 1916** **Sharif Hussein of Mecca**, guardian of Islam's holy cities, rose against the Ottomans with British money and arms. His son **Faisal** led Arab forces north, with the British liaison officer **T. E. Lawrence**, taking Aqaba (July 1917) and entering Damascus in October 1918.

**Three promises that contradicted each other:**

1. **The McMahon–Hussein correspondence (1915–16):** Britain's High Commissioner in Egypt promised to support Arab independence in return for the revolt. The exact borders were left vague, and whether they included Palestine is still disputed.
2. **The Sykes–Picot Agreement (May 1916):** a secret British-French plan to divide the Arab lands into zones of control, with Russia's consent. The Bolsheviks published it in late 1917.
3. **The Balfour Declaration (2 November 1917):** Britain announced it viewed "with favour the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people," while saying nothing should be done to prejudice "the civil and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities in Palestine" (text as printed by the Avalon Project, Yale).

**Why it mattered.** The Ottoman war left behind the **mandates** of 1920 (British Iraq, Palestine and Transjordan; French Syria and Lebanon), broken promises remembered across the Arab world, the Palestine question, and, amid it all, the deportation and destruction of the Armenians, the subject of a separate lesson.
The war in Africa, Asia and the Pacific,:
The First World War was fought on every continent but the Americas and Antarctica, because the warring empires reached everywhere. Their colonies supplied men, labour, food and battlefields.

**Africa.** Germany's four colonies were attacked from the first weeks.

| Colony | Fate |
| --- | --- |
| **Togoland** | taken by British and French forces, August 1914 |
| **Kamerun** (Cameroon) | conquered by early 1916 |
| **German South West Africa** (Namibia) | conquered by South African forces, July 1915; South Africa's own Boer rebellion of 1914 against joining the war was put down first (see the South African Politics curriculum) |
| **German East Africa** (Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi) | never fully taken; **Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck**'s small force of German officers and African *askari* soldiers fought on until **25 November 1918**, two weeks after the armistice |

**The East African campaign was fought on African backs.** Armies there moved on foot through bush and disease country, so both sides used hundreds of thousands of African **carriers** (porters). **Tens of thousands died of disease, hunger and overwork; some estimates put the total above 100,000.** Requisitions of food and men brought famine to parts of Tanzania.

**Africans in Europe.** France recruited about **200,000 soldiers from West Africa** (the *tirailleurs sénégalais*, drawn from many colonies, not only Senegal), many of whom fought at Verdun and on the Somme. North Africa sent many more soldiers and workers.

**India.** About **1.3 million Indians served** in the war as soldiers and labourers, and **over 70,000 died**. Indian troops held the line in France in 1914–15 and made up most of the army in Mesopotamia. India also paid much of the cost. Many Indian nationalists supported the war expecting self-government in return; the disappointment of 1919 (the next lessons) came from that.

**East Asia.** **Japan** joined the Allies in August 1914 and seized Germany's leased port of **Qingdao (Tsingtao)** in China (November 1914) and Germany's Pacific islands north of the equator. In **January 1915** Japan presented China with the **Twenty-One Demands**, aimed at turning it into a dependent. China joined the Allies in 1917 and sent about **140,000 labourers** (the Chinese Labour Corps) to dig trenches and unload ships in France.

**Oceania.** **New Zealand took German Samoa (August 1914)**, and **Australia took German New Guinea (September 1914)**. Australia and New Zealand then sent their armies to Gallipoli, the Middle East and France; Australia, from fewer than five million people, lost about 60,000 dead.

**Why it mattered.** Colonial peoples learned three things: that **their rulers needed them**, that **Europeans could be beaten and could slaughter one another**, and that **service had been promised a reward**. Those lessons fed the nationalist movements of the 1920s.
The Armenian genocide, 1915–1917:
In 1914 about **1.5 to 2 million Armenians** lived in the Ottoman Empire, mostly in eastern Anatolia and in its cities. They were an ancient Christian people who had lived in the region for over two thousand years. **Within about two years, most of them had been killed or driven from their homeland.**

**Background.** Armenians had been massacred before, under Sultan Abdülhamid II in **1894–96** (perhaps 100,000 to 300,000 dead) and at **Adana in 1909**. The CUP government that took the empire to war in 1914 was increasingly committed to a Turkish-Muslim national core for what remained of the empire. After the defeat at Sarıkamış in January 1915, its leaders blamed Armenians as a Russian fifth column, pointing to Armenian volunteers in the Russian army and to self-defence at **Van** in April 1915.

**What happened:**

1. **24 April 1915.** About 250 Armenian intellectuals and community leaders were arrested in Constantinople; most were later killed. Armenians mark this as the start.
2. **Disarming and killing the men.** Armenian soldiers in the Ottoman army were put into labour battalions, and many were shot.
3. **Deportation.** A **deportation law of May 1915** sent whole communities on foot south into the **Syrian desert**. Along the routes, columns were attacked by the **Special Organization** (irregular units), gendarmes and local bands; women were raped and abducted, children taken for conversion, and great numbers died of thirst, hunger and exhaustion.
4. **The camps around Deir ez-Zor** in Syria, where many survivors were massacred in 1916.

**The numbers are debated, the event is not.** Estimates of Armenian dead run from about **600,000 to 1.5 million**; many scholars give **around one million or more**. Assyrian and Greek Christians of the empire also suffered mass killing and deportation in these years.

**The evidence is extensive:** reports by German and Austrian diplomats (allies of the Ottomans), the American ambassador **Henry Morgenthau**, missionaries and survivors; and the **Ottoman courts-martial of 1919–20**, which tried CUP leaders and found them guilty. Talat Pasha, the interior minister who organised the deportations, was condemned to death in absence and assassinated by an Armenian survivor in Berlin in 1921.

**Is "genocide" the right word?** The lawyer **Raphael Lemkin**, who coined the word in 1944, cited the Armenians as a case that shaped his thinking. **The large majority of historians and genocide scholars call it genocide**, and many states recognise it as such. The **Turkish state rejects the term**, arguing that deaths came from wartime deportation, disease and intercommunal fighting in which Muslims also died in great numbers, and that no central order to exterminate has been proven. A small number of Western scholars have made a version of that argument. The scholarly majority answers that **the pattern of killing across the whole empire, the separation and killing of men, and the deportation of women and children into the desert** show intent regardless of whether a single written order survives.

**Why it mattered.** It destroyed Armenian life in Anatolia and became a precedent, studied as one, for the genocides of the twentieth century.
Russia's two revolutions of 1917 and the:
In early 1917 Russia had lost millions of men, its cities were short of bread, and the tsar, **Nicholas II**, had taken personal command at the front, leaving government discredited at home. (Russia then used the old Julian calendar, 13 days behind the West; dates here are given in the old style, with the Western date where it matters.)

**The February Revolution.** Bread queues and strikes in **Petrograd** (St Petersburg) in late February 1917 grew into mass demonstrations; the soldiers of the garrison refused to fire and joined them. **Nicholas II abdicated on 2 March (15 March) 1917**, ending three centuries of Romanov rule. Power was split between a **Provisional Government** of liberals and moderate socialists and the **Petrograd Soviet**, a council of workers' and soldiers' deputies. This was called **"dual power."**

**Why the Provisional Government failed.** It kept fighting the war, put off land reform and elections until a Constituent Assembly could meet, and lost the army. **Lenin**, leader of the Bolshevik faction of Marxists, returned from Swiss exile in April 1917 (on a train the Germans let through, hoping he would knock Russia out of the war) and demanded **"Peace, land and bread"** and **"All power to the soviets."** After a right-wing general, **Kornilov**, appeared to threaten a coup in August, the Bolsheviks won majorities in the Petrograd and Moscow soviets.

**The October Revolution.** On **25 October (7 November) 1917**, Bolshevik-led forces organised by **Leon Trotsky** seized the Winter Palace and key points in Petrograd with little bloodshed. A Congress of Soviets endorsed the new government. Lenin's decrees gave the land to the peasants and called for peace.

**From revolution to dictatorship:**

| Date | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **December 1917** | the **Cheka** secret police founded |
| **November 1917–January 1918** | elections to the Constituent Assembly give the Bolsheviks about a quarter of the vote (the peasant Socialist Revolutionaries won most); **the Bolsheviks close it after one day** |
| **3 March 1918** | **Treaty of Brest-Litovsk**: Russia gives up Poland, the Baltic lands, Finland and Ukraine, most of it falling under German control |
| **July 1918** | the tsar and his family shot at Yekaterinburg |

**The Civil War, 1918–1921.** The **Reds** (Bolsheviks) fought the **Whites** (former officers, conservatives, some liberals, with Allied intervention forces at the edges), as well as peasant armies, anarchists, and national movements in Ukraine, the Caucasus and Central Asia. **The Reds won because they held the industrial centre and railways, were united under one leadership, and the Whites could not promise peasants their land.** Both sides used terror; the Bolshevik **Red Terror** was declared in September 1918. A Bolshevik drive west was turned back by Poland at **Warsaw in August 1920**. War, requisitioning ("War Communism") and drought brought the **famine of 1921–22, which killed perhaps five million people.**

After a sailors' revolt at **Kronstadt** in March 1921, Lenin allowed private trade again (the **New Economic Policy**). The **Soviet Union was founded in December 1922**; Lenin died in January 1924.

**Revolution or coup? A real debate.** One reading (Richard Pipes) sees October as **a coup by a small, disciplined party** that hijacked a popular revolution and built dictatorship from the start. The other (social historians such as Alexander Rabinowitch) sees the Bolsheviks as **genuinely carried by workers and soldiers in 1917**, with dictatorship growing out of civil war. Local studies of the soviets, factory committees and elections are the evidence each side uses, and the two can be partly true together: popular in the cities in 1917, minority rule by 1918.
1917–1918: America enters, Germany gambl:
By early 1917 the war was a contest of endurance. Germany, squeezed by a British naval blockade that brought hunger to its cities, made two gambles. The first lost the war; the second nearly won it.

**Gamble one: unrestricted submarine warfare.** In **February 1917** Germany began sinking merchant ships on sight, neutral or not, expecting to starve Britain out before America could matter. Britain intercepted the **Zimmermann Telegram**, in which Germany's foreign secretary offered Mexico an alliance and the return of Texas, New Mexico and Arizona if the United States entered the war. **The United States declared war on Germany on 6 April 1917.** Convoys defeated the submarines by late 1917, and American troops, slow to arrive, numbered about two million in France by November 1918.

**Russia leaves the war.** The Bolshevik revolution and the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (March 1918) freed German divisions from the east.

**Gamble two: the Spring Offensive.** On **21 March 1918** Germany's army, now under the effective direction of **Ludendorff**, launched a great offensive in the west using new **storm-trooper** infiltration tactics and short, intense bombardments. It advanced further than anyone had in four years, to the Marne in May–June, less than 100 kilometres from Paris, but it outran its supplies, cost Germany its best troops, and achieved no decisive break.

**The Allies strike back.** Under a single Allied commander, **Ferdinand Foch**, the Allies counter-attacked at the **Second Marne (July 1918)**, and on **8 August 1918** British, Australian, Canadian and French forces broke through at **Amiens** with tanks, aircraft and artillery working together. Ludendorff later called it the black day of the German army. Through the **Hundred Days** offensive, the German army was pushed back steadily.

**Germany's allies fall away:**

| Date (1918) | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **29 September** | **Bulgaria** signs an armistice |
| **30 October** | the **Ottoman Empire** signs the Armistice of Mudros |
| **3 November** | **Austria-Hungary**, already breaking into national states, signs at Villa Giusti |
| **early November** | sailors mutiny at **Kiel**; revolution spreads across Germany |
| **9 November** | **Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicates**; a republic is proclaimed in Berlin |
| **11 November** | **armistice** signed in a railway carriage at **Compiègne**, effective at 11 a.m. |

**The cost.** About **9 to 10 million soldiers died**, along with millions of civilians from hunger, disease, massacre and the flu that followed (estimates for the civilian dead vary widely). Some 20 million were wounded.

**A dangerous myth.** Because the armistice came while German armies still stood on foreign soil, and because the generals let civilian politicians sign it, many Germans came to believe the army had been **"stabbed in the back"** by socialists and Jews at home. **Historians agree this was false**: the army itself, through Ludendorff, demanded an armistice in late September 1918 because it was losing. But the myth poisoned the new German republic.
The influenza pandemic of 1918–1920:
In 1918, as the war ended, a new strain of influenza swept the world in waves. **It killed more people than the war itself.**

**What it was.** An **H1N1 influenza A** virus, identified long afterwards: scientists reconstructed it in **2005** from preserved tissue, including the body of a victim buried in Alaskan permafrost. It came in **three main waves**: a milder one in spring 1918, a terrible one from about **September to December 1918**, and a third in early 1919, with outbreaks into 1920.

**Why it was called "Spanish."** Neutral Spain's newspapers were not censored and reported the disease openly, while warring countries hid it. So it looked as if it came from Spain. It did not.

**Where it began is unknown.** The main theories:

| Theory | Evidence for it |
| --- | --- |
| **Kansas, USA** | early outbreak at **Camp Funston** army camp, March 1918 |
| **Northern France** | respiratory outbreaks among troops at the British base at **Étaples** in 1916–17 |
| **China** | the movement of the Chinese Labour Corps across North America to France |

None is proven. Better genetic evidence from early samples would settle it.

**How many died.** Perhaps a **third of the world's people were infected**. Death estimates range from about **17 million to 50 million**, and some go higher; the uncertainty comes from countries such as India and China with poor records.

**Strange features:**

- **It killed young adults.** Most flu kills the very old and very young; this strain killed many healthy people aged about **20 to 40**, perhaps through an over-strong immune reaction, and often with bacterial pneumonia (there were no antibiotics).
- **It was fast.** People could be well in the morning and dead by night, their faces turning blue from lack of oxygen.

**Across the world:**

- **India** suffered the most deaths of any country, with estimates of **about 12 to 20 million**, worsened by a failed monsoon and famine conditions.
- **Western Samoa**, under New Zealand rule, lost about **a fifth of its population** after an infected ship was allowed to land in November 1918. **American Samoa**, next door, imposed a strict quarantine and **recorded no deaths**.
- **South Africa** was among the worst-hit countries in proportion to its population, with the disease spreading along the railways from the ports in late 1918.
- **Troopships and demobilisation** carried it everywhere, from the Western Front to the Pacific islands and Alaska.

**Why it is half-forgotten.** It came at the same moment as the armistice, killed without heroes or villains, and left few monuments. Only after 2020's pandemic did it return to general memory. **It changed public health**: several countries built national health ministries in the years after.
Primary source: Wilson's Fourteen Points:
On **8 January 1918**, ten months after the United States entered the war, President **Woodrow Wilson** told a joint session of Congress in Washington what America was fighting for. It was the most detailed public statement of war aims made by any of the warring governments (Britain's Lloyd George had given a shorter one three days earlier), and it became the basis on which Germany asked for an armistice.

**The text** (Woodrow Wilson, address to Congress, 8 January 1918; written in English, so no translation; from the *Congressional Record*, 65th Congress, 2nd Session, as given in the Internet Modern History Sourcebook). The purpose, as Wilson put it:

> "What we demand in this war, therefore, is nothing peculiar to ourselves. It is that the world be made fit and safe to live in; and particularly that it be made safe for every peace-loving nation which, like our own, wishes to live its own life, determine its own institutions, be assured of justice and fair dealing by the other peoples of the world as against force and selfish aggression."

Three of the fourteen points:

> "I. Open covenants of peace, openly arrived at, after which there shall be no private international understanding of any kind but diplomacy shall proceed always frankly and in the public view."

> "V. A free, open-minded, and absolutely impartial adjustment of all colonial claims, based upon a strict observance of the principle that in determining all such questions of sovereignty the interests of the populations concerned must have equal weight with the equitable claims of the government whose title is to be determined."

> "XIV. A general association of nations must be formed under specific covenants for the purpose of affording mutual guarantees of political independence and territorial integrity to great and small states alike."

**Read it closely:**

| Phrase | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **"Open covenants … openly arrived at"** | an attack on **secret treaties** like Sykes–Picot and the Treaty of London. The Bolsheviks had just published the Allies' secret treaties, and Wilson was answering Lenin's call for peace |
| **"the interests of the populations concerned"** (point V) | colonial peoples' interests were to count, but only with **"equal weight"** beside their rulers' claims. It does not promise independence |
| **"great and small states alike"** (point XIV) | the seed of the **League of Nations** |
| the other points | specific: Belgium restored, Alsace-Lorraine returned to France, an independent **Poland** with access to the sea, "autonomous development" for the peoples of Austria-Hungary and the non-Turkish peoples of the Ottoman Empire |

**What is not there.** The famous phrase **"self-determination" does not appear in the Fourteen Points.** Wilson used it in a later speech, in February 1918. Yet across Egypt, India, Korea and China, people read the speech as promising it, and the historian Erez Manela has called the hopes of 1919 the "Wilsonian moment."

**A lesson about sources.** Printed versions of the speech differ in small wording. Wikisource's text of point I reads "Open covenants of peace must be arrived at…", while the *Congressional Record* text quoted here reads "openly arrived at." Variants like this are why a historian always states which printing a quotation comes from.

**Who it was for.** Several audiences at once: Congress and the American public, the Allies (whose secret aims it quietly rebuked), the German people (whom it invited to make peace over their government's head), and Russia's Bolsheviks. Elsewhere in the speech Wilson said **"The day of conquest and aggrandizement is gone by"** (Wikisource text). The peace of 1919 would test that claim.
The Paris peace of 1919 and the League o:
The peace conference opened in **Paris on 18 January 1919**. Germany and the other defeated powers were not invited to negotiate; they were handed terms. The decisions were made by the **"Big Four"**: **Wilson** (USA), **Georges Clemenceau** (France), **David Lloyd George** (Britain) and **Vittorio Orlando** (Italy).

**Each wanted something different.** France, invaded twice in fifty years, wanted security against Germany. Britain wanted German naval and colonial power ended, without crushing Germany as a trading partner. Wilson wanted his League. Italy wanted the lands it had been promised in 1915.

**The treaties:**

| Treaty | With | Signed | Main terms |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Versailles** | Germany | **28 June 1919** | lost about 13% of its European territory (Alsace-Lorraine, lands to Poland) and all colonies; army limited to **100,000**; Rhineland demilitarised; **Article 231** on responsibility for the war; reparations |
| **Saint-Germain** | Austria | September 1919 | Austria reduced to a small German-speaking republic, forbidden to unite with Germany |
| **Neuilly** | Bulgaria | November 1919 | land lost to Greece, Yugoslavia, Romania |
| **Trianon** | Hungary | June 1920 | lost about **two-thirds of its territory**; millions of Hungarians left outside it |
| **Sèvres** | Ottoman Empire | August 1920 | partition; overturned by the Turkish national movement and replaced at Lausanne in 1923 |

**New states** filled central and eastern Europe: **Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Austria, Hungary, Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania**. Each contained minorities, and borders were drawn by nationality only where the victors found it convenient.

**Reparations** were set in 1921 at **132 billion gold marks**, although much of that sum was in bonds few expected ever to be paid.

**Was Versailles too harsh? A lasting argument.**

- **Too harsh.** In *The Economic Consequences of the Peace* (1919), the British economist **John Maynard Keynes** called it a *Carthaginian peace*, a peace of destruction, that would wreck Europe's economy and breed revenge.
- **Not harsh enough, or not enforced.** Historians such as **Sally Marks** and **Margaret MacMillan** (*Peacemakers*, 2001) argue Germany kept its unity and industry, paid only a fraction of reparations, and was left potentially Europe's strongest state. The failure was in **enforcement** in the 1930s, not the terms.
- What would settle it is counterfactual, so evidence is indirect: what Germany actually paid, and whether its economic crises of 1923 and 1930 owed more to reparations or to its own policies.

**The world beyond Europe.** Japan's proposal to write **racial equality** into the League Covenant was blocked in April 1919. Germany's rights in **Shandong** went to Japan, setting off China's **May Fourth Movement** (4 May 1919). Egypt rose in revolution in March 1919; Korea's **March First Movement** was crushed. **Colonial peoples learned that the peace was for Europeans.**

**The League of Nations** met first in January 1920, at **Geneva**. Germany's colonies and the Ottoman Arab lands became **mandates**, run by Britain, France, Belgium, Japan, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand under League supervision. **The US Senate refused to ratify the treaty** (votes of November 1919 and March 1920), so America never joined. The League settled small disputes (the Åland Islands, 1921), helped refugees with the **Nansen passport** (1922) and fought disease, but it had no army; it failed over **Manchuria (1931)** and **Ethiopia (1935)**.
The end of the Ottomans and Atatürk's Tu:
At the armistice of **Mudros (30 October 1918)** the Ottoman Empire was beaten. Its Arab lands were in British and French hands, Allied fleets lay off **Constantinople**, and the CUP leaders had fled. Within five years the empire was gone and a Turkish republic stood in its place.

**The partition that failed.** In **May 1919**, with Allied backing, a **Greek army landed at Smyrna (İzmir)** on the Aegean coast, where many Greeks lived. Days later, on **19 May 1919**, **Mustafa Kemal**, the hero of Gallipoli, landed at **Samsun** on the Black Sea, supposedly to restore order, and instead organised resistance. A rival government, the **Grand National Assembly**, opened at **Ankara** in April 1920. The Sultan's government signed the **Treaty of Sèvres (August 1920)**, which would have given land to Greece, an independent Armenia and a possible Kurdistan, and left only a rump of Anatolia under Turkish rule. **Kemal's movement refused it.**

**The war of independence, 1919–1922:**

| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **1920–21** | Turkish nationalists defeat the short-lived Armenian republic in the east and make terms with Soviet Russia and France |
| **Aug–Sept 1921** | the Greek advance on Ankara is stopped at the **Sakarya** river |
| **August–September 1922** | the Greek army is routed; Turkish forces take Smyrna, and **much of the city burns**, its Greek and Armenian quarters destroyed |
| **November 1922** | the **sultanate abolished** |
| **24 July 1923** | **Treaty of Lausanne**: the Allies recognise Turkey's borders, much as they still stand |

**The population exchange.** Greece and Turkey agreed in January 1923 to a compulsory exchange: about **1.2 million Orthodox Christians** left Turkey for Greece and about **400,000 Muslims** left Greece for Turkey. Religion, not language, decided who went. **It was the first large internationally agreed population transfer**, and it was later cited as a model, for good and ill.

**The republic.** Turkey was proclaimed a republic on **29 October 1923**, with Kemal as president and **Ankara** as capital. What followed was a revolution from above:

- **1924**: the **caliphate abolished**, ending an institution as old as Islam's first century; religious courts closed.
- **1925**: the fez banned in favour of Western hats.
- **1926**: new civil code based on Switzerland's; polygamy banned.
- **1928**: the Arabic script replaced by a **Latin alphabet**.
- **1934**: women given the vote in national elections; **surnames** made compulsory, and the assembly gave Kemal the name **Atatürk**, "Father of the Turks."

**The other side of it.** The republic was a **one-party state** until after the Second World War. Kurdish revolts, such as **Sheikh Said's (1925)** and that of **Dersim (1937–38)**, were crushed with great loss of life, and Kurdish identity was denied. Non-Muslim minorities kept shrinking.

**How to judge Atatürk is argued.** One reading sees a **modernising nation-builder** who saved a Turkish state from partition and gave it secular law and women's rights decades before many neighbours. Another stresses **authoritarian, ethnic nationalism** that suppressed Kurds, religion and dissent. Both rest on the same facts; the dispute is how to weigh them. Atatürk died on **10 November 1938**.

**The wider Middle East.** **Reza Khan** took power in Persia and crowned himself Shah in **1925**, with a similar modernising programme. **Ibn Saud** united most of Arabia, proclaiming the kingdom of **Saudi Arabia in 1932**. Egypt gained nominal independence in **1922**, Iraq in **1932**, both under heavy British influence.
Empires under challenge between the wars:
The First World War did not end the European empires; at their peak, in the early 1920s, Britain's and France's were larger than ever. But across the world, colonised peoples organised against them with new methods.

**India.** In **1919** the British passed the **Rowlatt Acts**, keeping wartime powers of arrest without trial. On **13 April 1919**, at the **Jallianwala Bagh** in **Amritsar**, General **Reginald Dyer** ordered troops to fire on an unarmed crowd that had no way out. The official count was **379 dead**; Indian estimates were far higher. **Mohandas Gandhi**, a lawyer who had developed mass non-violent resistance (*satyagraha*, "truth-force") in South Africa between 1893 and 1914, led the **Non-Cooperation movement (1920–22)**: boycotts of British goods, schools and courts. He called it off after a crowd killed 22 policemen at **Chauri Chaura** in February 1922.

**The Salt March.** From **12 March to 6 April 1930** Gandhi walked about **380 kilometres** to the sea at **Dandi** to make salt, breaking the government's salt monopoly. Tens of thousands were arrested in the campaign that followed. **The genius of it was the choice of target**: a tax every poor Indian paid, which the world could understand. The **Government of India Act 1935** gave Indians elected provincial governments, which the Congress party won in 1937. The **Muslim League** under **Muhammad Ali Jinnah** grew more distant from Congress, a division that would matter enormously in 1947.

**Ireland.** The **Easter Rising** in Dublin (April 1916) was crushed, but the execution of its leaders turned opinion. After a war of independence (1919–21) the **Anglo-Irish Treaty (December 1921)** created the **Irish Free State**, while six north-eastern counties remained in the UK as **Northern Ireland**. A civil war among Irish nationalists over the treaty followed (1922–23).

**Egypt.** After the arrest and exile of the nationalist leader **Saad Zaghlul**, Egypt rose in the **revolution of 1919**. Britain declared Egypt independent in **1922**, but kept troops there and control of the Suez Canal.

**Africa.** Organised opposition grew in many forms:

| Movement | Where and when |
| --- | --- |
| **Pan-African Congresses** | Paris 1919 and after, organised by the African American scholar **W. E. B. Du Bois** |
| **Marcus Garvey's UNIA** | a mass movement from New York in the 1920s: "Africa for the Africans" |
| **Harry Thuku** | Kenya, 1922: arrested for organising against forced labour and taxes; police killed protesters in Nairobi |
| **The Women's War** | south-eastern Nigeria, **1929**: thousands of Igbo women protested taxation and British-appointed chiefs |
| **Copperbelt strikes** | Northern Rhodesia (Zambia), 1935 |

**The Americas.** The United States occupied **Haiti (1915–34)** and intervened repeatedly in Central America; in **Nicaragua**, **Augusto Sandino** fought US Marines from 1927 to 1933. Franklin Roosevelt's **"Good Neighbor" policy** (1933) ended the occupations.

**East and South-East Asia.** Korea's **March First Movement (1919)** against Japanese rule was put down with thousands killed. In **Vietnam**, a young **Ho Chi Minh** petitioned the Paris conference in 1919 and later founded the Indochinese Communist Party (1930). In the Dutch East Indies, **Sukarno** founded the Indonesian Nationalist Party in **1927**.

**Why it mattered.** None of these movements won full independence before 1939, apart from Ireland's partial victory and Egypt's and Iraq's nominal ones. But they built the parties, leaders and methods that would end the empires after 1945.
Stalin's revolution from above: collecti:
After Lenin's death in January 1924, **Joseph Stalin**, the party's General Secretary, outmanoeuvred his rivals: **Trotsky** was expelled from the party in 1927 and from the country in 1929. By 1929 Stalin was the master of the Soviet Union, and he set out to transform it at a speed no state had attempted.

**The plan.** The **First Five-Year Plan (1928–32)** demanded vast new steel mills, dams, tractor factories and whole new cities, such as **Magnitogorsk** in the Urals. To pay for industry and feed the cities, the state needed grain from the peasants, who were most of the population and who had been selling less of it to the state at its low prices.

**Collectivisation.** From late **1929** peasants were forced to give up their land and animals and join **collective farms (kolkhozy)**. In **December 1929** Stalin called for the **"liquidation of the kulaks as a class"**: better-off peasants, or anyone labelled one. About **1.8 million people were deported as kulaks in 1930–31** to labour settlements in Siberia, the Urals and Kazakhstan, where many died. Peasants resisted by slaughtering their animals rather than surrendering them; the Soviet Union lost about half its livestock.

**The famine.** Grain quotas stayed high even as harvests fell. In **1932–33** famine struck Ukraine, the Kuban (in southern Russia, with many Ukrainians), the Volga and above all **Kazakhstan**, where forced settlement of nomads destroyed the herds.

| Region | Estimated deaths (about) |
| --- | --- |
| **Ukraine** | **3.5 to 5 million**; demographers often give about 3.9 million |
| **Kazakhstan** | about **1.5 million**, perhaps a third or more of all Kazakhs |
| **USSR in total** | roughly **5.5 to 8.7 million** |

**What the state did.** Grain was still exported. A law of **August 1932** made theft of collective property, including gleaning, punishable by death or ten years. Villages that missed quotas were **"blacklisted"** and cut off from goods. A directive of **22 January 1933**, signed by Stalin and Molotov, **stopped starving peasants from leaving Ukraine and the Kuban** to look for food. The famine was denied in public, and foreign journalists who reported it, such as **Gareth Jones**, were attacked.

**Was it genocide? The historians' debate.** Ukrainians call it the **Holodomor**, "death by hunger." That the famine happened, and that Stalin's policies caused it, is not disputed by serious historians. The argument is over **intent**:

- **Genocide, aimed at Ukrainians as a nation.** Robert Conquest (*The Harvest of Sorrow*, 1986), and in a related form **Anne Applebaum** (*Red Famine*, 2017), argue that measures in late 1932 and early 1933 targeted **Ukraine specifically**: the border closure, the blacklists, and a simultaneous assault on Ukrainian culture and the Ukrainian Communist Party. Ukraine's parliament declared it genocide in 2006, and many states have since agreed.
- **A Soviet-wide catastrophe, not an ethnic one.** R. W. Davies and **Stephen Wheatcroft** (*The Years of Hunger*, 2004) argue that Stalin's ruthlessness towards peasants everywhere, his ideology and his refusal to admit failure explain the famine; they point out that **Kazakhs died at an even higher rate**, and that some relief grain was eventually released.

**What would settle it** is evidence of the Politburo's purpose in late 1932: whether its orders aimed at Ukrainians as Ukrainians, or at peasants who resisted. The archives opened since 1991 have been read both ways.
The Great Terror and the Gulag, 1934–193:
On **1 December 1934** **Sergei Kirov**, the party boss of Leningrad, was shot dead in his offices. Stalin used the murder as the pretext for a campaign of arrests that rose, in **1937–38**, into the **Great Terror**, one of the largest peacetime killings by any state of its own people.

**The show trials.** In three great public trials in Moscow (**August 1936, January 1937, March 1938**), the old Bolshevik leaders, **Zinoviev, Kamenev** and later **Bukharin** among them, confessed to absurd crimes: plotting with Trotsky, Germany and Japan to murder Stalin and restore capitalism. They were shot. **The confessions were extracted by threats to their families, sleeplessness and torture.**

**The purge of the army.** In June 1937 Marshal **Mikhail Tukhachevsky** and other top commanders were shot. Thousands of officers were arrested. The army that met Hitler in 1941 had lost many of its most experienced leaders.

**The mass operations.** Most victims were not famous. **NKVD Order No. 00447 (July 1937)** set regional quotas, region by region, of "anti-Soviet elements" to be shot or sent to camps: former kulaks, priests, criminals. Further **"national operations"** targeted Poles, Germans, Latvians, Koreans and others as potential spies; the Polish operation alone shot over 100,000 people.

**The numbers, from the Soviet archives.** NKVD records for **1937–38** count about **1.5 million arrests** and about **680,000 executions**, at a rate of over 1,500 a day. Historians generally accept these as a minimum.

**The Gulag.** The Gulag (an acronym for the Main Camp Administration) was a system of hundreds of labour camps across Siberia, the Arctic and Kazakhstan. Prisoners dug canals, mined gold at **Kolyma**, and cut timber. Anne Applebaum estimates that about **18 million people passed through** the camps and colonies between 1929 and Stalin's death in 1953. Recorded deaths in the camps run to **about 1.5 to 1.7 million**, and many more died soon after release or in exile settlements.

**Who drove the Terror? A debate partly settled by the archives.**

- **From the top (the "totalitarian" reading).** Robert Conquest's *The Great Terror* (1968) argued that **Stalin planned and directed it**.
- **From below (the "revisionist" reading).** Historians such as **J. Arch Getty**, writing in the 1980s, stressed chaos, local officials' rivalries and pressures from below, and argued earlier death estimates were too high.
- **What the archives showed after 1991.** Stalin and his inner circle **personally signed lists of thousands of names for execution**, and set and raised the quotas, which supports the top-down case. The numbers were large but generally **lower than Conquest's highest estimates**, which supports some revisionist caution. Most historians now hold both: **Stalin started and steered it; local officials magnified it**.

**Why Stalin did it** is still argued: to destroy any possible alternative leadership before a coming war, out of paranoia, or to complete the revolution by removing every "enemy." **Trotsky**, his last great rival, was murdered by a Soviet agent in **Mexico in August 1940**.
Mussolini and the invention of fascism,:
Italy had been on the winning side in 1918, but many Italians felt cheated: the Paris conference did not give them all the land promised in 1915. The poet **Gabriele D'Annunzio** called it a ***mutilated victory***, and in September 1919 led irregulars to seize the port of **Fiume** (Rijeka), which he held for over a year.

**The first fascists.** In **Milan on 23 March 1919**, **Benito Mussolini**, a former socialist newspaper editor and war veteran, founded the **Fasci di Combattimento**. The name came from the *fasces*, the bundle of rods carried before Roman magistrates: **strength through unity**. In the **"two red years" (1919–20)** of strikes and factory and land occupations, landowners and industrialists turned to fascist squads, the **Blackshirts**, who beat and killed socialists and burned their offices, often with police looking away.

**Into power.** On **28 October 1922**, fascist columns converged on the capital in the **March on Rome**. King **Victor Emmanuel III** refused to declare martial law and instead appointed Mussolini prime minister. **It was less a seizure of power than a handing-over**, by a king and establishment who thought they could use him.

**From government to dictatorship:**

| Year | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1923** | the **Acerbo Law** gives two-thirds of seats to the party with the most votes |
| **June 1924** | the socialist deputy **Giacomo Matteotti**, who had denounced fascist violence, is murdered by fascists |
| **January 1925** | Mussolini takes responsibility in a speech and moves to one-party rule; opposition parties banned by 1926 |
| **1929** | the **Lateran Pacts** with the Pope create Vatican City and settle the Church's relations with the state |

**The regime** called itself **totalitarian**, a word it made popular, meaning that no part of life should lie outside the state. In practice it shared power with the monarchy, the Church, the army and big business. It built roads, drained the Pontine marshes, and organised youth, leisure and propaganda.

**Empire in Africa.** In **Libya**, Italy crushed resistance by moving much of the population of Cyrenaica into **concentration camps**, where tens of thousands died; the resistance leader **Omar Mukhtar** was hanged in **1931**. In **October 1935** Italy invaded **Ethiopia**, using **poison gas** against soldiers and civilians, and took Addis Ababa in **May 1936**. Emperor **Haile Selassie** appealed to the League of Nations in Geneva in June 1936; its sanctions were weak and soon dropped.

**What was fascism? Historians disagree.**

- **A set of ideas.** Roger Griffin defines it as **"palingenetic ultranationalism"**: the myth of a nation's rebirth from decadence through violence and unity.
- **A pattern of behaviour.** Robert Paxton (*The Anatomy of Fascism*, 2004) says watch what fascists did: mass movements that **allied with conservative elites** to take power in a crisis of democracy.
- **A class weapon.** Marxist historians saw it as capitalism's defence against the workers' movement.
- **Only Italy's.** Some argue the word should not be stretched over Nazism and others at all.

The test of each definition is whether it fits Italy and Germany while excluding ordinary dictatorships, such as military ones.
The Great Depression across the world, 1:
In **October 1929** share prices on the **New York Stock Exchange** collapsed, on **Black Thursday (24 October)** and **Black Tuesday (29 October)**. The crash began the worst economic slump of the industrial age, and because the world economy was joined by trade, loans and the gold standard, **it spread to every continent**.

**How bad it got in the United States.** By 1932–33 industrial production had fallen by nearly half, about **a quarter of the workforce was unemployed**, and thousands of banks had failed, taking people's savings with them. Farm prices collapsed; in the 1930s the **Dust Bowl** of the southern plains drove families west.

**How it spread:**

1. **American loans stopped.** American money had kept Germany and central Europe afloat since 1924. It was called home.
2. **Trade shrank.** The US **Smoot–Hawley tariff (1930)** raised duties, and others retaliated. World trade fell by about two-thirds in value between 1929 and 1933.
3. **Banks fell like dominoes.** The failure of Austria's **Creditanstalt** in **May 1931** set off a banking crisis in central Europe; Germany's banks followed in July.
4. **The gold standard tied hands.** Countries whose currencies were fixed to gold had to raise interest rates and cut spending to defend them, deepening the slump. **Britain left gold in September 1931**, the United States in 1933, France not until 1936.

**Around the world:**

| Region | What the Depression did |
| --- | --- |
| **Germany** | about **six million unemployed** by early 1932; the Nazi vote rose with it |
| **Latin America** | export prices (coffee, beef, tin, copper) collapsed; military coups or revolts in **Argentina, Brazil** (Getúlio Vargas, October 1930), Peru and others around 1930–32. Many turned to building their own industries. In **1938** Mexico's president **Lázaro Cárdenas** nationalised foreign oil companies |
| **Africa** | prices for cocoa, groundnuts, palm oil and copper fell; colonial taxes did not, driving many into migrant labour; the **Gold Coast cocoa hold-up** of 1937–38 protested low prices |
| **India** | farm prices halved; peasants' debts soared, feeding Gandhi's civil disobedience |
| **Japan** | silk and rice prices fell steeply; rural misery strengthened the army and nationalist radicals |
| **USSR** | largely cut off from world markets; its planned growth during the slump impressed many outside observers who did not see the famine |

**The responses.** **Franklin Roosevelt**, elected US president in 1932, launched the **New Deal** from **1933**: bank rescues, public works, farm support, and later Social Security (1935). Sweden's Social Democrats tried public works and spending. Germany under the Nazis cut unemployment by rearmament and public works. In 1936 **Keynes** published *The General Theory*, arguing that governments should spend to fight unemployment when private demand collapses.

**Why was it so deep? Three explanations, largely compatible:**

- **Demand collapsed** (Keynes): spending fell, so production fell, so incomes fell further.
- **Money shrank** (Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz, 1963): the US central bank let the money supply fall by about a third as banks failed.
- **The gold standard spread it** (Barry Eichengreen, *Golden Fetters*, 1992). The strongest evidence: **countries that left gold early recovered sooner** than those that held on.

Economists now broadly agree all three mattered; they still argue how much each did, and whether the New Deal sped recovery or slowed it.

**Why it mattered politically.** The Depression discredited liberal democracy and free markets in the eyes of millions. **It made Hitler's rise possible, strengthened militarists in Japan**, and made communism and fascism both look like the future.
From Weimar to Hitler's dictatorship, 19:
Germany's first democracy was born in defeat. In **November 1918** revolution swept the Kaiser away; in **August 1919** a national assembly meeting at **Weimar** adopted a democratic constitution. It gave women the vote and used proportional representation, and its **Article 48** let the president rule by emergency decree.

**The republic's hard birth:**

| Year | Crisis |
| --- | --- |
| **January 1919** | the communist **Spartacist** rising in Berlin is crushed by army and *Freikorps* volunteers; **Rosa Luxemburg** and **Karl Liebknecht** murdered |
| **1920** | the right-wing **Kapp Putsch** fails when workers strike |
| **1922** | foreign minister **Walther Rathenau**, a Jew, is murdered by nationalists |
| **1923** | France and Belgium occupy the **Ruhr** over unpaid reparations; **hyperinflation**: by November a US dollar cost about **4.2 trillion marks**, and savings were wiped out |
| **8–9 November 1923** | **Adolf Hitler**'s **Beer Hall Putsch** in Munich fails; in prison he writes *Mein Kampf* |

**Hitler** was Austrian-born, a front-line soldier in the war, and leader since 1921 of the small **National Socialist German Workers' Party (NSDAP)**. His creed joined extreme nationalism, the "stab in the back" myth, the demand for **"living space" (*Lebensraum*) in the east**, and above all a murderous **antisemitism** that blamed Jews for defeat, communism and capitalism alike.

**The good years, 1924–29.** A new currency, American loans under the **Dawes Plan (1924)** and the diplomacy of **Gustav Stresemann** (the Locarno treaties, 1925; League membership, 1926) brought calm. Berlin's culture flowered. The Nazis won just **2.6%** of the vote in 1928.

**The Depression destroyed it.** After 1930, chancellors ruled by presidential decree under Article 48, bypassing a deadlocked parliament. The Nazi vote soared:

| Election | Nazi share |
| --- | --- |
| **September 1930** | **18.3%** |
| **July 1932** | **37.3%**, the largest party |
| **November 1932** | **33.1%** |

**Hitler did not win power; he was given it.** Conservative politicians around President **Paul von Hindenburg**, led by **Franz von Papen**, believed they could control him, and on **30 January 1933** Hindenburg appointed Hitler chancellor.

**Eighteen months to dictatorship:**

1. **27–28 February 1933**: the **Reichstag fire**; an emergency decree suspends civil liberties. Communists are rounded up; the first concentration camp opens at **Dachau** in March.
2. **23 March 1933**: the **Enabling Act** lets the government make laws without parliament.
3. **1 April 1933**: boycott of Jewish shops; Jews purged from the civil service.
4. **July 1933**: all parties except the Nazis banned.
5. **30 June–2 July 1934**: the **Night of the Long Knives**; Hitler has the leaders of his own stormtroopers (SA) and other rivals killed.
6. **August 1934**: Hindenburg dies; Hitler becomes **Führer**, and the army swears an oath to him personally.

**Who voted Nazi? A debate.** An older view saw the **lower middle class** (shopkeepers, clerks, artisans) as the core. Electoral studies since the 1980s (by Jürgen Falter and others) found the Nazis drew from **almost every group**, a "people's party of protest," strongest among **Protestants and in the countryside**, weakest among Catholics and organised workers. **The unemployed themselves tended to vote Communist.** Historians also argue whether Weimar was doomed by Versailles and the Depression, or was destroyed by choices, above all the elites' choice of January 1933.
China divided: the Republic, the Nationa:
In **October 1911** an army mutiny at **Wuchang** set off a revolution, and in **February 1912** the last Qing emperor, the child **Puyi**, abdicated. More than two thousand years of imperial rule ended. The **Republic of China** had a revolutionary hero in **Sun Yat-sen**, but power went to the general **Yuan Shikai**, who tried to make himself emperor and died in 1916.

**The warlord era, 1916–1928.** China fractured. Regional military strongmen (warlords) controlled their own provinces, while governments in **Beijing** came and went.

**The May Fourth Movement.** On **4 May 1919**, students in Beijing protested the Paris peace's transfer of German rights in **Shandong** to Japan. The protests grew into a wider movement for **science, democracy and a new culture** against Confucian tradition. Out of it came many of the founders of the **Chinese Communist Party**, established in **Shanghai in July 1921**, with **Mao Zedong** among the delegates.

**Two parties, one alliance, then war:**

| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **1923–27** | **First United Front**: Sun's **Nationalist Party (Guomindang, GMD)** and the Communists work together, with Soviet advisers |
| **March 1925** | Sun Yat-sen dies; **Chiang Kai-shek** rises to lead the Nationalist army |
| **1926–28** | the **Northern Expedition**: Chiang's armies march north and defeat or absorb the warlords |
| **April 1927** | in **Shanghai** Chiang turns on his Communist allies; thousands are killed |
| **1928** | Chiang's **Nationalist government at Nanjing** claims to rule China |

**The Nationalist decade, 1928–37.** Chiang's government built railways, schools and a modern army, and won back some rights from foreign powers. But it never controlled all of China; corruption spread; and it relied on landlords in the countryside.

**The Communists in the countryside.** Driven from the cities, the Communists built a base, the **Jiangxi Soviet**, in the south-east, where Mao developed the idea of a **revolution of peasants**, not factory workers. Chiang's encirclement campaigns forced them out, and in **October 1934** about 86,000 began the **Long March**: thousands of kilometres (the official figure is about **12,500**, and some researchers put the main route nearer 6,000) over a year, through mountains and swamps, to **Yan'an** in the north-west. Perhaps **one in ten** arrived (figures vary). At **Zunyi (January 1935)**, Mao won a leading voice in the party. **The Long March became the founding legend of the Communist state**, and parts of the legend have been questioned since, but the march itself and its losses are real.

**The Xi'an Incident.** Chiang wanted to destroy the Communists before fighting Japan, which had seized Manchuria in 1931. In **December 1936** two of his own generals kidnapped him at **Xi'an** until he agreed to a **Second United Front** against Japan.

**Why it mattered.** When full war with Japan came in **July 1937**, China had two governments, two armies and two visions of its future. The war against Japan would weaken the Nationalists and strengthen the Communists, who won the civil war that followed in 1949 (Stage 11).
Japan's expansion and the Nanjing massac:
In the 1920s Japan was a parliamentary monarchy under the emperor, with party cabinets and, from **1925**, votes for all men. The same year it passed the **Peace Preservation Law** against communists and other "dangerous thoughts." Over the next decade, power shifted to the army and navy.

**Why the army gained ground.** The Depression ruined Japanese farmers and silk producers. Nationalists blamed party politicians and big business, and argued that Japan, short of raw materials and shut out of Western markets, needed an empire on the Asian mainland. Japan already ruled **Taiwan** (since 1895) and **Korea** (since 1910), and kept troops in southern **Manchuria** to guard its railway.

**Manchuria, 1931.** On **18 September 1931**, Japanese officers of the **Kwantung Army** blew up a stretch of their own railway near **Mukden** (Shenyang) and blamed Chinese troops. Without orders from Tokyo, the army conquered all Manchuria. In **1932** Japan set up the puppet state of **Manchukuo**, with the last Qing emperor, **Puyi**, as its figurehead. When the League of Nations' **Lytton Report** condemned the conquest, **Japan left the League (announced 1933)**.

**Government by assassination.** Young officers murdered a prime minister, **Inukai Tsuyoshi**, in May **1932**. A larger army rising in Tokyo on **26 February 1936** was put down, but it left the military stronger in government. Japan signed the **Anti-Comintern Pact** with Germany in November 1936.

**Full war with China, 1937.** A skirmish at the **Marco Polo Bridge** near Beijing on **7 July 1937** grew into full-scale war. Chinese forces fought hard for **Shanghai** from August to November 1937; Japan then advanced up the Yangtze to the Nationalist capital, **Nanjing**.

**The Nanjing massacre.** Japanese troops took **Nanjing on 13 December 1937**. For about six weeks they killed captured soldiers and civilians in great numbers and raped women and girls on a mass scale. A small group of foreigners, including the German businessman **John Rabe** and the American missionary teacher **Minnie Vautrin**, ran a **Safety Zone** that sheltered perhaps 200,000 people, and their diaries and letters are among the key sources.

**The numbers are disputed; the massacre is not.**

| Estimate | Source |
| --- | --- |
| **over 200,000** | the **Tokyo war crimes tribunal** (1946–48) |
| **300,000** | the figure of the Chinese government and the Nanjing memorial |
| **tens of thousands, around 40,000** | some Japanese historians, such as **Hata Ikuhiko** |

The range depends on how one counts: the area and period included, and whether disarmed soldiers are counted as massacre victims. Japanese nationalist writers who deny the massacre altogether are rejected by mainstream historians in Japan and elsewhere. **Tens of thousands of women were raped**, by most estimates.

**What came after.** China moved its capital up the Yangtze to **Chongqing** and kept fighting. Japan held the coast and the cities but could not end the war. Its army ran a biological warfare programme in Manchuria, **Unit 731**, which experimented on prisoners. In **Korea**, colonial rule hardened: Koreans were pressed to take Japanese names, and later conscripted for labour, and many women were forced into military brothels as so-called **"comfort women."**

**Turning south.** Japan's army also fought the Soviet Union, on the Mongolian border at **Khalkhin Gol (Nomonhan)** in **1939**, and was badly beaten by Soviet forces under **Georgy Zhukov**. **That defeat helped push Japan to expand south instead**, towards the oil and rubber of South-East Asia, and so towards war with Britain, the Netherlands and the United States.
The Spanish Civil War, 1936–1939:
Spain stayed out of the First World War, but it was divided between landowners and landless labourers, a powerful Catholic Church and fierce anticlericals, centralists and regions such as **Catalonia** and the **Basque Country** that wanted self-rule. In **April 1931** the king left and the **Second Republic** was proclaimed.

**The Republic's five years.** Governments of the left (1931–33) pushed land reform, cut the Church's role in education and gave Catalonia autonomy; a right-wing government (1933–35) undid much of it and crushed a miners' rising in **Asturias** in October 1934. In **February 1936** a **Popular Front** of left parties narrowly won the election. Political violence spread on both sides.

**The coup.** On **17–18 July 1936**, army officers rose against the Republic, starting in Spanish Morocco. **The coup half-failed**: it won much of the north and west, but in **Madrid, Barcelona** and most cities, workers' militias and loyal forces defeated it. A failed coup became a civil war. General **Francisco Franco**, commanding the army in Morocco, soon led the rebels, who called themselves **Nationalists**.

**A war the world joined:**

| Side | Help |
| --- | --- |
| **Nationalists** | **Nazi Germany** (aircraft and the **Condor Legion**) and **Fascist Italy** (tens of thousands of troops); German planes flew Franco's army across from Morocco |
| **Republicans** | the **Soviet Union** (tanks, aircraft, advisers, paid for with Spain's gold reserves); Mexico; the **International Brigades**, perhaps 35,000 volunteers from over fifty countries |
| **Britain and France** | a **Non-Intervention** policy, which in practice hurt the Republic most |

**Revolution inside the war.** In Republican Catalonia and Aragon, **anarchists** and other revolutionaries collectivised factories and farms in 1936, and attacked the Church: about **6,800 priests, monks and nuns were killed**, most of them in the first months.
