It circled the Earth every 96 minutes, broadcasting a beep anyone with a radio could hear. It went up on a version of the **R-7**, the world's first intercontinental ballistic missile, first flown successfully six weeks earlier. **The message was not lost: a rocket that could reach orbit could reach America.**

The American response was close to panic:
- **NASA** was founded (October 1958) to run a civilian space programme.
- The **National Defense Education Act (1958)** poured money into science teaching.
- The first US satellite, **Explorer 1**, went up on **31 January 1958**, using a rocket built by a team under **Wernher von Braun**, the former Nazi rocket engineer brought to America in 1945.

**The Soviet firsts:**

| Date | |
| --- | --- |
| November 1957 | **Laika**, a dog, the first animal in orbit (she died within hours) |
| 1959 | **Luna 2** hits the Moon; **Luna 3** photographs its far side |
| **12 April 1961** | **Yuri Gagarin**, the first human in space, orbits the Earth once in **108 minutes** |
| June 1963 | **Valentina Tereshkova**, the first woman in space |
| March 1965 | **Alexei Leonov** makes the first spacewalk |

Much of this was the work of one man, the chief designer **Sergei Korolev**, whose name was kept secret until his death in **January 1966**.

**The Moon.** Six weeks after Gagarin and a month after the Bay of Pigs, Kennedy asked Congress on **25 May 1961** to commit to "landing a man on the moon and returning him safely to the earth" "before this decade is out". **Apollo** came to employ about **400,000 people** at its peak and cost about **$25 billion** at the time.
- A fire killed three astronauts in **Apollo 1 (January 1967)**; the Soviet **Soyuz 1** crashed in April, killing Vladimir Komarov.
- **Apollo 8** orbited the Moon at Christmas **1968**.
- **Apollo 11**: **Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the Moon on 20 July 1969**, while Michael Collins circled above. Hundreds of millions watched on television.

Twelve men walked on the Moon in six landings; the last left in **December 1972**. The Soviet Moon rocket, the **N1**, exploded on all four of its launches.

**Others joined.** France (1965), Japan and **China (both 1970)** launched their own satellites; India's first, **Aryabhata (1975)**, went up on a Soviet rocket.

**How it ended.** In **July 1975** an American Apollo and a Soviet Soyuz **docked in orbit**, and their crews shook hands: détente in space. The race had also produced the **Outer Space Treaty (1967)**, banning nuclear weapons in orbit, and the satellites for weather, communications and navigation that the world now depends on.
The Vietnam War, 1955–1975:
The longest war of the Cold War, and the one the United States lost.

**Two Vietnams.** After Geneva (1954) the north was ruled by **Ho Chi Minh's** communists from Hanoi, the south by **Ngo Dinh Diem** from Saigon, a Catholic anti-communist backed by the US. Diem cancelled the 1956 elections, which Ho was expected to win. In **1960** southern communists, backed by Hanoi, formed the **National Liberation Front**, called the **Viet Cong** by its enemies. Diem's government was unpopular, and after Buddhist protests (a monk burned himself to death in Saigon in June 1963) his own generals **killed him in November 1963**, after the US had let them know it would not oppose a coup.

**The American war:**

| Date | |
| --- | --- |
| end of 1963 | about **16,000 US military advisers** |
| **August 1964** | reported attacks on US destroyers in the **Gulf of Tonkin** (the second attack almost certainly did not happen); Congress gives Johnson power to wage war |
| **March 1965** | sustained bombing of the North (**Rolling Thunder**) and the first US combat troops land at Da Nang |
| 1968–69 | US troops peak at over **half a million** |
| **30 January 1968** | the **Tet Offensive**: attacks on over 100 towns, even the US embassy in Saigon. A military defeat for the communists, but a political shock in America |
| March 1968 | US soldiers massacre about **500 villagers at My Lai** |
| 1969–72 | Nixon's **"Vietnamisation"**: US troops withdrawn while bombing widens to **Cambodia and Laos** |
| **27 January 1973** | **Paris Peace Accords**; the last US combat troops leave |
| **30 April 1975** | North Vietnamese tanks enter Saigon; the South surrenders |

**The cost.** About **58,000** Americans died. Vietnamese deaths are far less certain: from about **1 million to over 3 million**, soldiers and civilians, North and South (Vietnam's own figure is about 3 million). Some 800,000 or more "boat people" later fled by sea.

**Cambodia and Laos.** The war spread. In Cambodia, the **Khmer Rouge** under **Pol Pot** took **Phnom Penh on 17 April 1975**, emptied the cities and set out to build an agrarian communism from "Year Zero". About **1.5 to 2 million people**, close to a quarter of the population, died from execution, starvation and overwork before **Vietnam invaded and drove them out in January 1979**. Laos became communist in 1975.

**The arguments over the war.**
- **What kind of war was it?** One reading: a **war of national liberation**, a continuation of the fight against France, which the US misread as Soviet or Chinese expansion. The other: **North Vietnamese aggression** against a southern state with real anti-communist support, aided throughout by the USSR and China. Archives from Hanoi show the North **directed** the southern war; southern grievances against Diem were also real.
- **Could the US have won?** The **orthodox** view (most historians): no; no level of American force could build a government in Saigon that its people would fight for. The **revisionist** view (for example Mark Moyar, *Triumph Forsaken*, 2006): the war was winnable, and lost through errors such as abandoning Diem, or through Congress cutting aid after 1973.

What would settle it is what can never be tested: a different set of choices. **Note which question an author is answering**: whether the war was right, or whether it could have been won.
The civil rights movement in the United:
In fourteen years, black Americans in the South, through courts, boycotts, marches and votes, broke the legal system of segregation that had ruled the region since the 1890s.

**What they faced.** In the former slave states, **"Jim Crow" laws** separated black and white people in schools, buses, restaurants and cemeteries. Poll taxes, literacy tests and terror kept most black Southerners from voting: in Mississippi in the early 1960s, **fewer than 7%** of black adults were registered. Lynching had killed thousands since the 1880s.

**The milestones:**

| Date | |
| --- | --- |
| 1948 | Truman orders the **armed forces desegregated** |
| **17 May 1954** | ***Brown v. Board of Education***: the Supreme Court rules segregated schools unconstitutional, overturning "separate but equal" (1896) |
| August 1955 | **Emmett Till**, aged 14, murdered in Mississippi; his mother insists on an open coffin |
| **December 1955 – December 1956** | **Rosa Parks** refuses to give up her bus seat in **Montgomery, Alabama**; a 381-day bus boycott, led by a 26-year-old minister, **Martin Luther King Jr.**, wins |
| 1957 | **Little Rock, Arkansas**: Eisenhower sends paratroops to escort nine black students into a white high school |
| February 1960 | four students sit in at a whites-only lunch counter in **Greensboro, North Carolina**; sit-ins spread across the South |
| 1961 | the **Freedom Rides** on interstate buses, met by mobs in Alabama |
| 1963 | **Birmingham, Alabama**: police turn fire hoses and dogs on children; **the March on Washington (28 August)**, about 250,000 people, King's "I have a dream" speech |
| **2 July 1964** | the **Civil Rights Act** outlaws segregation in public places and discrimination in employment |
| **7 March 1965** | **"Bloody Sunday"** at **Selma, Alabama**: marchers beaten on the Edmund Pettus Bridge |
| **6 August 1965** | the **Voting Rights Act**; black registration in the South rises fast |
| **4 April 1968** | King assassinated in **Memphis** |

**The movement was not one thing.** King's **non-violence**, drawing on Christian teaching and **Gandhi**, was one strand. Student activists of **SNCC** organised in the most dangerous counties. **Malcolm X** (killed in **February 1965**) and, from 1966, **"Black Power"** argued for self-defence and black pride, especially in the cities of the North, where segregation was by housing and jobs, not law.

**The Cold War link.** **Mary Dudziak** (*Cold War Civil Rights*, 2000) showed that American leaders knew Soviet propaganda used every lynching and school riot to win over newly independent Africa and Asia. Segregation was a foreign-policy liability, and that helped push Washington to act.

**Who made the change?** One reading credits **national leaders and courts**: the Supreme Court, Kennedy and especially **Lyndon Johnson**, who drove the laws through Congress. The other, now dominant among historians, credits **local, grass-roots organising**, often by women and the young, which forced national leaders to act. **Jacquelyn Dowd Hall** and others speak of a **"long civil rights movement"** reaching back to the 1930s and forward past 1968. The evidence of the bills' timing supports both: the laws followed the marches, but needed the votes.

**Its reach.** The movement inspired others worldwide, from Catholic civil rights marchers in **Northern Ireland (1968)** to campaigners against apartheid.
Apartheid South Africa, 1948–1990, in br:
South Africa is taught in depth in the South African Politics curriculum. Here is its place in the world story of these decades.

**Apartheid, "separateness", was the opposite of the age's trend.** As colonies across Africa won independence, South Africa's white minority, about a fifth of the population, built a stricter system of racial rule.

**The National Party** won the whites-only election of **May 1948** under **D. F. Malan**. Its laws, in the first years:
- the **Population Registration Act (1950)**, classifying everyone by race;
- the **Group Areas Act (1950)**, assigning each race its own residential areas, and forcing out those in the "wrong" one;
- **Bantu Education (1953)**, a deliberately inferior schooling for black children;
- tightened **pass laws**, controlling where black people could live and work.

From the **1960s** the government set up ten **"homelands"** and declared four of them "independent", stripping millions of their South African citizenship. **About 3.5 million people** were forcibly moved between 1960 and the early 1980s (the figure of the Surplus People Project).

**Resistance and repression:**

| Date | |
| --- | --- |
| 1955 | the **Freedom Charter**, adopted at Kliptown: "South Africa belongs to all who live in it" |
| **21 March 1960** | **Sharpeville**: police kill **69** people protesting the pass laws; the ANC and PAC are banned |
| 1961 | the ANC turns to armed struggle (**Umkhonto we Sizwe**); South Africa leaves the Commonwealth and becomes a republic |
| 1964 | **Nelson Mandela** and others sentenced to life at the **Rivonia trial** |
| **16 June 1976** | **Soweto**: police fire on schoolchildren protesting against teaching in Afrikaans; hundreds die in the months of unrest that follow |
| 1977 | **Steve Biko**, of the Black Consciousness movement, dies in police custody; the UN imposes an arms embargo |

**The world's part.** The **UN** condemned apartheid from the 1950s; the newly independent African states made it their cause. Western governments were slower: South Africa was rich, anti-communist and sold gold and strategic minerals. Sports and cultural **boycotts** grew from the 1960s, and economic **sanctions** came in the 1980s (the US Congress passed them over Reagan's veto in **1986**).

**The regional war.** As Portugal's empire fell in **1975**, South Africa fought Cuban-backed governments and guerrillas in **Angola** and **Namibia**, which it occupied. After the battles around **Cuito Cuanavale (1987–88)**, negotiations led to Cuban withdrawal and **Namibia's independence (21 March 1990)**.

**The end.** On **2 February 1990** President **F. W. de Klerk** lifted the bans on the ANC and other movements; **Mandela walked free on 11 February 1990**. Negotiations led to the first democratic election on **27 April 1994**. Why the regime gave way when it did (sanctions, the economy, township revolt, the end of the Soviet threat) is argued in the South African Politics curriculum.
The Arab–Israeli wars and the oil shocks:
Two wars in the Middle East, and the oil weapon used after the second, ended the long post-war boom in the West.

**The Six-Day War (5–10 June 1967).** After Nasser closed the **Straits of Tiran** to Israeli shipping and moved troops into Sinai, Israel struck first. In six days it took the **Sinai and Gaza** from Egypt, the **West Bank and East Jerusalem** from Jordan, and the **Golan Heights** from Syria. About **a quarter of a million more Palestinians** became refugees. **UN Resolution 242** (November 1967) called for Israeli withdrawal from territories occupied in exchange for peace and recognition. Whether Israel's first strike was pre-emption against a real threat or a war of choice is debated; most historians agree that neither side's leaders fully planned what happened.

**The Yom Kippur War, or Ramadan War (6–25 October 1973).** Egypt under **Anwar Sadat** and Syria attacked on the Jewish holy day. Israel was surprised, then recovered with a massive American airlift. Both superpowers went on alert before a ceasefire held.

**The oil weapon.** **OPEC**, founded at **Baghdad in September 1960** by Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela, had been gaining control of prices from the Western oil companies. In **October 1973** the Arab members **cut production** and placed an **embargo on the United States and the Netherlands** for supporting Israel. It lasted until **March 1974**.

**The price of oil roughly quadrupled, from about $3 to about $12 a barrel.**

**The second shock (1979).** The **Iranian revolution** cut Iran's output, and panic buying did the rest: the price **more than doubled** by 1980.

**The effects:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **In the West** | **"stagflation"**, rising prices and rising unemployment together, which the post-war economics had said could not happen; queues at petrol stations; the end of the boom that had run since about 1950 |
| **In the oil states** | vast wealth: Saudi Arabia, the Gulf and Iran built cities, armies and welfare states |
| **For the poorest countries** | crushing import bills |
| **The petrodollars** | oil money, deposited in Western banks, was lent to **Latin American and African governments**. When interest rates rose sharply after 1979, **Mexico declared it could not pay in August 1982**, starting a **debt crisis** and a "lost decade" across Latin America |
| **The long reply** | new oil from **the North Sea and Alaska**; more efficient cars and factories, led by Japan |

**Did the embargo cause the price rise?** One reading: yes, OPEC used its power as a political weapon. Another stresses **markets**: US oil production had peaked in **1970**, demand was soaring, and price controls in America worsened the shortages. Most economists combine the two: the embargo struck a tight market.

**Peace on one front.** Sadat flew to **Jerusalem in November 1977**. At **Camp David (September 1978)**, with President Carter, Sadat and **Menachem Begin** agreed the terms, and the **Egypt–Israel peace treaty (March 1979)** returned Sinai to Egypt. Sadat was **assassinated by Islamist soldiers in October 1981**.
The Iranian revolution, 1979:
In 1979 a mass revolution overthrew one of America's closest allies and set up the first modern state ruled by clerics. Almost no one had predicted it.

**Background: oil and the coup of 1953.** In **1951** Iran's elected prime minister, **Mohammad Mosaddegh**, nationalised the British-owned **Anglo-Iranian Oil Company**. In **August 1953** a coup organised by the **CIA and British intelligence** overthrew him and restored the power of the young shah, **Mohammad Reza Pahlavi**. The CIA's role, long known, was officially acknowledged in documents released in **2013**. Many Iranians never forgot it.

**The shah's Iran (1953–1978).**
- The **White Revolution (1963)**: land reform, votes for women, literacy campaigns.
- Oil money, above all after **1973**, paid for fast growth, a large army and lavish spectacle.
- Political parties were suppressed, and the secret police, **SAVAK**, used torture.
- A cleric, **Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini**, who denounced the reforms and American influence, was exiled in **1964**, and preached from Iraq and, from 1978, France. His sermons spread on **cassette tapes**.

**The revolution (1978–79).**

| Date | |
| --- | --- |
| January 1978 | protests in Qom after a newspaper attack on Khomeini; deaths, then mourning protests every forty days, in the Shia custom |
| **8 September 1978** | **"Black Friday"**: troops fire on crowds in Tehran |
| autumn 1978 | strikes, including in the **oil fields**; marches of millions |
| **16 January 1979** | the **shah leaves Iran** |
| **1 February 1979** | **Khomeini returns** to a vast crowd in Tehran |
| 11 February | the army declares itself neutral; the old regime falls |
| March–April 1979 | a referendum makes Iran an **Islamic Republic** |
| December 1979 | a constitution based on **velayat-e faqih**, rule by the senior Islamic jurist, with Khomeini as Supreme Leader |

**A coalition, then a takeover.** The revolution was made by an alliance of clerics, bazaar merchants, students, liberals, nationalists and communist and Islamic-left groups. Within about three years Khomeini's followers had **crushed or executed their former allies**.

**The hostage crisis.** On **4 November 1979** students seized the **US embassy**; **52 Americans were held for 444 days**, released on **20 January 1981**, minutes after Carter left office.

**The Iran–Iraq war (September 1980 – August 1988).** **Saddam Hussein** of Iraq invaded, expecting a quick win against a state in chaos. It became an eight-year war of trenches, human-wave attacks and **Iraqi poison gas**, killing **hundreds of thousands** (estimates commonly run from about 500,000 upward), and ended where it began.

**Why it happened is argued.** Explanations stress **too-fast, uneven modernisation**; **oil-boom inflation** and inequality after 1973; the shah's **dependence on America**; the organising power of the **mosque network**; or Khomeini's **leadership**. **Charles Kurzman** (*The Unthinkable Revolution*, 2004) argued that each of these explains less than it seems, and that the revolution grew as **people came to believe it could succeed**, which is why no one foresaw it.

**Its reach.** The same year, militants **seized the Grand Mosque in Mecca** (November 1979) and the USSR invaded Afghanistan: **1979 is often taken as the year political Islam entered world politics in force**.
The Soviet–Afghan war, 1979–1989:
The USSR invaded Afghanistan to save a communist government and stayed for nine years. It was the Soviet Union's Vietnam, and it had long consequences for the world.

**How it began.** Afghanistan, a landlocked, mostly rural kingdom between the USSR, Iran and Pakistan, had taken aid from both superpowers. In **1973** **Mohammed Daoud** overthrew his cousin the king. In **April 1978** the communist **People's Democratic Party** killed Daoud and seized power (the **Saur Revolution**). Its land reforms, attacks on religion and mass arrests set off revolts across the country, and its own factions fought each other: **Hafizullah Amin** had the president, Taraki, killed in **October 1979**.

**The invasion.** Fearing that Afghanistan would fall to Islamist rebels or turn to the West, the Soviet leadership sent in troops on **24–27 December 1979**. Soviet special forces **killed Amin** and installed **Babrak Karmal**.

**The war.** The Soviets held the cities and roads; the resistance, the **mujahideen**, "those who wage jihad", held the mountains and villages.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Soviet troops** | about **100,000** at a time; over 600,000 served in all |
| **Their backers** | the **US** (through the CIA, by way of **Pakistan's intelligence service**, the ISI), **Saudi Arabia**, which matched US money, China, and others |
| **Weapons** | from **1986**, American **Stinger** missiles that shot down Soviet helicopters |
| **Foreign volunteers** | a few thousand Arab fighters, among them a young Saudi, **Osama bin Laden** |

**The costs.** About **15,000 Soviet soldiers** died. Afghan deaths are estimated at about **1 million** (estimates run from about 500,000 to 2 million), and about **5 to 6 million refugees** fled, mostly to **Pakistan and Iran**: perhaps a third of the population.

**The withdrawal.** **Gorbachev** called the war a **"bleeding wound" (1986)**. Under the **Geneva Accords (April 1988)** the Soviets left; the last troops crossed the bridge at Termez on **15 February 1989**. The communist government of **Najibullah** held out until **1992**. Then the mujahideen fought each other, and the **Taliban** took Kabul in **1996** (Stage 12).

**The arguments.**
- **Did the Stingers win the war?** One reading: yes, they broke Soviet air power and forced the decision to leave. Another: the Politburo had **decided to withdraw in late 1985 or 1986**, before Stingers mattered, for reasons of cost and Gorbachev's wider reforms. Soviet archives tend to support the second, but the debate continues.
- **"Blowback."** Did arming the mujahideen create the jihadist movement that later struck the US? Critics say the CIA's money fed the most radical groups through the ISI. Defenders reply that the CIA did not fund the Arab volunteers like bin Laden, and that **al-Qaeda** (founded about **1988**) grew from other roots. Both claims rest on partial evidence.

**Its effects.** The war **weakened the Soviet army's prestige and the regime's legitimacy at home**, sent veterans and refugees across the region, made Pakistan a front-line state, and trained a generation of fighters who would reappear in the 1990s.
Latin America's dictatorships, 1954–1990:
From the 1950s to the 1980s most of Latin America was ruled at some point by soldiers, often with American support, in the name of saving their countries from communism.

**Guatemala, 1954.** **Jacobo Árbenz**, elected president in **1950**, began a land reform (1952) that took unused land, including much belonging to the American **United Fruit Company**. In **June 1954** a small invasion of exiles organised by the **CIA** frightened the army into abandoning him. The military regimes that followed fought a **civil war (1960–1996)** that killed about **200,000** people. A UN-backed truth commission (1999) found that the army had committed **acts of genocide** against Maya communities.

**The Cuban effect.** After **1959** Washington feared "another Cuba". Kennedy's **Alliance for Progress (1961)** offered aid and reform; at the same time the US trained Latin American officers in counter-insurgency. Guerrilla movements inspired by Cuba spread; **Che Guevara** was killed in **Bolivia in October 1967**.

**The wave of coups:**

| Country | Military or dictatorial rule |
| --- | --- |
| **Paraguay** | General Stroessner, **1954–1989** |
| **Brazil** | army coup **1964**; military rule until **1985** |
| **Uruguay** | 1973–1985 |
| **Chile** | **11 September 1973**; Pinochet until **1990** |
| **Argentina** | **24 March 1976 – 1983** |

**Chile.** **Salvador Allende**, a Marxist, was elected president in **1970** with **36.6%** of the vote, and nationalised the copper mines. Nixon ordered the CIA to undermine him, and his economy fell into inflation and shortages. On **11 September 1973** the army under **General Augusto Pinochet** bombed the presidential palace; **Allende killed himself** inside. Official commissions later counted about **3,000 dead or disappeared** and about **38,000** survivors of political imprisonment and torture. Pinochet's economists, the **"Chicago Boys"**, imposed free-market reforms. He lost a **plebiscite in October 1988** and handed over power in **March 1990**.

**Argentina.** The junta's **"Dirty War"** against the left kidnapped, tortured and **"disappeared"** people, many dropped alive from planes into the sea. The truth commission's report, ***Nunca Más*** (1984), documented about **9,000**; human-rights groups estimate up to **30,000**. From **1977** the **Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo** marched weekly for their missing children. The junta's invasion of the British **Falkland Islands (April 1982)** ended in defeat in June, and the regime fell.

**Central America in the 1980s.** In **Nicaragua** the **Sandinistas** overthrew the Somoza dictatorship in **July 1979**; the Reagan administration funded the **Contra** rebels against them. In **El Salvador**, a civil war (**1980–1992**) between a US-backed government and leftist guerrillas killed about **75,000**; Archbishop **Óscar Romero** was shot dead while saying Mass in **March 1980**.

**How much did Washington drive it?** One reading puts the **US** at the centre: it trained the officers, funded the coups and covered up the crimes. Another stresses **local actors**: Latin American armies, elites and middle classes who feared revolution acted on their own, and the US often followed. Declassified US documents (many released since the 1990s) show **deep American involvement in Guatemala and Chile**, and much less direct control elsewhere. Most historians now hold both.
Deng Xiaoping's reforms and Tiananmen, 1:
In 1978 China began the economic changes that made it, within a generation, the world's workshop. In 1989 its leaders showed where the political limits lay.

**After Mao.** Mao died on **9 September 1976**; the **Gang of Four** were arrested in **October**. **Deng Xiaoping**, purged twice and twice rehabilitated, outmanoeuvred Mao's chosen successor, Hua Guofeng, and by the **Third Plenum of December 1978** was the real leader. He never held the top formal title. His slogan was to "**seek truth from facts**", and his attitude was summed up in a saying he had used since the 1960s: it does not matter whether a cat is black or white, so long as it catches mice.

**The reforms, step by step:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The countryside** | in **Xiaogang village, Anhui, in late 1978**, farmers secretly divided the collective land into family plots. The party saw harvests rise and, as the **household responsibility system**, spread it across China by the early 1980s. The communes were dissolved |
| **Special Economic Zones (1980)** | **Shenzhen**, next to Hong Kong, and three others opened to foreign investment and exports. Shenzhen grew from a small town to a city of millions |
| **Opening** | full **diplomatic relations with the US (1 January 1979)**; Deng toured America weeks later |
| **The one-child policy (from 1980)** | enforced with fines and often forced abortions and sterilisations |

**Growth averaged close to 10% a year** through the 1980s and beyond, and hundreds of millions of people were eventually lifted out of extreme poverty. The reforms also brought **inflation, corruption** and resentment of officials' families getting rich.

**Who drove reform?** One reading credits **Deng and the leaders** in Beijing. Another, argued for example by **Kate Xiao Zhou** (*How the Farmers Changed China*, 1996), holds that **farmers moved first**, as in Xiaogang, and the party mostly approved what was already happening. The evidence suggests both: local experiments, then central decisions that let them spread.

**Political limits.** In **1978–79** posters on Beijing's **"Democracy Wall"** called for freedom; the electrician **Wei Jingsheng** demanded a "fifth modernisation", democracy, and was jailed for fifteen years.

**Tiananmen (April–June 1989).** When the reformist former party chief **Hu Yaobang** died on **15 April 1989**, students gathered in **Tiananmen Square** to mourn him and stayed to protest against corruption and for freedom of speech. At their height the protests drew **a million people** in Beijing, and spread to many other cities. Students went on hunger strike while **Gorbachev visited in May**. The party leader **Zhao Ziyang**, who visited the hunger strikers, was purged and kept under house arrest until his death in 2005. Martial law was declared on **20 May**. On the night of **3–4 June** the army fought its way into the centre of Beijing.

**How many died is not known.** The government gave about 200 to 300; other estimates run from **several hundred to several thousand**. The archives that would settle it are closed, and in China the subject is still censored.

**The lesson the party drew**, unlike the one drawn in Moscow: **economic opening without political opening**. Deng restarted reform on his **"southern tour" of 1992** (Stage 12).
Japan's miracle and the Asian tigers:
In 1945 Japan lay in ruins and South Korea was among the poorest countries on Earth. By 1990 they, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore were rich. How it happened is one of the great arguments of economic history.

**Japan.** Under **American occupation (1945–1952)**, led by General **Douglas MacArthur**:
- a new **constitution (1947)** kept the emperor as a symbol, gave women the vote, and in **Article 9** renounced war;
- **land reform** turned tenants into owners;
- the great industrial combines were partly broken up.

Then the **Korean War** brought American orders. From the mid-1950s to **1973**, Japan's economy grew at about **10% a year**. The **bullet train** and the **Tokyo Olympics** (both **1964**) announced its return; by **1968** it was the world's **second-largest economy**. Cars, steel, ships, cameras and electronics flooded world markets. The ministry of trade and industry (**MITI**) steered credit and protected key industries.

**The four tigers:**

| | How it rose |
| --- | --- |
| **South Korea** | General **Park Chung-hee** took power in **1961** and drove exports through huge family firms, the ***chaebol*** (Samsung, Hyundai), with cheap state credit and tight discipline. Park was assassinated in **1979**; the army killed protesters at **Gwangju (May 1980)**; mass protests won **democracy in 1987** |
| **Taiwan** | the Nationalist government, under **martial law (1949–1987)**, carried out land reform and grew through thousands of small export firms, later electronics |
| **Hong Kong** | a British colony swollen by refugees from China; free trade, textiles and later finance. The **Sino-British Joint Declaration (1984)** set its return to China for 1997 |
| **Singapore** | expelled from Malaysia, it became independent on **9 August 1965**. **Lee Kuan Yew** built a clean, strict, one-party-dominant state that invited in foreign companies |

**What they shared.** High savings and investment, **heavy spending on education**, export-led growth, land reform in Japan, Korea and Taiwan, American markets and aid, and, for most of the period, **authoritarian governments**.

**Why did it work? The strongest readings:**
- **The market reading:** they succeeded by **exporting into world markets**, with stable money and open trade, unlike countries that protected themselves behind tariffs.
- **The developmental-state reading:** **Chalmers Johnson** (*MITI and the Japanese Miracle*, 1982), **Alice Amsden** (*Asia's Next Giant*, 1989) and **Robert Wade** (*Governing the Market*, 1990) argued that the **state picked industries, directed credit and disciplined firms**, deliberately "getting prices wrong".
- The **World Bank**'s *East Asian Miracle* (1993) took a middle path: mostly sound basics, some intervention that worked.
- **Paul Krugman** ("The Myth of Asia's Miracle", 1994) argued growth came mostly from **more inputs**, more workers, schooling and machines, not rising efficiency, so it would slow.

**What would settle it:** careful measurement of productivity, and comparison with countries that tried the same policies and failed. That work goes on. Meanwhile **ASEAN**, founded in **1967**, and later Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia, followed in the tigers' path, and so, from 1978, did China.
The European Community, 1950–1992:
Western Europe, which had fought two world wars in thirty years, bound its old enemies together by trade, law and shared institutions.

**The idea.** On **9 May 1950** the French foreign minister **Robert Schuman**, with a plan drafted by **Jean Monnet**, proposed pooling French and German **coal and steel**, the materials of war, under a common authority, so that war between them would become "not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible". The day is still celebrated as Europe Day.

**The building blocks:**

| Date | |
| --- | --- |
| 1951 | **Treaty of Paris**: the **European Coal and Steel Community**, six members: **France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg** |
| 1954 | a European army (the European Defence Community) is **rejected by the French parliament** |
| **25 March 1957** | **Treaty of Rome**: the **European Economic Community** (a customs union and common market) and Euratom, from 1 January 1958 |
| 1962 | the **Common Agricultural Policy**, which for decades took most of the budget |
| 1963 and 1967 | **de Gaulle vetoes British entry** |
| **1973** | **Britain, Ireland and Denmark** join; Norway's voters say no |
| 1979 | first direct elections to the **European Parliament** |
| 1981; 1986 | **Greece**; then **Spain and Portugal** |
| 1986 | the **Single European Act**: a **single market** by the end of 1992 |
| **February 1992** | the **Maastricht Treaty** creates the **European Union** (in force 1993) and plans a single currency |

**Democracy in the south.** Spain, Portugal and Greece had been dictatorships. Portugal's army overthrew the regime on **25 April 1974** (the **Carnation Revolution**), which also ended its African empire; Greece's colonels fell in **July 1974**; **Franco** died in **November 1975**. **Joining the Community anchored all three as democracies**, a pattern repeated after 1989 in the east.

**The other half.** The communist states had their own bloc, **Comecon (1949)**, which coordinated economies under Soviet direction but never became a common market. Britain and others outside the EEC formed the looser **European Free Trade Association (1960)**.

**Why did integration happen? The strongest readings:**
- **The idealist reading:** visionaries such as Monnet and Schuman, scarred by war, built a new kind of union step by step, each step creating pressure for the next.
- **Alan Milward** (*The European Rescue of the Nation-State*, 1992): governments joined to **strengthen their own nation-states**, securing growth, farm incomes and welfare they could not secure alone.
- **Andrew Moravcsik** (*The Choice for Europe*, 1998): each big step was a **bargain between national governments** driven by economic interests, especially those of France and Germany.
- **The Cold War reading:** the US pushed integration, through the Marshall Plan's demands for cooperation, to strengthen Europe against the Soviet bloc.

They are not exclusive. What tests them is the archival record of each negotiation, where national interest and idealism can be weighed case by case.
Gorbachev and the revolutions of 1989:
In one year, the communist governments of eastern Europe fell, and, apart from Romania, almost without bloodshed. The man who made it possible had meant to save communism.

**Earlier risings, crushed.** East Germany (**June 1953**); **Hungary (October–November 1956)**, where Soviet tanks killed about 2,500 Hungarians and some 200,000 fled; and the **Prague Spring of 1968**, "socialism with a human face", ended by a Warsaw Pact invasion in **August 1968**. The **Brezhnev Doctrine** said the bloc would intervene to keep any member socialist. In **Poland** the independent trade union **Solidarity**, founded in the **Gdańsk** shipyards in **August 1980** under **Lech Wałęsa**, gained about **10 million members** before **martial law** suppressed it in **December 1981**.

**Gorbachev.** By the 1980s the Soviet economy was stagnant, the war in Afghanistan was unwinnable, and arms spending with Reagan's America was ruinous. Three elderly leaders died between **1982 and 1985**. **Mikhail Gorbachev**, aged 54, became general secretary on **11 March 1985**. His programme:
- **perestroika**, restructuring the economy;
- **glasnost**, openness, which the cover-up of the **Chernobyl** reactor explosion (**26 April 1986**) made urgent;
- **"new thinking"** abroad: the **INF Treaty (December 1987)** abolished a whole class of nuclear missiles, and in a speech to the **UN in December 1988** he announced troop cuts and said every nation must have **freedom of choice**.

**1989, country by country:**

| Country | |
| --- | --- |
| **Poland** | round-table talks with Solidarity; in partly free elections on **4 June**, Solidarity wins almost every seat it may contest. A non-communist prime minister in August |
| **Hungary** | reformist communists **open the border with Austria**, cutting the fence in May, letting East Germans out in September |
| **East Germany** | mass flight; **Monday demonstrations** in Leipzig (70,000 on 9 October); Honecker removed. On **9 November** a confused announcement leads crowds to the crossings, and **the Berlin Wall opens** |
| **Bulgaria** | the leader of 35 years, **Todor Zhivkov**, removed on 10 November |
| **Czechoslovakia** | the **Velvet Revolution** from 17 November; the playwright **Václav Havel** elected president on **29 December** |
| **Romania** | the only violent one: from **Timișoara (16 December)** to Bucharest; **Nicolae and Elena Ceaușescu shot on 25 December**; about **1,100** dead |

**Germany reunited on 3 October 1990.**

**Why did Moscow let them go?** Gorbachev's spokesman joked about a **"Sinatra Doctrine"**: let them do it their way. The readings:
- **Gorbachev's choice:** he refused to use force, out of conviction, and the regimes, stripped of the Soviet guarantee, collapsed.
- **Western pressure**: Reagan's arms build-up and support for dissidents left Moscow unable to compete.
- **People power:** the crowds, the churches, Solidarity and the dissidents made the revolutions.
- **Bankruptcy:** the bloc was deep in debt to Western banks and could not pay for its own survival.

Most historians combine them. The test: compare 1989 with **Tiananmen, the same year**, where the leadership chose force.
The end of the Soviet Union, 1991:
On **25 December 1991** Mikhail Gorbachev resigned and the red flag was lowered over the Kremlin. The USSR, a superpower of 290 million people, broke into fifteen states without a major war among them.

**The nations awake.** Glasnost let long-suppressed grievances be spoken. The USSR's fifteen republics were nominally sovereign; their peoples now took it literally.
- **Nagorno-Karabakh (from 1988)**: Armenians and Azerbaijanis fought over the Armenian-majority enclave, and there were pogroms.
- **Tbilisi (April 1989)**: Soviet troops killed about twenty Georgian protesters.
- The **Baltic Way (23 August 1989)**: some 2 million Estonians, Latvians and Lithuanians joined hands in a line across the three republics, on the fiftieth anniversary of the Nazi–Soviet Pact that had led to their annexation.
- **Lithuania declared independence on 11 March 1990**. In **January 1991** Soviet troops killed fourteen people at the Vilnius television tower.

**Two rivals in Moscow.** Gorbachev had ended the party's monopoly of power (**1990**) but would not abandon the Union. **Boris Yeltsin**, a party boss turned radical, was elected chairman of Russia's parliament in **1990** and, on **12 June 1991**, **president of Russia** by popular vote, an authority Gorbachev never had. In a **referendum in March 1991**, about **three quarters** of those voting backed a renewed union, though six republics boycotted it.

**The August coup.** On **19 August 1991**, the day before a new treaty loosening the Union was to be signed, hard-liners including the heads of the KGB and the army put Gorbachev under house arrest at his holiday home at **Foros, in Crimea**. Crowds gathered at Russia's parliament, the **White House**; **Yeltsin climbed onto a tank** to denounce the coup; key army units would not fire. **It collapsed in three days**; three young men were killed.

**The end:**

| Date | |
| --- | --- |
| August–September 1991 | the Baltic states win recognition; **Ukraine declares independence (24 August)** |
| **1 December 1991** | **Ukraine's referendum**: about **90%** for independence |
| **8 December** | **Belovezha Accords**: the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus declare the USSR at an end, and form a **Commonwealth of Independent States** |
| 21 December | eleven republics join the Commonwealth at **Alma-Ata** |
| **25 December** | Gorbachev resigns |

**Why did it collapse? The strongest readings:**
- **The economic reading:** central planning could not keep up with the information age; falling oil prices after 1986 emptied the treasury. **Stephen Kotkin** (*Armageddon Averted*, 2001) stresses a system already in terminal decline.
- **The Gorbachev reading:** a system that could have lasted for decades, as China's did, was **broken by its reformer**, whose half-reforms wrecked the old economy without building a new one, and whose glasnost destroyed belief in the party. **Vladislav Zubok** (*Collapse*, 2021) argues this.
- **The nationalities reading:** the republics, Ukraine above all, broke it apart. **Serhii Plokhy** (*The Last Empire*, 2014) shows that Ukraine's vote was decisive, and that **President Bush wanted the Union to survive**: in Kyiv on **1 August 1991** he warned against "a suicidal nationalism based upon ethnic hatred".
- **The Western-pressure reading:** Reagan's arms race and support for the Afghan resistance broke the Soviet budget.

What would settle it is a counterfactual: whether a different leader could have reformed the USSR without ending it. **China after 1989 is the case each side cites.**
Connections: the world at the end of the:
The stage closes in **1991**: one superpower left, nearly a hundred new states, and a world economy about to join together. Here is how its threads ran.

**Who fought whom, mostly through others.** The superpowers never fought each other directly. Instead the Cold War was fought by **proxy**, in places that had just become independent or were trying to:

| Where | Backed by the US side | Backed by the Soviet side |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Korea, 1950–53** | South Korea, UN forces | North Korea, China |
| **Vietnam, 1955–75** | South Vietnam | North Vietnam, the NLF |
| **Angola, 1975–2002** | UNITA (with South Africa) | MPLA (with Cuban troops) |
| **The Horn of Africa, 1977–78** | Somalia, after it switched sides | Ethiopia's Marxist **Derg**, with Cubans |
| **Afghanistan, 1979–89** | the mujahideen | the Kabul government and Soviet army |
| **Central America, 1980s** | El Salvador's government, the Contras | the Sandinistas, Salvadoran guerrillas |

**What moved across the world.**
- **Arms**: the superpowers and their allies armed both sides of dozens of wars.
- **Ideas**: Marxism in its Soviet, Maoist and Cuban forms; anti-colonial nationalism and pan-Africanism; Fanon; non-violence, from Gandhi to King; political Islam after 1979; human rights after Helsinki (1975).
- **Money and goods**: the dollar system; oil and petrodollars; the **shipping container** (first used in 1956), which cut the cost of moving goods around the world; Japanese and then Asian exports.
- **People**: partition's migrants; Palestinian refugees; migrants from former colonies to Britain (the *Empire Windrush*, **1948**), France and the Netherlands; Turkish workers to West Germany; the boat people.
- **Food**: the **Green Revolution** of the 1960s, high-yield wheat and rice, saved India and Mexico from expected famines.

**What changed in forty-six years.**
- The **UN grew from 51 members to over 160**. The European empires were gone, except in fragments.
- World population roughly **doubled**, from about 2.5 billion in 1950 to about **5.4 billion in 1991**.
- Life expectancy rose across most of the world, and **smallpox was eradicated (1980)**.
- The world was **divided less by empire than by wealth**: a rich North, the rising East Asian economies, and a South often in debt.

**What carries over into Stage 12.**
1. **One superpower.** The US stood alone; the **Gulf War (1990–91)**, which drove Iraq out of Kuwait under a UN mandate, looked like the model of a new order.
2. **New wars at the edges of the old empires**: Yugoslavia began to break up in **1991**; Soviet successor states quarrelled over borders and minorities.
3. **China's rise**, built on Deng's reforms and the political line drawn at Tiananmen.
4. **Political Islam**, from Iran's revolution and the Afghan war.
5. **The networked world**: ARPANET (**1969**) grew into the internet, and **Tim Berners-Lee** at CERN made the first **World Wide Web** site public in **1991**.
6. **The Middle East's unfinished business**: Palestinians, Israel and their neighbours met at the **Madrid Conference (October 1991)**.

**Look back at the whole stage:** two superpowers, armed to destroy the world, did not use their weapons on each other, while new states across Africa and Asia fought for, won and struggled to use their independence. The questions that run through it, **who started the Cold War, why the empires ended, and why the Soviet Union fell**, are still argued from archives that are still opening.
Map: the world in 1991:
Where everyone stood in the year the Cold War ended. Every later lesson in this stage starts from this map.

**The Soviet Union ended on 26 December 1991.** Gorbachev had resigned the day before, and fifteen republics became independent states: Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, the three Baltic states, Moldova, the three Caucasus states and five in Central Asia. Germany had reunified in October 1990. The Warsaw Pact dissolved in July 1991. In a few months the second superpower was gone, and **the United States was the only one left**.

**The world, region by region, at the start of 1992:**

| Region | Where things stood |
| --- | --- |
| **North America** | the US had just led a coalition of about 35 states to expel Iraq from Kuwait (January–February 1991), under a UN Security Council mandate |
| **Europe** | the West was about to sign the Maastricht Treaty (February 1992); the East was leaving communism; **Yugoslavia had begun to break apart** (June 1991) |
| **Russia and the former USSR** | a new Russia under Boris Yeltsin, launching rapid market reform into a collapsing economy |
| **The Near East and North Africa** | Iraq defeated but Saddam Hussein still in power; the Madrid peace conference on Israel and the Arabs (October 1991) |
| **Sub-Saharan Africa** | one-party states and military regimes under pressure to hold elections; **South Africa negotiating the end of apartheid**; civil war in Somalia; Rwanda already at war (since 1990) |
| **South Asia** | **India in a balance-of-payments crisis**, about to open its economy (July 1991) |
| **East Asia** | China recovering its growth after the Tiananmen killings of June 1989; Japan's asset bubble bursting (from 1990–91), beginning its "lost decade"; South Korea and Taiwan newly democratic |
| **South-East Asia** | the "tiger" economies booming; the Paris accords to end Cambodia's war (October 1991) |
| **Latin America** | almost every state now an elected democracy after the military regimes of the 1970s–80s; debt crisis giving way to free-market reform |
| **Oceania** | Australia and New Zealand turning their trade towards Asia |

**Three facts about this map that the stage turns on:**

1. **About 5.4 billion people** lived on Earth in 1991 (UN estimates); by 2022 there were 8 billion. Most of the growth was in Asia and Africa.
2. **Most of humanity was poor.** By the World Bank's measure, more than a third of the world lived in extreme poverty around 1990, most of them in China and India.
3. **The internet barely existed for the public.** The first website went online at CERN, near Geneva, in 1991.

**A warning about the word "now".** This stage covers events whose endings are not known. Lessons on matters still unfolding are stamped **as of November 2026**, and say what is settled and what is not. Treat those parts as a snapshot, to be checked against later sources.
The end of history? Fukuyama and Hunting:
Two American political scientists offered the two most famous guesses about what the post-Cold War world would be. Both are still argued over, and the argument is a good way into the whole stage.

**Francis Fukuyama: "The End of History?" (1989).** In an essay in *The National Interest* in summer 1989, expanded into *The End of History and the Last Man* (1992), Fukuyama argued that with communism's failure, **liberal democracy combined with a market economy had no serious ideological rival left**. He meant "history" in the sense of the German philosopher Hegel: the long contest of ideas about how to organise society. Events would go on happening; what had ended, he said, was the search for a better system.

**He did not say nothing more would happen.** That is the commonest misreading. He also worried, in the "last man" half of the book, that a comfortable liberal world might leave people restless for recognition and struggle.

**Samuel Huntington: "The Clash of Civilizations?" (1993).** In *Foreign Affairs* in 1993, expanded into a book in 1996, Huntington replied that **the great divisions of the future would be cultural, not ideological**. He named about eight civilisations (Western, Orthodox, Islamic, Sinic, Hindu, Japanese, Latin American and possibly African) and predicted that the most dangerous conflicts would come along the "fault lines" between them.

| | Fukuyama | Huntington |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Core claim** | one model has won the argument | the world divides by culture |
| **What drives conflict** | resistance from the losers of modernity | identity, religion, civilisation |
| **Looked right when** | the 1990s: democracy spread to Eastern Europe, Latin America, parts of Africa | after 9/11 (2001), and with the wars in Bosnia and the Caucasus |
| **Looked wrong when** | China grew rich without democratising; democracy retreated after about 2006 | most wars since 1991 have been **inside** a civilisation: Rwanda, Congo, Syria, Russia against Ukraine |

**The strongest case for each, and what would settle it.** Fukuyama's defenders say no rival *model* has yet won people's free choice: rich autocracies have not produced a system others voluntarily copy, and people still migrate towards liberal democracies. Huntington's defenders say identity has plainly beaten economics as a force in politics, from Hindu nationalism to Russian claims about a "Russian world". **What would settle it is time:** whether China's state-led model keeps delivering and attracts imitators, and whether the democratic retreat measured since the late 2000s by groups such as Freedom House and V-Dem reverses or deepens.

**Read the rest of this stage with both in mind.** Almost every lesson that follows has been claimed as evidence by one side or the other.
Globalisation and the World Trade Organi:
Globalisation means the world's economies binding together through trade, investment, migration and communication. It is old (the Silk Roads, the Atlantic economy, the 1870–1914 boom), but after 1991 it ran faster and wider than ever before.

**The rule-book: the WTO.** The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) of 1947 had cut tariffs among mostly Western states. Its eighth round of talks, the **Uruguay Round (1986–94)**, ended at Marrakesh in April 1994 and created the **World Trade Organization, which opened in Geneva on 1 January 1995**. It went beyond goods to services and intellectual property, and it had a binding **dispute settlement** system: a state that lost a case could face legal retaliation.

**The great entries.** **China joined the WTO on 11 December 2001**, after fifteen years of negotiation. Russia joined in 2012. The WTO has about 166 members, covering nearly all world trade.

**Regional blocs grew too.** NAFTA joined the US, Canada and Mexico from 1 January 1994. Mercosur in South America (1991), ASEAN's free-trade area in South-East Asia, and later the African Continental Free Trade Area (in force 2019, trading from 2021).

**Container ships, supply chains and the "China shock".** Cheap shipping and the internet let firms split production across continents: an iPhone designed in California, with parts from Japan, Korea and Taiwan, assembled in China. **World trade rose from under 40% to over 50% of world output** between the early 1990s and 2008.

**What everyone agrees on:**
- **Extreme poverty fell faster than at any time in history**, from more than a third of humanity around 1990 to under a tenth by the late 2010s (World Bank), mostly because of growth in China, India and East Asia.
- **Manufacturing jobs left older industrial regions.** Economists David Autor, David Dorn and Gordon Hanson (2013) showed that US districts most exposed to Chinese imports lost jobs that did not come back for years.

**What is contested.** Economist Branko Milanović's "elephant curve" showed that between 1988 and 2008 the biggest gains went to Asia's new middle classes and to the very richest, with little for the lower middle classes of rich countries. **One reading:** globalisation was a huge net good, and the losers needed better help at home. **The other:** it was managed for capital, and its costs bred the populism of the 2010s. Protests began early: about 40,000 marched against the WTO in **Seattle in November 1999**.

**As of November 2026.** Settled: the WTO's **Doha Round** (launched 2001) never concluded; its **Appellate Body has not worked since December 2019**, when the US blocked new judges. Not settled: whether the large US tariffs imposed from 2025 and the China–US trade conflict mark a lasting turn away from open trade, or a pause. Economists disagree, and the data is still coming in.
The European Union and the euro:
After 1991 Western Europe's common market became a political union, gained a single currency, and doubled its membership. It is the largest experiment in states pooling sovereignty in history.

**Maastricht, 1992.** Signed in the Dutch city of Maastricht on 7 February 1992, in force on 1 November 1993, the Treaty on European Union renamed the European Community the **European Union**, created EU citizenship, began common foreign and justice policies, and set the path to a single currency. Danish voters rejected it at first (June 1992) and French voters only just accepted it (51%): **from the start, the union was more popular with governments than with every electorate**.

**The euro.** On **1 January 1999** eleven states fixed their exchange rates and handed monetary policy to the **European Central Bank** in Frankfurt. Notes and coins followed on 1 January 2002. Britain and Denmark kept opt-outs; Sweden stayed out by choice.

**Enlargement to the east.** On **1 May 2004** ten states joined at once, eight of them former communist countries (Poland, Hungary, Czechia, Slovakia, Slovenia and the three Baltic states), plus Cyprus and Malta. Romania and Bulgaria followed in 2007 and Croatia in 2013, making 28. **For Eastern Europe this was the real end of the Cold War**: membership required democracy, courts and market rules, and brought large transfers of money.

**The crises:**

| Years | Crisis | What happened |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **2010–12** | the eurozone debt crisis | Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Cyprus and Spain needed rescues; harsh cuts in Greece; ECB head Mario Draghi's pledge in July 2012 to do **"whatever it takes"** calmed the markets |
| **2015** | migration | over a million asylum seekers, many fleeing Syria, reached the EU; members quarrelled over sharing them |
| **2016–20** | Brexit | the UK voted to leave on **23 June 2016, by 52% to 48%**, and left on **31 January 2020** |
| **2022–** | war in Ukraine | sanctions on Russia; Ukraine and Moldova made candidates for membership |

**The contested question: did the euro work?** One reading: it bound Europe together, survived crises that critics said would break it, and grew to twenty members (Croatia in 2023). The other, put by many economists from the start: **one interest rate cannot suit both Germany and Greece**, and without a shared budget the poorer members bore the cost of every shock. The evidence both sides cite is the same decade, 2008–18, read differently.

**As of November 2026.** Settled: **Bulgaria adopted the euro on 1 January 2026**, making 21 members; the UK is outside the EU. Not settled: whether the EU enlarges again (Ukraine, Moldova and the Western Balkans are candidates), and how far it builds a common defence.
The wars of Yugoslavia, 1991–2001:
While Western Europe united, the multi-national federation of Yugoslavia broke apart in the bloodiest wars Europe had seen since 1945. They brought a phrase back into the language: ethnic cleansing.

**The federation.** Communist Yugoslavia, held together under Josip Broz Tito until his death in 1980, had six republics: Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbia, Montenegro and Macedonia, with two autonomous provinces in Serbia (Kosovo and Vojvodina). Serbs, Croats and Bosnian Muslims (Bosniaks) spoke closely related languages but were divided by religion and memory, including the massacres of the Second World War. After 1987 **Slobodan Milošević**, leader of Serbia, built his power on Serb nationalism; Croatia's Franjo Tuđman answered with Croatian nationalism.

**The wars in order:**

| Dates | War | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **June–July 1991** | Slovenia, the "Ten-Day War" | Slovenia independent, few deaths |
| **1991–95** | Croatia | Serb rebels backed by the Yugoslav army took about a quarter of Croatia; Croatia retook most of it in August 1995, and some 150,000–200,000 Serbs fled |
| **1992–95** | Bosnia-Herzegovina | the worst: Serb, Croat and Bosniak forces; the **siege of Sarajevo** (April 1992 to February 1996) |
| **1998–99** | Kosovo | Serbian forces against the Albanian-majority province; NATO bombing |
| **2001** | Macedonia | a short Albanian insurgency, ended by the Ohrid Agreement |

**Srebrenica, July 1995.** Bosnian Serb forces under Ratko Mladić overran a UN "safe area" guarded by Dutch peacekeepers and **killed about 8,000 Bosniak men and boys**. The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY, The Hague) and the International Court of Justice both ruled it **genocide**. Total deaths in the Bosnian war are now put at about **100,000** from a careful name-by-name count, lower than the 200,000+ often given at the time.

**The peace.** After NATO air strikes in August–September 1995, the **Dayton Agreement** (negotiated in Ohio, signed in Paris in December 1995) split Bosnia into two entities under a weak central state. It ended the killing; it still governs Bosnia, and many Bosnians say it froze the divisions.

**Kosovo and a precedent.** NATO bombed Serbia for 78 days, March–June 1999, **without a UN Security Council mandate**, because Russia and China would have vetoed one. Defenders call it a humanitarian rescue; critics, including Russia ever since, call it an illegal war that broke the UN Charter. Kosovo declared independence in 2008; Serbia and Russia do not recognise it. Milošević was sent to The Hague in 2001 and **died in his cell in 2006 before a verdict**. Mladić and the Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadžić were convicted of genocide.

**Why it broke: two readings.** "Ancient hatreds", popular in the early 1990s, said the peoples had always fought. Most historians now reject it: **these peoples had lived mixed, and intermarried, for long periods; the wars were made by leaders** who used nationalism to keep power as communism collapsed. The weight of the evidence (the speeches, the planning, the role of state media) supports the second reading.
Rwanda, 1994: the genocide against the T:
In about a hundred days in 1994, in a small, crowded country in the hills of central Africa, perhaps three-quarters of the Tutsi population was murdered, mostly by neighbours with machetes, while the world watched and withdrew.

**Background.** Rwanda's people were Hutu (the large majority), Tutsi (about one in seven) and Twa. Belgian colonial rulers (from 1916) **hardened these into fixed racial categories**, recorded on identity cards from the 1930s, and ruled through a Tutsi elite. At independence in 1962 a Hutu government took power; waves of violence drove hundreds of thousands of Tutsi into exile. In **October 1990** the Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF), a Tutsi-led exile army from Uganda, invaded. The Arusha Accords (August 1993) promised power-sharing; Hutu extremists organised to stop them, with militias (the *Interahamwe*) and a hate radio station, RTLM.

**The genocide.** On **6 April 1994** the plane carrying President Juvénal Habyarimana was shot down over Kigali. Within hours, roadblocks went up and killing began from prepared lists: Tutsi, and Hutu who opposed the extremists. It ended when the **RPF under Paul Kagame took Kigali on 4 July** and then the whole country. The killing ran from 7 April to about mid-July.

**The numbers are debated, and the debate is about method, not fact.** Estimates run from about **500,000** (Human Rights Watch's historian Alison Des Forges) through the widely used **800,000** to over **1 million** (the Rwandan government's census of victims). Every serious account agrees it was **genocide: the deliberate destruction of the Tutsi as a group**.

**The world's failure.** A small UN force (UNAMIR) under the Canadian general **Roméo Dallaire** was already in Rwanda. In January 1994 Dallaire warned the UN of plans for extermination and was told not to act. After ten Belgian peacekeepers were murdered, **the Security Council cut the force to about 270 in April**. Governments avoided the word "genocide" because the Genocide Convention (1948) would oblige them to act. France, an ally of the old regime, ran a late intervention (Opération Turquoise, June–August) that also let many killers escape. A French historians' commission (the Duclert report, 2021) found France bore "heavy and overwhelming responsibilities" but not complicity in the killing itself.

**What remains contested:** **who shot down the plane.** Two French judicial investigations pointed in turn at the RPF and then, from ballistic evidence, at Hutu extremists; the case was dropped in 2018 without a finding. Also contested: the scale of RPF reprisal killings in 1994.

**Aftermath across Africa.** About two million Hutu fled into Zaire (now the DR Congo), with the killers among them. Rwanda and Uganda invaded in 1996, toppling Mobutu in 1997; the **Second Congo War (1998–2003)** drew in nine African states. Deaths, mostly from hunger and disease, are put in the millions, a figure fiercely disputed. In Rwanda, a UN tribunal sat at Arusha (set up in November 1994, closed in 2015) and local *gacaca* courts tried about 1.9 million cases. Kagame has ruled since, presiding over fast growth and tight political control.
South Africa's 1994 election and Africa':
South Africa's peaceful transfer of power was one of the great hopeful events of the 1990s. It is kept brief here: **the South African Politics curriculum** teaches it in full.

**South Africa, in outline.** President F. W. de Klerk unbanned the ANC and freed **Nelson Mandela on 11 February 1990**. Negotiations (CODESA, 1991–93) went on through violence that killed thousands, above all in KwaZulu-Natal and the townships around Johannesburg. On **27 April 1994** South Africans of every race voted together for the first time; the ANC won about 62%, and **Mandela was inaugurated as president on 10 May 1994**. A new constitution followed in 1996, and a **Truth and Reconciliation Commission** under Archbishop Desmond Tutu (from 1996) traded amnesty for full confession. Mandela and de Klerk shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993.

**The rest of Africa since 1991.** The continent's story after the Cold War is not one story. Its 54 states went very different ways:

| Theme | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| **Elections return** | Benin (1991) and Zambia (1991) voted out their founding rulers; **Nigeria returned to civilian rule in 1999** after long military government; Ghana has passed power peacefully between parties several times |
| **Wars of the 1990s** | Somalia (state collapse from 1991; the US withdrew after the Mogadishu battle of October 1993); Liberia and Sierra Leone (diamonds and child soldiers, to about 2002–03); the Congo wars |
| **Institutions** | the **African Union** replaced the Organisation of African Unity in 2002 |
| **Growth** | from about 2000 many economies grew fast on commodity prices and Chinese demand; mobile phones spread faster than landlines ever had, and Kenya's **M-Pesa** (2007) made phone money ordinary |
| **New wars** | South Sudan's independence (2011) and its civil war (2013–18); jihadist insurgencies in the Sahel and north-east Nigeria (Boko Haram, from 2009); Ethiopia's Tigray war (2020–22) |

**Population is the long fact.** Sub-Saharan Africa had about half a billion people in 1990 and over **1.2 billion** by the mid-2020s (UN estimates); by the UN's projections, about a quarter of humanity will be African by 2050. Projections are not history, but they shape every plan made now.

**As of November 2026.** Settled: South Africa's democracy has held through seven national elections; in 2024 the ANC lost its majority for the first time and formed a coalition. Not settled: Sudan's war, which broke out in **April 2023** between the army and the Rapid Support Forces, had produced what the UN called the world's largest displacement crisis, and had not ended. Military coups in Mali (2020, 2021), Burkina Faso (2022) and Niger (2023) reversed the trend to elections in the Sahel, and those governments remain in power.
The internet and the digital revolution:
The biggest change in daily life in this stage was not a war or a treaty. It was a network of computers that, within thirty years, most of humanity carried in a pocket.

**Origins in the Cold War.** ARPANET, funded by the US Defense Department, linked its first computers in **1969**. In the 1970s Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn designed the TCP/IP rules that let different networks join into one "internet" (adopted on ARPANET on 1 January 1983). For twenty years it belonged to universities and the military.

**The web, 1989–93.** At **CERN**, the physics laboratory near Geneva, the English scientist **Tim Berners-Lee** proposed in March 1989 a system of linked pages: the World Wide Web. The first website went online in 1991. In **April 1993 CERN put the web's software in the public domain**, free for anyone, and the Mosaic browser (1993) made it point-and-click. That decision is one reason the web grew as an open network rather than a company's product.

**The timeline of a revolution:**

| Year | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **1995** | Amazon and eBay founded; Windows 95; about 16 million people online |
| **1998** | Google founded in California |
| **2000** | the **dot-com crash**: the Nasdaq lost about three-quarters of its value by 2002 |
| **2004** | Facebook founded |
| **2007** | Apple's **iPhone**; the smartphone era begins |
| **2010s** | social media becomes the main news source for many; China builds a separate, censored internet ("the Great Firewall") with its own giants (Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu) |
| **2022** | OpenAI releases **ChatGPT** (30 November); generative AI reaches the public |

**Who is online.** The UN's telecommunications agency (ITU) counted about **5.5 billion** internet users in 2024, around two-thirds of humanity. The gap is wide: most people in rich countries, far fewer in the poorest. Mobile phones carried the internet to Africa and South Asia without the wired networks the West had built first.

**What historians can already say.** Like printing after the 1450s, the internet **cut the cost of copying and spreading words to almost nothing**, with the same double result: more knowledge, more propaganda, and fierce fights over who controls it. The Arab Spring of 2011 was called a "Facebook revolution"; by the late 2010s governments everywhere were using the same tools to watch and steer their citizens.

**As of November 2026.** Settled: the internet's spread and its economic weight (the largest companies on Earth by market value are now mostly digital). Not settled, and genuinely disputed among researchers: **whether social media has measurably damaged democracy or young people's mental health**, where studies point in different directions; and how far artificial intelligence will change work. Both are too recent to judge, and the honest answer is that the evidence is not in.
9/11 and the war in Afghanistan:
On a clear Tuesday morning in September 2001, nineteen men with box-cutters turned four airliners into missiles. The response shaped the next twenty years of world politics.

**The attacks.** On **11 September 2001** hijackers from the Islamist network **al-Qaeda** flew two planes into the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York and one into the Pentagon near Washington; on the fourth, passengers fought back and it crashed in a field in Pennsylvania. **2,977 people were killed**, from more than 90 countries. Fifteen of the hijackers were Saudi citizens.

**Who and why.** Al-Qaeda ("the base") grew from Arab volunteers in the war against the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan (1979–89). Its leader, the Saudi **Osama bin Laden**, declared war on the US in 1996 and 1998, citing US troops in Saudi Arabia, sanctions on Iraq and US support for Israel. It had already bombed US embassies in Kenya and Tanzania (August 1998, 224 dead). From 1996 it was sheltered in Afghanistan by the **Taliban**, a movement of Pashtun religious students who had taken Kabul that year. The US government's **9/11 Commission (report, July 2004)** found that US agencies had warnings but failed to share and act on them.

**The war.** The Taliban refused to hand over bin Laden. The US and Britain began bombing on **7 October 2001**, working with the Afghan Northern Alliance; **Kabul fell on 13 November** and the Taliban regime was gone by December. A conference at Bonn installed Hamid Karzai, and NATO took command of the international force in 2003, the alliance's first major operation outside Europe. NATO had invoked Article 5, its mutual-defence clause, for the only time in its history, on 12 September 2001.

**The long war.** The Taliban regrouped from Pakistan and fought back from about 2005. US troop numbers peaked at about 100,000 in 2010–11. **Bin Laden was killed by US special forces at Abbottabad, Pakistan, on 2 May 2011.** In February 2020 the US signed the **Doha Agreement** with the Taliban, promising withdrawal. As the last troops left, the Afghan government collapsed: **the Taliban entered Kabul on 15 August 2021**, and the airlift ended on 30 August amid scenes of desperation and a suicide bombing that killed about 170 Afghans and 13 US troops.

**The costs.** Brown University's Costs of War project estimates that over 170,000 people died in the Afghan war directly, among them about 2,400 US service members; other estimates differ, and indirect deaths are higher.

**Why did it fail? The readings.** That the mission drifted from punishing al-Qaeda to building a state nobody knew how to build; that Pakistan's sheltering of the Taliban made victory impossible; that the war was lost by **the diversion of attention and troops to Iraq from 2003**; that corruption hollowed out the Afghan state the West funded. These are not exclusive, and historians weigh them differently.

**As of November 2026.** Settled: the Taliban rule Afghanistan, and have **barred girls from school beyond the sixth grade and women from most work**. Not settled: international recognition of their government. Russia became the first state to recognise it formally, in July 2025.
The Iraq War, 2003–2011:
The invasion of Iraq was the most divisive war of the period: fought on a claim that proved false, legal or illegal depending on whom you ask, and followed by a sectarian civil war and the rise of the Islamic State.

**The case for war.** After 9/11 the administration of **George W. Bush** argued that Saddam Hussein's Iraq held **weapons of mass destruction (WMD)** in breach of UN resolutions, and might pass them to terrorists. Britain's Tony Blair joined. On **5 February 2003** Secretary of State Colin Powell presented the case to the UN Security Council. France, Germany and Russia opposed war; there was **no new Security Council resolution authorising force**. On 15 February 2003 millions marched against it, in the largest coordinated protest in history up to then.

**The invasion.** US-led forces crossed from Kuwait on **20 March 2003**. Baghdad fell on 9 April; the statue of Saddam in Firdos Square came down. Saddam was captured in December 2003, tried by an Iraqi court, and **hanged on 30 December 2006**.

**No weapons.** The US Iraq Survey Group's final report (the Duelfer Report, September 2004) found that **Iraq had destroyed its stockpiles in 1991 and had no active WMD programmes** by 2003. Britain's Chilcot Inquiry (2016) concluded that the UK went to war before peaceful options were exhausted, on intelligence presented with unjustified certainty.

**The occupation and civil war:**

| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **May 2003** | the US occupation authority **dissolves the Iraqi army and bans senior Ba'ath party members**, putting hundreds of thousands of armed men out of work |
| **2004** | insurgency spreads; the Abu Ghraib prison abuse photographs |
| **February 2006** | bombing of the Shia shrine at Samarra; **sectarian civil war** between Sunni and Shia |
| **2007** | the US "surge" of about 30,000 more troops, and Sunni tribes turning against al-Qaeda in Iraq; violence falls |
| **December 2011** | the last US troops leave |
| **June 2014** | **the Islamic State (ISIS)**, heir of al-Qaeda in Iraq, takes Mosul and declares a "caliphate" across Iraq and Syria; it is driven out of Mosul in 2017 |

**How many died is fiercely disputed.** Iraq Body Count, which records documented civilian deaths, counts **over 200,000** violent civilian deaths from 2003 onward. Survey-based studies run from about 150,000 violent deaths by mid-2006 (the Iraq Family Health Survey) to over 600,000 (a *Lancet* study of 2006 whose methods were strongly criticised). The gap comes from method: counting reported deaths versus extrapolating from household surveys.

**Legality.** UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan said in September 2004 that the invasion was **"not in conformity with the UN Charter"** and, from the Charter's point of view, illegal. The US and UK argued that earlier resolutions from 1990–91 and 2002 already gave authority. International lawyers mostly side with Annan; the governments involved never accepted it.

**What carried forward.** Iran's influence in Iraq grew; the war's failure made Western publics wary of intervening in Syria after 2011; and **Russia has cited Iraq ever since** when accused of breaking international law.
The rise of China:
The largest change in the balance of the world since 1991 is China's return to the position it held for most of history: the biggest economy, or close to it.

**Deng's bargain.** After the army crushed the Tiananmen Square protests in Beijing on **4 June 1989** (the death toll is unknown; estimates range from several hundred to several thousand), conservatives in the Communist Party tried to slow reform. **Deng Xiaoping's "southern tour" of January–February 1992**, to the boom city of Shenzhen next to Hong Kong, restarted it. The bargain held for a generation: **fast growth and rising living standards, under one-party rule with no political opening**.

**The growth.** From 1978 to the 2010s China's economy grew at close to 10% a year on official figures, the fastest sustained growth of any large country in recorded history. Hundreds of millions moved from villages to factory cities; the World Bank counts **about 800 million Chinese lifted out of extreme poverty** since 1978. Key steps:

| Year | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1997** | Britain hands **Hong Kong** back, under "one country, two systems" promised for fifty years |
| **2001** | China joins the **WTO** |
| **2008** | the Beijing Olympics; China's huge stimulus cushions the world financial crisis |
| **2010** | China passes Japan as the world's **second-largest economy** at market exchange rates |
| **2013** | Xi Jinping launches the **Belt and Road Initiative**: ports, railways and loans across Asia, Africa and beyond |

**Xi Jinping, from 2012.** Xi became party leader in November 2012. He ran a vast anti-corruption campaign, built up the navy and fortified islands in the South China Sea, and in **2018 abolished the presidential term limit**. In **Xinjiang**, from about 2017, perhaps a million or more Uyghurs and other Muslims were held in internment camps (the figure rests on leaked documents, satellite images and survey extrapolations; China calls them vocational training centres). The UN human rights office (2022) said the abuses may amount to crimes against humanity. In **Hong Kong**, after mass protests in 2019, a **National Security Law (June 2020)** ended the open opposition and free press the city had kept.

**Contested points:**
- **How big, really?** Some economists argue China's official growth figures are inflated; others think the distortions are modest. On purchasing-power measures, China's economy has been the world's largest since the mid-2010s (IMF and World Bank figures).
- **"Peak China"?** One reading holds that a shrinking population (falling since 2022), heavy local-government debt and a property slump (Evergrande defaulted in 2021) mean China's rise has crested. The other points to China's lead in electric cars, batteries, solar panels and shipbuilding. The next decade's numbers will settle it.

**As of November 2026.** Settled: China is the world's leading manufacturer and largest trading nation in goods. Not settled: the future of Taiwan, which China claims and which governs itself as a democracy, and the course of the US–China rivalry.
India's growth since 1991:
In 1991 India nearly ran out of money. Its response opened the economy of the world's largest democracy and began a long rise that has made it, by UN estimates, the most populous country on Earth.

**The crisis.** In mid-1991 India had foreign reserves to cover only about **two or three weeks of imports**; it pledged gold to the Bank of England and the Bank of Japan to borrow. The Gulf War had raised oil prices and cut workers' remittances, and the Soviet Union, a major trading partner, was collapsing.

**The reform.** The new Congress government of **P. V. Narasimha Rao**, with the economist **Manmohan Singh** as finance minister, presented its budget on **24 July 1991**. It devalued the rupee, cut tariffs, opened the door to foreign investment and began dismantling the "**licence raj**", the permits a firm needed to make or expand almost anything. Singh closed his speech by quoting Victor Hugo: no power on earth can stop an idea whose time has come.

**What followed:**

| Years | Development |
| --- | --- |
